citations.quote:
If $\sigma\in S_n$ has $c_k$ cycles of length $k$, including fixed points when
$k=1$, then
$$|C_{S_n}(\sigma)|=\prod_{k=1}^n k^{c_k}c_k!.$$
The formula uses the empty product $1$ when $n=0$.

Let $n\ge 0$ and let $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)\vdash n$ be a partition
with Young diagram $[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Throughout, $S_n$
denotes the symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, with $S_0=\{1\}$.

**Standard Young subgroups.** For $1\le i\le k$ let
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
be the $i$-th **block** of $\lambda$. The blocks are consecutive intervals of
integers, they are pairwise disjoint, each has $|B_i|=\lambda_i$, and together
they partition $\{1,\dots,n\}$. The **standard Young subgroup** of type
$\lambda$ is
$$S_\lambda:=\{\,\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(B_i)=B_i\text{ for every }1\le i\le k\,\}.$$
This is a subgroup of $S_n$, namely the direct product
$S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$ of the symmetric groups of the individual
blocks, each acting on its block and fixing the remaining entries pointwise;
as in [[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]], the product
decomposition is unique because the blocks are pairwise disjoint and cover
$\{1,\dots,n\}$, so $|S_\lambda|=\lambda_1!\cdots\lambda_k!$. A **Young
subgroup of type $\lambda$** is a subgroup of $S_n$ conjugate to
$S_\lambda$. For $k=0$, that is for $\lambda=\varnothing$ and $n=0$, there are
no blocks and $S_\varnothing=S_0=\{1\}$.

**Row equivalence and tabloids.** Let $t$ and $u$ be $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). We say that $t$ and $u$
are **row equivalent**, and write $t\sim u$, when they have the same row sets:
for every row $i$,
$$\{\,t(i,j):1\le j\le\lambda_i\,\}=\{\,u(i,j):1\le j\le\lambda_i\,\}.$$
Equivalently, $t\sim u$ if and only if $u=\rho\cdot t$ for some $\rho\in R_t$:
if $u=\rho\cdot t$ then $\rho$ merely permutes the entries inside each row of
$t$, and conversely, if the row sets agree, then
$\rho(t(i,j)):=u(i,j)$ defines a permutation $\rho$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ that
preserves each row set of $t$, so $\rho\in R_t$ and $\rho\cdot t=u$. Hence
$\sim$ is an equivalence relation on the $\lambda$-tableaux, and the
equivalence class
$$\{t\}:=\{\,u:u\sim t\,\}=\{\,\rho\cdot t:\rho\in R_t\,\}$$
is the **tabloid** of $t$. We draw $\{t\}$ as the diagram $[\lambda]$ filled
with the entries of $t$ and bars between the rows, recording that the order of
the entries inside a row is forgotten. A tabloid is **standard** when it
contains a standard tableau.

**The permutation module.** Let $\Omega_\lambda$ be the finite set of
$\lambda$-tabloids. For $\sigma\in S_n$ and a tabloid $\{t\}$ define
$$\sigma\cdot\{t\}:=\{\sigma\cdot t\}.$$
This is well defined: if $t,u$ are $\lambda$-tableaux with $t\sim u$, then the
row sets of $\sigma\cdot u$ are the $\sigma$-images of the row sets of $u$,
which are the $\sigma$-images of the row sets of $t$, and these are exactly
the row sets of $\sigma\cdot t$
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]); so
$\sigma\cdot u\sim\sigma\cdot t$ and the tabloids $\{\sigma\cdot u\}$ and
$\{\sigma\cdot t\}$ coincide. Because the action on tableaux is a left action,
the induced rule on tabloids satisfies $\mathrm{id}\cdot\{t\}=\{t\}$ and
$\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot\{t\})=(\sigma\tau)\cdot\{t\}$, so $S_n$ acts on
$\Omega_\lambda$ from the left. The **Young permutation module** attached to
$\lambda$ is the complex vector space
$$M^\lambda:=\mathbb C^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$$
with the tabloids as basis, again written $\{t\}$ for the basis vector of the
tabloid $\{t\}$, equipped with the linear extension of the action above:
$$\sigma\cdot\sum_{\{t\}\in\Omega_\lambda}a_{\{t\}}\,\{t\}:=\sum_{\{t\}\in\Omega_\lambda}a_{\{t\}}\,\{\sigma\cdot t\}.$$
This is the permutation representation of $S_n$ on the finite set
$\Omega_\lambda$ ([[def-trivial-regular-and-permutation-representations]]),
so $M^\lambda$ is a finite-dimensional complex representation of $S_n$.

**The stabilizer of a tabloid.** For every $\lambda$-tableau $t$ one has
$$\sigma\cdot\{t\}=\{t\}\iff \sigma\cdot t\sim t\iff \sigma\in R_t,$$
so the stabilizer in $S_n$ of the tabloid $\{t\}$ is exactly the row
stabilizer $R_t$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]). The action
on $\Omega_\lambda$ is transitive: given tabloids $\{t\}$ and $\{s\}$, the
permutation $\sigma$ determined by $\sigma(t(i,j)):=s(i,j)$ satisfies
$\sigma\cdot t=s$, hence $\sigma\cdot\{t\}=\{s\}$. In particular, for the
**standard row-filled $\lambda$-tableau** $t_0$, whose row $i$ carries the
entries of $B_i$ in increasing order, the row sets of $t_0$ are precisely the
blocks $B_1,\dots,B_k$, so $R_{t_0}=S_\lambda$ and the stabilizer of the
tabloid $\{t_0\}$ is the standard Young subgroup $S_\lambda$.

The conjugacy classes of $S_n$ are in bijection with the tuples of
nonnegative integers $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ satisfying
$$\sum_{k=1}^n kc_k=n.$$
For $n=0$, the unique empty tuple indexes the identity class of $S_0$.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$,
with diagrams $[\lambda]$ and $[\mu]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For content counts
only, set $\mu_i:=0$ for $i$ beyond the number of parts of $\mu$; these
zeros are not additional parts of the partition.

A **semistandard tableau of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$**, also called a
semistandard tableau of shape $\lambda$ and **type $\mu$**, is a filling
$T:[\lambda]\to\{1,2,\dots\}$ of the boxes of $[\lambda]$ with positive
integers such that:

1. **content:** for every $i\ge 1$ the entry $i$ occurs in exactly $\mu_i$
   boxes of $[\lambda]$, so the multiset of entries is
   $\{1^{\mu_1},2^{\mu_2},\dots\}$ and in particular every entry lies between
   $1$ and the number of parts of $\mu$;
2. **rows:** the entries weakly increase along every row, that is,
   $T(i,j)\le T(i,j+1)$ whenever $(i,j)$ and $(i,j+1)$ are both in
   $[\lambda]$;
3. **columns:** the entries strictly increase down every column, that is,
   $T(i,j)<T(i+1,j)$ whenever $(i,j)$ and $(i+1,j)$ are both in $[\lambda]$.

The **Kostka number** $K_{\lambda,\mu}$ is the number of semistandard
tableaux of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$:
$$K_{\lambda,\mu}:=\#\{\,T:T\text{ is a semistandard }\lambda\text{-tableau of content }\mu\,\}.$$
This is well defined and finite: a filling of the $n$ boxes of $[\lambda]$ by
positive integers has at most $n^n$ possibilities for $n\ge1$ once each entry is required
to lie between $1$ and the number of parts of $\mu$, and conditions 1--3 cut this
finite set down to the semistandard tableaux, so $K_{\lambda,\mu}$ is a
nonnegative integer. It is zero when the conditions cannot be met.

Two entries may be equal inside a row, but never inside a column: a repeated
entry in a column would contradict the strict increase of condition 3, so the
repetitions of a label forced by the content $\mu$ must be spread across
distinct columns of $[\lambda]$. For $\lambda=\mu=\varnothing$ there is a
single filling, the empty one, so
$$K_{\varnothing,\varnothing}=1 .$$

**Relation to standard tableaux.** Because a tableau of content $(1^n)$ uses
each of the numbers $1,\dots,n$ exactly once, its entries are pairwise
distinct, and weak increase along a row is then strict increase along that
row; a filling of $[\lambda]$ with content $(1^n)$ is therefore semistandard
exactly when it is a standard $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]), that is,
$$K_{\lambda,(1^n)}=f^\lambda ,$$
the number of standard tableaux of shape $\lambda$. In particular, for $n\ge1$,
$K_{(n),(1^n)}=K_{(n),(n)}=1$, since the single row carries either the
standard entries $1,2,\dots,n$ or the $n$ copies of the entry $1$, and
$K_{(1^n),(1^n)}=1$, realized by the single column $1,2,\dots,n$ read from
top to bottom.

Let $n\ge1$ and fix an ordering of the partitions of $n$ that is a linear
extension of the dominance order with the most dominant partition first (for
example James's dictionary order, in which $(n),(n-1,1),\dots,(1^n)$ appear in
this order). For $\lambda,\rho\vdash n$ let $\chi^\lambda$ be the irreducible
character of the Specht module $S^\lambda$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]],
[[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]]), let $C_\rho$ be the conjugacy
class of cycle type $\rho$
([[cor-symmetric-conjugacy-classes-are-indexed-by-cycle-types]]) and let
$S_\lambda$ be the standard Young subgroup
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). Define
$$A:=(a_{\lambda\rho}),\quad a_{\lambda\rho}:=|S_\lambda\cap C_\rho|,\qquad M:=\operatorname{diag}(z_\rho)_{\rho\vdash n},\quad z_\rho:=\prod_{i\ge1}i^{m_i(\rho)}m_i(\rho)!,$$
where $m_i(\rho)$ is the number of parts of $\rho$ equal to $i$, so that
$z_\rho=|C_{S_n}(\rho)|=n!/|C_\rho|$
([[thm-centralizer-cardinality-from-cycle-type]]); let
$C:=(\chi^\lambda(C_\rho))$ be the character table of $S_n$
([[def-character-table-of-a-finite-group]], a row for each $\lambda$, a column
for each class, entries the common values) and set
$B:=(b_{\lambda\nu}):=CA^{\mathsf T}$. Then:

1. $b_{\lambda\nu}=\sum_{\rho\vdash n}\chi^\lambda(C_\rho)\,a_{\nu\rho}=|S_\nu|\,(\chi^\lambda,1_{S_\nu}\!\!\uparrow^{S_n})=|S_\nu|\,K_{\lambda\nu}$
   ([[thm-youngs-rule-for-permutation-modules]],
   [[cor-frobenius-reciprocity-for-complex-characters]]); hence $B$ is a
   nonnegative integer matrix, upper triangular in the fixed order
   ($b_{\lambda\nu}=0$ unless $\lambda\unrhd\nu$) with diagonal
   $b_{\nu\nu}=|S_\nu|=\prod_i\nu_i!>0$
   ([[lem-kostka-change-of-basis-is-dominance-unitriangular]]).

2. **(Gram equation.)** $B^{\mathsf T}B=AMA^{\mathsf T}$, that is,
   $\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}b_{\lambda\nu}b_{\lambda\mu}=\sum_{\rho\vdash n}z_\rho\,a_{\nu\rho}a_{\mu\rho}$
   for all $\nu,\mu\vdash n$
   ([[thm-first-orthogonality-relation-for-irreducible-complex-characters]],
   [[thm-orbit-stabilizer]]).

3. $B$ is the unique nonnegative, upper-triangular matrix with positive
   diagonal satisfying the Gram equation of (2) in the fixed order, and its
   diagonal is necessarily $b_{\nu\nu}=|S_\nu|$. The matrix $A$ is invertible
   with $\det A=\prod_{\lambda\vdash n}\prod_i(\lambda_i-1)!$; consequently the
   character table is recovered from $A$ and the Gram equation alone as
   $$C=B\,(A^{\mathsf T})^{-1},\qquad \det C=\prod_{\lambda\vdash n}\prod_i\lambda_i,$$
   the product of all parts of all partitions of $n$
   ([[thm-irreducible-complex-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis-of-the-class-functions]]).
   No choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge0$, let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, let $M^\mu$ be the complex Young
permutation module of shape $\mu$ with its tabloid basis
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]), and let
$S^\lambda\subseteq M^\lambda$ be the complex Specht module
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). Write
$K_{\lambda,\mu}$ for the Kostka number
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]) and, for an integer $r\ge0$,
let $(S^\lambda)^{\oplus r}$ denote a direct sum of $r$ copies of
$S^\lambda$, the zero module when $r=0$. Then:

1. **(Isomorphism type.)** $M^\mu$ is completely reducible and there is an
   isomorphism of $\mathbb C S_n$-modules
   $$M^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n}(S^\lambda)^{\oplus K_{\lambda,\mu}},$$
   the sum being over the finitely many partitions of $n$.
2. **(Multiplicity.)** In every decomposition of $M^\mu$ as a direct sum of
   irreducible subrepresentations the number of summands isomorphic to
   $S^\lambda$ equals $K_{\lambda,\mu}$; that is, the multiplicity
   $[M^\mu:S^\lambda]$ is well defined and equal to the Kostka number
   $K_{\lambda,\mu}$, independently of the decomposition.

For two class functions $\varphi,\psi\in\mathrm{cf}(G)$
([[def-class-function-and-the-space-of-complex-class-functions]]), define

$$\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\varphi(g)\,\overline{\psi(g)},$$

the finite sum being that of
([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]) for the additive commutative
monoid of $\mathbb C$. This is the standard Hermitian form on
the complex vector space of class functions.

This assignment is an inner product in the exact sense of the published
definition ([[def-inner-product-space]]), with the inner product linear in the
first argument. Linearity in the first slot is immediate from the pointwise
vector-space structure of $\mathrm{cf}(G)$ and linearity of the finite sum. The
conjugate-symmetry clause holds because conjugation
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) is an involution:
$\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle=\frac1{|G|}\sum_g\psi(g)\overline{\varphi(g)}
=\overline{\frac1{|G|}\sum_g\varphi(g)\overline{\psi(g)}}
=\overline{\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle}$. For definiteness,
$\langle\varphi,\varphi\rangle=\frac1{|G|}\sum_g|\varphi(g)|^2$ is a sum of
nonnegative real numbers, hence nonnegative real; it is $0$ exactly when every
term $|\varphi(g)|^2$ is $0$, and since $|z|=0$ holds only for $z=0$ in
$\mathbb C$, that says exactly $\varphi=0$ as a function.

Let $G$ be a finite group. A **virtual character** of $G$ is an integral linear
combination of irreducible complex characters:

$$ \vartheta=\sum_i n_i\chi_i, \qquad n_i\in\mathbb Z, $$

with only finitely many nonzero coefficients. Since irreducible characters are
class functions, every virtual character is a class function on $G$
([[def-class-function-and-the-space-of-complex-class-functions]],
[[def-irreducible-complex-character]]).

The set of all virtual characters is the **character ring** $R(G)$. Addition is
pointwise addition of class functions, and multiplication is the bilinear
extension of tensor-product multiplication on honest characters:

$$ (\chi_V+\chi_W)(g)=\chi_V(g)+\chi_W(g), \qquad (\chi_V\chi_W)(g)=\chi_{V\otimes W}(g) $$

([[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]).

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r$ be the irreducible complex
characters of $G$, one per equivalence class
([[def-irreducible-complex-character]]), and let $g_1,\dots,g_s$ be
representatives of the distinct conjugacy classes of $G$
([[def-conjugacy-class-and-centralizer]]). The **character table** of $G$ is
the array whose rows are indexed by $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r$, whose columns are
indexed by $g_1,\dots,g_s$, and whose $(i,j)$ entry is $\chi_i(g_j)$.

The array is written with a top row recording the conjugacy-class sizes
$|\operatorname{Cl}_G(g_j)|$ above the column labels, and with the first column
recording the degrees $\chi_i(1)$ beside the row labels. The ordering of the
rows and of the columns is arbitrary: permuting either does not change the table
as data. Because each $\chi_i$ is constant on each conjugacy class, the entry
$\chi_i(g_j)$ is independent of the choice of representative $g_j$. That the
number of rows equals the number of columns is a theorem about the table, proved
later on this page as
[[cor-the-character-table-is-square-and-invertible]], not part of the present
definition.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected, $2\times2$-free skew diagram with complement a Young diagram.
Every strip node $(p,q)$ lies on the rim: if $(p+1,q+1)$ belonged to
$[\lambda]$, it could not belong to $[\nu]$, since that would force
$(p,q)\in[\nu]$; and the partition inequalities then put all four nodes of
the corresponding $2\times2$ block in the strip, a contradiction. The rim
nodes in row $p$ have columns $\max(1,\lambda_{p+1}),\dots,\lambda_p$,
where missing row lengths are zero. Read each such interval from right to
left, then move down at column $\lambda_{p+1}$ to the next row: these are
exactly the rim nodes and their side-adjacencies. Thus the rim is a single
path moving left or down, and its connected subsets are subpaths. The
$r-1$ steps of $\xi$ consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ leftward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $G$ be a finite group. A **virtual character** of $G$ is an integral linear
combination of irreducible complex characters:

$$ \vartheta=\sum_i n_i\chi_i, \qquad n_i\in\mathbb Z, $$

with only finitely many nonzero coefficients. Since irreducible characters are
class functions, every virtual character is a class function on $G$
([[def-class-function-and-the-space-of-complex-class-functions]],
[[def-irreducible-complex-character]]).

The set of all virtual characters is the **character ring** $R(G)$. Addition is
pointwise addition of class functions, and multiplication is the bilinear
extension of tensor-product multiplication on honest characters:

$$ (\chi_V+\chi_W)(g)=\chi_V(g)+\chi_W(g), \qquad (\chi_V\chi_W)(g)=\chi_{V\otimes W}(g) $$

([[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]).

Let $r\ge1$, $\lambda\vdash n$ and $\nu\vdash n-r$, and let
$c^\lambda_{\nu\mu}$ be the Littlewood–Richardson coefficient, the number of
Littlewood–Richardson tableaux of shape $\lambda/\nu$ and content $\mu$
([[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]]); thus
$\chi^\nu\circ\chi^\mu=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}c^\lambda_{\nu\mu}\chi^\lambda$
with $\circ$ the outer induction product
([[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]],
[[def-outer-induction-product-for-symmetric-group-characters]]). If $\nu\not\subseteq\lambda$, all coefficients below are zero by definition. Otherwise write
$\lambda/\nu$ as the disjoint union of its edge-connected components.

1. **(LR multiplicities.)** $c^\lambda_{\nu,(x,1^{r-x})}=0$ for every $x$
   unless $\lambda/\nu$ is a union of $m\ge1$ pairwise disjoint skew hooks with
   $r$ nodes in total; precisely, this means that $\lambda/\nu$ contains no
   $2\times2$ block, and then its $m$ edge-connected components are the skew
   hooks (for $m=1$, $\lambda/\nu$ is a removable border strip in the sense of
   [[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]). If $\lambda/\nu$ is such a union
   occupying $c$ columns in total, then
   $$c^\lambda_{\nu,(x,1^{r-x})}=\binom{m-1}{c-x}\qquad(1\le x\le r),$$
   with the convention $\binom{m-1}{c-x}=0$ when $c-x<0$ or $c-x>m-1$.

2. **(Alternating cancellation.)** With the same convention,
   $$\sum_{x=1}^{r}(-1)^{r-x}c^\lambda_{\nu,(x,1^{r-x})}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{r-c},& \lambda/\nu\text{ is a connected border strip occupying }c\text{ columns},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$
   where "otherwise" covers both unions of $m\ge2$ disjoint skew hooks and skew
   diagrams that are not unions of disjoint skew hooks. In the first case
   $c\ge m$, because distinct components have disjoint columns by column-convexity and each component occupies at least one
   column, so the terms $x=c-m+1,\dots,c$ all occur in the range $1\le x\le r$,
   and the sum is
   $\sum_{x}(-1)^{r-x}\binom{m-1}{c-x}=(-1)^{r-c}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(-1)^k\binom{m-1}{k}=0$.

3. **(Character form.)** Since a connected border strip with $r$ nodes and $c$
   columns has height $r-c$
   ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]),
   $$\sum_{x=1}^{r}(-1)^{r-x}\chi^\nu\circ\chi^{(x,1^{r-x})}=\sum_{\substack{\lambda\vdash n\\ \lambda/\nu\text{ a removable border strip of size }r}}(-1)^{\operatorname{ht}(\lambda/\nu)}\,\chi^\lambda,$$
   so every disconnected union of skew hooks cancels in the alternating hook
   induction of size $r$. No choice principle is used.

For $m,n\ge0$, $S_m$ is the symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,m\}$,
with $S_0=\{1\}$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). Identify
$S_m\times S_n$ ([[def-external-direct-product-of-groups]]) with the subgroup
of $S_{m+n}$ preserving each of the two blocks: the first factor acts on
$\{1,\dots,m\}$ and the second on $\{m+1,\dots,m+n\}$, so that
$(\sigma,\tau)$ acts as $\sigma$ on the first block and as $\tau$ on the
second after shifting its labels by $m$. Either block may be empty; its
symmetric group is trivial. These actions give an injective homomorphism,
and every permutation preserving the blocks has a unique pair of restrictions,
so its image is exactly the stated subgroup. For honest characters $\chi$ of $S_m$ and $\psi$ of $S_n$, let
$\chi\boxtimes\psi$ be the character of $S_m\times S_n$ on the tensor product
$V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$ of representations affording $\chi$ and $\psi$, with
$(\sigma,\tau)\cdot(v\otimes w):=\sigma v\otimes\tau w$, so that

$$(\chi\boxtimes\psi)(\sigma,\tau)=\chi(\sigma)\psi(\tau)$$

([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]).

Every virtual character $f\in R(S_m)$ is an integral combination
$f=\sum_ia_i\chi_i$ of the irreducible characters $\chi_i$ of $S_m$
([[def-virtual-character-and-character-ring-of-a-finite-group]]), and the
coefficients $a_i$ are unique because the irreducible characters of a finite
group are orthonormal, hence $\mathbb Z$-linearly independent, in
$\mathrm{cf}(S_m)$
([[thm-irreducible-complex-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis-of-the-class-functions]]).
So for $f=\sum_ia_i\chi_i$ and $g=\sum_jb_j\psi_j$ we may set

$$f\boxtimes g:=\sum_{i,j}a_ib_j\,(\chi_i\boxtimes\psi_j)\in R(S_m\times S_n),$$

an integral combination of honest characters of $S_m\times S_n$. Its value at
$(\sigma,\tau)$ is $f(\sigma)g(\tau)$ by the displayed character formula,
and uniqueness of the coefficients makes $f\boxtimes g$ well defined. The assignment
is $\mathbb Z$-bilinear in $(f,g)$. The **outer induction product** is

$$f\circ g:=\sum_{i,j}a_ib_j\,\operatorname{Ind}_{S_m\times S_n}^{S_{m+n}}\bigl(\chi_i\boxtimes\psi_j\bigr)\in R(S_{m+n}),$$

the induction of honest characters in the sense of
[[def-induced-character-of-a-complex-representation]]. The trivial character
of $S_0$ is the unit of degree zero. This is the outer product, defined across
different symmetric groups; the same-rank tensor product $f\cdot g$ on a single
$R(S_n)$ is a different operation, and the two are never conflated. No choice
principle is used.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $H\le G$, and let $W$ be a finite-dimensional
complex representation of $H$ with character $\chi_W$
([[def-character-of-a-complex-representation]]).

The **induced character** of $\chi_W$ is the character of the induced
representation:

$$ \operatorname{Ind}_H^G\chi_W := \chi_{\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W}. $$

When the representation affording $\chi_W$ is denoted simply by $W$, one also
writes $\chi_{\operatorname{Ind}_H^G W}$.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $H\le G$, and let $\chi$ be the character of a
finite-dimensional complex representation of $H$. Then for every $g\in G$,

$$ \operatorname{Ind}_H^G\chi(g) = \frac1{|H|} \sum_{\substack{x\in G\\x^{-1}gx\in H}} \chi(x^{-1}gx). $$

Let $n\ge1$ and let $\rho\in S_n$ be a cycle of length $n$ (for $n=1$, the identity on the sole point)
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]). Then for every
partition $\lambda\vdash n$, taking $\lambda_2=0$ for a one-row partition, with $\chi^\lambda$ the character of the complex
Specht module $S^\lambda$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]],
[[def-virtual-character-and-character-ring-of-a-finite-group]]),

$$\chi^\lambda(\rho)=\begin{cases}(-1)^{n-x},& \lambda=(x,1^{n-x})\text{ for some }1\le x\le n,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$

where $(x,1^{n-x})$ denotes the hook partition of $n$ with first part $x$. In
particular $\chi^{(n)}(\rho)=1$ and $\chi^{(1^n)}(\rho)=(-1)^{n-1}$, and
$\chi^\lambda(\rho)=0$ whenever $[\lambda]$ contains a $2\times2$ block of
nodes, equivalently whenever $\lambda_2\ge2$; in the hook case
$\lambda=(x,1^{n-x})$ the numbers of rows and columns are $n-x+1$ and $x$. No
choice principle is used.

For two class functions $\varphi,\psi\in\mathrm{cf}(G)$
([[def-class-function-and-the-space-of-complex-class-functions]]), define

$$\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\varphi(g)\,\overline{\psi(g)},$$

the finite sum being that of
([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]) for the additive commutative
monoid of $\mathbb C$. This is the standard Hermitian form on
the complex vector space of class functions.

This assignment is an inner product in the exact sense of the published
definition ([[def-inner-product-space]]), with the inner product linear in the
first argument. Linearity in the first slot is immediate from the pointwise
vector-space structure of $\mathrm{cf}(G)$ and linearity of the finite sum. The
conjugate-symmetry clause holds because conjugation
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) is an involution:
$\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle=\frac1{|G|}\sum_g\psi(g)\overline{\varphi(g)}
=\overline{\frac1{|G|}\sum_g\varphi(g)\overline{\psi(g)}}
=\overline{\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle}$. For definiteness,
$\langle\varphi,\varphi\rangle=\frac1{|G|}\sum_g|\varphi(g)|^2$ is a sum of
nonnegative real numbers, hence nonnegative real; it is $0$ exactly when every
term $|\varphi(g)|^2$ is $0$, and since $|z|=0$ holds only for $z=0$ in
$\mathbb C$, that says exactly $\varphi=0$ as a function.

Let $G$ be a finite group and let $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r$ be the irreducible
complex characters of $G$, one from each equivalence class. Then

$$\langle\chi_i,\chi_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\qquad(1\le i,j\le r).$$

Let $G$ be a finite group. The irreducible complex characters of $G$,
$\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r$, form an orthonormal basis of the complex vector space
$\mathrm{cf}(G)$ of class functions on $G$, with respect to the standard
inner product.

For every $n\ge0$, the modules $\{S^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list, up to isomorphism, of finite-dimensional irreducible
complex $S_n$-representations.

For every $n\ge0$ and every $\lambda\vdash n$, let $S^\lambda$ be the complex
Specht module of shape $\lambda$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]) and $\chi^\lambda$
its character, an irreducible character of $S_n$
([[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]]). Then

$$\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda\in\Lambda^n,$$

the stable Schur function of shape $\lambda$
([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]). In particular $\operatorname{ch}$
maps the $\mathbb Z$-basis $\{\chi^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $R(S_n)$ to the
$\mathbb Z$-basis $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $\Lambda^n$, and all values
$\chi^\lambda(\rho)$ are integers.

For $\sigma,\tau\in S_n$, there is a $g\in S_n$ with
$\tau=g\sigma g^{-1}$ if and only if $\sigma$ and $\tau$ have the same cycle
type, including their numbers of fixed points.

Let $X$ be a finite set and let $\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, with cycle
notation and composition as in [[def-symmetric-group]].

The **support** and **fixed-point set** of $\sigma$ are

$$\operatorname{supp}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)\ne x\},\qquad \operatorname{Fix}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)=x\}.$$

A cycle $(a_0\,a_1\,\ldots\,a_{k-1})$ has **length** $k$ and support
$\{a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\}$. Two cycles are **disjoint** when their supports are
disjoint. A **disjoint-cycle decomposition** of $\sigma$ is an expression for
$\sigma$ as a product of pairwise disjoint cycles of length at least $2$.
One-cycles are omitted, and the empty product is the identity permutation.

When $|X|=n$, the **cycle type** of $\sigma$ is the list of natural numbers
$c_1(\sigma),\ldots,c_n(\sigma)$, where $c_k(\sigma)$ is the number of
$k$-element orbits of the action generated by $\sigma$. Thus $c_1(\sigma)$ is
the number of fixed points. Equivalently, the cycle type records the lengths of
all cycles after each fixed point is inserted as a one-cycle.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, so that $n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). The
**symmetric group on $n$ letters** is

$$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(n)=\operatorname{Sym}(\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}),$$

the group of all bijections of $n$ under composition ([[def-symmetric-group]]),
with the composition convention

$$(\sigma\tau)(i):=(\sigma\circ\tau)(i)=\sigma(\tau(i))\qquad(i\in n),$$

so that in a product the right-hand factor acts first. An element of $S_n$ is
named by either of the two notations below.

**One-line notation.** For $\sigma\in S_n$, its **one-line form** is the list of
its values in order of their arguments,

$$\sigma=[\sigma(0),\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n-1)].$$

This list has length $n$ and its entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$, each occurring
once, because $\sigma$ is a bijection of $n$. Conversely, a list
$[b_0,b_1,\dots,b_{n-1}]$ whose entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$ each occurring once
is the one-line form of exactly one element of $S_n$, namely the map sending
each $i\in n$ to $b_i$: that map is injective because the entries are distinct,
and surjective because every element of $n$ occurs among them. So one-line
notation is a bijection from $S_n$ to the arrangements of $0,1,\dots,n-1$ in a
list. For $n=0$ the one-line form of the unique element of $S_0$ is the empty
list.

**Cycle notation.** For distinct $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{k-1}\in n$ with $k\ge2$, the
symbol $(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})$ denotes the element of $S_n$ that sends
$a_i$ to $a_{i+1}$ for each $i<k-1$, sends $a_{k-1}$ to $a_0$, and fixes every
element of $n$ outside $\{a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]); it is
called a **$k$-cycle**, and a $2$-cycle is a **transposition**. Writing cycle
symbols side by side means composing them, so $(a\,b)(c\,d)$ is
$(a\,b)\circ(c\,d)$, and the empty juxtaposition of cycle symbols is the
identity $\operatorname{id}$.

Unlike one-line notation, cycle notation does not name each permutation once:
the symbol may be started at any of its entries, so

$$(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})=(a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1}\,a_0)$$

and each $k$-cycle is written by exactly $k$ symbols of this shape. A cycle
symbol also does not record $n$, which must be supplied by the context.

derivations.claim:
By the character form of the cancellation lemma [F2], $\sum_{x=1}^{r}(-1)^{r-x}\chi^
u\circ\chi^{(x,1^{r-x})}=\Psi_
u$; since the outer product is $\mathbb Z$-bilinear [F3] and $\psi_r=\sum_{x=1}^{r}(-1)^{r-x}\chi^{(x,1^{r-x})}$ by [F1], the same sum is $\chi^
u\circ\psi_r$. Hence $\Psi_
u=\chi^
u\circ\psi_r$ in $R(S_n)$.

We prove the evaluation $\psi_r=r\cdot 1_C$, where $C$ is the conjugacy class of the $r$-cycles of $S_r$ and $1_C$ is its indicator function. Let $\rho\in S_r$ be an $r$-cycle. For every $\lambda\vdash r$, orthonormality [F6] gives $\langle\psi_r,\chi^\lambda\rangle=\sum_{x=1}^{r}(-1)^{r-x}\langle\chi^{(x,1^{r-x})},\chi^\lambda\rangle$, which equals $(-1)^{r-\lambda_1}$ if $\lambda=(\lambda_1,1^{r-\lambda_1})$ is a hook and $0$ otherwise; by the full-cycle lemma [F5] this is exactly $\chi^\lambda(\rho)$. On the other hand, for $f:=r\cdot 1_C$ the definition of the standard inner product [F6], the integrality $\overline{\chi^\lambda(\sigma)}=\chi^\lambda(\sigma)$ [F7] and the constancy of $\chi^\lambda$ on $C$ give $\langle f,\chi^\lambda\rangle=\frac{1}{r!}\,r\sum_{\sigma\in C}\chi^\lambda(\sigma)=\frac{r\,|C|}{r!}\,\chi^\lambda(\rho)=\chi^\lambda(\rho)$, because $C$ consists of the $r!/r=(r-1)!$ cyclic orderings of the $r$ points up to rotation. Thus $\langle\psi_r-f,\chi^\lambda\rangle=0$ for every $\lambda\vdash r$; the $\chi^\lambda$ exhaust the irreducible characters of $S_r$ and form an orthonormal basis of the class functions [F6], so $\psi_r-f=0$, that is, $\psi_r(\rho)=r$ for every $r$-cycle $\rho$ and $\psi_r(\tau)=0$ for every $\tau\in S_r$ that is not an $r$-cycle.

Let $\sigma\in S_n$ have cycle type with no part equal to $r$; we show $\Psi_
u(\sigma)=0$. By step 1.1, $\Psi_
u=\chi^
u\circ\psi_r$, and by [F3] this outer product is $\operatorname{Ind}_K^{S_n}(\chi^
u oxtimes\psi_r)$ for the two-block subgroup $K=\operatorname{Sym}(B_1)	imes\operatorname{Sym}(B_2)$ with $B_1=\{0,\dots,n-r-1\}$ and $B_2=\{n-r,\dots,n-1\}$; applying Frobenius' formula [F4] to the honest characters of the finite expansion of $\chi^
u oxtimes\psi_r$ and extending by linearity gives $$(\chi^
u\circ\psi_r)(\sigma)= rac{1}{|K|}\sum_{\substack{x\in S_n\ x^{-1}\sigma x\in K}}(\chi^
u oxtimes\psi_r)(x^{-1}\sigma x).$$ For an index $x$ of the sum write $x^{-1}\sigma x=(u,v)$ with $u\in\operatorname{Sym}(B_1)$ and $v\in\operatorname{Sym}(B_2)$; then $(\chi^
u oxtimes\psi_r)(u,v)=\chi^
u(u)\psi_r(v)$ by [F3]. If $r=1$, then $K$ fixes the single point of $B_2$, so no conjugate of $\sigma$ (which has no fixed point) lies in $K$ and the sum is empty; hence assume $r\ge2$. If $v$ were an $r$-cycle on $B_2$, then the disjoint-cycle decomposition of $x^{-1}\sigma x$ would contain that $r$-cycle, so the cycle type of $x^{-1}\sigma x$ would have a part equal to $r$, contradicting [F8] and the hypothesis on $\sigma$. Therefore $v$ is not an $r$-cycle, so $\psi_r(v)=0$ by step 1.2 and every term of the sum vanishes; hence $(\chi^
u\circ\psi_r)(\sigma)=0$ and therefore $\Psi_
u(\sigma)=0$ by step 1.1.

Step 1.1 identifies $\Psi_
u$ with the outer product $\chi^
u\circ\psi_r$, step 1.2 shows that $\psi_r$ equals $r$ on the class of $r$-cycles of $S_r$ and vanishes on every other class, and step 2.1 shows $\Psi_
u(\sigma)=0$ for every $\sigma\in S_n$ whose cycle type has no part equal to $r$. These are exactly the three assertions of the statement.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, so that $n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). The
**symmetric group on $n$ letters** is

$$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(n)=\operatorname{Sym}(\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}),$$

the group of all bijections of $n$ under composition ([[def-symmetric-group]]),
with the composition convention

$$(\sigma\tau)(i):=(\sigma\circ\tau)(i)=\sigma(\tau(i))\qquad(i\in n),$$

so that in a product the right-hand factor acts first. An element of $S_n$ is
named by either of the two notations below.

**One-line notation.** For $\sigma\in S_n$, its **one-line form** is the list of
its values in order of their arguments,

$$\sigma=[\sigma(0),\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n-1)].$$

This list has length $n$ and its entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$, each occurring

list.

**Cycle notation.** For distinct $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{k-1}\in n$ with $k\ge2$, the
symbol $(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})$ denotes the element of $S_n$ that sends
$a_i$ to $a_{i+1}$ for each $i<k-1$, sends $a_{k-1}$ to $a_0$, and fixes every
element of $n$ outside $\{a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]); it is

symbols side by side means composing them, so $(a\,b)(c\,d)$ is

$$(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})=(a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1}\,a_0)$$

and each $k$-cycle is written by exactly $k$ symbols of this shape. A cycle
symbol also does not record $n$, which must be supplied by the context.

Let $0\le r\le n$ and let $K\le S_n$ be the subgroup preserving each of the
two blocks $B_1=\{0,\dots,n-r-1\}$ and $B_2=\{n-r,\dots,n-1\}$ of the
underlying set $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]); under the order-preserving relabelling $i\mapsto i-1$, these are the two blocks of sizes $n-r$ and $r$ in the outer-product definition ([[def-outer-induction-product-for-symmetric-group-characters]]); it is the image of the external direct product $S_{n-r}\times S_r$ acting on
$B_1$ and $B_2$ ([[def-external-direct-product-of-groups]]). Identify the
complex character ring $R(K)$ with $R(S_{n-r})\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R(S_r)$ by
external tensor products $\chi\boxtimes\psi$ of characters
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[lem-character-ring-of-a-direct-product-is-the-tensor-product]]). For a
partition $\lambda\vdash n$ let $\chi^\lambda$ be the character of the complex
Specht module $S^\lambda$, an irreducible character of $S_n$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]],
[[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]]), and let $c^\lambda_{\nu\mu}$
be the Littlewood–Richardson coefficient
([[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]]). Then, in $R(K)$,
$$\chi^\lambda\big|_{K}=\sum_{\nu\vdash n-r}\ \sum_{\mu\vdash r}c^\lambda_{\nu\mu}\,(\chi^\nu\boxtimes\chi^\mu).$$

In particular the multiplicity of the irreducible character
$\chi^\nu\boxtimes\chi^\mu$ in the restricted character $\chi^\lambda|_K$
equals $c^\lambda_{\nu\mu}$; for $r=n$ this says that the multiplicity is $1$
if $\mu=\lambda$ and $0$ otherwise. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda,
u$ be partitions with $[\lambda]\subseteq[
u]$, and let $\mu$ be a partition with $|
u|=|\lambda|+|\mu|$. Use the conventions of [[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]] for the skew diagram $
u/\lambda$ and for semistandard skew tableaux of shape $
u/\lambda$, and those of [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] for the content of a tableau; recall that entries of a semistandard skew tableau weakly increase along rows and strictly increase down columns ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]] fixes the English row and column coordinates).

The **reading word** $w(T)$ of a semistandard skew tableau $T$ of shape $
u/\lambda$ is the word obtained by reading the rows of $T$ from right to left, beginning with the top row and proceeding to the bottom row. The word $w(T)=a_1a_2\cdots a_N$ is a **lattice word** (a lattice permutation) if in every prefix $a_1\cdots a_p$ and for every $i\ge1$ the number of letters $i$ in the prefix is at least the number of letters $i+1$; the empty word is a lattice word vacuously.

A **Littlewood--Richardson tableau** (LR tableau) of shape $
u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$ is a semistandard skew tableau of shape $
u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$ whose reading word is a lattice word. The **Littlewood--Richardson coefficient** $c^
u_{\lambda\mu}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ is the number of LR tableaux of shape $
u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$; it is $0$ when $[\lambda]
ot\subseteq[
u]$, when $|
u|
e|\lambda|+|\mu|$, or when no such tableau exists. For $\mu=\varnothing$ and $
u=\lambda$ the empty skew tableau is the unique tableau of content $\varnothing$, its reading word is empty, and hence $c^\lambda_{\lambda\varnothing}=1$; more generally $c^\lambda_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\mu=\varnothing$, and $c^
u_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\lambda\subseteq
u$ and $|
u|=|\lambda|+|\mu|$.

Let $G,H$ be finite groups. For finite-dimensional complex representations $V$ of $G$ and $W$ of $H$, their **external tensor product** is the representation of $G\times H$ on $V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$ with

$$
(g,h)\cdot(v\otimes w):=(gv)\otimes(hw).
$$

Its character satisfies $\chi_{V\boxtimes W}(g,h)=\chi_V(g)\chi_W(h)$. Extend this operation $\mathbb Z$-bilinearly from irreducible characters to $R(G)\times R(H)$, using the irreducible-character bases. Then:

(i) the induced map $R(G)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R(H)\to R(G\times H)$, $\chi\otimes\psi\mapsto\chi\boxtimes\psi$, is an isomorphism of rings, carries $1\otimes1$ to the trivial character, and satisfies

$$
(\chi\boxtimes\psi)(\chi'\boxtimes\psi')=(\chi\chi')\boxtimes(\psi\psi')
$$

for all $\chi,\chi'\in R(G)$ and $\psi,\psi'\in R(H)$; and

(ii) as $\chi$ and $\psi$ range over the irreducible characters, the elements $\chi\boxtimes\psi$ are pairwise distinct and form an orthonormal $\mathbb Z$-basis of $R(G\times H)$. In particular, every honest character of $G\times H$ is a nonnegative integral combination of these external products. No choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $\rho\in S_n$ be a cycle of length $n$ (for $n=1$, the identity on the sole point)
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]). Then for every
partition $\lambda\vdash n$, taking $\lambda_2=0$ for a one-row partition, with $\chi^\lambda$ the character of the complex
Specht module $S^\lambda$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]],
[[def-virtual-character-and-character-ring-of-a-finite-group]]),

$$\chi^\lambda(\rho)=\begin{cases}(-1)^{n-x},& \lambda=(x,1^{n-x})\text{ for some }1\le x\le n,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$

where $(x,1^{n-x})$ denotes the hook partition of $n$ with first part $x$. In
particular $\chi^{(n)}(\rho)=1$ and $\chi^{(1^n)}(\rho)=(-1)^{n-1}$, and
$\chi^\lambda(\rho)=0$ whenever $[\lambda]$ contains a $2\times2$ block of
nodes, equivalently whenever $\lambda_2\ge2$; in the hook case
$\lambda=(x,1^{n-x})$ the numbers of rows and columns are $n-x+1$ and $x$. No
choice principle is used.

Let $r\ge1$, $\lambda\vdash n$ and $\nu\vdash n-r$, and let
$c^\lambda_{\nu\mu}$ be the Littlewood–Richardson coefficient, the number of
Littlewood–Richardson tableaux of shape $\lambda/\nu$ and content $\mu$
([[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]]); thus
$\chi^\nu\circ\chi^\mu=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}c^\lambda_{\nu\mu}\chi^\lambda$
with $\circ$ the outer induction product
([[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]],
[[def-outer-induction-product-for-symmetric-group-characters]]). If $\nu\not\subseteq\lambda$, all coefficients below are zero by definition. Otherwise write
$\lambda/\nu$ as the disjoint union of its edge-connected components.

1. **(LR multiplicities.)** $c^\lambda_{\nu,(x,1^{r-x})}=0$ for every $x$
   unless $\lambda/\nu$ is a union of $m\ge1$ pairwise disjoint skew hooks with
   $r$ nodes in total; precisely, this means that $\lambda/\nu$ contains no
   $2\times2$ block, and then its $m$ edge-connected components are the skew
   hooks (for $m=1$, $\lambda/\nu$ is a removable border strip in the sense of
   [[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]). If $\lambda/\nu$ is such a union
   occupying $c$ columns in total, then
   $$c^\lambda_{\nu,(x,1^{r-x})}=\binom{m-1}{c-x}\qquad(1\le x\le r),$$
   with the convention $\binom{m-1}{c-x}=0$ when $c-x<0$ or $c-x>m-1$.

2. **(Alternating cancellation.)** With the same convention,
   $$\sum_{x=1}^{r}(-1)^{r-x}c^\lambda_{\nu,(x,1^{r-x})}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{r-c},& \lambda/\nu\text{ is a connected border strip occupying }c\text{ columns},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$
   where "otherwise" covers both unions of $m\ge2$ disjoint skew hooks and skew
   diagrams that are not unions of disjoint skew hooks. In the first case
   $c\ge m$, because distinct components have disjoint columns by column-convexity and each component occupies at least one
   column, so the terms $x=c-m+1,\dots,c$ all occur in the range $1\le x\le r$,
   and the sum is
   $\sum_{x}(-1)^{r-x}\binom{m-1}{c-x}=(-1)^{r-c}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(-1)^k\binom{m-1}{k}=0$.

3. **(Character form.)** Since a connected border strip with $r$ nodes and $c$
   columns has height $r-c$
   ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]),
   $$\sum_{x=1}^{r}(-1)^{r-x}\chi^\nu\circ\chi^{(x,1^{r-x})}=\sum_{\substack{\lambda\vdash n\\ \lambda/\nu\text{ a removable border strip of size }r}}(-1)^{\operatorname{ht}(\lambda/\nu)}\,\chi^\lambda,$$
   so every disconnected union of skew hooks cancels in the alternating hook
   induction of size $r$. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected, $2\times2$-free skew diagram with complement a Young diagram.
Every strip node $(p,q)$ lies on the rim: if $(p+1,q+1)$ belonged to
$[\lambda]$, it could not belong to $[\nu]$, since that would force
$(p,q)\in[\nu]$; and the partition inequalities then put all four nodes of
the corresponding $2\times2$ block in the strip, a contradiction. The rim
nodes in row $p$ have columns $\max(1,\lambda_{p+1}),\dots,\lambda_p$,
where missing row lengths are zero. Read each such interval from right to
left, then move down at column $\lambda_{p+1}$ to the next row: these are
exactly the rim nodes and their side-adjacencies. Thus the rim is a single
path moving left or down, and its connected subsets are subpaths. The
$r-1$ steps of $\xi$ consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ leftward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, so that $n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). The
**symmetric group on $n$ letters** is

$$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(n)=\operatorname{Sym}(\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}),$$

the group of all bijections of $n$ under composition ([[def-symmetric-group]]),
with the composition convention

$$(\sigma\tau)(i):=(\sigma\circ\tau)(i)=\sigma(\tau(i))\qquad(i\in n),$$

so that in a product the right-hand factor acts first. An element of $S_n$ is
named by either of the two notations below.

**One-line notation.** For $\sigma\in S_n$, its **one-line form** is the list of
its values in order of their arguments,

$$\sigma=[\sigma(0),\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n-1)].$$

This list has length $n$ and its entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$, each occurring
once, because $\sigma$ is a bijection of $n$. Conversely, a list
$[b_0,b_1,\dots,b_{n-1}]$ whose entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$ each occurring once
is the one-line form of exactly one element of $S_n$, namely the map sending
each $i\in n$ to $b_i$: that map is injective because the entries are distinct,
and surjective because every element of $n$ occurs among them. So one-line
notation is a bijection from $S_n$ to the arrangements of $0,1,\dots,n-1$ in a
list. For $n=0$ the one-line form of the unique element of $S_0$ is the empty
list.

**Cycle notation.** For distinct $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{k-1}\in n$ with $k\ge2$, the
symbol $(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})$ denotes the element of $S_n$ that sends
$a_i$ to $a_{i+1}$ for each $i<k-1$, sends $a_{k-1}$ to $a_0$, and fixes every
element of $n$ outside $\{a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]); it is
called a **$k$-cycle**, and a $2$-cycle is a **transposition**. Writing cycle
symbols side by side means composing them, so $(a\,b)(c\,d)$ is
$(a\,b)\circ(c\,d)$, and the empty juxtaposition of cycle symbols is the
identity $\operatorname{id}$.

Unlike one-line notation, cycle notation does not name each permutation once:
the symbol may be started at any of its entries, so

$$(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})=(a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1}\,a_0)$$

and each $k$-cycle is written by exactly $k$ symbols of this shape. A cycle
symbol also does not record $n$, which must be supplied by the context.

Let $X$ be a finite set and let $\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, with cycle
notation and composition as in [[def-symmetric-group]].

The **support** and **fixed-point set** of $\sigma$ are

$$\operatorname{supp}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)\ne x\},\qquad \operatorname{Fix}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)=x\}.$$

A cycle $(a_0\,a_1\,\ldots\,a_{k-1})$ has **length** $k$ and support
$\{a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\}$. Two cycles are **disjoint** when their supports are
disjoint. A **disjoint-cycle decomposition** of $\sigma$ is an expression for
$\sigma$ as a product of pairwise disjoint cycles of length at least $2$.
One-cycles are omitted, and the empty product is the identity permutation.

When $|X|=n$, the **cycle type** of $\sigma$ is the list of natural numbers
$c_1(\sigma),\ldots,c_n(\sigma)$, where $c_k(\sigma)$ is the number of
$k$-element orbits of the action generated by $\sigma$. Thus $c_1(\sigma)$ is
the number of fixed points. Equivalently, the cycle type records the lengths of
all cycles after each fixed point is inserted as a one-cycle.

Let $n\ge 0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $t$ be a $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Use the left action of
$S_n$ on tableaux, tabloids, and $M^\lambda$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). For each
$\gamma\in C_t$, let $\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)$ be its inversion sign in
$S_n$. The order-preserving relabelling
$\iota_n:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, $i\mapsto i-1$, carries each
inversion pair $(i,j)$ bijectively to $(i-1,j-1)$; thus this sign is exactly
the published inversion sign on the finite ordinal
([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). For $n=0$, both groups are
trivial and the sign is $1$.

The **column antisymmetrizer**, **polytabloid**, and **Specht space** are
$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma\quad\in\mathbb C[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}\quad\in M^\lambda,\qquad S^\lambda:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{e_s:s\text{ is a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\}.$$
The elements of the sum are in the finite subgroup $C_t$, and each acts by the
declared left action on the tabloid basis, so these are well-defined finite
expressions.

For every tableau, $C_t\cap R_t=\{1\}$: a permutation in both stabilizers
preserves the row and column of each entry, and each row-column intersection
contains at most one node. Thus $\gamma\{t\}$ are distinct as $\gamma$ ranges
over $C_t$, and the coefficient of $\{t\}$ in $e_t$ is $1$. In particular,
$e_t\ne0$. When $n=0$, the empty tableau has $C_t=\{1\}$, so
$\kappa_t=1$, $e_t=\{\varnothing\}$, and $S^\varnothing=\mathbb C$.

citations.quote:
Let $1\le r\le n$ and choose a set $D\subseteq\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ of $r$ points. Let $\rho\in S_n$ act as a single cyclic permutation on $D$ and fix its complement. For $r=1$ this means $\rho=1$ with a specified point $D=\{d\}$; for $r\ge2$, $D=\operatorname{supp}(\rho)$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]], [[def-permutation-support-disjoint-cycles-and-cycle-type]]). Let $\sigma\in S_n$ fix $D$ pointwise, and identify its restriction to the complement of $D$ with an element of $S_{n-r}$ using the unique order-preserving bijection onto $\{0,\dots,n-r-1\}$. Then for every
$\lambda\vdash n$,
$$\chi^\lambda(\sigma\rho)=\sum_{\substack{\nu\vdash n-r\\ \lambda/\nu\text{ a removable border strip of size }r}}(-1)^{\operatorname{ht}(\lambda/\nu)}\,\chi^\nu(\sigma),$$
the sum running over the removable border strips of $\lambda$ of size $r$
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]) and being $0$ when there is none.
Applied to the parts of a cycle type in succession, the rule computes
$\chi^\lambda$ on every class of $S_n$. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. Let $H(x)$ be the hook of $x$,
with arm length $a(x)=\lambda_i-j$, leg length $\ell(x)=\lambda'_j-i$ and hook
length $h(x)=a(x)+\ell(x)+1$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); its two endpoints are the last node
$(i,\lambda_i)$ of its arm and the last node $(\lambda'_j,j)$ of its leg. Let
$\xi(x)$ be the unique edge-connected set of nodes of $[\lambda]$ with
endpoints $(i,\lambda_i)$ and $(\lambda'_j,j)$ that lies in the rim of
$[\lambda]$, i.e. consists of nodes $(p,q)$ with $(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Then:

1. $\xi(x)$ is a removable border strip of $\lambda$ of size $h(x)$ and height
   $\ell(x)$ ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]), and
   $[\lambda]\setminus\xi(x)$ is a Young diagram, so $\lambda\setminus\xi(x)$ is
   a partition of $n-h(x)$;
2. every removable border strip of $\lambda$ equals $\xi(x)$ for exactly one
   node $x\in[\lambda]$; hence $x\mapsto\xi(x)$ is a bijection from the nodes
   of $[\lambda]$ onto the removable border strips of $\lambda$.

Consequently the sizes of the removable border strips of $\lambda$ are exactly
the hook lengths of $\lambda$, the height of $\xi(x)$ is the leg length
$\ell(x)$, and $x$ is removable as a node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) if and only if $\xi(x)$
has size $1$. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and let
$x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. The **hook of $x$** is the set
$$H(x):=\{(i,j')\in[\lambda]:j'\ge j\}\cup\{(i',j)\in[\lambda]:i'\ge i\},$$
the union of the boxes of $[\lambda]$ weakly to the right of $x$ in row $i$
and weakly below $x$ in column $j$; the box $x$ itself belongs to both parts
and is counted once. The **arm** $\operatorname{arm}(x)$ is the part in row
$i$ strictly to the right of $x$, so
$\operatorname{arm}(x)=\{(i,j'):j<j'\le\lambda_i\}$; the **leg**
$\operatorname{leg}(x)$ is the part in column $j$ strictly below $x$, so
$\operatorname{leg}(x)=\{(i',j):i<i'\le\lambda'_j\}$. The **arm length** is
$a(x):=\lambda_i-j$, the **leg length** is $\ell(x):=\lambda'_j-i$, and the
**hook length** is

$$h(x):=a(x)+\ell(x)+1=\lambda_i-j+\lambda'_j-i+1,$$

so that $H(x)$ has exactly $h(x)$ boxes. Here $\lambda'_j$ is the number of
rows of $[\lambda]$ of length at least $j$, so the boxes of column $j$ below
row $i$ are exactly the rows $i+1,\dots,\lambda'_j$ and the arm has
$\lambda_i-j$ boxes; the arm, the leg and the anchor $x$ are pairwise disjoint
and exhaust $H(x)$, which gives the count.

A box is removable in the sense of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] if and only if it is the
last box of its row and of its column, i.e. if and only if $h(x)=1$: a row
endpoint $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable exactly when no box lies immediately
below it, that is when $\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$, and then
$a(x)=\lambda_i-\lambda_i=0$ and $\ell(x)=\lambda'_{\lambda_i}-i=0$; conversely
$h(x)=1$ forces $a(x)=\ell(x)=0$, so $x$ ends both its row and its column. The
empty partition has no boxes.

Finally $P(\lambda):=\prod_{x\in[\lambda]}h(x)$ denotes the **hook product**
of $\lambda$, the empty product $P(\varnothing)=1$ being part of the
convention. This fixes the off-by-one convention used by the whole page: the
anchor box contributes $1$, the arm contributes $\lambda_i-j$ and the leg
contributes $\lambda'_j-i$. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected, $2\times2$-free skew diagram with complement a Young diagram.
Every strip node $(p,q)$ lies on the rim: if $(p+1,q+1)$ belonged to
$[\lambda]$, it could not belong to $[\nu]$, since that would force
$(p,q)\in[\nu]$; and the partition inequalities then put all four nodes of
the corresponding $2\times2$ block in the strip, a contradiction. The rim
nodes in row $p$ have columns $\max(1,\lambda_{p+1}),\dots,\lambda_p$,
where missing row lengths are zero. Read each such interval from right to
left, then move down at column $\lambda_{p+1}$ to the next row: these are
exactly the rim nodes and their side-adjacencies. Thus the rim is a single
path moving left or down, and its connected subsets are subpaths. The
$r-1$ steps of $\xi$ consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ leftward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $X$ be a finite set and let $\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, with cycle
notation and composition as in [[def-symmetric-group]].

The **support** and **fixed-point set** of $\sigma$ are

$$\operatorname{supp}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)\ne x\},\qquad \operatorname{Fix}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)=x\}.$$

A cycle $(a_0\,a_1\,\ldots\,a_{k-1})$ has **length** $k$ and support
$\{a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\}$. Two cycles are **disjoint** when their supports are
disjoint. A **disjoint-cycle decomposition** of $\sigma$ is an expression for
$\sigma$ as a product of pairwise disjoint cycles of length at least $2$.
One-cycles are omitted, and the empty product is the identity permutation.

When $|X|=n$, the **cycle type** of $\sigma$ is the list of natural numbers
$c_1(\sigma),\ldots,c_n(\sigma)$, where $c_k(\sigma)$ is the number of
$k$-element orbits of the action generated by $\sigma$. Thus $c_1(\sigma)$ is
the number of fixed points. Equivalently, the cycle type records the lengths of
all cycles after each fixed point is inserted as a one-cycle.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, so that $n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). The
**symmetric group on $n$ letters** is

$$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(n)=\operatorname{Sym}(\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}),$$

the group of all bijections of $n$ under composition ([[def-symmetric-group]]),
with the composition convention

$$(\sigma\tau)(i):=(\sigma\circ\tau)(i)=\sigma(\tau(i))\qquad(i\in n),$$

so that in a product the right-hand factor acts first. An element of $S_n$ is
named by either of the two notations below.

**One-line notation.** For $\sigma\in S_n$, its **one-line form** is the list of
its values in order of their arguments,

$$\sigma=[\sigma(0),\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n-1)].$$

This list has length $n$ and its entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$, each occurring
once, because $\sigma$ is a bijection of $n$. Conversely, a list
$[b_0,b_1,\dots,b_{n-1}]$ whose entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$ each occurring once
is the one-line form of exactly one element of $S_n$, namely the map sending
each $i\in n$ to $b_i$: that map is injective because the entries are distinct,
and surjective because every element of $n$ occurs among them. So one-line
notation is a bijection from $S_n$ to the arrangements of $0,1,\dots,n-1$ in a
list. For $n=0$ the one-line form of the unique element of $S_0$ is the empty
list.

**Cycle notation.** For distinct $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{k-1}\in n$ with $k\ge2$, the
symbol $(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})$ denotes the element of $S_n$ that sends
$a_i$ to $a_{i+1}$ for each $i<k-1$, sends $a_{k-1}$ to $a_0$, and fixes every
element of $n$ outside $\{a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]); it is
called a **$k$-cycle**, and a $2$-cycle is a **transposition**. Writing cycle
symbols side by side means composing them, so $(a\,b)(c\,d)$ is
$(a\,b)\circ(c\,d)$, and the empty juxtaposition of cycle symbols is the
identity $\operatorname{id}$.

Unlike one-line notation, cycle notation does not name each permutation once:
the symbol may be started at any of its entries, so

$$(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})=(a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1}\,a_0)$$

and each $k$-cycle is written by exactly $k$ symbols of this shape. A cycle
symbol also does not record $n$, which must be supplied by the context.

derivations.claim: Select a cycle of length $r$, with its set $D$ of $r$ points; for $r=1$ select a fixed point and put $c=1$, otherwise let $c$ be its cyclic permutation. Put $\sigma:=\rho c^{-1}$, the product of the remaining disjoint cycles. Then $\rho=\sigma c$, and $\sigma$ fixes $D$ pointwise, because the supports of the cycles of $\rho$ are pairwise disjoint.

By the hook/rim-hook correspondence [F2], the removable border strips of $\lambda$ are exactly the rim hooks $\xi(x)$ indexed by the nodes of $[\lambda]$, and the size of $\xi(x)$ is the hook length $h(x)$. Therefore $\lambda$ has a removable border strip of size $r$ if and only if some hook length of $\lambda$ equals $r$, so the two hypotheses of the statement are equivalent.

Apply the Murnaghan–Nakayama rule [F1] to the specified cycle $(D,c)$ and the compatible permutation $\sigma$ of step 1.1: $\chi^\lambda(ho)=\chi^\lambda(\sigma c)=\sum_{\lambda/
u}(-1)^{\operatorname{ht}(\lambda/
u)}\chi^
u(\sigma)$, the sum running over the removable border strips $\lambda/
u$ of size $r$. By hypothesis $\lambda$ has no such strip, so the index set is empty and the empty sum is $0$; thus $\chi^\lambda(ho)=0$. By the equivalence of step 1.2 the same conclusion holds under the hook-length hypothesis.

Let $r\ge1$, $n\ge r$ and $\nu\vdash n-r$, and put
$$\Psi_\nu:=\sum_{\substack{\lambda\vdash n\\ \lambda/\nu\text{ a removable border strip of size }r}}(-1)^{\operatorname{ht}(\lambda/\nu)}\,\chi^\lambda\in R(S_n),$$
a virtual character of $S_n$
([[def-virtual-character-and-character-ring-of-a-finite-group]],
[[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]), and
$$\psi_r:=\sum_{x=1}^{r}(-1)^{r-x}\chi^{(x,1^{r-x})}\in R(S_r).$$
Then
$$\Psi_\nu(\sigma)=0\qquad\text{for every }\sigma\in S_n\text{ whose cycle type has no part equal to }r$$
([[def-permutation-support-disjoint-cycles-and-cycle-type]]); equivalently,
the signed sum over the partitions $\lambda$ obtained from $\nu$ by adding an
$r$-border strip vanishes on all classes that contain no $r$-cycle. Moreover
$\Psi_\nu$ is the outer induction product $\Psi_\nu=\chi^\nu\circ\psi_r$
([[def-outer-induction-product-for-symmetric-group-characters]]), and $\psi_r$
vanishes on every class of $S_r$ other than the class of $r$-cycles: it is the
function that takes the value $r$ on every $r$-cycle and the value $0$ on every
other element of $S_r$. No choice principle is used.

border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and let
$x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. The **hook of $x$** is the set
$$H(x):=\{(i,j')\in[\lambda]:j'\ge j\}\cup\{(i',j)\in[\lambda]:i'\ge i\},$$
the union of the boxes of $[\lambda]$ weakly to the right of $x$ in row $i$
and weakly below $x$ in column $j$; the box $x$ itself belongs to both parts
and is counted once. The **arm** $\operatorname{arm}(x)$ is the part in row
$i$ strictly to the right of $x$, so
$\operatorname{arm}(x)=\{(i,j'):j<j'\le\lambda_i\}$; the **leg**
$\operatorname{leg}(x)$ is the part in column $j$ strictly below $x$, so
$\operatorname{leg}(x)=\{(i',j):i<i'\le\lambda'_j\}$. The **arm length** is
$a(x):=\lambda_i-j$, the **leg length** is $\ell(x):=\lambda'_j-i$, and the
**hook length** is

$$h(x):=a(x)+\ell(x)+1=\lambda_i-j+\lambda'_j-i+1,$$

so that $H(x)$ has exactly $h(x)$ boxes. Here $\lambda'_j$ is the number of
rows of $[\lambda]$ of length at least $j$, so the boxes of column $j$ below
row $i$ are exactly the rows $i+1,\dots,\lambda'_j$ and the arm has
$\lambda_i-j$ boxes; the arm, the leg and the anchor $x$ are pairwise disjoint
and exhaust $H(x)$, which gives the count.

A box is removable in the sense of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] if and only if it is the
last box of its row and of its column, i.e. if and only if $h(x)=1$: a row
endpoint $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable exactly when no box lies immediately
below it, that is when $\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$, and then
$a(x)=\lambda_i-\lambda_i=0$ and $\ell(x)=\lambda'_{\lambda_i}-i=0$; conversely
$h(x)=1$ forces $a(x)=\ell(x)=0$, so $x$ ends both its row and its column. The
empty partition has no boxes.

Finally $P(\lambda):=\prod_{x\in[\lambda]}h(x)$ denotes the **hook product**
of $\lambda$, the empty product $P(\varnothing)=1$ being part of the
convention. This fixes the off-by-one convention used by the whole page: the
anchor box contributes $1$, the arm contributes $\lambda_i-j$ and the leg
contributes $\lambda'_j-i$. No choice principle is used.

Let $1\le r\le n$ and choose a set $D\subseteq\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ of $r$ points. Let $\rho\in S_n$ act as a single cyclic permutation on $D$ and fix its complement. For $r=1$ this means $\rho=1$ with a specified point $D=\{d\}$; for $r\ge2$, $D=\operatorname{supp}(\rho)$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]], [[def-permutation-support-disjoint-cycles-and-cycle-type]]). Let $\sigma\in S_n$ fix $D$ pointwise, and identify its restriction to the complement of $D$ with an element of $S_{n-r}$ using the unique order-preserving bijection onto $\{0,\dots,n-r-1\}$. Then for every
$\lambda\vdash n$,
$$\chi^\lambda(\sigma\rho)=\sum_{\substack{\nu\vdash n-r\\ \lambda/\nu\text{ a removable border strip of size }r}}(-1)^{\operatorname{ht}(\lambda/\nu)}\,\chi^\nu(\sigma),$$
the sum running over the removable border strips of $\lambda$ of size $r$
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]) and being $0$ when there is none.
Applied to the parts of a cycle type in succession, the rule computes
$\chi^\lambda$ on every class of $S_n$. No choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $\rho\in S_n$ be a cycle of length $n$ (for $n=1$, the identity on the sole point)
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]). Then for every
partition $\lambda\vdash n$, taking $\lambda_2=0$ for a one-row partition, with $\chi^\lambda$ the character of the complex
Specht module $S^\lambda$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]],
[[def-virtual-character-and-character-ring-of-a-finite-group]]),

$$\chi^\lambda(\rho)=\begin{cases}(-1)^{n-x},& \lambda=(x,1^{n-x})\text{ for some }1\le x\le n,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$

where $(x,1^{n-x})$ denotes the hook partition of $n$ with first part $x$. In
particular $\chi^{(n)}(\rho)=1$ and $\chi^{(1^n)}(\rho)=(-1)^{n-1}$, and
$\chi^\lambda(\rho)=0$ whenever $[\lambda]$ contains a $2\times2$ block of
nodes, equivalently whenever $\lambda_2\ge2$; in the hook case
$\lambda=(x,1^{n-x})$ the numbers of rows and columns are $n-x+1$ and $x$. No
choice principle is used.

For every $n\ge0$ and every $\lambda\vdash n$, the number $f^\lambda$ of
standard $\lambda$-tableaux is
$$f^\lambda=\frac{n!}{\prod_{x\in[\lambda]}h(x)},$$
the empty product for $\lambda=\varnothing$ being $1$, so that
$f^\varnothing=1$ and, for $n\ge1$, $f^\lambda=1$ for $\lambda=(n)$ and $\lambda=(1^n)$. In
particular, over $\mathbb C$,
$$\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda=\frac{n!}{\prod_{x\in[\lambda]}h(x)}$$
for the Specht module $S^\lambda$, including $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\varnothing=1$.

derivations.claim: A partition $\lambda\vdash8$ contains $(3,2)$ exactly when $\lambda_1\ge3$ and $\lambda_2\ge2$, leaving the eleven candidates $(6,2),(5,2,1),(4,2,2),(4,2,1,1),(3,2,2,1),(3,2,1,1,1),(5,3),(4,3,1),(3,3,2),(3,3,1,1),(4,4)$; among their skew differences $\lambda/(3,2)$, which all have $3$ nodes, exactly four are edge-connected and contain no $2\times2$ block, namely the horizontal strip $\{(1,4),(1,5),(1,6)\}$ with $c=3$ columns in $\lambda=(6,2)$, the corners $\{(1,4),(2,3),(2,4)\}$ and $\{(3,1),(3,2),(4,1)\}$ with $c=2$ in $\lambda=(4,4)$ and $\lambda=(3,2,2,1)$, and the vertical strip $\{(3,1),(4,1),(5,1)\}$ with $c=1$ in $\lambda=(3,2,1,1,1)$; the other seven differences are disconnected, for instance $\lambda=(5,3)$, where the node $(2,3)$ is not adjacent to $(1,4)$ or $(1,5)$. The heights are $3-c$, namely $0,1,1,2$, so the four signs $+,-,-,+$ and the displayed expression for $\Psi_{(3,2)}$ follow.

The four dimensions of [F5] give $\Psi_{(3,2)}(1)=20-14-70+64=0$; equivalently $\Psi_{(3,2)}=\chi^{(3,2)}\circ\psi_3$ by [F1] and $\psi_3(1)=0$ because the identity of $S_3$ is not a $3$-cycle, so the degree vanishes.

On the class of $8$-cycles each of the four shapes contains a $2\times2$ block (rows $1$ and $2$, columns $1$ and $2$), so none is a hook and $\chi^\lambda=0$ on that class for all four $\lambda$ by the full-cycle lemma [F4]; hence $\Psi_{(3,2)}$ vanishes there.

On the class $(4,4)$ the rule [F3] gives: $\chi^{(6,2)}=0$, since the unique $4$-strip takes $(6,2)$ to $(2,2)$ with height $0$ and $(2,2)$ has no $4$-strip; $\chi^{(4,4)}=+1-(-1)=2$ from the strips to $(4)$ (height $0$) and to $(3,1)$ (height $1$), with $\chi^{(4)}(4)=1$ and $\chi^{(3,1)}(4)=-1$; $\chi^{(3,2,2,1)}=(-1)+(-1)=-2$ from the strips to $(3,1)$ and to $(1^4)$, both of height $2$, with $\chi^{(3,1)}(4)=\chi^{(1^4)}(4)=-1$; and $\chi^{(3,2,1,1,1)}=0$ because $(3,2,1,1,1)$ has no $4$-strip. Hence $\Psi_{(3,2)}=+0-2-(-2)+0=0$ on the class $(4,4)$, whose cycle type has no part $3$.

Steps 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 verify the vanishing predicted by [F1] on the identity class, the class of $8$-cycles and the class $(4,4)$, all of which are classes of $S_8$ without a $3$-cycle, confirming the displayed value $\Psi_{(3,2)}=0$ there.
