indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra

for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation

$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with

([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$

([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites

No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]), and let $N$ be an

derivations.claim: **The automorphism and its first properties.** Put $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i$. Since $T_i^{-1}=q^{-1}(T_i-(q-1))$ by [F1], one has $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$. The assignment satisfies the Hecke relations: $\theta(T_i)^2=(q-1)^2-2(q-1)T_i+T_i^2=(q-1)^2-2(q-1)T_i+(q-1)T_i+q=(q-1)\theta(T_i)+q$; the braid relation holds because $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$ multiplies every generator by the same scalar $-q$, and inverses satisfy the braid relations; the distant commutation holds similarly, and the scalar squares cancel. Since $H$ is presented by these relations, the assignment extends uniquely to an $R$-algebra endomorphism $\theta$ of $H$; applying it twice fixes each generator, so $\theta^2=\mathrm{id}_H$ by [F2] and $\theta$ is an involutive automorphism. For a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$ one gets $\theta(T_w)=(-q)^\ell T_{i_1}^{-1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}^{-1}=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$, and $\theta$ commutes with $*$ because both sides of $\theta(T_w^*)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_w^{-1}$ and $\theta(T_w)^*=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-*}=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_w^{-1}$ agree. All generator images have coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, so $\theta$ is compatible with base change by [F5].

**Pullback of modules.** If $M$ is a right $H$-module, then $M^\theta$ with $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$ is a right $H$-module, because $(m\cdot h)\cdot k=m\theta(h)\theta(k)=m\theta(hk)=m\cdot(hk)$. Since $\theta$ is an involutive automorphism, the assignments $M\mapsto M^\theta$ on modules and $N\mapsto N$ on underlying $R$-modules are inverse bijections on submodules: a subset $N\subseteq M$ is closed under the old action if and only if it is closed under the new one, since $\theta$ is bijective and $\theta(H)=H$. Hence $(-)^\theta$ is exact, preserves submodules and quotients, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$; it also carries simple modules to simple modules and preserves the length of finite composition series with multiplicities, because the two module structures have exactly the same submodule lattice.

**Contragredient modules.** For a right $H$-module $M$, put $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with $(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$. Then $((f\cdot h)\cdot k)(m)=f(mk^*h^*)=f(m(hk)^*)$ by [F2], so $f\cdot(hk)=(f\cdot h)\cdot k$ and $M^\circ$ is a right $H$-module. If $M\cong R^r$ is finite free, then $M^\circ\cong R^r$ by [F4] applied with $N=R$, and the dual-basis identification is natural in $R$, so $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change. Finally $(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$: both have underlying module $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$, and for the two actions one computes $(f\cdot h)(m)=f(m\theta(h^*))$ for the first and $(f\cdot h)(m)=f(m\theta(h)^*)=f(m\theta(h^*))$ for the second, using that $\theta$ commutes with $*$ by step 1.1.

**The common eigenspace.** Let $H_\lambda$ be the $R$-span of $\{T_w:w\in S_\lambda\}$, the subalgebra generated by the $T_i$ with $s_i\in S_\lambda$; it is $\theta$-stable because $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i\in H_\lambda$. The element $\theta(x_\lambda)$ lies in $H_\lambda$ and satisfies $T_i\theta(x_\lambda)=\theta(\theta(T_i)x_\lambda)=\theta(((q-1)-T_i)x_\lambda)=\theta((q-1)x_\lambda-qx_\lambda)=-\theta(x_\lambda)$ for every generator $T_i$ of $S_\lambda$, by [F3]; so it is a common left eigenvector for eigenvalue $-1$. Conversely let $a=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}a_wT_w\in H_\lambda$ satisfy $T_ia=-a$ for all these generators. Comparing in the expansion $T_ia=\sum_wa_wT_iT_w$, using the left multiplication rule of [F1], the coefficient of $T_v$ equals $qa_{s_iv}$ when $\ell(s_iv)=\ell(v)+1$ and equals $(q-1)a_v+a_{s_iv}$ when $\ell(s_iv)=\ell(v)-1$, and it must equal $-a_v$; the first case gives $a_{s_iv}=-q^{-1}a_v$, and the second gives the same relation with the roles of $v$ and $s_iv$ exchanged. Hence $a_{s_iu}=-q^{-1}a_u$ whenever $\ell(s_iu)=\ell(u)+1$. Every nonidentity $w\in S_\lambda$ is a length-increasing product of generators of $S_\lambda$: the permutation $w^{-1}$ restricted to some row block $B_r$ is not the identity, hence has an adjacent descent, which exhibits a generator $s_i$ of $S_\lambda$ with $\ell(s_iw)=\ell(w)-1$. Iterating, $a_w=(-q)^{-\ell(w)}a_1$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$, so $a=a_1y_\lambda$: the common eigenspace is exactly the free line $Ry_\lambda$, and it contains $\theta(x_\lambda)$.

**The case $q=1$.** At $q=1$ the quadratic relation is $T_i^2=1$, so $T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}=T_w$ and step 1.1 gives $\theta(T_w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}T_w=\operatorname{sgn}(w)T_w$. The relations $T_i^2=1$, braid and distant commutation are the Coxeter relations of the adjacent transpositions of $S_n$, so the specialization $H_{R,1}(S_n)$ is the group algebra $R[S_n]$ with $T_w$ the group basis element $w$; the displayed identity then says that $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$. For $N=0$, as in the shapes $\varnothing$ and $(1^n)$, the unit below is $q^0=1$.

**The unit.** By step 2.2 write $\theta(x_\lambda)=c\,y_\lambda$ with $c\in R$. In the expansion $\theta(T_w)=\prod_j\theta(T_{i_j})=\prod_j((q-1)-T_{i_j})$ of a reduced word, every term other than the full product of the $-T_{i_j}$ has fewer than $\ell(w)$ generator factors and so cannot contribute to the standard basis element of length $N$; hence the coefficient of $T_{w_0(S_\lambda)}$ in $\theta(x_\lambda)=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}\theta(T_w)$ is $(-1)^N$, the contribution of $w=w_0(S_\lambda)$ alone. In $c\,y_\lambda$ the coefficient of $T_{w_0(S_\lambda)}$ is $c(-q)^{-N}$, so $c=(-1)^N(-q)^N=q^N$. Therefore $\theta(x_\lambda)=q^Ny_\lambda$, and applying the involution $\theta$ and using $\theta(q^N)=q^N$ gives $\theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-N}x_\lambda$.

Statements (1), (2), (3) and (4) are established by steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1, with the $q=1$ clause in step 2.3 and the unit $q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$ displayed in step 3.1. Only the presentation of $H$, inversion counts, the standard basis and finite free duality are used; no choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra over $R$ with generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, quadratic relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant
commutation relations, and standard basis $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); here
$\ell(w)$ is the inversion length of $w\in S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). All modules below are right
modules.

**The star anti-involution.** Let $\sigma\mapsto\sigma^*$ be the unique
$R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $T_i^*=T_i$ for every generator: it
exists because reversal of words preserves the ideal of defining relations
(the quadratic and braid relators are fixed, while a distant commutation relator is sent to its negative), so reversal descends from the free algebra to $H$, and it is
unique because the generators generate $H$. On the standard basis
$T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, since reversing a reduced word for $w$ is a reduced word
for $w^{-1}$.

**Tableau conventions.** Write $t\cdot\sigma$ for the right action of $S_n$ on
tableaux defined by $(t\cdot\sigma)(c):=\sigma^{-1}(t(c))$; it is the inverse
of the left action $(\sigma\cdot t)(c)=\sigma(t(c))$ of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]], and it is a right action.
A $\lambda$-tableau is **row standard** when its entries strictly increase
along every row; columns are not constrained. Let $t^\lambda$ be the row-filled
$\lambda$-tableau, whose row $i$ carries
$\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i$ from left
to right, and let $t_\lambda$ be the column-filled $\lambda$-tableau, whose
column $j$ carries consecutive integers downward; equivalently
$t_\lambda(i,j)=t^{\lambda'}(j,i)$, so that $t_\lambda$ is the transpose of
$t^{\lambda'}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

**The row subgroup and the coset representatives.** Let $S_\lambda$ be the
**row subgroup** of $\lambda$, the subgroup of $S_n$ preserving every row of
$t^\lambda$; writing
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
for the $i$-th row block of $t^\lambda$, one has
$S_\lambda=S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$, the direct product of the
symmetric groups of the individual row blocks. Let
$$D_\lambda:=\{d\in S_n:t^\lambda\cdot d\text{ is row standard}\}.$$
This is the set of minimal-length right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in
$S_n$: every right coset $S_\lambda d$ has exactly one element $d_0$ for which
$t^\lambda\cdot d_0$ is row standard, and it satisfies
$\ell(wd_0)=\ell(w)+\ell(d_0)$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). Let
$w_\lambda\in S_n$ be the unique element with $t^\lambda\cdot w_\lambda=t_\lambda$;
existence and uniqueness hold because the action of $S_n$ on $\lambda$-tableaux
is free and transitive.

**Generators and modules.** For a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ put
$$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w,\qquad y_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w,\qquad z_\lambda:=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'},$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition of $\lambda$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). The **row
permutation module** is the right ideal $M(\lambda):=x_\lambda H\subseteq H$,
and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is
$P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid
generator.

**The forms.** The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ determined on the distinguished family
$\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by
$$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}\qquad(d,e\in D_\lambda),$$
and the **DJ form** is the restriction of $\beta$ to $P(\lambda)$. That family
is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]), so the displayed
values define a unique bilinear form; the family is $\{x_\varnothing\}=\{1\}$
for the empty partition.

**Small cases and base change.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set
$x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that
$M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form; for
$n=0,1$ there are no generators and $H=R$. Every base change
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, produces all
objects above over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers of this page prove
that the distinguished families and the form are compatible with such base
change. No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

For every $n\ge0$,
$$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2=n!,$$
where $f^\lambda$ is the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux and
$f^\varnothing=1$, $0!=1$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$\alpha,\nu\vdash n$ be partitions of $n$ with conjugate $\nu'$ and
$x_\alpha,y_\nu\in H_{R,q}(S_n)$ as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. If $\alpha$
is not dominated by $\nu'$ in the sense of
[[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]], that is, if
$\sum_{i\le k}\alpha_i>\sum_{i\le k}\nu'_i$ for some $k\ge1$, then
$$x_\alpha Hy_\nu=0.$$
The vanishing is a universal Laurent-polynomial identity, remains valid at
singular parameters and uses no cancellation of $q+1$. The proof explicitly
sorts parabolic double cosets and uses the zero product
$(1+T_i)(1-q^{-1}T_i)=0$. Empty shapes and $n=0,1$ are included. No choice
principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: **Compositions.** A composition of $n$ is a finite sequence $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ of nonnegative integers with $\sum\alpha_i=n$; its row blocks $B_r$, row group $S_\alpha$, row-filled tableau $t^\alpha$, row-standard tableaux, set $D_\alpha$, distinguished elements $d_\alpha(u)$, and elements $x_\alpha=\sum_{w\in S_\alpha}T_w$, $b_u:=x_\alpha T_{d_\alpha(u)}$ are defined exactly as for partitions in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], and for row-standard $\alpha$-tableaux $s,t$ put $m^\alpha_{st}:=T_{d_\alpha(s)}^*x_\alpha T_{d_\alpha(t)}$, so that $b_t=m^\alpha_{t^\alpha t}$. Every statement of [F2] was proved for partitions but uses only that the row group is a product of symmetric groups on consecutive blocks, so it applies verbatim to compositions.

**Dominance of tableaux by counting.** For $\alpha$-tableaux $u,v$ and integers $m\ge0$, $k\ge1$ put $c_{m,k}(u):=\#\{x\in B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_k:u(x)\le m\}$; write $u\unrhd v$ when $c_{m,k}(u)\ge c_{m,k}(v)$ for all $m,k$, and $u\equiv v$ when all these numbers agree. Passing from $u$ to $u\cdot s_i$ exchanges the labels $i$ and $i+1$, so it changes only the counts at $m=i$, and $c_{i,k}(u\cdot s_i)=c_{i-1,k}(u)+[i+1\text{ lies in the first }k\text{ blocks of }u]$ because the label $i$ is replaced by $i+1$ and all other labels $\le i$ stay put. In particular $u\equiv v$ implies $u\cdot s_i\equiv v\cdot s_i$, and if $u,v$ are both row standard then $u\equiv v$ if and only if $u=v$, because the numbers $c_{m,k}$ determine the multiset of entries of each block and a row-standard tableau is its block multisets sorted increasingly. Suppose now that $s$ is row standard, that $s':=s\cdot s_i$ is row standard, and that the labels $i,i+1$ lie in rows $a<b$ of $s$, so that $s'$ is obtained from $s$ by moving $i$ down into row $b$ and $i+1$ up into row $a$. Then for every row-standard $r$ with $r\unrhd s$ one has $r\unrhd s'$ and $r\cdot s_i\unrhd s'$. Indeed for $m\ne i$ the counts are unchanged by both swaps, so $c_{m,k}(r)\ge c_{m,k}(s)=c_{m,k}(s')$ and the same for $r\cdot s_i$; for $m=i$ one has $c_{i,k}(s')=c_{i-1,k}(s)+[k\ge b]$, while $c_{i,k}(r)\ge c_{i,k}(s)\ge c_{i-1,k}(s)+[k\ge b]=c_{i,k}(s')$ for every $k$, and $c_{i,k}(r\cdot s_i)=c_{i-1,k}(r)+[i+1\text{ lies in the first }k\text{ blocks of }r]\ge c_{i-1,k}(r)\ge c_{i-1,k}(s)=c_{i,k}(s')$ for $k<b$, while for $k\ge b$ the sharper bound $c_{i,k}(r\cdot s_i)\ge c_{i+1,k}(r)-1\ge c_{i+1,k}(s)-1=c_{i-1,k}(s)+1=c_{i,k}(s')$ holds, the first inequality by $[i\text{ lies in the first }k\text{ blocks of }r]\le1$ and the last because both labels then lie in the first $k$ blocks of $s$.

**The trace pairing.** Define $\tau:H\to R$ by $\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$. The multiplication rules give $\tau(T_wT_i)=\tau(T_iT_w)=q\delta_{w,s_i}$ for every $w$ and every generator $T_i$: in the two-case formulas the identity $T_1$ occurs only in the descent case $w=s_i$, with coefficient $q$. Moving generator letters across one another successively gives $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ for all $a,b\in H$, and $\tau(a^*)=\tau(a)$ since $\tau$ is $R$-linear and $*$ permutes the standard basis. Let $B_0$ be the bilinear form defined on the standard basis by $B_0(T_u,T_v):=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$. Every right $s_i$-orbit $\{T_w,T_{ws_i}\}$ has two elements; writing $w$ for the element with $\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1$, right multiplication by $T_i$ on the block spanned by the orbit has matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&q\\1&q-1\end{pmatrix}$, and the restriction of $B_0$ to the block has matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(q^{\ell(w)},q^{\ell(w)+1})$ with $A^{\mathsf T}D=DA$; distinct blocks are orthogonal, so $B_0(xT_i,y)=B_0(x,yT_i)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Iterating along a reduced word $T_u=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_r}$ gives $B_0(T_u,T_v)=B_0(T_1,T_vT_{i_r}\cdots T_{i_1})=B_0(T_1,T_vT_u^*)$, and $B_0(T_1,y)=\tau(y)$ for every $y$ by the definitions; hence $B_0(T_u,T_v)=\tau(T_vT_u^*)=\tau(T_{u^{-1}}T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$. In particular the bilinear form $(a,b)\mapsto\tau(a^*b)$ equals $B_0$ and has diagonal Gram matrix with unit entries $q^{\ell(u)}$ in the standard basis, so it is unimodular.

**The support lemma.** Let $g$ be a row-standard $\alpha$-tableau, let $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_r}$ be a reduced word, put $t:=g\cdot w$ and $g_k:=g\cdot(s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k})$, and assume $\ell(d_\alpha(t))=\ell(d_\alpha(g))+\ell(w)$. If $v$ is a row-standard $\alpha$-tableau with $vhd g$, then every row-standard tableau $u$ whose basis element $b_u$ is involved in $b_vT_w$ satisfies $uhd t$. The assumed length equality makes the concatenation of a reduced word for $d_\alpha(g)$ and the displayed word for $w$ reduced, since $d_\alpha(t)=d_\alpha(g)w$. Starting at the row-standard $t$ and removing its final letters backwards, each removed letter is a right descent. A right descent exchanges consecutive labels in reversed row-reading order; they cannot lie in one increasing row, so the swap preserves row standardness by [F2]. Thus every $g_k$ is row standard, $d_\alpha(g_k)=d_\alpha(g)s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, and $\ell(d_\alpha(g_k))=\ell(d_\alpha(g))+k$. Hence each step replaces $g_k$ by the row-standard tableau $g_k\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}$ with $\ell(d_\alpha(g_k\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}))=\ell(d_\alpha(g_k))+1$, so the three-case rule of [F2] gives $b_{g_k}T_{i_{k+1}}=b_{g_{k+1}}$: the swapped tableau is row standard and the length increases. The labels $i,i+1$ therefore lie in different rows of $g_k$ (otherwise the swap would stay in one row and the rule would return a multiple of $b_{g_k}$), and since $g_{k+1}$ is row standard with $\ell(d_\alpha(g_k)s_{i_{k+1}})=\ell(d_\alpha(g_k))+1$, the row-reading position of $i$ precedes that of $i+1$, so $i$ lies in a strictly upper row of $g_k$; this is exactly the configuration of step 1.2. We now show by induction on $k$ that every row-standard $u$ with $b_u$ involved in $b_vT_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_k}$ satisfies $u\unrhd g_k$ and $u
ot\equiv g_k$. For $k=0$ we have $v\unrhd g$ and $v
e g$, and $v\equiv g$ would give $g\unrhd v$, so $v
ot\equiv g$. For the step, the action rule of [F2] shows that $b_uT_{i_{k+1}}$ is a combination of $b_u$ and, when $u\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}$ is row standard, $b_{u\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}}$; step 1.2 applied to $s:=g_k$, $s'=g_{k+1}$ gives $u\unrhd g_{k+1}$ and $u\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}\unrhd g_{k+1}$ whenever the swapped tableau is row standard. Neither output is $\equiv g_{k+1}$: if $u\equiv g_{k+1}$ then $u\unrhd g_k\unrhd g_{k+1}\equiv u$ forces $u\equiv g_k$, and if $u\cdot s_{i_{k+1}}\equiv g_{k+1}$ then applying the swap to the two equivalent tableaux gives $u\equiv g_k$, both contradicting the induction hypothesis. At the end $t$ is row standard, so $u\unrhd t$ together with $u
ot\equiv t$ says exactly that $uhd t$.

**Compositions to partitions.** Let $\alpha$ be a composition and $\beta$ the partition obtained by rearranging its parts. Choose $d$ mapping each row block of $\beta$ increasingly onto a row block of $\alpha$ of the same size. Then $d^{-1}$ is increasing on each $\alpha$-block, $d$ is increasing on each $\beta$-block, $d\in D_\alpha$, $d^{-1}\in D_\beta$, and $d^{-1}S_\alpha d=S_\beta$. Hence $x_\alpha T_d=\sum_{w\in S_\alpha}T_{wd}=\sum_{u\in S_\alpha d}T_u$ and $T_dx_\beta=\sum_{v\in S_\beta}T_{dv}=\sum_{u\in dS_\beta}T_u$, and these agree because $S_\alpha d=d(d^{-1}S_\alpha d)=dS_\beta$. Thus $x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ and $T_d$ is invertible. Since $Hx_\beta$ is free with basis $\{T_{d_\beta(s)}^*x_\beta\}$ (the star of the basis of $x_\beta H$) and $x_\beta H$ is free with basis $\{x_\beta T_{d_\beta(u)}\}$ by [F2], expanding $T_{d_\alpha(s)}^*T_d$ and $T_d^{-1}T_{d_\alpha(t)}$ expresses $m^\alpha_{st}$ as an $R$-linear combination of $m^\beta_{uv}$ with $u,v$ row standard; all coefficients are Laurent polynomials in $q$, with no quantum factorial inverted.

**The Garnir belt identity.** Let $\rho$ be a partition and $(i,j)$ a node with $j\le\rho_{i+1}$. Let $\alpha$ replace the two consecutive parts $\rho_i,\rho_{i+1}$ by $j-1,\rho_i+1,\rho_{i+1}-j$, deleting zeros; its blocks are those of $\rho$ except that the belt $a,\dots,b$, where $a=t^\rho(i,j)$ and $b=t^\rho(i+1,j)$, is cut into three consecutive blocks of sizes $j-1$, $\rho_i+1$ and $\rho_{i+1}-j$; the middle block is the interval $a,\dots,b$ itself, of size $\rho_i+1=b-a+1$. Put $D:=S_\alpha\cap D_\rho$ and $E:=S_\rho\cap D_\alpha$. Then $$x_\rho\sum_{d\in D}T_d=\sum_{v\in E}T_v^*x_\alpha.$$ Put $K=S_\rho\cap S_\alpha$. Sorting a permutation of $S_\alpha$ within each $\rho$-block preserves the $\alpha$-blocks, because every intersection of the two interval blocks is an interval. The unique sorted result is in $D$, so $D$ is a transversal for the right cosets $K\backslash S_\alpha$; likewise $E$ is a transversal for $K\backslash S_\rho$. Two products $ud$ and $u'd'$ coincide only if $d,d'$ lie in the same $K$-coset, which forces $d=d'$ and then $u=u'$. Inverting the representatives in $E$ gives the corresponding transversal for the cosets of $K$ on the other side. Thus the products $S_\rho\times D\to S_\rho S_\alpha$, $(u,d)\mapsto ud$, and $E\times S_\alpha\to S_\rho S_\alpha$, $(v,u)\mapsto v^{-1}u$, are bijections with length-additive products, because $D\subseteq D_\rho$, $E\subseteq D_\alpha$ and $\ell(u^{-1}v)=\ell(v^{-1}u)$ for all $u\in S_\alpha$, $v\in D_\alpha$; expanding both sides in the standard basis therefore gives $\sum_{w\in S_\rho S_\alpha}T_w$ for the left side and the same sum for the right side, since $T_v^*=T_{v^{-1}}$.

**The Garnir tableau.** With $\rho,\alpha,(i,j)$ as in step 2.3, let $g$ be the row-standard tableau agreeing with $t^\rho$ outside the belt $a,\dots,b$, whose row $i+1$ carries the $j$ smallest belt entries increasingly in its first $j$ positions and whose row $i$ carries the remaining belt entries increasingly in its last $\rho_i-j+1$ positions. Among the tableaux $t^\rho\cdot d$, $d\in D$, exactly one fails to be standard, namely $g$, and every other one strictly dominates $g$: each of them agrees with $t^\rho$ outside the belt and is determined by the $j$-element subset $S$ of belt entries that it places increasingly in the first $j$ positions of row $i+1$, the complementary belt entries occupying increasingly the last $\rho_i-j+1$ positions of row $i$; column $j$ fails exactly when $\min(\mathrm{belt}\setminus S)>\max(S)$, that is, when $S$ consists of the $j$ smallest belt entries, which is $g$. For the dominance comparison, the cumulative counts $c_{m,k}$ of step 1.2 for $k\le i-1$ and $k\ge i+1$ do not depend on $S$; for $k=i$ row $i$ carries the belt complement of $S$, and $g$ carries the largest $\rho_i-j+1$ belt entries, whose count function is pointwise minimal, so every other belt tableau strictly dominates $g$.

The cells in row $i+1$ through column $j$ must then precede every cell in row $i$ from column $j$ onward. The label order of $t$ is a linear extension of this partial order. The label order of the Garnir tableau $g$ in step 3.1 is the row-reading order with precisely these two consecutive groups interchanged. Its inverted cell pairs relative to row reading are exactly the forced pairs between these groups. Sort the label-ordered cell list of $t$ into the label order of $g$ by swapping adjacent entries that occur in the opposite order in $g$. The swapped entries are incomparable in the partial order, because both lists are linear extensions; thus every intermediate list remains a linear extension and its tableau remains row standard with the chosen column violation. Each swapped pair is reversed relative to row reading, since the only reversals of $g$ are forced pairs which cannot be reversed in $t$. Consequently every swap exchanges consecutive labels at a right descent of the distinguished permutation and decreases its inversion length by one. The finite sorting ends at $g$. Reversing the $r$ swaps gives $t=g\cdot w$ and $d(t)=d(g)w$, with $\ell(d(t))=\ell(d(g))+r$. After the second index is standard, the left index is treated symmetrically using $m^\rho_{st}=m^\rho_{ts}{}^*$, and the finite dominance order on row-standard tableaux makes the inner induction terminate. Composing with step 2.2, every $m^\alpha_{st}$ with $\alpha$ a composition is a combination of partition-indexed $m^\nu_{uv}$ with $u,v$ standard.

**The Murphy basis.** For $\alpha=(1^n)$ one has $x_{(1^n)}=1$, so every standard basis element is a Murphy element and the standard Murphy family spans $H$ by step 5.1. Its cardinality is $\sum_\rho(f^\rho)^2=n!$ by [F3], equal to the rank of the free module $H$, so writing the family in the standard basis gives a square matrix that, having a right inverse, has unit determinant; hence the family including the empty shape is an $R$-basis of $H$, and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$ follows from $x_\rho^*=x_\rho$ and [F1]. **Lexicographic ideals and the first-index law.** Let $J^{\rhd_{\mathrm{lex}}\rho}$ be the span of all $m_{uv}$ whose shape is strictly lexicographically larger than $\rho$. Both are therefore two-sided ideals of $H$.

**The cell law and the cell module.** Let $s,t$ be standard $\rho$-tableaux and $h\in H$. Since $x_\rho T_{d(t)}h\in M(\rho)=\bigoplus_v R\,x_\rho T_{d(v)}$ with $v$ running over the row-standard $\rho$-tableaux, there are unique $c_{tv}(h)\in R$ with $x_\rho T_{d(t)}h=\sum_v c_{tv}(h)x_\rho T_{d(v)}$; multiplying on the left by $T_{d(s)}^*$ gives the exact identity $m_{st}h=\sum_v c_{tv}(h)m_{sv}$, whose coefficients do not involve $s$. For $v$ non-standard, step 5.1 writes $m_{sv}=\sum_{w\in\operatorname{Std}(\rho)}b_{vw}m_{sw}+j_v$ with $b_{vw}\in R$ independent of the first index $s$ and $j_v\in J^{\rhd_{\mathrm{lex}}\rho}$; step 8.1 puts $m_{sv}$ and the $m_{sw}$ in $I^{\unrhd\rho}$, so $j_v\in J^{\rhd_{\mathrm{lex}}\rho}\cap I^{\unrhd\rho}$. Both spans are spanned by Murphy basis elements, of shapes $\rhd_{\mathrm{lex}}\rho$ and $\unrhd\rho$ respectively, and the Murphy basis is independent, so their intersection is spanned by the basis elements whose shapes satisfy both conditions; a shape $\mu\ne\rho$ satisfying $\mu\unrhd\rho$ and $\mu\rhd_{\mathrm{lex}}\rho$ is exactly a shape $\mu\rhd\rho$. Hence $j_v\in I^{\rhd\rho}$ and $$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\rho)}r_{tv}(h)\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\rho}}$$ with coefficients $r_{tv}(h)$ independent of the first index. By step 6.1 the quotient $I^{\unrhd\rho}/I^{\rhd\rho}$ is free with basis the classes of $\{m_{uv}:u,v\in\operatorname{Std}(\rho)\}$, and $x_\rho T_{d(v)}=m^\rho_{t^\rho v}$; the congruence with $s=t^\rho$ shows that the image of $M(\rho)$ in this quotient is spanned by the $f^\rho$ independent classes $m_t=x_\rho T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\rho}$, with kernel $M(\rho)\cap I^{\rhd\rho}$. Therefore $C_{\mathrm M}(\rho)=M(\rho)/(M(\rho)\cap I^{\rhd\rho})$ is free with basis $\{m_t:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\rho)\}$ and satisfies the displayed cell law. This is clauses (2) and (3).

**The cell form.** Let $u,v,s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\rho)$. Applying the cell law of step 9.1 to $m_{us}m_{tv}$ with $h=m_{tv}$ gives $m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\sum_w r_{sw}(m_{tv})m_{uw}$, and applying it to $m_{vt}m_{su}=m_{tv}^*m_{us}^*$ with $h=m_{su}$ and starring gives $m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\sum_w r_{tw}(m_{su})m_{wv}$. Comparing coefficients in the basis $\{m_{ab}:a,b\in\operatorname{Std}(\rho)\}$ of $I^{\unrhd\rho}/I^{\rhd\rho}$ yields $r_{sw}(m_{tv})=0$ for $w\ne v$ and $r_{sv}(m_{tv})=r_{tu}(m_{su})$, a scalar $G_\rho(m_s,m_t)\in R$ independent of $u$ and $v$; hence $m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\rho(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\rho}}$, and $G_\rho$ is the unique bilinear form with this property. Starring the defining congruence and exchanging $(s,t)$ with $(u,v)$ gives $G_\rho(m_t,m_s)=G_\rho(m_s,m_t)$. This is clauses (4) and (5), and since only the presentation of $H$, inversion counting, the local double-coset vanishing, the trace computation and finite free duality were used, no choice principle is used.

The support induction establishes row standardness backwards; the belt transversals use the intersection parabolic and both additive coset orientations. In 4.2 the only cell inversions of the canonical Garnir list are forced lower-prefix/upper-tail pairs; adjacent inversions against that list are incomparable and right descents, giving finite length-additive reduction. Right straightening fixes s; higher shapes decrease through a finite descending lexicographic induction. Square spanning matrix gives a basis over any commutative ring. The perfect mixed trace blocks and zero products isolate exactly dominance-upward spans; 9.1 retains coefficients independent of s and 10.1 yields the symmetric contravariant form. Empty/one-box/zero-ring and all unit q cases hold without factorial division or AC. Read Mathas 3.9 and complete 3.12-3.15 arguments; local mixed-trace dominance proof was independently checked. The new auxiliary Statement clauses only expose proved identities.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition
$\alpha$ and the partition $\beta$ obtained by sorting its parts,
$x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ with a block-reordering permutation $d$
(step 2.2); and for the Garnir composition $\alpha$ at a node of $\rho$,
$x_\rho\sum_{d\in S_\alpha\cap D_\rho}T_d
=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).
The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

For every $n\ge0$,
$$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2=n!,$$
where $f^\lambda$ is the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux and
$f^\varnothing=1$, $0!=1$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$\alpha,\nu\vdash n$ be partitions of $n$ with conjugate $\nu'$ and
$x_\alpha,y_\nu\in H_{R,q}(S_n)$ as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. If $\alpha$
is not dominated by $\nu'$ in the sense of
[[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]], that is, if
$\sum_{i\le k}\alpha_i>\sum_{i\le k}\nu'_i$ for some $k\ge1$, then
$$x_\alpha Hy_\nu=0.$$
The vanishing is a universal Laurent-polynomial identity, remains valid at
singular parameters and uses no cancellation of $q+1$. The proof explicitly
sorts parabolic double cosets and uses the zero product
$(1+T_i)(1-q^{-1}T_i)=0$. Empty shapes and $n=0,1$ are included. No choice
principle is used.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

For all partitions $\lambda$ and $\mu$ of the same integer $n$,
$$\lambda\unrhd\mu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\mu'\unrhd\lambda'.$$

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

derivations.claim: **The order on row-standard tableaux.** For an $\alpha$-tableau $u$ and integers $m\ge0$, $k\ge1$ put $c_{m,k}(u):=\#\{x\in B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_k:u(x)\le m\}$, where $B_1,B_2,\dots$ are the row blocks of the shape, and write $u\le v$ when $c_{m,k}(u)\le c_{m,k}(v)$ for all $m,k$. Swapping the labels $i$ and $i+1$ changes only the counts at $m=i$, and $c_{i,k}(u\cdot s_i)=c_{i-1,k}(u)+[\,i+1$ lies in the first $k$ blocks of $u\,]$, because the label $i$ is replaced by $i+1$ and every other label $\le i$ stays put. Hence for row-standard $u,v$ the relations $u\le v$ and $v\le u$ hold simultaneously only when $u=v$: the numbers $c_{m,k}$ record the multiset of labels in each row block, and a row-standard tableau is its row multisets sorted increasingly. Moreover, interchanging consecutive labels $i,i+1$ in incomparable cells of a standard tableau preserves standardness: every other label is either smaller than both or larger than both, so inequalities with neighbouring cells persist, and the swapped cells impose no inequality on each other.

**Ascending standard chains and their local shape.** Let $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)$, $t\ne t^\mu$, and put $d:=d_\mu(t)\ne1$. Since $d$ is not the identity there is an index $i$ with $d(i)>d(i+1)$; such an index is a right descent, so $\ell(ds_i)=\ell(d)-1$. In the row-reading word of $t$ the value $i$ occurs at position $d(i)$ and the value $i+1$ at the earlier position $d(i+1)$. The two cells are incomparable: the cell of $i+1$ is not northwest of the cell of $i$, since in a standard tableau a northwest cell carries the smaller value, and it is not southeast either, since a southeast cell is later in row-reading order. Therefore $t\cdot s_i$ is standard and $d_\mu(t\cdot s_i)=ds_i$. Iterating gives a descending chain from $t$ to $t^\mu$ in which each step is a standard adjacent swap of incomparable cells and decreases $\ell(d_\mu(\cdot))$ by one; reversing it gives an ascending chain $t_0=t^\mu,t_1,\dots,t_r=t$ of standard $\mu$-tableaux with $t_{j+1}=t_j\cdot s_{i_j}$ and $\ell(d_\mu(t_{j+1}))=\ell(d_\mu(t_j))+1$. In such a step the value $i:=i_j$ precedes the value $i+1$ in the row-reading order of $t_j$, so the two cells are distinct and lie in different rows, with the row of $i$ strictly above the row of $i+1$; the cell of $i$ also lies in a strictly later column than the cell of $i+1$, since otherwise the cell in the row of $i$ and the column of $i+1$ would carry an integer strictly between $i$ and $i+1$. Transposing, the standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s_j:=t_j'$ satisfy $s_{j+1}=s_j\cdot s_i$, the value $i$ lies in a row strictly below the row of $i+1$ in $s_j$, and $\ell(d_\lambda(s_j)s_i)=\ell(d_\lambda(s_j))-1$.

**Base case of the triangular expansion.** Let $u\in S_\mu$. The group $S_\mu$ permutes the intervals $B_j=\{\lambda'_1+\cdots+\lambda'_{j-1}+1,\dots,\lambda'_1+\cdots+\lambda'_j\}$, and these are exactly the label sets of the columns of $t_\lambda$; they are intervals, increasing in $j$. Hence row $i$ of $t_\lambda\cdot u$ carries the entries $u^{-1}(t_\lambda(i,j))$ for $j\le\lambda_i$, and these increase with $j$ because $u^{-1}(t_\lambda(i,j))$ lies in $B_j$ and every element of $B_j$ is smaller than every element of $B_{j+1}$. The permutation $w_\lambda$ is increasing on each $\mu$-block: its values are the row-reading positions of the entries in a column of $t_\lambda$, and these increase down that column. Thus $w_\lambda^{-1}\in D_\mu$; applying the row-module length-additivity proof to $u^{-1}w_\lambda^{-1}$ and then taking inverses yields $\ell(w_\lambda u)=\ell(w_\lambda)+\ell(u)$ and $T_{w_\lambda}T_u=T_{w_\lambda u}$. Thus $w_\lambda u\in D_\lambda$ and $x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda u}=b_{r_u}$ with $r_u:=t_\lambda\cdot u$, so that $z_\lambda=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}(-q)^{-\ell(u)}b_{r_u}$. For fixed $m,k$, the first $k$ cells of column $j$ of $r_u$ carry $u^{-1}$ of the first $\min(k,\lambda'_j)$ labels of $B_j$, an arbitrary subset of that size, and the number of labels $\le m$ in such a subset is at most $\min(\min(k,\lambda'_j),t_j)$ with $t_j:=\#\{x\in B_j:x\le m\}$; this bound is exactly the number of labels $\le m$ in the first $\min(k,\lambda'_j)$ cells of column $j$ of $t_\lambda$. Summing over $j$ gives $r_u\le t_\lambda$. If $r_u=t_\lambda$ then $u^{-1}$ fixes every label in every column of $t_\lambda$, so $u=1$; therefore $r_u<t_\lambda$ for $u\ne1$, and the coefficient of $b_{t_\lambda}$ in $z_\lambda$ is $(-q)^0=1$. Since $t_\lambda=(t^\mu)'$ and $d_\mu(t^\mu)=1$, this proves clause 2 for $t=t^\mu$.

**The unit minor and the splitting.** By clause 2, the coefficient of $b_{t'}$ in $e_u$ equals $q^{\ell(d_\mu(u))}$ for $t=u$ and vanishes unless $t'\le u'$. Choose a linear extension of the order $\le$ restricted to $\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)=\{t':t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ and order both sides of the square matrix $C$ with entries $C_{t,u}:=[$coefficient of $b_{t'}$ in $e_u]$ by it. Then $C$ is triangular with diagonal entries $q^{\ell(d_\mu(u))}\in R^\times$, so $C$ is invertible and $\{e_t:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is $R$-linearly independent. Define $\pi\colon M(\lambda)\to E:=\sum_tRe_t$ by reading the coordinates of a vector in the basis $\{b_r\}$ at the rows $t'$, applying $C^{-1}$ and forming the corresponding combination of the $e_t$. Then $\pi$ is $R$-linear, $\pi|_{E}=\mathrm{id}_E$ since the $t'$-coordinates of $e_u$ are the $u$-th column of $C$, and the image of $\pi$ is $E$; hence $E$ is free of rank $f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$ and a direct summand of $M(\lambda)$.

Both $C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta$ and $E$ are free of rank $f^\mu=f^\lambda$ by [F4] and step 3.1. Choose preimages under $\pi F$ of the finitely many basis vectors of $E$; their coordinate columns form a right inverse of the square matrix of $\pi F$, so the determinant of that matrix is a unit of $R$ and $\pi F$ is an isomorphism. If $p\in P(\lambda)$ and $\pi(p)=0$, choose $u$ with $F(u)=p$; then $\pi F(u)=0$ gives $u=0$ and $p=0$. For arbitrary $p\in P(\lambda)$ the difference $p-\pi(p)$ lies in $P(\lambda)$ and is killed by $\pi$, so it vanishes and $p=\pi(p)\in E$. Therefore $P(\lambda)=E$: the family $\{e_t\}$ is an $R$-basis of $P(\lambda)$, the module $P(\lambda)$ is free of rank $f^\lambda$, and it is a split direct summand of $M(\lambda)$ by step 3.1. This is clause 1.

**Finite straightening.** Expand $z_\lambda T_w$ in the distinguished row basis by the finite standard-basis multiplication rules. Read its coordinates at the standard rows $t'$ and apply the inverse unit-triangular matrix $C^{-1}$ of step 3.1. The resulting coordinates give its unique expansion in $\{e_t\}$, since step 4.1 proves $P(\lambda)=E$ and $\pi|_P=\mathrm{id}_P$. All operations use Laurent-polynomial coefficients; the inverse of $C$ is obtained by finite triangular substitution. The signed Garnir identities of step 2.2 hold for this expansion as well. Thus clause 4 supplies valid relations and the unit minor supplies an exact finite straightening, without requiring an additional unproved signed-belt induction.

**The DJ form, base change and degenerate cases.** For $t,u$ one has $B_{tu}=\beta(e_t,e_u)=\sum_r a_{r,t}a_{r,u}q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}$ by clause 2 and the defining diagonal values of $\beta$, which is clause 3; no claim of invertibility of $B$ is made, and $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ may well be degenerate. For $\lambda=\varnothing$ and $n=0$ one has $\mu=\varnothing$, $z_\lambda=1$, $\operatorname{Std}(\mu)=\{\varnothing\}$ and clause 2 reads $e_\varnothing=b_\varnothing$; for $n=1$ the two shapes are the single node with $z_\lambda=1$. All constructions above use only the presentation [F1], the row-module rules [F2], the automorphism $\theta$ [F3], the Murphy theory [F4], the vanishing [F5] and the dominance facts [F6], whose coefficients lie in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$; the determinant argument of step 4.1 inverts a square matrix whose entries are Laurent polynomials and whose determinant is a unit, so its inverse has entries in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, and every identity specializes along $v\mapsto q$ by [F7]. This is clause 5; no generic semisimplicity, no division by a quantum factorial and no choice principle are used.

risk_review.notes: Checked all ten steps and clauses over arbitrary R with unit q. Adjacent standard swaps reverse transposed lengths; column-block expansion and the count induction give a unit triangular minor. The signed quotient maps onto zH and kills higher ideals by opposite dominance; the square surjection pi F is invertible, proving spanning and splitting without semisimplicity. Gram coefficients include diagonal and zeros, and finite straightening uses C inverse rather than an asserted signed-belt induction. Confirmed refuter:12:1 at lambda=(3,2): w=(1,4,2,5,3) is increasing on mu blocks, its inverse is not; corrected Proof 1.3 to w inverse in D_mu. Confirmed refuter:12:2: F3 is partition-only; Proof 2.2 now defines composition y_alpha,N_alpha and derives its common sign eigenspace and longest coefficient. Sorting parts preserves N, so the conjugation scalar cancels. Universal Laurent identities and n=0,1/zero-ring/degenerate-form boundaries hold; no AC or quantum-factorial division.

boundaries.evidence: n=0 with lambda=emptyset: the Murphy basis has the single element m=1, theta(1)=1, the image ideals theta(I^{unrhd emptyset})=H and theta(I^{rhd emptyset})=0 coincide with the originals, and the constructions of steps 1.1-3.1 specialize to the identity module R, the identity isomorphism and the unit form.

The zero ring is allowed. For n=2 the two ideals differ over the generic Laurent ring and whenever q != -1; when q=-1 the vectors q-T_1 and 1+T_1 are unit multiples, so the ideals coincide. The transported form is defined without division. Statement clause 1 and Proof 2.1 explicitly qualify the witness.
n=1: H=R with theta=id, the unique partition (1) has a one-element Murphy basis, and clauses 1-4 reduce to the identity statement as in steps 1.1-1.2.

Single row lambda=(n): the transport formula of step 1.1 uses theta(m_(n))=q^N y_(n) and the transported cell is rank one; single column lambda=(1^n): x=1 and theta(1)=1; both are covered by the same basis-image argument of steps 1.1-1.2 with no shape-specific hypothesis.

The transported filtration is indexed by the finite dominance poset with endpoints (n) and (1^n), whose shape spans are the images described in step 1.2; the limiting case where transport visibly moves the subspace, the two-element poset at n=2, lambda=(2), is exactly the check of step 2.1.
Statement clause 4 records that no choice principle is used; every transported object is the image under the fixed automorphism theta along steps 1.1-2.2.

boundaries.reason: The Statement asserts transformed-basis and isomorphism statements outright; the only equivalence-shaped claim, the well-definedness of m+K maps to theta(m)+theta(K) in step 2.2, is proved as a bijection inside step 2.2.
No converse is claimed; clause 1 explicitly asserts that the ideal subspaces are in general different, so no equality of ideals is asserted in either direction.

citations.quote:
For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put

where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.
