Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda$ be the set of partitions
of $n$ ordered by dominance $\unrhd$
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), and for $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let
$T(\lambda)=\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ be the set of standard $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Then the **Murphy basis
theorem** holds: the family
$$\mathcal M=\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$$
is an $R$-basis of $H$, and $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ is a cellular basis of $H$ in
the sense of [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]. Explicitly:
(i) $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all $\lambda$ and $s,t$; and (ii) for every
$\lambda$, every $t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ and every $h\in H$ there exist
$r_v\in R$ with
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}},$$
where $H^{\rhd\lambda}$ is spanned by the $m_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. The
theorem holds over every commutative coefficient ring with $q\in R^{\times}$
and assumes no semisimplicity; the total number of Murphy elements is
$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}|\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)|^2=n!$
([[cor-sum-of-squares-of-standard-tableau-numbers]]), matching the rank of $H$.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with
standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-automorphism $*$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For a
composition (in particular a partition) $\mu$ of $n$ put
$m_\mu:=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w\in H$, the **row symmetrizer** of the standard
Young subgroup $S_\mu$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]); the sum has
$|S_\mu|=\prod_i\mu_i!$ terms.

A tableau is **row standard** when its entries increase along each row. Use the right tableau action $t\cdot w:=w^{-1}\cdot t$, where the left action applies $w$ to the entries. For a row-standard $\mu$-tableau $s$, let $d(s)$ be the unique permutation with $s=t^\mu\cdot d(s)$, where $t^\mu$ is filled by $1,2,\dots,n$ in row-major order. Explicitly, if $s$ carries entry $a$ in the $p$-th node in that order, then $d(s)(a)=p$: $d(s)$ is the **inverse** of the row-reading permutation. The action on tableaux is free; the stabilizer of the row tabloid of $t^\mu$ is $S_\mu$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]).

Write $D_\mu$ for these distinguished permutations. Row-standardness says that $d^{-1}$ is increasing on each canonical row block. The coset $S_\mu d$ consists exactly of the tableaux with the same row sets, so sorting each row produces its unique representative in $D_\mu$. Moreover,
$$\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)\qquad(w\in S_\mu,\ d\in D_\mu).$$
To verify this, count inversions of $(wd)^{-1}=d^{-1}w^{-1}$. Pairs of labels within one canonical block contribute exactly the inversions of $w^{-1}$, since $d^{-1}$ is increasing there. For labels in different blocks, $w^{-1}$ permutes the labels within their respective blocks, so the total number of cross-block inversions equals that of $d^{-1}$. The two contributions give the displayed equality, using inversion invariance of length. It also proves minimality and uniqueness in $S_\mu d$. These conventions extend to compositions by using their consecutive row blocks.
For row-standard $\mu$-tableaux $s,t$ define the **Murphy element**
$$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}\,m_{\mu}\,T_{d(t)}\in H,$$
and for a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ write the diagonal element as $m_{tt}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$;
the notation $m_t$ is reserved for a cell-module vector, rather than an element of $H$. Then $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all
row-standard $s,t$ of the same shape: applying the anti-automorphism, which
fixes $m_\mu$ because $m_\mu^*=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_{w^{-1}}=m_\mu$, gives
$$m_{st}^{*}=(T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(t)})^{*}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu^{*}T_{d(s)}^{**}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(s)}=m_{ts}.$$
Finally, $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ for every $w\in S_\mu$: it suffices to
prove this for $w=s_i$ a simple transposition with $i,i+1$ in the same block of
$\mu$, since any $w\in S_\mu\setminus\{1\}$ has a reduced expression
$w=w's_i$ with $\ell(w)=\ell(w')+1$ and the claim follows by induction,
$m_\mu T_w=m_\mu T_{w'}T_i=q^{\ell(w')}m_\mu T_i=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$. For such
$i$ the right multiplication $v\mapsto vs_i$ is an involution of the finite
group $S_\mu$, and pairing the summands of $m_\mu T_i=\sum_{v\in S_\mu}T_vT_i$
in twos gives, in the two cases of the standard-basis multiplication rule
$T_vT_i=T_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)+1$ and
$T_vT_i=(q-1)T_v+qT_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)-1$,
$$T_vT_i+T_{vs_i}T_i=q\,(T_v+T_{vs_i}),$$
so summing over the $\tfrac12|S_\mu|$ pairs yields $m_\mu T_i=qm_\mu$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional cellular algebra over a field $F$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) with cell modules
$C_\lambda$ and cell-form quotients $D_\lambda=C_\lambda/R_\lambda$. Then:

1. every nonzero $D_\lambda$ is an absolutely simple head, all simple
   $A$-modules occur exactly once this way, and $[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\ne0$ implies
   $\lambda\ge\mu$, with $[C_\mu:D_\mu]=1$ whenever $D_\mu\ne0$; here
   "nonzero quotient" means nonzero form, not necessarily a nondegenerate form
   on $C_\lambda$;
2. every nonzero cell module, including labels with zero-form quotient, has
   all its composition factors in a single block
   ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]);
3. two nonzero cell modules share a block exactly when they are linked by a
   finite chain of nonzero cell modules whose neighbouring terms share a
   simple composition factor;
4. for one primitive idempotent $e_\mu$ per simple,
   $$\dim_Fe_\mu Ae_\nu=\sum_\lambda[C_\lambda:D_\mu]\,[C_\lambda:D_\nu].$$

If the cellular index set $T(\lambda)$ is empty, then $C_\lambda=D_\lambda=0$.
Its block support, the set of primitive central idempotents $b$ with
$C_\lambda b\ne0$, is empty, and it has no simple composition factors.
It does not participate in the nonzero-cell linkage criterion of (3), and
its term in the corner sum of (4) is zero.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition
$\alpha$ and the partition $\beta$ obtained by sorting its parts,
$x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ with a block-reordering permutation $d$
(step 2.2); and for the Garnir composition $\alpha$ at a node of $\rho$,
$x_\rho\sum_{d\in S_\alpha\cap D_\rho}T_d
=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).
The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with its basis $\{m_t\}$, $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$, the permutation form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ and the DJ form on $P(\lambda)$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Then:

1. Setting $B_\lambda(m_s,p):=\beta(x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(s)},p)$ for $s\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ and $p\in P(\lambda)$ defines an explicit $R$-bilinear pairing $B_\lambda\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\times P(\lambda)\to R$ that is $H$-balanced, $B_\lambda(mh,p)=B_\lambda(m,ph^*)$, and whose adjoint $c\mapsto B_\lambda(c,-)$ is an isomorphism of right $H$-modules $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ onto the star-contragredient module of [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. No nondegeneracy of the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ is required.

2. Equivalently, the kernel of the quotient map $M(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is the orthogonal complement $P(\lambda)^\perp=\{a\in M(\lambda):\beta(a,p)=0\text{ for all }p\in P(\lambda)\}$, namely $M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$; the pairing matrices in the bases $\{m_s\}$ and $\{e_t\}$ have entries $B_\lambda(m_s,e_t)=q^{\ell(d_\lambda(s))}a_{d_\lambda(s),t}$ with $e_t=\sum_d a_{d,t}b_d$, and determinant a unit of $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. Their inverses are finite tableau formulas given by the adjugate divided by this unit.

3. All statements are compatible with every base change $A\to R$, $v\mapsto q$; the construction uses no generic semisimplicity, no nondegeneracy of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ and no choice principle.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: The row-double-coset identity and membership. For a semistandard tableau $S$ of shape $\lambda$ and type $\rho$ and a standard $t$ of shape $\lambda$, every row-standard refinement $s$ of the column-strict tableau $S$ is standard, and $\sum_sT_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda$ is the sum of $T_w$ over the double coset $S_\rho d(s_0)^{-1}S_\lambda$, each $w$ occurring exactly once; its left $S_\rho$-coset expansion writes it as $x_\rho h_0$, and appending $T_{d(t)}$ gives $m_{(S,t)}=x_\rho h$ for some $h\in H_n$. Hence each $m_{(S,t)}$ lies in $x_\rho H_n$, and no row-intersection quantum factorial is introduced.

Independence and the Garnir coefficient rules. The sums $m_{(S,t)}$ are $R$-independent because their Murphy fibres (the index sets $\{s:ho(s)=S\}$) are disjoint and every coefficient in the expansion of $m_{(S,t)}$ in the $m_{st}$ basis is $1$; they therefore have disjoint unit pivots. For the coefficient rules, consider a violation at adjacent rows $i,i+1$ and column $j$ and the composition $
u=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{i-1},j-1,\lambda_i+1,\lambda_{i+1}-j,\lambda_{i+2},\dots)$; the two length-additive coset sums of $S_
u S_\lambda$ give $\sum_{w\in S_
u\cap D_\lambda}x_\lambda T_w =\sum_{v\in S_\lambda\cap D_
u}T_v^*x_
u,$ whose distinguished Garnir term occurs with coefficient $1$. Every other term in the original shape has strictly more dominant row tableaux, the reordered $
u$ has strictly higher lexicographic shape, and the ordinary Murphy dominance refinement places these shape errors in higher-cell ideals; a nonstandard tableau factors as that Garnir tableau followed by an additive-length word (removing inversions while keeping the column violation), and Bruhat subword support preserves the strict tableau-prefix inequality. In the isolated relation for consecutive $a,a+1$ in one column, sorting the Garnir belt has a unique standard term whose single adjacent swap produces the distinguished Garnir term, with coefficient $-1$, and every other same-shape term is strictly more dominant. This yields the displayed congruence of the Statement, and the right analogue follows by the cellular involutions $*$.

The row eigenspace test. For a fixed $a$ the left $z$-eigenspace of $T_a$ in $H_n$ is $(1+T_a)H_n$: in the $T_w$ basis pair $w$ with $s_aw$ of larger length, and coefficient comparison in $T_ah=zh$ gives equality of the two coefficients, whose sum is $(1+T_a)T_w$. This argument uses only that $z$ is a unit. Over the universal domain, no element of this space has a nonzero Murphy coefficient at a tableau with $a,a+1$ in one column: choose a least shape and then a least left tableau in a dominance-compatible support order; higher-cell terms cannot contribute to its shape, and a column correction from another tableau can contribute only from a strictly less dominant left tableau, absent by minimality. If $a,a+1$ are in a column, its coefficient in $T_ah$ is the negative of its coefficient in $h$ by step 1.2, contradicting the eigenvalue equation since $z+1\ne0$ in the domain; if they share a row, the basis element is already a $z$-eigenvector and is subtracted; if their swap is standard, the exact two-tableau rules make the two coefficients equal and their sum is a $z$-eigenvector, which is subtracted. Each subtraction stays in the row ideal and removes the chosen support term without creating new ones, so induction on the finite support proves the column exclusion; specializing the resulting coordinate-zero identities gives it over every base ring, with no division by $z+1$ at a singular parameter.

The basis theorem. Let $h\in x_\rho H_n$. It is a $z$-eigenvector for every generator inside every $\rho$-row interval, so step 2.1 excludes any supported tableau with a consecutive pair inside one column; for an adjacent standard swap, comparison of the exact two-tableau equations makes the two coefficients equal (no column-state correction can interfere, since every such state has coefficient $0$). The standard refinements of a fixed row-label tableau are the linear extensions of the finite node posets of its repeated-label classes, and any two are connected by swaps of adjacent incomparable elements; finite induction on the inversion distance shows that if a repeated label occupies one column, a consecutive vertical cover realises an excluded state and forces the whole fibre coefficient to be $0$, while otherwise the row-label tableau is column-strict and every fibre coefficient equals one common value. Hence $h$ has zero coefficients off semistandard fibres and constant coefficients on each semistandard fibre, i.e. $h$ lies in the span of the $m_{(S,t)}$; with step 1.2 this proves that the $m_{(S,t)}$ form an $R$-basis of $x_\rho H_n$.

The two filtrations, keeping the ordinary dictionary explicit. The higher-shape Murphy-cell filtration obtained from [F1] has one quotient $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ for every semistandard tableau $S$ of shape $\lambda$ and type $\rho$: its second-index action is the fixed-first-index Murphy cell action. These quotients are free over $R$, so every short exact sequence of this filtration splits as a sequence of $R$-modules. Star duality is therefore exact on this filtration. On the distinguished coset basis $b_d=x_\rho T_d$ of $x_\rho H_n$, define $\beta(b_d,b_c)=\delta_{dc}z^{\ell(d)}$. The row-permutation generator cases prove contravariance: a same-row generator acts by $z$; a length-increasing adjacent coset pair acts by $b_dT_i=b_c$, $b_cT_i=z b_d+(z-1)b_c$, with $\ell(c)=\ell(d)+1$, and the diagonal weights give $\beta(b_dT_i,b_c)=z^{\ell(c)}=z\beta(b_d,b_d)$. All other entries are zero or the corresponding diagonal equality. Thus $\beta$ gives an $H_n$-isomorphism $x_\rho H_n\cong(x_\rho H_n)^\circ$, since every diagonal $z^{\ell(d)}$ is a unit. The independently proved same-shape bridge gives $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\circ\cong P(\lambda)$, the ordinary Dipper–James Specht module, by finite-free biduality. Dualize the split Murphy filtration and transport it through this permutation self-duality. The resulting reversed filtration is an ordinary Specht filtration with exactly the same multiplicities. The original Murphy filtration is not called the ordinary one. This preserves the full every-ring/unit-parameter existence Statement without generic semisimplicity or form nondegeneracy on a Specht module.

The generic multiplicity interpretation. Over the generic field the finite Hecke algebra is split semisimple: by [F2] every simple is a nonzero cellular head, a simple factor of an ordinary cell module has a word character from that module and from the head's own cell shape, and disjoint word sets force the shapes to agree; existence of a factor forces its own head to be nonzero, diagonal multiplicity $1$ forces the cell module to be simple, and the sum of squared dimensions equals the Hecke rank, so the algebra and each parabolic are split semisimple. Consequently the filtration multiplicity $\#\operatorname{SStd}_\rho(\lambda)$ equals the multiplicity of the trivial character of the $\rho$-row parabolic in $S^\lambda$, by induction/restriction adjunction in the semisimple category.

Conclusion. Steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1 prove the semistandard Murphy basis of $x_\rho H_n$, step 1.2 gives the explicit Garnir and same-column generator rules with their termination, step 4.1 gives the Specht filtration with multiplicity $\#\operatorname{SStd}_\rho(\lambda)$, and step 5.1 gives the generic parabolic-multiplicity interpretation. Everything is proved universally over $\mathbb Z[z,z^{-1}]$ and specializes; the row-double-coset membership uses each coset word once and introduces no quantum-factorial division.

citations.quote: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$, where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set.

Every idempotent $e$ in a finite-dimensional unital $k$-algebra $A$ is a finite sum of pairwise orthogonal primitive idempotents of $A$. Here primitive means nonzero and admitting no decomposition as two nonzero orthogonal idempotents; zero is the empty sum.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left $A$-module. Then $M$ has a projective cover. If $\pi:P\to M$ and $\rho:Q\to M$ are projective covers, then there is an isomorphism $f:P\to Q$ with $\rho\circ f=\pi$.
Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field and let $J=J(A)$. Then $J$ is nilpotent, and the quotient algebra $A/J$ is semisimple.
Any two composition series of a module have the same length, and their simple factors agree up to permutation and isomorphism.

A **composition series** of a left $R$-module $M$ is a finite chain $$0=M_0<M_1<\cdots<M_n=M$$ whose factors $M_i/M_{i-1}$ are simple. If such a series exists, the **length** $\ell_R(M)$ is its number $n$ of factors; [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]] proves independence of the chosen series.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre $Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

derivations.claim: The cell-form scalar and its symmetry. For basis elements $c^\lambda_{us},c^\lambda_{tv}$ the product $c^\lambda_{us}c^\lambda_{tv}$ equals a scalar $G_\lambda(s,t)$ times $c^\lambda_{uv}$ modulo $A^{>\lambda}$ with $G_\lambda(s,t)$ independent of $u,v$: the right cell axiom fixes the first index and the left cell axiom fixes the last one, and comparing the two evaluations leaves the same scalar. The cellular involution gives $G_\lambda(s,t)=G_\lambda(t,s)$. Associativity of the threefold product yields $\langle xa,y\rangle=\langle x,ya^*\rangle$, since both sides compute the coefficient in the cell layer of the same product. [F1, algebra]

Cell purity and the zero cell. If $T(\lambda)$ is empty, then $C_\lambda=0$, its Gram matrix and form quotient are zero, and every central block projection acts with zero image; thus its block support is empty and it has no simple factors. The corresponding cell layer $J_\lambda$ is zero as well. Now assume $C_\lambda\ne0$ and let $z$ be a central idempotent of $A$. On the cell layer $J_\lambda\cong C_\lambda^{\mathrm{left}}\otimes_FC_\lambda$ the equality of left and right multiplication by $z$ gives $B\otimes\operatorname{Id}=\operatorname{Id}\otimes A_\lambda$ for the first- and second-factor coefficient matrices; comparing matrix coefficients shows every off-diagonal entry of $B$ and $A_\lambda$ vanishes and all diagonal entries of $B$ and $A_\lambda$ are equal, so both are a single scalar $\theta_\lambda$ times the identity. Since $z$ is idempotent, $\theta_\lambda\in\{0,1\}$. Applying this to all primitive central idempotents, whose sum is $1$, exactly one acts as $1$ on the nonzero cell module $C_\lambda$ and the others as $0$; hence $C_\lambda$, and therefore every composition factor of it, lies in one block. This covers labels with zero-form quotient because the tensor argument never divides by the Gram matrix. [F1, F4, algebra]

Nonzero form gives a simple head. Let $R_\lambda:=\{x\in C_\lambda:\langle x,C_\lambda\rangle=0\}$ be the radical of the form. By step 1.1 the rank-one action is $xc^\lambda_{uv}=\langle x,c^\lambda_u\rangle c^\lambda_v$, which shows that $R_\lambda$ is a submodule and that every vector $x\notin R_\lambda$ generates $C_\lambda$: if $\langle x,c^\lambda_u\rangle\ne0$, then scaling $xc^\lambda_{uv}$ by the inverse scalar produces $c^\lambda_v$ for every $v$. Hence every proper submodule is contained in $R_\lambda$ and $D_\lambda=C_\lambda/R_\lambda$ is simple when the form is nonzero; the criterion is nonzero form, and a degenerate but nonzero form is allowed. Extending scalars preserves the Gram rank and the rank-one action, so $D_\lambda$ is absolutely simple. [F1, step 1.1]

Every simple occurs. Let $D$ be a simple $A$-module, and choose a cell ideal $I_\lambda$ acting nontrivially on $D$, maximal among such ideals in the finite cell order; then $A^{>\lambda}$ annihilates $D$, while $J_\lambda=I_\lambda/A^{>\lambda}$ does not, so $DJ_\lambda=D$. If the Gram matrix of $C_\lambda$ were zero, the cell-layer multiplication would satisfy $J_\lambda^2=0$ and $DJ_\lambda^2=0$, a contradiction; hence the form is nonzero. Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and let
$x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. The **hook of $x$** is the set
$$H(x):=\{(i,j')\in[\lambda]:j'\ge j\}\cup\{(i',j)\in[\lambda]:i'\ge i\},$$
the union of the boxes of $[\lambda]$ weakly to the right of $x$ in row $i$
and weakly below $x$ in column $j$; the box $x$ itself belongs to both parts
and is counted once. The **arm** $\operatorname{arm}(x)$ is the part in row
$i$ strictly to the right of $x$, so
$\operatorname{arm}(x)=\{(i,j'):j<j'\le\lambda_i\}$; the **leg**
$\operatorname{leg}(x)$ is the part in column $j$ strictly below $x$, so
$\operatorname{leg}(x)=\{(i',j):i<i'\le\lambda'_j\}$. The **arm length** is
$a(x):=\lambda_i-j$, the **leg length** is $\ell(x):=\lambda'_j-i$, and the
**hook length** is

$$h(x):=a(x)+\ell(x)+1=\lambda_i-j+\lambda'_j-i+1,$$

so that $H(x)$ has exactly $h(x)$ boxes. Here $\lambda'_j$ is the number of
rows of $[\lambda]$ of length at least $j$, so the boxes of column $j$ below
row $i$ are exactly the rows $i+1,\dots,\lambda'_j$ and the arm has
$\lambda_i-j$ boxes; the arm, the leg and the anchor $x$ are pairwise disjoint
and exhaust $H(x)$, which gives the count.

A box is removable in the sense of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] if and only if it is the
last box of its row and of its column, i.e. if and only if $h(x)=1$: a row
endpoint $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable exactly when no box lies immediately
below it, that is when $\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$, and then
$a(x)=\lambda_i-\lambda_i=0$ and $\ell(x)=\lambda'_{\lambda_i}-i=0$; conversely
$h(x)=1$ forces $a(x)=\ell(x)=0$, so $x$ ends both its row and its column. The
empty partition has no boxes.

Finally $P(\lambda):=\prod_{x\in[\lambda]}h(x)$ denotes the **hook product**
of $\lambda$, the empty product $P(\varnothing)=1$ being part of the
convention. This fixes the off-by-one convention used by the whole page: the
anchor box contributes $1$, the arm contributes $\lambda_i-j$ and the leg
contributes $\lambda'_j-i$. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected, $2\times2$-free skew diagram with complement a Young diagram.
Every strip node $(p,q)$ lies on the rim: if $(p+1,q+1)$ belonged to
$[\lambda]$, it could not belong to $[\nu]$, since that would force
$(p,q)\in[\nu]$; and the partition inequalities then put all four nodes of
the corresponding $2\times2$ block in the strip, a contradiction. The rim
nodes in row $p$ have columns $\max(1,\lambda_{p+1}),\dots,\lambda_p$,
where missing row lengths are zero. Read each such interval from right to
left, then move down at column $\lambda_{p+1}$ to the next row: these are
exactly the rim nodes and their side-adjacencies. Thus the rim is a single
path moving left or down, and its connected subsets are subpaths. The
$r-1$ steps of $\xi$ consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ leftward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. Let $H(x)$ be the hook of $x$,
with arm length $a(x)=\lambda_i-j$, leg length $\ell(x)=\lambda'_j-i$ and hook
length $h(x)=a(x)+\ell(x)+1$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); its two endpoints are the last node
$(i,\lambda_i)$ of its arm and the last node $(\lambda'_j,j)$ of its leg. Let
$\xi(x)$ be the unique edge-connected set of nodes of $[\lambda]$ with
endpoints $(i,\lambda_i)$ and $(\lambda'_j,j)$ that lies in the rim of
$[\lambda]$, i.e. consists of nodes $(p,q)$ with $(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Then:

1. $\xi(x)$ is a removable border strip of $\lambda$ of size $h(x)$ and height
   $\ell(x)$ ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]), and
   $[\lambda]\setminus\xi(x)$ is a Young diagram, so $\lambda\setminus\xi(x)$ is
   a partition of $n-h(x)$;
2. every removable border strip of $\lambda$ equals $\xi(x)$ for exactly one
   node $x\in[\lambda]$; hence $x\mapsto\xi(x)$ is a bijection from the nodes
   of $[\lambda]$ onto the removable border strips of $\lambda$.

Consequently the sizes of the removable border strips of $\lambda$ are exactly
the hook lengths of $\lambda$, the height of $\xi(x)$ is the leg length
$\ell(x)$, and $x$ is removable as a node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) if and only if $\xi(x)$
has size $1$. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Pad $\lambda$ with zeros to length $m$. By [F3], $h_i=\lambda_i+m-i$. Below $h_i$ there are exactly $m-i$ beads, hence $h_i-(m-i)=\lambda_i$ gaps. For a node $(i,j)$ put $g_j=h_i-h_{i,j}(\lambda)=m+j-1-\lambda'_j$. These values are distinct by [F1], satisfy $0\le g_j<h_i$, and are gaps: equality $g_j=h_x=\lambda_x+m-x$ would give $\lambda_x-j+\lambda'_j-x+1=0$. If $x\le\lambda'_j$, both differences are nonnegative; otherwise both are at most $-1$, since $\lambda_x<j$. Neither case gives zero. Thus the $\lambda_i$ numbers $g_j$ exhaust the gaps below $h_i$, including the empty set when $\lambda_i=0$.

Fix $(i,j)$ and put $r=\lambda'_j$ and $g=m+j-1-r$. The rim strip of [F4] has complement with rows $\mu_p=\lambda_p$ outside $i\le p\le r$, $\mu_p=\lambda_{p+1}-1$ for $i\le p<r$, and $\mu_r=j-1$: in row $p$ the strip occupies the rim nodes with column at least $j$, whose complement ends at $\max(j-1,\lambda_{p+1}-1)$. For $p<r$ one has $\lambda_{p+1}\ge j$, while $\lambda_{r+1}<j$. These formulas give the displayed partition in (ii), with trailing zeros deleted, and its size is $n-h_{i,j}(\lambda)$.

Consequently, for $h\ge0$, $h\in H_i(\lambda)$ exactly when $h\le h_i$ and $h_i-h\notin X$: at $h=0$ the latter fails because $h_i\in X$, and for $h>h_i$ its first inequality fails. For $1\le h\le h_i$ this is the gap correspondence in step 1.1. The bead $h_i$ determines $i$, and the distinct row hook lengths determine $j$, so $(i,j)\mapsto(h_i,g_j)$ is the asserted bijection with length $h_i-g_j$.

The new value $g$ is below $h_r$ because $h_r-g=\lambda_r-j+1\ge1$, and, if $r<m$, above $h_{r+1}$ because $g-h_{r+1}=j-\lambda_{r+1}\ge1$. Hence the decreasing list of $X'=(X\setminus\{h_i\})\cup\{g\}$ is $h_1,\ldots,h_{i-1},h_{i+1},\ldots,h_r,g,h_{r+1},\ldots,h_m$. Applying [F2] gives precisely the parts $\mu_p$ in step 1.2. Thus $P(X')=\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}$, and the abacus change is the relocation of the bead $h_i$ to $g$.

The length is $b-g$, so $e\mid h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ exactly when $b\equiv g\pmod e$. In that case the bead remains on its runner, moves up $h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e$ rows, and all runner bead counts are unchanged. Without this divisibility assumption the relocation may change runners. In row $i$ a hook of length $e$ exists exactly when $h_i\ge e$ and $h_i-e\notin X$, by step 2.1; existential quantification over $i$ gives the final bead criterion in (iii).

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.

For every $d\ge0$ and partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash d$,
$$h_\mu=\sum_{\lambda\vdash d}K_{\lambda\mu}s_\lambda.$$
Moreover, $K_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, and
$K_{\mu\mu}=1$. Thus, after ordering the partitions of $d$ by any linear
extension of dominance from smaller to larger, the matrix
$(K_{\lambda\mu})_{\lambda,\mu\vdash d}$ is lower unitriangular over
$\mathbb Z$.

Let $\mathcal C$ be an essentially small abelian category
([[def-abelian-category]]). Its set of isomorphism classes is denoted
$\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)$. The **Grothendieck group** of $\mathcal C$ is

$$ G_0(\mathcal C):=\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]\big/\langle e_Y-e_X-e_Z:\ 0\to X\to Y\to Z\to 0\text{ is short exact in }\mathcal C\rangle. $$

where $\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]$ is the free abelian group on
that set ([[def-free-abelian-group]]) and $[X]$ denotes the image of the
generator for the isomorphism class of $X$. Thus the defining relation is
$[Y]=[X]+[Z]$ for every short exact sequence
([[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]]).
This is the short-exact-sequence group, distinguished below from split
Grothendieck groups of projectives. No free abelian group on the possibly
class-sized collection of all objects is formed. The sequence
$0\to0\to0\to0$ in particular gives $[0]=0$.

derivations.claim: Multiplication by the central idempotent $\epsilon_B$ is the projection of every right $S$-module onto its $B$-summand: $N=\bigoplus_iN\epsilon_i$ by [F1], so $N\epsilon_B$ is that direct summand and is a submodule, and $N\epsilon_B=N$ exactly when all composition factors of $N$ lie in $B$. The assignment $N\mapsto N\epsilon_B$ is exact, because it is the projection onto a direct summand of the identity functor: for $f:N\to N'$ one has $f(N\epsilon_B)=f(N)\epsilon_B$, $\ker(f|_{N\epsilon_B})=(\ker f)\epsilon_B$ and $\operatorname{im}(f|_{N\epsilon_B})=(\operatorname{im}f)\epsilon_B$, so it preserves kernels and images.

A nonzero finite-dimensional module has a simple quotient: choose a proper submodule of maximal vector-space dimension. If a Weyl module had two nonzero summands, each would have a nonzero head, so its head would not be simple, contrary to [F2]. Thus it is indecomposable. Its block decomposition [F1] has precisely one nonzero summand, the block containing its head $L^\lambda$; hence $W^\lambda\epsilon_B$ is either $W^\lambda$ or $0$.

Apply the exact projection of step 1.1 to the class identity of the hypothesis. Since $M\epsilon_B=M$ by the hypothesis that all composition factors of $M$ lie in $B$, and since $W^{\lambda}\epsilon_B$ is $W^{\lambda}$ or $0$ by step 1.2, the induced identity in $G_0$ reads $$[M]=\sum_{\lambda:\,W^{\lambda}\in B}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}].$$ Subtracting it from the given identity $[M]=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$ yields $$\sum_{\lambda:\,W^{\lambda}\notin B}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]=0$$ in $G_0(S\text{-mod})$.

By the linear independence of the Weyl classes [F3], all coefficients in the vanishing combination of step 2.1 are zero: $a_{\lambda}=0$ for every $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}\notin B$, which is the contrapositive of the assertion that $a_{\lambda}\ne0$ implies $W^{\lambda}\in B$.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a
$\beta$-set for $\lambda$, so that $P(X)=\lambda$
([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Write $H_i(\lambda)$ for
the set of hook lengths in row $i$ of $[\lambda]$: thus $h\in H_i(\lambda)$
means $h=h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ for some node $(i,j)\in[\lambda]$, and
$H_i(\lambda)=\emptyset$ for $i>\ell(\lambda)$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]).

(i) For every $h\ge0$ and every $i\in[m]$, $h\in H_i(\lambda)$ if and only if
$h\le h_i$ and $h_i-h\notin X$. Equivalently, the hooks of $\lambda$
correspond bijectively to the **bead-gap pairs** $(b,g)$ with $b\in X$,
$g\notin X$ and $0\le g<b$; the hook $H_{i,j}(\lambda)$ corresponds to
$$(b,g)=\bigl(h_i,\;h_i-h_{i,j}(\lambda)\bigr),$$
and then $|H_{i,j}(\lambda)|=b-g$.

(ii) Fix a node $(i,j)\in[\lambda]$ and let $(b,g)$ be its bead-gap pair as in
(i). Then
$$X':=(X\setminus\{b\})\cup\{g\}$$
is again a $\beta$-set, now for the partition $\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}$
obtained from $\lambda$ by removing the removable border strip $R_{i,j}$ that
corresponds to the hook of $(i,j)$, of size $h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ and height
$\ell(i,j)=\lambda'_j-i$
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]); in terms of parts, with
$b_0:=\ell(i,j)=\lambda'_j-i$,
$$\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}=\bigl(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{i-1},\,\lambda_{i+1}-1,\dots,\lambda_{i+b_0}-1,\,j-1,\,\lambda_{i+b_0+1},\dots\bigr),$$
so that $|\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}|=n-h_{i,j}(\lambda)$. Finally $X'$ is
obtained from the configuration $A_X$ by moving the bead from position $b$ to
the gap $g$.

(iii) In particular $e\mid h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ if and only if $b\equiv g\pmod e$,
that is, if and only if the bead $b$ and the gap $g$ lie on the same runner of
the $e$-abacus; then $g=b-e\cdot(h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e)$ and the move in (ii) is
the slide of the bead $b$ up $h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e$ rows on its own runner. A
hook of length $e$ in row $i$ of $\lambda$ exists if and only if $h_i\ge e$
and $h_i-e\notin X$; Thus $\lambda$ has a hook of length $e$ if and only if some bead of $X$ has a gap
in the position $e$ labels above it on its own runner.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected, $2\times2$-free skew diagram with complement a Young diagram.
Every strip node $(p,q)$ lies on the rim: if $(p+1,q+1)$ belonged to
$[\lambda]$, it could not belong to $[\nu]$, since that would force
$(p,q)\in[\nu]$; and the partition inequalities then put all four nodes of
the corresponding $2\times2$ block in the strip, a contradiction. The rim
nodes in row $p$ have columns $\max(1,\lambda_{p+1}),\dots,\lambda_p$,
where missing row lengths are zero. Read each such interval from right to
left, then move down at column $\lambda_{p+1}$ to the next row: these are
exactly the rim nodes and their side-adjacencies. Thus the rim is a single
path moving left or down, and its connected subsets are subpaths. The
$r-1$ steps of $\xi$ consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ leftward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. Let $H(x)$ be the hook of $x$,
with arm length $a(x)=\lambda_i-j$, leg length $\ell(x)=\lambda'_j-i$ and hook
length $h(x)=a(x)+\ell(x)+1$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); its two endpoints are the last node
$(i,\lambda_i)$ of its arm and the last node $(\lambda'_j,j)$ of its leg. Let
$\xi(x)$ be the unique edge-connected set of nodes of $[\lambda]$ with
endpoints $(i,\lambda_i)$ and $(\lambda'_j,j)$ that lies in the rim of
$[\lambda]$, i.e. consists of nodes $(p,q)$ with $(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Then:

1. $\xi(x)$ is a removable border strip of $\lambda$ of size $h(x)$ and height
   $\ell(x)$ ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]), and
   $[\lambda]\setminus\xi(x)$ is a Young diagram, so $\lambda\setminus\xi(x)$ is
   a partition of $n-h(x)$;
2. every removable border strip of $\lambda$ equals $\xi(x)$ for exactly one
   node $x\in[\lambda]$; hence $x\mapsto\xi(x)$ is a bijection from the nodes
   of $[\lambda]$ onto the removable border strips of $\lambda$.

Consequently the sizes of the removable border strips of $\lambda$ are exactly
the hook lengths of $\lambda$, the height of $\xi(x)$ is the leg length
$\ell(x)$, and $x$ is removable as a node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) if and only if $\xi(x)$
has size $1$. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Fix a $\beta$-set $X$ of a partition $\mu$ and write its elements as $h_1>\cdots>h_m$. By [F1] the hooks of length $e$ of $\mu$ correspond bijectively to the beads $b=h_i$ with $h_i\ge e$ and $h_i-e\notin X$, the correspondence sending such a bead to the rim strip $R_{i,j}(\mu)$ attached to the node with $h_{i,j}(\mu)=e$, and removal of that strip replaces $X$ by $X'=(X\setminus\{h_i\})\cup\{h_i-e\}$, a $\beta$-set for $\mu\setminus R_{i,j}(\mu)$ of the same size $m$. In particular $\mu$ has no hook of length $e$ exactly when no bead of $X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own runner.

Compute the shift directly. For $Y=X+1$, its runner sets are $Y^{(e)}_0=(X^{(e)}_{e-1})+1$ and $Y^{(e)}_i=X^{(e)}_{i-1}$ for $1\le i<e$: the last runner wraps to runner $0$ one row lower, and the shift adds the bead at $0$. Its counts are $(c_{e-1}+1,c_0,\ldots,c_{e-2})$. Packing with these counts gives $Y^{(e)}=(X^{(e)})+1$, so $P(Y^{(e)})=P(X^{(e)})$ by [F3]. Iteration proves core independence for all beta-sets of $\lambda$. After $e$ shifts, every runner row-label set has undergone one beta-set shift by $1$, so its partition is unchanged. Normalised beta-sets differ by a multiple of $e$, proving independence of the ordered quotient and its total size.

Call a bead of $X$ *movable* when the position $e$ labels above it on its runner is a gap, so that by step 1.1 the movable beads are exactly the hooks of length $e$ of $\mu$; moving a bead up one row replaces $X$ by a $\beta$-set of $\mu$ minus that hook, and the counts $|X^{(e)}_i|$ of beads on each runner are unchanged. A configuration is top-packed precisely when it has no movable bead: a top-packed runner carries beads in the rows $0,1,\dots,c_i-1$, so the row above a bead is a bead again (and row $0$ has no row above it), while if some runner is not top-packed there are a gap in row $g$ and a bead in a row $a>g$ on that runner; choosing $a$ minimal among the bead rows larger than $g$, the row $a-1$ is a gap, so the bead in row $a$ is movable.

Every sequence of moves of steps 1.1 and 2.1 is finite: the quantity $\Phi:=\sum_{i}\sum_{a\in X^{(e)}_i}a$ is the total of the row labels of all beads, and each move replaces a bead's row label $a$ by $a-1$, so $\Phi$ decreases by exactly $1$ and is a nonnegative integer. A sequence is maximal exactly when it stops at a configuration with no movable bead, that is, by step 2.1, exactly when it stops at the top-packed configuration of the counts $(c_i)$; and that configuration is unique, since a runner with $c_i$ beads has exactly one top-packed state, the rows $0,\dots,c_i-1$. Hence every maximal sequence of moves starting from $X$ ends at the same configuration, namely $X^{(e)}$, and therefore at the same terminal partition $P(X^{(e)})$.

By step 1.2 the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ does not depend on the chosen $\beta$-set $X$, so $C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)})$ is well-defined; by step 3.1 it is the common terminal partition of all maximal sequences of e-hook removals, and by step 2.1 a terminal configuration is top-packed, hence carries no movable bead, hence its partition has no hook of length $e$ by step 1.1; thus $C_e(\lambda)$ is an $e$-core. Every strip removed along such a sequence corresponds to a node hook of length exactly $e$ and so has size $e$ by [F4]. This proves all the asserted properties.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a
$\beta$-set for $\lambda$, so that $P(X)=\lambda$
([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Write $H_i(\lambda)$ for
the set of hook lengths in row $i$ of $[\lambda]$: thus $h\in H_i(\lambda)$
means $h=h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ for some node $(i,j)\in[\lambda]$, and
$H_i(\lambda)=\emptyset$ for $i>\ell(\lambda)$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]).

(i) For every $h\ge0$ and every $i\in[m]$, $h\in H_i(\lambda)$ if and only if
$h\le h_i$ and $h_i-h\notin X$. Equivalently, the hooks of $\lambda$
correspond bijectively to the **bead-gap pairs** $(b,g)$ with $b\in X$,
$g\notin X$ and $0\le g<b$; the hook $H_{i,j}(\lambda)$ corresponds to
$$(b,g)=\bigl(h_i,\;h_i-h_{i,j}(\lambda)\bigr),$$
and then $|H_{i,j}(\lambda)|=b-g$.

(ii) Fix a node $(i,j)\in[\lambda]$ and let $(b,g)$ be its bead-gap pair as in
(i). Then
$$X':=(X\setminus\{b\})\cup\{g\}$$
is again a $\beta$-set, now for the partition $\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}$
obtained from $\lambda$ by removing the removable border strip $R_{i,j}$ that
corresponds to the hook of $(i,j)$, of size $h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ and height
$\ell(i,j)=\lambda'_j-i$
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]); in terms of parts, with
$b_0:=\ell(i,j)=\lambda'_j-i$,
$$\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}=\bigl(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{i-1},\,\lambda_{i+1}-1,\dots,\lambda_{i+b_0}-1,\,j-1,\,\lambda_{i+b_0+1},\dots\bigr),$$
so that $|\lambda\setminus R_{i,j}|=n-h_{i,j}(\lambda)$. Finally $X'$ is
obtained from the configuration $A_X$ by moving the bead from position $b$ to
the gap $g$.

(iii) In particular $e\mid h_{i,j}(\lambda)$ if and only if $b\equiv g\pmod e$,
that is, if and only if the bead $b$ and the gap $g$ lie on the same runner of
the $e$-abacus; then $g=b-e\cdot(h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e)$ and the move in (ii) is
the slide of the bead $b$ up $h_{i,j}(\lambda)/e$ rows on its own runner. A
hook of length $e$ in row $i$ of $\lambda$ exists if and only if $h_i\ge e$
and $h_i-e\notin X$; Thus $\lambda$ has a hook of length $e$ if and only if some bead of $X$ has a gap
in the position $e$ labels above it on its own runner.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Write a hook $H=H_{i,j}(\lambda)$ of $e$-divisible length in its bead-gap form $(b,g)$ with $b\in X$, $g\notin X$, $0\le g<b$ and $h:=|H|=b-g$. By $e\mid h$ we have $b\equiv g\pmod e$; write the common residue as $s\in\{0,\dots,e-1\}$ and $$b=b'e+s,\qquad g=g'e+s,\qquad b'=\frac{b-s}{e}>g'=\frac{g-s}{e}\ge0.$$ The bead $b$ is a bead of $X$ on runner $s$ and the gap $g$ is a gap of $X$ on runner $s$.

Applying step 1.1 conversely, a bead $b'\in X^{(e)}_s$ and a gap $g'\notin X^{(e)}_s$ with $0\le g'<b'$ give the bead-gap pair $(b,g)=(b'e+s,g'e+s)$ of $X$ with $e\mid(b-g)$ and $b-g=e(b'-g')$. Hence $f(H):=$ the hook of $\lambda^{(s)}$ attached to the bead-gap pair $(b',g')$ of the $\beta$-set $X^{(e)}_s$ is well defined, and $f$ is bijective onto the hooks of $\bigsqcup_i\lambda^{(i)}$ because both sides are in bijection with the bead-gap pairs of $X$ whose two positions share a runner, respectively with the union over $s$ of the bead-gap pairs of $X^{(e)}_s$; the length identity is $|H|=b-g=e(b'-g')=e|f(H)|$.

For the removal identity, let $X'=(X\setminus\{b\})\cup\{g\}$ be the $\beta$-set of $\lambda\setminus H$ from [F1], again of size $m$ and hence normalised by [F3]. Because $b$ and $g$ lie on runner $s$, the beads of $X'$ on a runner $t\ne s$ are exactly the beads of $X$ on runner $t$, and the beads on runner $s$ have row labels $(X^{(e)}_s\setminus\{b'\})\cup\{g'\}$. Consequently, computing the quotient from the normalised sets by [F2], $$\lambda'^{(t)}=P\bigl((X')^{(e)}_t\bigr)=\lambda^{(t)}\ (t\ne s),\qquad \lambda'^{(s)}=P\bigl((X^{(e)}_s\setminus\{b'\})\cup\{g'\}\bigr),$$ and the last partition is $\lambda^{(s)}$ with its hook $f(H)$ removed, by [F1] applied to the $\beta$-set $X^{(e)}_s$ of $\lambda^{(s)}$. This is exactly the assertion $Q_e(\lambda\setminus H)=Q_e(\lambda)\setminus f(H)$.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 together exhibit the required bijection $f$ with the length and removal identities, and the description of $f$ on the abacus is the rescaling of step 1.1 followed by the bead-gap dictionary of the runner in step 2.1.
