citations.quote:
For all partitions $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$,
$$\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta} =\bigl\langle s_\alpha[X]s_\beta[Y]\,\big|\,\sigma[XY]\,s_\gamma[XY+X+Y]\bigr\rangle_{X,Y},$$
the inner product being the Hall inner product extended to symmetric functions
in the two alphabet variables $X,Y$, and $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ the
reduced Kronecker coefficient
([[def-reduced-kronecker-coefficient]]).

Equivalently, introducing a third alphabet $Z$,
$$\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\, s_\alpha[X]s_\beta[Y]s_\gamma[Z] =\sigma[XYZ+XY+XZ+YZ],$$
the symmetric Cauchy-type identity for the reduced coefficients, summed over
all triples of partitions and by total degree. Equivalently again, in the
notation of
[[lem-padding-completion-is-compatible-with-the-internal-product]],
$$R_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,s_\gamma,$$
the finite Schur expansion of the polynomial $R_{\alpha,\beta}$.

For partitions $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ define the **reduced (stable) Kronecker
coefficient** $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ to be the eventual value of the
padded sequence $n\mapsto g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ furnished by
[[thm-murnaghan-stability-for-kronecker-coefficients]]; equivalently
$$\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}:=\lim_{n\to\infty}g^{\gamma[n]}_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]},$$
where the sequence is defined for
$n\ge\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,|\beta|+\beta_1,|\gamma|+\gamma_1\}$ and set to
$0$ below by the convention in [[thm-murnaghan-stability-for-kronecker-coefficients]]
(the size-indexed coefficients of [[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]] themselves are defined
only on that common domain; see also
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

**Well-definedness.** The sequence is eventually constant by the Murnaghan
stability theorem, and the eventual value of an eventually constant sequence
of nonnegative integers is a unique nonnegative integer; no choice is
involved. Two immediate conventions: (i) $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}=
\bar g^\gamma_{\beta,\alpha}$ for all $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, because
$V_\mu\otimes V_\nu\cong V_\nu\otimes V_\mu$ and the Kronecker coefficients
are symmetric in their two lower indices; (ii) for fixed $\alpha,\beta$ only
finitely many $\gamma$ have $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\ne0$, because the
finite set $S(\alpha,\beta)$ of the stability theorem carries the whole
support. The values used later and verified in the source's introduction for
$\alpha=\beta=(2)$ are $\bar g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}=2$ and
$\bar g^{(4)}_{(2),(2)}=1$; they are read off from the displayed stable row
and are not used as logical inputs anywhere on this page.

For partitions $\alpha,\beta$ put $a=|\alpha|$, $b=|\beta|$ and define
$$R_{\alpha,\beta}[Z]:=\langle s_\alpha[A]s_\beta[B]\,|\,\sigma[ZAB+ZA+ZB+AB]\rangle_{A,B},$$
the Hall pairing in the alphabet variables $A,B$
([[def-hall-inner-product-on-symmetric-functions]],
[[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]]).

1. $R_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a finite symmetric-function polynomial in $Z$ of
   degree at most $a+b$.
2. For every integer $n\ge0$,
   $$(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)=U_nR_{\alpha,\beta},$$
   where $U_n$ is the Jacobi–Trudi completion and $*$ the internal product
   ([[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]],
   [[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]]); this holds for every
   $n\ge0$, including those $n$ for which the padded sequences $\alpha[n]$,
   $\beta[n]$ are not partitions. Equivalently, with $t$ a one-letter formal
   alphabet,
   $$\sum_{n\ge0}(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)\,t^n =\sigma[tX]\,R_{\alpha,\beta}[tX-1].$$
3. The same polynomial is the finite Littlewood expression
   $$R_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_{\delta,\epsilon,\tau} \bigl((s_\delta s_\tau)^{\perp}s_\alpha\bigr) \bigl((s_\epsilon s_\tau)^{\perp}s_\beta\bigr) \bigl(s_\delta*s_\epsilon\bigr),$$
   the sum over all triples of partitions, all factors evaluated at $Z$.

**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$, with missing parts read as zero, the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]). When this sequence is used as
a partition label, omit trailing zero entries; in particular
$\varnothing[0]=\varnothing$ and the missing first part is zero.

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is
$0$; if $\min_jq_j\ge0$ then $\nu$, after deleting trailing zero entries, is a partition of $|\mu|$
with at most $m$ parts and the Jacobi–Trudi identity gives the value
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)s_\nu$. In particular $s_{\alpha[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{\alpha[n]}=0$ for $n<0$: every term of the
determinant expansion has total degree $n$, so for $n<0$ some factor has
negative index and vanishes.

**The operators $U_n$ and $V$.** The Schur functions form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of
$\Lambda$ ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n(\Lambda)\subseteq\Lambda^n$ for $n\ge0$ (and $U_n=0$ for
$n<0$), while $V$ raises degree by one; in particular $V(1)=s_{(1)}$. The operators
are extended linearly, and $V^k$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of $V$.

**The stabilization index.** The internal product $*$ on $\Lambda$ is the
degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that
$$s_{\alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{\beta[n_0+k]}=V^k\bigl(s_{\alpha[n_0]}*s_{\beta[n_0]}\bigr) \qquad\text{for all }k>0,$$
following the source. This definition records the source's convention only: it
does not assert that such an $n_0$ exists, nor that a value of $n_0$ satisfying
the display is least for any other property. Existence, least-ness and the
exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

Let $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ be a partition with $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let $n\ge0$ be
an integer. Read $|\varnothing|=0$ and $\alpha_1=0$ when
$\alpha=\varnothing$. Whenever

$$n\;\ge\;|\alpha|+\alpha_1,$$

define the **first-row padding** of $\alpha$ to size $n$ to be
$$\alpha[n]:=\bigl(n-|\alpha|,\ \alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \dots,\ \alpha_k\bigr).$$

The threshold is exact.

**Above the threshold.** Suppose $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$. Then
$n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1\ge0$, so every entry of the displayed sequence is a
nonnegative integer, the entries sum to $(n-|\alpha|)+|\alpha|=n$, and the
sequence is weakly decreasing because $n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1$ and $\alpha$ is
weakly decreasing ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
If $\alpha$ is nonempty then $\alpha_1\ge1$, hence $n-|\alpha|\ge1$ and the
displayed sequence is a partition of $n$ with positive parts. If
$\alpha=\varnothing$ then the displayed sequence is $(n)$; this is a partition
of $n$ for every $n\ge1$, while for $n=0$ one takes $\varnothing[0]:=\varnothing$,
the unique partition of $0$. Thus the padding is defined and is a partition of
$n$ on the whole displayed range.

**Below the threshold.** If $\alpha$ is nonempty and $n<|\alpha|+\alpha_1$,
then $n-|\alpha|<\alpha_1$; if also $n\ge|\alpha|$ the leading entry is
nonnegative but smaller than the second entry $\alpha_1$, and if $n<|\alpha|$
it is negative. In both cases the displayed sequence is not a partition, so
$\alpha[n]$ is left undefined. The threshold $|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is therefore
the exact size at which the padded family begins: for nonempty $\alpha$, at
$n=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ the padding equals $(\alpha_1,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$,
which is a partition with a repeated first part when $\alpha$ is nonempty.

**Neutrality of the notation.** This definition records a family of partitions;
it asserts no constancy of any quantity along the family and no stability
property. The same notation is used by the FI-module and
representation-stability developments; no FI-module structure or generation
degree is asserted here.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the

reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition, by
[[thm-isotypic-decomposition-of-a-completely-reducible-representation-is-unique]]
(Proof step 2.1 identifies each grouped block with the defining isotypic sum).
In particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.

For every $d\ge0$, the stable Schur functions $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$
form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $\Lambda^d$ and are orthonormal for the Hall form:
$$\langle s_\lambda,s_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$.

**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$, with missing parts read as zero, the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]). When this sequence is used as
a partition label, omit trailing zero entries; in particular
$\varnothing[0]=\varnothing$ and the missing first part is zero.

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is
$0$; if $\min_jq_j\ge0$ then $\nu$, after deleting trailing zero entries, is a partition of $|\mu|$
with at most $m$ parts and the Jacobi–Trudi identity gives the value
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)s_\nu$. In particular $s_{\alpha[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{\alpha[n]}=0$ for $n<0$: every term of the
determinant expansion has total degree $n$, so for $n<0$ some factor has
negative index and vanishes.

**The operators $U_n$ and $V$.** The Schur functions form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of
$\Lambda$ ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n(\Lambda)\subseteq\Lambda^n$ for $n\ge0$ (and $U_n=0$ for
$n<0$), while $V$ raises degree by one; in particular $V(1)=s_{(1)}$. The operators
are extended linearly, and $V^k$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of $V$.

**The stabilization index.** The internal product $*$ on $\Lambda$ is the
degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that
$$s_{\alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{\beta[n_0+k]}=V^k\bigl(s_{\alpha[n_0]}*s_{\beta[n_0]}\bigr) \qquad\text{for all }k>0,$$
following the source. This definition records the source's convention only: it
does not assert that such an $n_0$ exists, nor that a value of $n_0$ satisfying
the display is least for any other property. Existence, least-ness and the
exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

Let $\alpha$ be a partition and $t$ a formal variable. With the Jacobi-Trudi
convention of [[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]]
for the integer sequences $\alpha[n]=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$, one
has an identity of formal Laurent series with coefficients in the symmetric
function ring
([[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]]):
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}s_{\alpha[n]}[X]\,t^n=\sigma[tX]\cdot s_\alpha[tX-1] =t^{|\alpha|}\cdot\sigma[tX]\cdot s_\alpha[X-t^{-1}],$$
where $s_\alpha[tX-1]$ is evaluated through $p_k\mapsto t^kp_k[X]-1$ and
$s_\alpha[X-t^{-1}]$ through $p_k\mapsto p_k[X]-t^{-k}$. Equivalently,
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}s_{\alpha[n]}[X]\,t^n =\sigma[tX]\sum_{\mu:\ \alpha/\mu\ \text{a vertical strip}} (-1)^{|\alpha|-|\mu|}t^{|\mu|}s_\mu[X].$$

For partitions $\alpha,\beta$ put $a=|\alpha|$, $b=|\beta|$ and define
$$R_{\alpha,\beta}[Z]:=\langle s_\alpha[A]s_\beta[B]\,|\,\sigma[ZAB+ZA+ZB+AB]\rangle_{A,B},$$
the Hall pairing in the alphabet variables $A,B$
([[def-hall-inner-product-on-symmetric-functions]],
[[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]]).

1. $R_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a finite symmetric-function polynomial in $Z$ of
   degree at most $a+b$.
2. For every integer $n\ge0$,
   $$(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)=U_nR_{\alpha,\beta},$$
   where $U_n$ is the Jacobi–Trudi completion and $*$ the internal product
   ([[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]],
   [[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]]); this holds for every
   $n\ge0$, including those $n$ for which the padded sequences $\alpha[n]$,
   $\beta[n]$ are not partitions. Equivalently, with $t$ a one-letter formal
   alphabet,
   $$\sum_{n\ge0}(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)\,t^n =\sigma[tX]\,R_{\alpha,\beta}[tX-1].$$
3. The same polynomial is the finite Littlewood expression
   $$R_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_{\delta,\epsilon,\tau} \bigl((s_\delta s_\tau)^{\perp}s_\alpha\bigr) \bigl((s_\epsilon s_\tau)^{\perp}s_\beta\bigr) \bigl(s_\delta*s_\epsilon\bigr),$$
   the sum over all triples of partitions, all factors evaluated at $Z$.

No choice principle is used.

The **reading word** $w(T)$ of a semistandard skew tableau $T$ of shape $
u/\lambda$ is the word obtained by reading the rows of $T$ from right to left, beginning with the top row and proceeding to the bottom row. The word $w(T)=a_1a_2\cdots a_N$ is a **lattice word** (a lattice permutation) if in every prefix $a_1\cdots a_p$ and for every $i\ge1$ the number of letters $i$ in the prefix is at least the number of letters $i+1$; the empty word is a lattice word vacuously.

u_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\lambda\subseteq
u$ and $|
u|=|\lambda|+|\mu|$.

Let $\operatorname{ch}:R_S\to\Lambda$ be the Frobenius characteristic restricted
to the graded ordinary representation ring of the symmetric groups
([[def-frobenius-characteristic-map]],
[[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). By
[[thm-frobenius-characteristic-is-an-isometric-graded-ring-isomorphism]] it is a
degree-preserving $\mathbb Z$-module isomorphism onto the stable symmetric
function ring $\Lambda=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}\Lambda^m$, so its restriction
$\operatorname{ch}:R(S_m)\to\Lambda^m$ is an isomorphism for every $m\ge0$.

For $f\in\Lambda^m$ and $g\in\Lambda^n$ define
$$f*g:=\begin{cases}\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)\cdot\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)\bigr),&m=n,\\[2pt]0,&m\ne n,\end{cases}$$
where $\cdot$ is the pointwise (internal tensor) product of class functions on
$S_m$; extend $*$ bilinearly to all of $\Lambda$. Call $*$ the
**internal (Kronecker) product** of symmetric functions.

**Well-definedness.** For $m=n$ the class functions $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)$
and $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)$ lie in $R(S_m)$, the integral span of the
irreducible characters of $S_m$
([[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). The
pointwise product of two honest characters of $S_m$ is again an honest
character, namely the character of the tensor product of the underlying
representations ([[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]),
and products of $\mathbb Z$-combinations of characters are computed
bilinearly; hence the pointwise product of two elements of $R(S_m)$ lies in
$R(S_m)$, and applying the isomorphism $\operatorname{ch}$ lands in $\Lambda^m$.
The product is therefore well defined and takes $\Lambda^m\times\Lambda^m$ to
$\Lambda^m$.

**Basic properties.** The product is bilinear by construction and inherits
commutativity and associativity from the pointwise product of class functions.
It preserves degrees, in the sense that $\Lambda^m*\Lambda^n\subseteq\Lambda^m$
for $m=n$ and is $0$ for $m\ne n$. On $\Lambda^n$ the unit is
$h_n=s_{(n)}=\operatorname{ch}(\text{trivial character of }S_n)$ for $n>0$,
and in degree zero it is $h_0=s_\varnothing=1$, because the
trivial character is the unit for pointwise multiplication on $R(S_n)$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]]
identifies $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^{(n)})=s_{(n)}=h_n$). The graded direct sum
$\Lambda$ has **no global unit** for $*$: if $e\in\Lambda$ had finite degree
support and $n$ were a degree with $e_n=0$ while $\Lambda^n\ne0$, then
$(e*h_n)_n=e_n*h_n=0\ne h_n$, so $e*h_n\ne h_n$; a global unit would require
$e_n$ to be a unit of $(\Lambda^n,*)$ for every $n$. In particular the ordinary
product unit $1\in\Lambda^0$ is not a unit for $*$ on the positive degrees.

**Schur expansion.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the definition and
the Specht character dictionary $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]])
give
$$s_\lambda*s_\mu=\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\chi^\lambda\cdot\chi^\mu\bigr)=\operatorname{ch}\Bigl(\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\chi^\nu\Bigr)=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\,s_\nu,$$
because $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the character of
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ and its decomposition has multiplicities
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the transport goes through the
choice-free Frobenius characteristic isomorphism and finite-dimensional
representation theory of finite groups.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $R_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_\gamma$ with finitely many nonzero terms.

*Local reduced coefficients for $(2),(2)$.* In the Littlewood expression of [F6], $(s_\delta s_\tau)^\perp s_{(2)}$ is nonzero only when $\delta=(m)$ and $\tau=(r)$ are rows with $m+r\le2$ (a row LR target forces every factor to be a row); it then equals $s_{(2-m-r)}$. The analogous condition holds for $\epsilon$, and $s_\delta*s_\epsilon=0$ unless their degrees agree, in which case it is $s_{(m)}$ by the unit rule. Here $(0)$ means $\varnothing$. Hence $R_{(2),(2)}=\sum_{m+r\le2}s_{(2-m-r)}^2s_{(m)}=s_{(2)}^2+s_{(1)}^2+1+s_{(1)}^3+s_{(1)}+s_{(2)}$. Counting row LR tableaux gives $s_{(2)}^2=s_{(4)}+s_{(3,1)}+s_{(2,2)}$ and $s_{(1)}^2=s_{(2)}+s_{(1,1)}$; adding one box to these two shapes gives $s_{(1)}^3=s_{(3)}+2s_{(2,1)}+s_{(1,1,1)}$. Thus $R_{(2),(2)}=1+s_{(1)}+2s_{(2)}+s_{(1,1)}+s_{(1,1,1)}+2s_{(2,1)}+s_{(2,2)}+s_{(3)}+s_{(3,1)}+s_{(4)}$, whose coefficients are exactly the reduced coefficients by [F1].

By [F2], $(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)=U_nR_{\alpha,\beta}$ for every $n\ge0$; by [F5], $U_nR_{\alpha,\beta}$ is the coefficient of $t^n$ in $\sigma[tX]R_{\alpha,\beta}[tX-1]$, and since $U_n$ is $\mathbb Z$-linear with $U_n(s_\gamma)=s_{\gamma[n]}$ by [F3], it equals $\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_{\gamma[n]}$, a finite sum. Hence the displayed identity holds for every $n\ge0$ at the level of Jacobi–Trudi completions.

In the admissible range $n\ge\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,|\beta|+\beta_1\}$ the padded sequences $\alpha[n],\beta[n]$ are partitions, so by [F3] the left side of step 2.1 is the internal product $s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}$ of two honest Schur functions; this proves the first display in exactly the stated range and shows that the range is the full set of $n$ for which both inputs are partitions.

*Rank-four cancellation.* Apply $U_4$ to the ten terms of step 1.2. The tails $\varnothing,(1),(2),(1,1),(1,1,1)$ give $s_{(4)},s_{(3,1)},s_{(2,2)},s_{(2,1,1)},s_{(1,1,1,1)}$ respectively. The tails $(2,1),(2,2)$ give zero by repeated straightening indices. The tails $(3),(3,1),(4)$ give $-s_{(2,2)},-s_{(2,1,1)},-s_{(3,1)}$ respectively by [F3]–[F4]. With their multiplicities from step 1.2, the sum is $s_{(4)}+s_{(1,1,1,1)}+s_{(2,2)}$; in particular its $(2,2)$ coefficient is $2-1=1$, whereas the reduced $(2)$ coefficient is $2$. This proves the announced cancellation locally.

*Coefficient form.* For $\delta\vdash n$, pair the identity of step 2.1 against $s_\delta$ using orthonormality [F4]: the left side gives $\langle s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]},s_\delta\rangle_H=g^\delta_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]}$ by [F4], and the right side gives $\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\langle s_{\gamma[n]},s_\delta\rangle_H$, where each factor is a Hall pairing of the Jacobi–Trudi determinant $s_{\gamma[n]}$ with a Schur function, hence a signed multiplicity of a Schur constituent, $0$ or $\pm1$ by [F4]. This is the second display, and it shows that individual coefficients can receive both positive and negative contributions from different $\gamma$ and need not equal $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$.

*Choice and finiteness.* Every step uses finite sums: the Schur expansion of $R_{\alpha,\beta}$ is finite by [F1], the sum over $\gamma$ in step 2.1 is finite, and the coefficient extraction of step 4.1 uses the finite degree-$n$ part of the Schur basis. No form of the axiom of choice is used; the identity is asserted for all admissible ranks, not only for the eventually stable ones.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ one has the finite nonnegative
expansion
$$\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta} =\sum_{\mu,\lambda,\eta,\rho,\theta,\pi} c^\gamma_{\mu,\theta,\pi}\,c^\alpha_{\rho,\lambda,\theta}\, c^\beta_{\rho,\eta,\pi}\,g^\mu_{\lambda,\eta},$$
the sum over all six-tuples of partitions (only finitely many summands are
nonzero), where the $c$'s are the threefold Schur coefficients
([[def-iterated-schur-coefficients]]) and the $g$'s are the ordinary Kronecker
coefficients ([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

Consequences.

1. $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}>0$ if and only if there exist partitions
   $\mu,\lambda,\eta,\rho,\theta,\pi$ with all four coefficients
   $c^\gamma_{\mu,\theta,\pi}$, $c^\alpha_{\rho,\lambda,\theta}$,
   $c^\beta_{\rho,\eta,\pi}$ and $g^\mu_{\lambda,\eta}$ positive.
2. For every nonzero summand the degree equations
   $|\alpha|=|\rho|+|\lambda|+|\theta|$,
   $|\beta|=|\rho|+|\eta|+|\pi|$,
   $|\gamma|=|\mu|+|\theta|+|\pi|$ and $|\mu|=|\lambda|=|\eta|$ hold.
3. For fixed $\alpha,\beta$ the index set is finite: for a nonzero summand
   $\rho,\lambda,\theta$ are contained in $\alpha$, $\rho,\eta,\pi$ are
   contained in $\beta$, and $|\mu|=|\lambda|$.
4. All summands are nonnegative integers, so no cancellation occurs.

**threefold Schur coefficient**
$$c^\delta_{a,b,c}:=[s_\delta]\,s_a s_b s_c,$$
the coefficient of $s_\delta$ in the ordinary product of the three Schur
functions of $\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]); when
$|\delta|\ne|a|+|b|+|c|$ the coefficient is $0$, the product being homogeneous
of degree $|a|+|b|+|c|$. Since
$s_as_b=\sum_\phi c^\phi_{a,b}s_\phi$ with

([[thm-littlewood-richardson-schur-product-expansion]],
[[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]]), substituting gives
$$c^\delta_{a,b,c}=\sum_\phi c^\phi_{a,b}\,c^\delta_{\phi,c} =\sum_\psi c^\psi_{a,c}\,c^\delta_{\psi,b},$$

each $c^\delta_{a,b,c}$ is a nonnegative integer, and the two displayed

$$c^\delta_{a,b,c}=\langle s_a s_b s_c,\,s_\delta\rangle_H,$$

([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]). No fourfold or
longer iterated coefficient is introduced here; iterating the two identities
above gives every nested product of three factors, and the symmetry of the
three subscripts is used throughout this page.

Since $|\gamma|=|\alpha|+|\beta|$, this gives $2|\rho|+|\mu|=0$, so $\rho=\mu=\varnothing$ and then $|\lambda|=|\eta|=0$, so $\lambda=\eta=\varnothing$.

*Collapse of the sum.* With $\rho=\lambda=\eta=\mu=\varnothing$, the only possibly nonzero summands have $c^\alpha_{\varnothing,\varnothing,\theta}=[s_\alpha]s_\theta=\delta_{\alpha,\theta}$ and $c^\beta_{\varnothing,\varnothing,\pi}=[s_\beta]s_\pi=\delta_{\beta,\pi}$, and $g^\varnothing_{\varnothing,\varnothing}=1$; hence $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}=c^\gamma_{\varnothing,\alpha,\beta}=c^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ by the symmetry of the threefold coefficient in [F2], which is the first display.

If $\beta=\varnothing$, the skew shape is empty and its unique empty tableau proves this; this is also the induction base. Suppose $\beta\ne\varnothing$. Existence: fill row $i$ of the skew shape $(\alpha+\beta)/\alpha$, which has $\beta_i$ cells, with the letter $i$; the rows are constant and hence weakly increasing, the columns are strictly increasing because the letters increase down the rows, and the reading word is $1^{\beta_1}2^{\beta_2}\cdots$, which is lattice because $\beta$ is weakly decreasing. Uniqueness: let $T$ be a Littlewood–Richardson tableau of shape $(\alpha+\beta)/\alpha$ and content $\beta$. The first letter of its reading word is the rightmost cell of the first skew row; the lattice condition on the prefix of length one forces that letter to be $1$, and since the row is weakly increasing every cell of the first row is $1$. The first row is read first and consists of exactly $\beta_1$ cells, so it exhausts the $\beta_1$ letters $1$ of the content. Deleting the first row leaves the shape $(\alpha'+\beta')/\alpha'$ with $\alpha'=(\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\dots)$, $\beta'=(\beta_2,\beta_3,\dots)$, carrying no letter $1$; its reading word, with every letter decreased by one, satisfies the lattice condition: the comparisons among letters $\ge2$ hold because they hold for the corresponding prefixes of the original lattice word, and the comparison with letter $1$ is not required after the shift. For all partitions $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ one has the finite nonnegative
expansion
$$\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta} =\sum_{\mu,\lambda,\eta,\rho,\theta,\pi} c^\gamma_{\mu,\theta,\pi}\,c^\alpha_{\rho,\lambda,\theta}\, c^\beta_{\rho,\eta,\pi}\,g^\mu_{\lambda,\eta},$$
the sum over all six-tuples of partitions (only finitely many summands are
nonzero), where the $c$'s are the threefold Schur coefficients
([[def-iterated-schur-coefficients]]) and the $g$'s are the ordinary Kronecker
coefficients ([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

Consequences.

1. $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}>0$ if and only if there exist partitions
   $\mu,\lambda,\eta,\rho,\theta,\pi$ with all four coefficients
   $c^\gamma_{\mu,\theta,\pi}$, $c^\alpha_{\rho,\lambda,\theta}$,
   $c^\beta_{\rho,\eta,\pi}$ and $g^\mu_{\lambda,\eta}$ positive.
2. For every nonzero summand the degree equations
   $|\alpha|=|\rho|+|\lambda|+|\theta|$,
   $|\beta|=|\rho|+|\eta|+|\pi|$,
   $|\gamma|=|\mu|+|\theta|+|\pi|$ and $|\mu|=|\lambda|=|\eta|$ hold.
3. For fixed $\alpha,\beta$ the index set is finite: for a nonzero summand
   $\rho,\lambda,\theta$ are contained in $\alpha$, $\rho,\eta,\pi$ are
   contained in $\beta$, and $|\mu|=|\lambda|$.
4. All summands are nonnegative integers, so no cancellation occurs.

derivations.claim: Since $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}>0$ is a sum of nonnegative integers, some summand is positive; fix such a summand, whose four coefficients are positive and whose sizes satisfy the degree equations of [F1].

*The three differences.* Using the degree equations and $|\lambda|=|\eta|=|\mu|$, compute $|\alpha|+|\beta|-|\gamma|=(|\rho|+|\lambda|+|\theta|)+(|\rho|+|\eta|+|\pi|)-(|\mu|+|\theta|+|\pi|)=2|\rho|+|\lambda|+|\eta|-|\mu|=2|\rho|+|\mu|\ge0$; next $|\alpha|+|\gamma|-|\beta|=(|\rho|+|\lambda|+|\theta|)+(|\mu|+|\theta|+|\pi|)-(|\rho|+|\eta|+|\pi|)=|\lambda|+|\mu|+2|\theta|-|\eta|=|\mu|+2|\theta|\ge0$; and symmetrically $|\beta|+|\gamma|-|\alpha|=(|\rho|+|\eta|+|\pi|)+(|\mu|+|\theta|+|\pi|)-(|\rho|+|\lambda|+|\theta|)=|\mu|+2|\pi|\ge0$. Each difference is a sum of nonnegative integers, giving the three inequalities for this summand.

Since these inequalities depend only on the sizes of $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ and not on the chosen positive summand, they hold whenever $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}>0$, that is, for every $\gamma\in\operatorname{Supp}(\alpha,\beta)$. This is precisely the assertion that the support lies in the triangle region cut out by the three size inequalities. The argument is a finite computation with nonnegative integers and uses no choice principle; the empty partition is allowed, and then the corresponding inequality is the trivial nonnegativity bound.

For partitions $\delta,a,b,c$ with $|\delta|=|a|+|b|+|c|$, define the
**threefold Schur coefficient**
$$c^\delta_{a,b,c}:=[s_\delta]\,s_a s_b s_c,$$
the coefficient of $s_\delta$ in the ordinary product of the three Schur
functions of $\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]); when
$|\delta|\ne|a|+|b|+|c|$ the coefficient is $0$, the product being homogeneous
of degree $|a|+|b|+|c|$. Since
$s_as_b=\sum_\phi c^\phi_{a,b}s_\phi$ with
$c^\phi_{a,b}$ the Littlewood–Richardson coefficients
([[thm-littlewood-richardson-schur-product-expansion]],
[[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]]), substituting gives
$$c^\delta_{a,b,c}=\sum_\phi c^\phi_{a,b}\,c^\delta_{\phi,c} =\sum_\psi c^\psi_{a,c}\,c^\delta_{\psi,b},$$
the sums over partitions $\phi$ of $|a|+|b|$ and $\psi$ of $|a|+|c|$; hence
each $c^\delta_{a,b,c}$ is a nonnegative integer, and the two displayed
expressions agree with the definition. These coefficients are symmetric in
$a,b,c$ because the product $s_as_bs_c$ is commutative, and equivalently
$$c^\delta_{a,b,c}=\langle s_a s_b s_c,\,s_\delta\rangle_H,$$
by the orthonormality of the Schur basis
([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]). No fourfold or
longer iterated coefficient is introduced here; iterating the two identities
above gives every nested product of three factors, and the symmetry of the
three subscripts is used throughout this page.

Let $\lambda,
u$ be partitions with $[\lambda]\subseteq[
u]$, and let $\mu$ be a partition with $|
u|=|\lambda|+|\mu|$. Use the conventions of [[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]] for the skew diagram $
u/\lambda$ and for semistandard skew tableaux of shape $
u/\lambda$, and those of [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] for the content of a tableau; recall that entries of a semistandard skew tableau weakly increase along rows and strictly increase down columns ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]] fixes the English row and column coordinates).

The **reading word** $w(T)$ of a semistandard skew tableau $T$ of shape $
u/\lambda$ is the word obtained by reading the rows of $T$ from right to left, beginning with the top row and proceeding to the bottom row. The word $w(T)=a_1a_2\cdots a_N$ is a **lattice word** (a lattice permutation) if in every prefix $a_1\cdots a_p$ and for every $i\ge1$ the number of letters $i$ in the prefix is at least the number of letters $i+1$; the empty word is a lattice word vacuously.

A **Littlewood--Richardson tableau** (LR tableau) of shape $
u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$ is a semistandard skew tableau of shape $
u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$ whose reading word is a lattice word. The **Littlewood--Richardson coefficient** $c^
u_{\lambda\mu}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ is the number of LR tableaux of shape $
u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$; it is $0$ when $[\lambda]
ot\subseteq[
u]$, when $|
u|
e|\lambda|+|\mu|$, or when no such tableau exists. For $\mu=\varnothing$ and $
u=\lambda$ the empty skew tableau is the unique tableau of content $\varnothing$, its reading word is empty, and hence $c^\lambda_{\lambda\varnothing}=1$; more generally $c^\lambda_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\mu=\varnothing$, and $c^
u_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\lambda\subseteq
u$ and $|
u|=|\lambda|+|\mu|$.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta$ and every integer
$n\ge\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,\,|\beta|+\beta_1\}$:
$$s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,s_{\gamma[n]},$$
an identity in the symmetric function ring, where $s_{\gamma[n]}$ is the
Jacobi–Trudi determinant attached to the integer sequence
$\gamma[n]=(n-|\gamma|,\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\dots)$, equal to $0$ or $\pm1$ times
a Schur function
([[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]],
[[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), and $*$ is the internal product
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

For an ordinary partition $\delta\vdash n$ the coefficient of $s_\delta$ is
$$g^\delta_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]} =\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\, \langle s_{\gamma[n]},s_\delta\rangle_H,$$
where each Hall factor is $0$ or a sign coming from Jacobi–Trudi
straightening ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]).
At small admissible ranks the signed terms can cancel or coalesce;
individual coefficients need not yet equal their reduced values. The range
displayed is precisely the set of $n$ for which $\alpha[n]$ and $\beta[n]$
are partitions.

**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$, with missing parts read as zero, the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]). When this sequence is used as
a partition label, omit trailing zero entries; in particular
$\varnothing[0]=\varnothing$ and the missing first part is zero.

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is

$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)s_\nu$. In particular $s_{\alpha[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{\alpha[n]}=0$ for $n<0$: every term of the
determinant expansion has total degree $n$, so for $n<0$ some factor has
negative index and vanishes.

$\Lambda$ ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n(\Lambda)\subseteq\Lambda^n$ for $n\ge0$ (and $U_n=0$ for
$n<0$), while $V$ raises degree by one; in particular $V(1)=s_{(1)}$. The operators
are extended linearly, and $V^k$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of $V$.

degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that
$$s_{\alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{\beta[n_0+k]}=V^k\bigl(s_{\alpha[n_0]}*s_{\beta[n_0]}\bigr) \qquad\text{for all }k>0,$$

the display is least for any other property. Existence, least-ness and the
exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

$$\langle s_\lambda,s_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$.

Let $\operatorname{ch}:R_S\to\Lambda$ be the Frobenius characteristic restricted
to the graded ordinary representation ring of the symmetric groups
([[def-frobenius-characteristic-map]],
[[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). By
[[thm-frobenius-characteristic-is-an-isometric-graded-ring-isomorphism]] it is a
degree-preserving $\mathbb Z$-module isomorphism onto the stable symmetric
function ring $\Lambda=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}\Lambda^m$, so its restriction
$\operatorname{ch}:R(S_m)\to\Lambda^m$ is an isomorphism for every $m\ge0$.

For $f\in\Lambda^m$ and $g\in\Lambda^n$ define
$$f*g:=\begin{cases}\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)\cdot\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)\bigr),&m=n,\\[2pt]0,&m\ne n,\end{cases}$$
where $\cdot$ is the pointwise (internal tensor) product of class functions on
$S_m$; extend $*$ bilinearly to all of $\Lambda$. Call $*$ the
**internal (Kronecker) product** of symmetric functions.

**Well-definedness.** For $m=n$ the class functions $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)$
and $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)$ lie in $R(S_m)$, the integral span of the
irreducible characters of $S_m$
([[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). The
pointwise product of two honest characters of $S_m$ is again an honest
character, namely the character of the tensor product of the underlying
representations ([[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]),
and products of $\mathbb Z$-combinations of characters are computed
bilinearly; hence the pointwise product of two elements of $R(S_m)$ lies in
$R(S_m)$, and applying the isomorphism $\operatorname{ch}$ lands in $\Lambda^m$.
The product is therefore well defined and takes $\Lambda^m\times\Lambda^m$ to
$\Lambda^m$.

**Basic properties.** The product is bilinear by construction and inherits
commutativity and associativity from the pointwise product of class functions.
It preserves degrees, in the sense that $\Lambda^m*\Lambda^n\subseteq\Lambda^m$
for $m=n$ and is $0$ for $m\ne n$. On $\Lambda^n$ the unit is
$h_n=s_{(n)}=\operatorname{ch}(\text{trivial character of }S_n)$ for $n>0$,
and in degree zero it is $h_0=s_\varnothing=1$, because the
trivial character is the unit for pointwise multiplication on $R(S_n)$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]]
identifies $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^{(n)})=s_{(n)}=h_n$). The graded direct sum
$\Lambda$ has **no global unit** for $*$: if $e\in\Lambda$ had finite degree
support and $n$ were a degree with $e_n=0$ while $\Lambda^n\ne0$, then
$(e*h_n)_n=e_n*h_n=0\ne h_n$, so $e*h_n\ne h_n$; a global unit would require
$e_n$ to be a unit of $(\Lambda^n,*)$ for every $n$. In particular the ordinary
product unit $1\in\Lambda^0$ is not a unit for $*$ on the positive degrees.

**Schur expansion.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the definition and
the Specht character dictionary $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]])
give
$$s_\lambda*s_\mu=\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\chi^\lambda\cdot\chi^\mu\bigr)=\operatorname{ch}\Bigl(\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\chi^\nu\Bigr)=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\,s_\nu,$$
because $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the character of
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ and its decomposition has multiplicities
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the transport goes through the
choice-free Frobenius characteristic isomorphism and finite-dimensional
representation theory of finite groups.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete
reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition, by
[[thm-isotypic-decomposition-of-a-completely-reducible-representation-is-unique]]
(Proof step 2.1 identifies each grouped block with the defining isotypic sum).
In particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.

derivations.claim: *Upper bound on the support.* Let $\gamma$ have $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\ne0$ and choose a nonzero summand of [F1]. First derive the needed row bounds from [F2]: if $c^\zeta_{a,b}>0$ and its first skew row is nonempty, the rightmost entry is the first reading-word letter and must be $1$; weak row increase forces all added first-row entries to be $1$. Thus $\zeta_1-a_1\le b_1$; an empty first skew row gives the same inequality. Iterating gives $\gamma_1\le\mu_1+\theta_1+\pi_1$. Containment, applied with $\theta$ (respectively $\pi$) first by symmetry, gives $\theta_1\le\alpha_1$, $\pi_1\le\beta_1$; the degree equations give $|\lambda|+|\theta|\le|\alpha|$ and $|\eta|+|\pi|\le|\beta|$. Therefore $\gamma_1\le\mu_1+\theta_1+\pi_1\le|\mu|+\theta_1+\pi_1$, so $|\gamma|+\gamma_1\le(|\mu|+|\theta|+|\pi|)+(|\mu|+\theta_1+\pi_1)=2|\mu|+|\theta|+\theta_1+|\pi|+\pi_1$; using $|\mu|=|\lambda|=|\eta|$ this is $(|\lambda|+|\theta|+\theta_1)+(|\eta|+|\pi|+\pi_1)\le(|\alpha|+\alpha_1)+(|\beta|+\beta_1)$ by [F2]. Hence every nonzero reduced coefficient has $|\gamma|+\gamma_1\le N$.

*Both inputs empty.* Here $N=0$, $\alpha[n]=\beta[n]=(n)$ for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{(n)}*s_{(n)}=s_{(n)}$ by [F7]; also $V^n(1)=V^n(s_\varnothing)=s_{(n)}$ by [F6], since $V$ adds a box to the first row and $s_{\varnothing}=1$. Hence $s_{\alpha[n+k]}*s_{\beta[n+k]}=s_{(n+k)}=V^k(s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]})$ for all $n\ge0,k>0$, with no negative-rank product invoked, so $\operatorname{stab}(\varnothing,\varnothing)=0$, the least possible value of the defining index.

*Attainment and identification of the maximum.* The partition $\gamma^\ast:=\alpha+\beta$ satisfies $|\gamma^\ast|+\gamma^\ast_1=|\alpha|+|\beta|+(\alpha_1+\beta_1)=N$ and $\bar g^{\gamma^\ast}_{\alpha,\beta}=c^{\gamma^\ast}_{\alpha,\beta}=1$ by [F4]; hence $\max\{|\gamma|+\gamma_1:\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\ne0\}=N$. In particular $|\gamma|+\gamma_1\le n$ for every support label and every $n\ge N$, so all support labels $\gamma[n]$ are ordinary partitions at such $n$; this proves the stated support maximum.

*$V$-stability from $N$.* For $n\ge N$ the identity of [F3] is available (the thresholds $|\alpha|+\alpha_1,|\beta|+\beta_1$ are $\le N$) and every $\gamma[n]$ in the finite support is a partition by step 2.1; applying [F3] at $n+k$ and using [F4] term by term gives $s_{\alpha[n+k]}*s_{\beta[n+k]}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_{\gamma[n+k]}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}V^k(s_{\gamma[n]})=V^k(s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]})$ for all $k>0$, together with the fixed nonnegative Schur expansion at every rank $n\ge N$. Hence $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)\le N$ in the sense of the Definition.

*$N$ is not in the image of $V$, when $N>0$.* If $N>0$ then $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is nonempty and the partition $(\alpha+\beta)[N]=(N-|\alpha|-|\beta|,(\alpha+\beta)_1,\dots)=(\alpha_1+\beta_1,\alpha_1+\beta_1,\dots)$ has equal first two parts, which are positive because at least one of $\alpha,\beta$ is nonempty. At rank $N$ the coefficient of $s_{(\alpha+\beta)[N]}$ in the product is $\bar g^{\alpha+\beta}_{\alpha,\beta}=1$ by [F4] and step 3.1. If $N>0$ and the product at $N$ lay in the image of $V$, then by [F6] its coefficient of $s_{(\alpha+\beta)[N]}$ would be $0$, a contradiction.

*Least-ness, both inputs nonempty.* Suppose $\alpha\ne\varnothing\ne\beta$. Then $N-1=|\alpha|+|\beta|+\alpha_1+\beta_1-1\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ and $\ge|\beta|+\beta_1$, since $|\beta|+\beta_1\ge1$ and $|\alpha|+\alpha_1\ge1$; so $N-1$ is an admissible rank and the product at $N-1$ is defined. If some $n_0<N$ satisfied the stabilization condition of the Definition, then the product at $N$ would equal $V^{N-n_0}$ of the product at $n_0$, which lies in the image of $V$, contradicting step 4.1; taking $n_0=N-1$ shows in particular that the product at $N$ is not $V$ of the product at $N-1$. Hence $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)=N$ in this case.

*Least-ness, exactly one input empty.* Say $ eta=\varnothing
e\alpha$, so $N=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is the least rank at which $\alpha[n]$ (and $ eta[n]=(n)$) is an ordinary partition. By [F5], every $\gamma$ with $ ar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\varnothing}
e0$ satisfies $|\gamma|\le|\alpha|\le|\emptyset|+|\gamma|=|\gamma|$, hence $|\gamma|=|\alpha|$, and then [F4] gives $ ar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\varnothing}=c^\gamma_{\alpha,\varnothing}=\delta_{\gamma,\alpha}$; so the product at rank $N$ is exactly $s_{\alpha[N]}$, whose first two parts are $\alpha_1,\alpha_1$ with $\alpha_1\ge1$. The obstruction of step 4.1 therefore applies at $N$: the product at $N$ does not lie in the image of $V$, so no $n_0<N$ can satisfy the stabilization condition, while $n_0=N$ does by step 3.1. The case $\alpha=\varnothing
e eta$ is symmetric.

*Conclusion.* Combining steps 3.1, 5.1, 5.2 and 1.2 gives $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)=N=|\alpha|+|\beta|+\alpha_1+\beta_1$ in all cases, with the fixed nonnegative expansion and $V$-stability from $N$ onward; the statement claims nothing about sharpness for an individual coefficient, and the proof used only finite sums, the proved all-rank expansion and the unit of the internal product. No choice principle is used.

For every partition $\lambda$, let $s_\lambda\in\Lambda$ be the stable Schur
function defined by bialternants
([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]). For any integers
$r\ge\ell(\lambda)$ and $c\ge\ell(\lambda')$, pad $\lambda$ and $\lambda'$
with zero parts to lengths $r$ and $c$, respectively. Then
$$s_\lambda=\det\bigl(h_{\lambda_i-i+j}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le r}=\det\bigl(e_{\lambda'_i-i+j}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le c},$$
where $h_k,e_k\in\Lambda$ are the stable complete and elementary functions
([[thm-elementary-and-complete-families-freely-generate-the-stable-ring]],
[[def-elementary-symmetric-polynomials]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]). In these
determinants use $h_0=e_0=1$, set $h_k=e_k=0$ for $k<0$, and take the empty
determinant to be $1$.

Work in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$. For a
partition $\rho$ write
$m_i(\rho):=\#\{j:\rho_j=i\}$ and
$z_\rho:=\prod_{i\ge1}i^{m_i(\rho)}m_i(\rho)!$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]).

For partitions $\lambda$ and $\rho$ of the same integer, let $N(\lambda,\rho)$
be the number of ways to distribute the cycles of a permutation $w$ of cycle
type $\rho$ among the $\ell(\lambda)$ rows, labelled $1,\dots,\ell(\lambda)$,
so that row $j$ receives cycles whose lengths sum to $\lambda_j$. Cycles of
equal length count as **distinct** here, because they are distinct cycles of
$w$; equivalently,

$$N(\lambda,\rho)=\sum_{(m_i^{(j)})}\ \prod_{i\ge1}\frac{m_i(\rho)!}{\prod_j m_i^{(j)}!},$$

the sum over all matrices $(m_i^{(j)})$ of nonnegative integers with
$\sum_j m_i^{(j)}=m_i(\rho)$ for every $i$ and
$\sum_i i\,m_i^{(j)}=\lambda_j$ for every $j$; each summand is the product
over $i$ of the number of ways to assign the $m_i(\rho)$ labelled cycles of
length $i$ to rows with the prescribed multiplicities $m_i^{(j)}$, so
$N(\lambda,\rho)$ is a nonnegative integer. Then

$$h_\lambda=\sum_{\rho\vdash|\lambda|}N(\lambda,\rho)\,\frac{p_\rho}{z_\rho}\qquad\text{in }\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}.$$

In particular $h_d=\sum_{\rho\vdash d}p_\rho/z_\rho$ for every $d\ge0$.

For every $n\ge0$ and every $\lambda\vdash n$, let $S^\lambda$ be the complex
Specht module of shape $\lambda$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]) and $\chi^\lambda$
its character, an irreducible character of $S_n$
([[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]]). Then

$$\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda\in\Lambda^n,$$

the stable Schur function of shape $\lambda$
([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]). In particular $\operatorname{ch}$
maps the $\mathbb Z$-basis $\{\chi^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $R(S_n)$ to the
$\mathbb Z$-basis $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $\Lambda^n$, and all values
$\chi^\lambda(\rho)$ are integers.

For all partitions $\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash n$,
$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=\bigl\langle\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu,\chi^\nu\bigr\rangle=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\chi^\lambda(\sigma)\chi^\mu(\sigma)\chi^\nu(\sigma),$$
where $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the pointwise product of class functions and the
sum uses the real-valuedness of the irreducible characters, so that no
conjugation appears on the third factor.

For every $n\ge0$ and every $\lambda\vdash n$, let $S^\lambda$ be the complex
Specht module of shape $\lambda$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]) and $\chi^\lambda$
its character, an irreducible character of $S_n$
([[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]]). Then

$$\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda\in\Lambda^n,$$

the stable Schur function of shape $\lambda$
([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]). In particular $\operatorname{ch}$
maps the $\mathbb Z$-basis $\{\chi^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $R(S_n)$ to the
$\mathbb Z$-basis $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $\Lambda^n$, and all values
$\chi^\lambda(\rho)$ are integers.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex

([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the

reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition, by
[[thm-isotypic-decomposition-of-a-completely-reducible-representation-is-unique]]
(Proof step 2.1 identifies each grouped block with the defining isotypic sum).
In particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.

For $\alpha=\beta=(2)$, every rank $n\ge4$ product is $U_nR_{(2),(2)}$, where
$$R_{(2),(2)}=1+s_{(1)}+2s_{(2)}+s_{(1,1)}+s_{(1,1,1)}+2s_{(2,1)}+s_{(2,2)}+s_{(3)}+s_{(3,1)}+s_{(4)}.$$
Its coefficients are the reduced coefficients, and all other reduced coefficients vanish. This finite polynomial and its rank-four cancellation are proved in steps 1.2 and 3.2 above.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta$ with missing parts read as zero,
$$\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)=N:=|\alpha|+|\beta|+\alpha_1+\beta_1,$$
with $\operatorname{stab}$ as in
[[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]].

More precisely. At every $n\ge N$ all support labels $\gamma[n]$ of the
finite support of $\bar g^\bullet_{\alpha,\beta}$ are ordinary partitions, the
full product has the fixed nonnegative Schur expansion
$s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_{\gamma[n]}$,
and the family is $V$-stable from $N$ onward. If both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are
nonempty, $N-1$ is admissible and the product at $N$ is not $V$ of the product
at $N-1$: the coefficient of $s_{(\alpha+\beta)[N]}$ is $1$, its first two
parts are equal, and no such Schur basis vector lies in the image of $V$. If
exactly one input is empty, $N$ is already the least ordinary input rank, and
the same image obstruction at $N$ excludes any earlier stabilization index in
the Jacobi–Trudi convention of the Definition. If both inputs are empty,
$N=0$, $s_{(n)}*s_{(n)}=s_{(n)}$ (including $s_{(0)}=1$) and $V^n(1)=s_{(n)}$,
so stabilization begins at zero and no negative-rank product is invoked. No
sharpness for an individual coefficient is claimed.

**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$, with missing parts read as zero, the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]). When this sequence is used as
a partition label, omit trailing zero entries; in particular
$\varnothing[0]=\varnothing$ and the missing first part is zero.

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is
$0$; if $\min_jq_j\ge0$ then $\nu$, after deleting trailing zero entries, is a partition of $|\mu|$
with at most $m$ parts and the Jacobi–Trudi identity gives the value
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)s_\nu$. In particular $s_{\alpha[n]}\in\Lambda^n$

$\Lambda$ ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n(\Lambda)\subseteq\Lambda^n$ for $n\ge0$ (and $U_n=0$ for

are extended linearly, and $V^k$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of $V$.

degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that
$$s_{\alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{\beta[n_0+k]}=V^k\bigl(s_{\alpha[n_0]}*s_{\beta[n_0]}\bigr) \qquad\text{for all }k>0,$$

does not assert that such an $n_0$ exists, nor that a value of $n_0$ satisfying
the display is least for any other property. Existence, least-ness and the
exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

Let $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ be a partition with $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let $n\ge0$ be
an integer. Read $|\varnothing|=0$ and $\alpha_1=0$ when
$\alpha=\varnothing$. Whenever

derivations.claim: *All six products from local straightening.* Apply $U_n$ to the ten-term polynomial of [F3]. The five tails $\varnothing,(1),(2),(1,1),(1,1,1)$ are already admissible for every $n\ge4$. For the remaining five tails, sorting the $q_j$ of [F4] gives the following values at ranks $4,5,6,7$; each becomes its ordinary padded Schur function once its threshold $|\gamma|+\gamma_1$ is reached: $\begin{array}{c|cccc}\gamma&4&5&6&7\\\hline(2,1)&0&s_{(2,2,1)}&s_{(3,2,1)}&s_{(4,2,1)}\\(2,2)&0&0&s_{(2,2,2)}&s_{(3,2,2)}\\(3)&-s_{(2,2)}&0&s_{(3,3)}&s_{(4,3)}\\(3,1)&-s_{(2,1,1)}&-s_{(2,2,1)}&0&s_{(3,3,1)}\\(4)&-s_{(3,1)}&-s_{(3,2)}&-s_{(3,3)}&0\end{array}$. Multiplying by the coefficients in [F3] and collecting terms yields precisely the four displayed products at ranks $4$ through $7$. At ranks $8,9$ every tail is admissible, and padding the same polynomial yields precisely the two displayed products, including zeros for every unlisted Schur label. This verifies the six products without assuming the source table.

*The reduced coefficients and stable ranks.* By [F3], the ten coefficients of $R_{(2),(2)}$ are exactly the listed reduced coefficients, and all others vanish. For $n\ge8$, [F4] sends each padded label to its rank-$(n+1)$ padding without changing its coefficient. Thus the rank-eight product maps to the rank-nine product term by term, and [F3] proves stability for all later ranks, with exact index $8=2+2+2+2$.

*Failure at rank seven.* The rank-seven expansion has the nine labels $(7),(4,1,1,1),(5,2),(6,1),(5,1,1),(4,2,1),(3,2,2),(4,3),(3,3,1)$, with coefficients $1,1,2,1,1,2,1,1,1$. Increasing their first parts by one gives exactly the rank-eight expansion minus $s_{(4,4)}$. That last term has coefficient one and is outside the image of $V$, since every $V(s_\delta)$ has strictly larger first part than second part. Hence the rank-eight product is not $V$ of the rank-seven product.

*The individual coefficient.* The computed rank-four and rank-five products have coefficient one at their $(n-2,2)$ labels; ranks six and seven have coefficient two, and every $n\ge8$ has the reduced coefficient two by step 2.1. Thus this coefficient first becomes constant at rank six, while the whole product first becomes $V$-stable at rank eight. All computations and comparisons are finite, and no choice principle is used.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta$ and every integer
$n\ge\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,\,|\beta|+\beta_1\}$:
$$s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,s_{\gamma[n]},$$
an identity in the symmetric function ring, where $s_{\gamma[n]}$ is the
Jacobi–Trudi determinant attached to the integer sequence
$\gamma[n]=(n-|\gamma|,\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\dots)$, equal to $0$ or $\pm1$ times
a Schur function
([[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]],
[[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), and $*$ is the internal product
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

For an ordinary partition $\delta\vdash n$ the coefficient of $s_\delta$ is
$$g^\delta_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]} =\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\, \langle s_{\gamma[n]},s_\delta\rangle_H,$$
where each Hall factor is $0$ or a sign coming from Jacobi–Trudi
straightening ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]).
At small admissible ranks the signed terms can cancel or coalesce;
individual coefficients need not yet equal their reduced values. The range
displayed is precisely the set of $n$ for which $\alpha[n]$ and $\beta[n]$
are partitions.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta$ with missing parts read as zero,
$$\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)=N:=|\alpha|+|\beta|+\alpha_1+\beta_1,$$
with $\operatorname{stab}$ as in
[[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]].

More precisely. At every $n\ge N$ all support labels $\gamma[n]$ of the
finite support of $\bar g^\bullet_{\alpha,\beta}$ are ordinary partitions, the
full product has the fixed nonnegative Schur expansion
$s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_{\gamma[n]}$,
and the family is $V$-stable from $N$ onward. If both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are
nonempty, $N-1$ is admissible and the product at $N$ is not $V$ of the product
at $N-1$: the coefficient of $s_{(\alpha+\beta)[N]}$ is $1$, its first two
parts are equal, and no such Schur basis vector lies in the image of $V$. If
exactly one input is empty, $N$ is already the least ordinary input rank, and
the same image obstruction at $N$ excludes any earlier stabilization index in
the Jacobi–Trudi convention of the Definition. If both inputs are empty,
$N=0$, $s_{(n)}*s_{(n)}=s_{(n)}$ (including $s_{(0)}=1$) and $V^n(1)=s_{(n)}$,
so stabilization begins at zero and no negative-rank product is invoked. No
sharpness for an individual coefficient is claimed.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group acting faithfully on its $r$-dimensional complex reflection representation $V$, and put $S=\mathbb C[V]$. Then $S^W$ is a polynomial algebra on $r$ homogeneous algebraically independent basic invariants, and $S$ is free of rank $|W|$ over $S^W$. More generally these conclusions hold for every finite subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ generated by complex reflections (nonidentity transformations fixing a hyperplane pointwise). In the Weyl case the generating root reflections have order two; no classification or Coxeter presentation is needed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite complex reflection group, in particular a finite Weyl reflection group, with $r=\dim V$. Put $S=\mathbb C[V]$, $R=S^W$, $I=SR_+$, and let $d_1,\ldots,d_r$ be the degrees of basic invariants. Then
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(S/I,t)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1+t+\cdots+t^{d_i-1}),\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}(S/I)=\prod_i d_i=|W|.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$. A **finite reduced crystallographic root system** is a finite subset $\Phi\subseteq E\setminus\{0\}$ spanning $E$, such that for every $\alpha,\beta\in\Phi$ the integer $\langle\beta,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2(\beta,\alpha)/(\alpha,\alpha)$ is integral, the reflection $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ preserves $\Phi$, and the only scalar multiples of $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ are $\alpha,-\alpha$. The **Weyl group** $W$ is the subgroup of linear isometries of $E$ generated by these reflections. A **root reflection** means one of the $s_\alpha$. The empty root system on $E=0$ is allowed, with $W=\{1\}$.

Choose $t\in E$ such that $(t,\alpha)\ne0$ for every root. Put $\Phi^+=\{\alpha:(t,\alpha)>0\}$ and $\Phi^-=-\Phi^+$. A positive root is **simple** if it is not the sum of two positive roots. The following positive-root lemma proves that the simple roots form a basis $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ and that the simple reflections $s_i=s_{\alpha_i}$ generate $W$; no such assertion is assumed by this definition. Once proved, let $\ell(w)$ be the least number of simple reflections in a word for $w$ and let $\operatorname{Inv}(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi^+:w\alpha\in\Phi^-\}$. A word is reduced if its length equals $\ell(w)$.

Identify $E$ with its dual by the displayed form, so $\alpha^\vee=2\alpha/(\alpha,\alpha)$. The root and coroot groups are $Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha$ and $Q^\vee=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha^\vee$. The **weight group** is $P=\{\lambda\in E:(\lambda,\alpha^\vee)\in\mathbb Z\text{ for all }\alpha\in\Phi\}$; the positive-root lemma proves it is a lattice with basis the vectors dual to the simple coroots. Put $Q_+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$, and write $\mu\le\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q_+$. The open and closed positive chambers are $\mathcal C=\{x:(x,\alpha_i)>0\text{ for all }i\}$ and $\overline{\mathcal C}=\{x:(x,\alpha_i)\ge0\text{ for all }i\}$. A weight is dominant if it belongs to $P\cap\overline{\mathcal C}$. More generally chambers are the connected components of $E\setminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}\alpha^\perp$. The closed-chamber representative and stabilizer assertions are proved later, not included as axioms.

Let $\Phi\subseteq E$ be a reduced crystallographic root system and let
$W=W(\Phi)$ be its Weyl group
([[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]]). Then $W$ acts simply transitively on
the set of open Weyl chambers of $\Phi$
([[def-open-and-closed-weyl-chambers]]): for any two open chambers $C,C'$
there is exactly one $w\in W$ with $w(C)=C'$.

Let $\Phi$ be the root system from [[thm-the-root-set-is-a-reduced-crystallographic-root-system]]. For a root $\alpha$, define the corresponding coroot by

$$\alpha^\vee:=\frac{2H_\alpha}{\alpha(H_\alpha)} \in \mathfrak h,$$

where $H_\alpha$ is the vector from [[def-killing-dual-vector-attached-to-a-root]]. The associated **root reflection** is the linear map

$$s_\alpha(\lambda):=\lambda-\lambda(\alpha^\vee)\alpha \qquad (\lambda\in \mathfrak h^*).$$

The subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak h^*)$ generated by these reflections is the **Weyl group** $W$, acting on $\mathfrak h^*$ in the usual way.

derivations.claim: Molien trace identity: for $|t|<1$, $$\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)=\sum_{d\ge0}\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^W)_dt^d=\frac1{|W|}\sum_{w\in W}\det(1-tw|_E)^{-1}.$$ Indeed the $W$-averaging operator $\pi=(1/|W|)\sum_ww$ is a projection onto $S^W$ in each finite-dimensional degree $S_d$, so $\dim(S^W)_d=\operatorname{tr}\pi|_{S_d}=(1/|W|)\sum_w\operatorname{tr}(w|_{S_d})$; on the other hand, for an operator with eigenvalues $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r$ on $E$, and hence $\mu_1^{-1},\dots,\mu_r^{-1}$ on $E^*$, the degree-$d$ trace $\operatorname{tr}(w|_{S_d})$ is the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial $h_d(\mu_1^{-1},\dots,\mu_r^{-1})$, whose generating function is $\prod_i(1-\mu_i^{-1}t)^{-1}=\det(1-tw^{-1}|_E)^{-1}$; averaging over $w$ and reindexing by $w\mapsto w^{-1}$ gives the displayed formula.

For $w\in W$ let $f$ be the dimension of its fixed space in $E$. Then $\det(1-tw|_E)=(1-t)^fg_w(t)$ with $g_w(t)=\prod_{\lambda
eq1}(1-t\lambda)$ over the remaining eigenvalues $\lambda$ of $w$ and $g_w(1)=\prod_{\lambda
eq1}(1-\lambda)
eq0$; all eigenvalues lie on the unit circle. In particular if $w
eq1$ fixes a hyperplane pointwise, then $f=r-1$, the remaining eigenvalue is $-1$, and $\det(1-tw|_E)=(1-t)^{r-1}(1+t)$.

If $w\in W$, $w
eq1$, fixes a hyperplane $H$ pointwise, then $H=\alpha^\perp$ for some root $\alpha$. Suppose $H$ is different from every root hyperplane. Then all intersections $H\cap eta^\perp$ are proper linear subspaces of $H$, whose finite union cannot cover it over the infinite field $\mathbb R$ (the product of nonzero defining linear forms is a nonzero polynomial). Thus choose $x\in H$ with $(x, eta)
eq0$ for every root $ eta$; then $x$ lies in an open chamber $C$, and $w(x)=x$ gives $x\in C\cap w(C)$. As $w$ permutes the chambers, $C\cap w(C)
eq\varnothing$ forces $w(C)=C$, so $w$ lies in the stabilizer of $C$, which is trivial by simple transitivity. Hence $H$ is contained in a root hyperplane, and since both are hyperplanes, $H=\alpha^\perp$ for a root $\alpha$.

Put $u=1-t$. Since $1-t^{d_i}=1-(1-u)^{d_i}=d_iu-\frac{d_i(d_i-1)}2u^2+O(u^3)$, one has $(1-t^{d_i})^{-1}=d_i^{-1}u^{-1}(1+\frac{d_i-1}2u+O(u^2))$, and therefore $$\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{d_i})^{-1}=\Bigl(\prod_id_i\Bigr)^{-1}u^{-r}\Bigl(1+\frac{\sum_i(d_i-1)}2u+O(u^2)\Bigr)=\frac1{|W|}u^{-r}\Bigl(1+\frac{\sum_i(d_i-1)}2u+O(u^2)\Bigr),$$ the last equality by [F1]; this product equals $\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)$ for $|t|<1$ by [F1].

The map $\alpha\mapsto s_\alpha$ induces a bijection from the set $\Phi^+$ of positive roots onto the set of reflections in $W$; consequently $W$ has exactly $|\Phi^+|$ reflections. Injectivity: $s_\alpha=s_\beta$ forces the two reflections to have the same fixed hyperplane, so $\beta=\pm\alpha$, and among positive roots $\beta=\alpha$. Surjectivity: every reflection of $W$ has a fixed hyperplane, which is $\alpha^\perp$ for some root $\alpha$ by step 1.3, and the reflection of $E$ with fixed hyperplane $\alpha^\perp$ is unique, namely $s_\alpha$. Since $s_\alpha=s_{-\alpha}$ and every root hyperplane is $\alpha^\perp$ for exactly one positive root by [F3], distinct positive roots give distinct reflections.

Expanding the right-hand side of step 1.1 at $t=1$ in the variable $u=1-t$ gives $$\frac1{|W|}\sum_{w\in W}\det(1-tw|_E)^{-1}=\frac1{|W|}\Bigl(u^{-r}+\frac{|\Phi^+|}2u^{-(r-1)}+O(u^{-(r-2)})\Bigr).$$ The identity $w=1$ contributes $u^{-r}$. A nonidentity $w$ with fixed space of dimension $r-1$ is a reflection, and there are exactly $|\Phi^+|$ of them by step 2.1; each contributes $\det(1-tw)^{-1}=(1-t)^{-(r-1)}(1+t)^{-1}=u^{-(r-1)}(\frac12+O(u))$ by step 1.2, because $(1+t)^{-1}=(2-u)^{-1}=\frac12+O(u)$. Every other nonidentity $w$ has $f\le r-2$, hence contributes $u^{-f}\cdot O(1)=O(u^{-(r-2)})$ by step 1.2.

Steps 1.4 and 3.1 compute the same meromorphic function of $u$ near $u=0$; comparing the coefficients of $u^{-(r-1)}$, which are finite, gives $\frac1{|W|}\cdot\frac{\sum_i(d_i-1)}2=\frac1{|W|}\cdot\frac{|\Phi^+|}2$, hence $\sum_i(d_i-1)=|\Phi^+|$.

With the page degree normalization $\deg E=2$ the basic invariant $w_i$ has page degree $2d_i$, so the coinvariant algebra has Hilbert series $\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})/(1-t^2)^r$ and its top degree is $\sum_i2d_i-2r=2\sum_i(d_i-1)=2|\Phi^+|=|\Phi|$, by step 4.1 and the published degree computation for the coinvariant algebra.
