For a polynomial Bott-Samelson bimodule $B$, $M=B\otimes_SR$ is finite free over the right $R$. A left denominator nonzero at the origin acts invertibly: modulo the right maximal ideal its constant plus positive-degree part is invertible, since positive left invariants annihilate the finite-dimensional coinvariant reduction and positive-degree operators there are nilpotent; Nakayama makes its matrix invertible over $R$. Both left and right actions therefore extend to $R$. Weyl invariants balance across every tensor factor, so these actions factor through $A$. Iterating the map in step 1.2 identifies the localized polynomial tensor word with $V_R$ of the deformed wall word, with empty word the identity graph $R=V_R\Delta_R(\lambda)$. All identifications preserve the generic tuple branches and the right parameter. The fixed average coordinate in the type-A permutation model is split off before this construction.

Let $Q,Q'$ be deformed block projectives. Their canonical comparison under $V_R$ is an isomorphism at every height-one prime. At nonroot primes, the distinct simple Verma components give one-label Morita equivalences; at root primes, each projective decomposes into the two elementary projectives of step 1.1 by lifting its actual residue decomposition with the projective Hom base-change maps in [F3], so that step verifies every pair of summands. The source Hom module is finite free over $R$ by [F3]. The target $\operatorname{Hom}_A(V_RQ,V_RQ')$ need not be assumed free in advance: it is the submodule of finite free $\operatorname{Hom}_R(V_RQ,V_RQ')$ satisfying the finitely many linear commutation equations for a finite $R$-basis of $A$. Inside the generic Hom space it is the intersection of its height-one localizations, since a rational matrix belongs to the free ambient matrix lattice precisely when all its height-one localizations do, and the $A$-linearity equations already hold generically. The coefficientwise UFD intersection argument of the central-action lemma gives the same intersection property for the source Hom lattice. Their height-one equalities therefore prove the comparison is an isomorphism over $R$; in particular the target is now free. This is full faithfulness on deformed projectives.

For polynomial Bott-Samelson modules $M,M'$ the module $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,M')$ is the localization of the polynomial Hom module, and the composite $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,M')\otimes_R\mathbb C\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_R}(Q_R,Q_R')\otimes_R\mathbb C\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(Q,Q')\cong\operatorname{Hom}_C(VQ,VQ')$ is the natural reduction map by step 3.1, projective Hom base change and the ordinary Struktursatz, all maps being the canonical composition maps; hence reduction-of-Hom holds for Bott-Samelson modules and, by taking summands, for all polynomial Soergel bimodules, the degree components giving the graded statement.

Absolute complex extension follows by the actual same equations as real extension, not by a real-only assertion. For the rational $B_w$, write $E_{\mathbb Q}^0$ for its finite-dimensional local degree-zero endomorphism algebra and $J_{\mathbb Q}$ for its nilpotent radical; [F4] gives $E_{\mathbb Q}^0/J_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q$. Fixed-degree maps are kernels of finite rational linear commutation equations on homogeneous generator images. Tensoring these equations with the flat field $\mathbb C$ identifies $E_{\mathbb C}^0=E_{\mathbb Q}^0\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$. Its ideal $J_{\mathbb Q}\otimes\mathbb C$ is nilpotent and its quotient is $\mathbb C$, so every element with nonzero scalar residue is invertible by a finite geometric series; hence this is a local algebra with residue $\mathbb C$. The same flat equations preserve its top graph and degree. Extending each rational word decomposition gives a complex decomposition into these absolutely indecomposable labels; finite Krull--Schmidt uniqueness then classifies every summand of every complex word. Thus the normalized polynomial $B_w$ has the required local degree-zero algebra over $\mathbb C$. Step 4.1 makes the degree-zero algebra of $\bar B_w$ its quotient, hence local. Here is the needed passage to ungraded endomorphisms. For the finite-dimensional graded algebra $E=\operatorname{End}(\bar B_w)$, grading scalings preserve its Jacobson radical $J$; interpolation in finitely many distinct scaling parameters extracts every homogeneous component, so $J$ is graded. The semisimple quotient $E/J$ is a product of matrix algebras by [F6]. Its grading derivation preserves each factor, since a derivation kills central idempotents. Every derivation $D$ of $\operatorname{Mat}_n(\mathbb C)$ is inner: with matrix units, $H=\sum_i D(e_{i1})e_{1i}$ satisfies $D(a)=Ha-aH$, by applying the product rule to $e_{ij}e_{k1}$ and summing in $k$. The grading derivation is diagonalizable; writing $H=H_s+H_n$ shows $\operatorname{ad}H_n=0$, because it is the commuting nilpotent part of $\operatorname{ad}H$. A scalar nilpotent matrix is zero, so $H$ is semisimple up to an irrelevant scalar. Its degree-zero centralizer is consequently a product of matrix algebras on its eigenspaces. Thus $(E/J)_0$ is semisimple. It is a quotient of the local $E_0$, so it equals $\mathbb C$; a product of such centralizers can have dimension one only if there is a single matrix factor of size one. Hence $E/J=\mathbb C$, and $E$ is local. This proves that $\bar B_w$ remains indecomposable after forgetting grading; it supplies the graded-algebra argument rather than attributing innerness to Wedderburn-Artin.

The normalized top summand is self-dual without assuming an unproved indecomposable-form assertion. In the unshifted tensor ring of a length-$k$ word, each added reflection factor is a quadratic finite free extension with basis $1,\alpha_s$ and relation $\alpha_s^2\in S^s$. The coefficient-of-$\alpha_s$ functional has perfect pairing matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; composing these functionals along the tensor tower gives a perfect right-$S$ pairing on its rank-$2^k$ basis. It is left-invariant by commutativity of the tensor ring. The total trace has degree $-2k$, so shifting the word by $(k)$ gives a degree-zero isomorphism from the Bott-Samelson bimodule to its invariant right dual $D B=\operatorname{Hom}_S(B,S)$. For a reduced word of $w$, $B_w$ is the unique summand with nonzero top graph $w$, of generic right rank one there; all other summands have strictly lower graph support by [F4]. Duality preserves generic graph branches: a left scalar on a rank-one branch acts by the same scalar on its right dual. Therefore $D B_w$ is an indecomposable summand of the very same self-dual word, has its $w$ branch, and must be the identical unique top summand, with no shift. Thus $B_w\cong D B_w$. Finite right projectivity makes duality commute with right origin reduction, so $\bar B_w$ has a graded self-duality centered at zero. Any two finite graded lifts with the same indecomposable underlying $C$-module differ by a shift: homogeneous components of an ungraded isomorphism and its inverse give $1=\sum_d g_{-d}f_d$ in the local degree-zero endomorphism algebra; one summand is a unit, so $f_d$ is an isomorphism after a shift (its source and target have the same finite dimension). A nonzero shift cannot preserve centered self-duality, by symmetry of the extreme degrees. This proves unique centered normalization; rank one has degrees $-1,1$, and an uncentered shift gives $0,2$.

Induction on Bruhat length gives the label dictionary: for a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$, $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ is the unique new top-label summand of $\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)$ by [F2], and applying $V$ and the iterated wall-crossing formula gives the new summand of the reduced left tensor word $\overline{B_{s_k}\cdots B_{s_1}}$, whose top graph label is the inverse $w^{-1}$, while every proper subexpression contributes already-matched smaller labels; full faithfulness of step 3.1 for the deformed side and the indecomposability of step 5.1 match the two new summands uniquely, so $VP(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\bar B_{w^{-1}}$, and distinct labels remain non-isomorphic because $V$ is fully faithful on projectives.

The type-A equivalence and normalized dictionary follow from steps 4.1 through 6.2. For a semisimple product of type-A factors, reflection words reorder into the independent factor words and their reductions are tensor products of the factor reductions. Their endomorphism algebra is the tensor product of the finite factor endomorphism algebras: in finite bases, the commutation equations for the two independent coefficient algebras give this tensor-Hom identity. Each factor algebra is local with residue $\mathbb C$ by step 5.1; the sum of its tensor-extended radicals is nilpotent and its quotient is $\mathbb C$, so the product reduction is indecomposable. The labels, inverse convention and centered self-duality therefore combine factorwise; a rank-zero factor contributes the unit. The ungraded equivalence for every complex semisimple type needs no unprovided diagrammatic classification: define its Weyl-group Soergel-module category as the additive category of summands of polynomial Bott-Samelson right reductions. For every reflection realization, $S=S^s\oplus\alpha_sS^s$, and Weyl invariants balance across the tensor factors; the elementary quotient computation gives $B_s\otimes_SC=(C\otimes_{C^s}C)(1)$ exactly as in the wall-crossing theorem. Thus forgetting shifts identifies all right-reduced words with the ordinary $V$-images of wall words starting at $V\Delta(\lambda)=\mathbb C$. Ordinary full faithfulness [F1] lifts every idempotent between these images uniquely to an idempotent of their projective words. Since all projectives occur as summands of such words by [F2], this is a fully faithful and essentially surjective equivalence in every type. Its indecomposable labels can be read from the unique new projective summands themselves. The additional type-A polynomial/diagrammatic label and centered self-dual normalization are exactly those established in steps 5.1 through 6.2; no type-A classification is substituted for a general-type classification.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and work in a regular integral type-A block over
$\mathbb C$. With the page's right wall-crossing convention and left
$C$-module values of $V$, there is an equivalence
$$V\colon\operatorname{Proj}(\mathcal O_\lambda)\xrightarrow{\sim}\{\text{ungraded Soergel modules }B\otimes_S\mathbb C\},\qquad P(w\cdot\lambda)\longmapsto\bar B_{w^{-1}}.$$
The target is the additive category of direct summands of the right reductions
of polynomial Bott-Samelson bimodules, or equivalently of iterated
$C\otimes_{C^s}(-)$ applied to the trivial module $\mathbb C$, not to the
regular module $C$. For a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$, the projective is the unique new
top-label summand of $\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)$; applying
$V$ gives the new summand of $\overline{B_{s_k}\cdots B_{s_1}}$, thus the
inverse label. These normalized indecomposable polynomial lifts supply
self-dual auxiliary gradings; in rank one the centered degrees are $-1,1$,
with degrees $0,2$ after an uncentered shift. Forgetting grading recovers the
projective dictionary. More generally the ungraded equivalence with
Weyl-group Soergel modules holds for every complex semisimple regular integral
block; the type-A diagrammatic label comparison applies only in type A.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be dominant regular integral,
$R=S(\mathfrak h)_{(0)}$ the localization at the origin, and use the selected
component $\mathcal D_R^{[\lambda]}(\lambda)$ of the tensor-generated deformed
family of [[def-the-deformed-category-o-family-and-its-specializations]]. For
every $x\in W$ there is a projective $P_R(x,\lambda)$ in the deformed
$\lambda$-block whose residue fiber is $P(x\cdot\lambda)$; it is unique up to
isomorphism, and every indecomposable of this selected tensor component is one
of these lifts. Each lift has a finite deformed Verma flag with the same
multiplicities as its closed fiber. More generally, a finite projective in this
block is a direct summand of a finite sum of truncated induced projectives
representing relative weight spaces; for every map of deformation algebras
$R\to R'$ its base change is projective in the corresponding truncated category
and
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_R}(P,N)\otimes_RR'\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_{R'}}(P\otimes_RR',N\otimes_RR').$$
For a finite Verma-filtered target $N$ this Hom module is finite free over
local $R$. A $\mathfrak g\otimes R$-linear map between such finite
projective/Verma-filtered objects whose residue fiber is an isomorphism is
itself an isomorphism, weight by weight. For a dot-dominant integral target
$\nu$, including singular $\nu$, the same local projective construction gives
all lifts in its deformed block, with labels the distinct cosets $W/W_\nu$,
where $W_\nu:=\operatorname{Stab}_W(\nu+\rho)$ is the dot stabilizer;
these lifts belong to the target component $\mathcal D_R^{[\nu]}(\lambda)$ of a
regular-source tensor family. It is neither necessary nor asserted that the
singular Verma itself generates every target projective, and the other central
components of the full tensor family are not claimed to have only these
indecomposables.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be dominant regular integral,
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$, $R=S_{(0)}$, and $P_R=P_R(w_0,\lambda)$ the deformed
antidominant projective. Write $\operatorname{HC}_\rho\colon Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to S^W$
for the published shifted Harish-Chandra isomorphism,
$\sigma_\lambda(f)(\epsilon)=f(\lambda+\rho+\epsilon)$, and define
$$a_\lambda\colon Z\otimes_{\mathbb C}R\longrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R,\qquad z\otimes r\longmapsto\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))\otimes r.$$
Then $a_\lambda$ and the action map $Z\otimes R\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)$
are surjective and have the same kernel, inducing a canonical $R$-algebra
isomorphism
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)\cong R\otimes_{R^W}R.$$
On a generic Verma constituent of highest weight $x\cdot\lambda+\epsilon$, $z$
acts by the scalar
$\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)(x(\lambda+\rho)+\epsilon)=\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))(x^{-1}\epsilon)$;
these scalars vary with $x$, and the center need not act by a single scalar on
$P_R$. After tensoring the right $R$ factor with the residue field at $0$, the
endomorphism algebra becomes $C=S/(S^W_+S)$. More generally, for dot-dominant
integral $\nu$ the corresponding algebra is $R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R$, where
$W_\nu$ is the dot stabilizer. Translation out of that facet identifies the
singular antidominant projective with the regular one; under these shifted
Harish-Chandra identifications, its induced endomorphism map is the inclusion
$R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R\hookrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a regular integral block and simple reflection
$s$, with $C=\operatorname{End}(P(w_0\cdot\lambda))$, there is a natural
isomorphism of functors to left $C$-modules
$$V\theta_s\cong C\otimes_{C^s}V.$$
Equivalently the functor is tensoring by the $(C,C)$-bimodule
$C\otimes_{C^s}C$, with left action on the first factor and right action on the
second. In type A over $\mathbb C$, its polynomial lift is tensoring on the
left by $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$; read up to the auxiliary suspension
normalisation fixed by the rank-one case, the right origin reduction of $B_s$
is the two-dimensional module of centered degrees $-1,1$, for $M=S$ the
coinvariant reduction satisfies
$B_s\otimes_SC\cong(C\otimes_{C^s}C)(1)$ in the same normalisation, and
$B_s\otimes_S\mathbb C$ itself is not the bimodule $C\otimes_{C^s}C$: the
former has vector-space dimension two, whereas the latter has dimension
$2|W|$. Forgetting the grading gives the displayed category-$\mathcal O$
formula, and no grading on arbitrary category-$\mathcal O$ objects is asserted.

**Graphs and supports.** Keep $k=\mathbb Q$, $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with
$\deg x_i=2$, and the affine scheme $V=\mathbb A^n_k=\operatorname{Spec}R$,
whose $k$-points are $V(k)=k^n$. Use the place-permuting action of $S_n$
from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of
the upper support submodule by the part supported strictly above $Gr(y)$.

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated
in degree $-d$; in particular $\Delta_e(0)=\nabla_e(0)=R_e=R$.

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

**Support filtrations.** A $\Delta$-flag of a graded $R$-bimodule $M$ is a
finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols
refer to a chosen compatible enumeration (the next items on this page prove that
they do not depend on it). With $T_x$ the Hecke basis of
[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and
$\widetilde T_x:=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$, the character sums attached to a flag are
$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

**Small $n$.** For $n\le1$ there is a single element $e$ and every object is a finite direct sum of shifts $\bigoplus_j R(d_j)$. Its one-graph flags have these summands as quotients, so $h_\Delta=\sum_jv^{d_j}\widetilde T_e$ and $h_\nabla=\sum_jv^{-d_j}\widetilde T_e$; in particular both characters send the unit $R$ to $1$.

**The reduction.** Work over the ring $S=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of the real
scalar-extension definition ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]),
with $S_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}S_d$ the ideal of positive-degree elements; the residue
field of the right action is
$$k:=S/S_+=\mathbb R,$$
with quotient map $S\twoheadrightarrow k$, $s\mapsto \bar s$. For a graded
$(S,S)$-bimodule $M$ that is finite free as a right $S$-module put
$$\overline M:=M\otimes_Sk=M/MS_+,$$
the **reduction** of $M$: a finite-dimensional graded $k$-vector space, on which
the left $S$-action descends because $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $MS_+$ is
stable under left multiplication. Write $\overline M^{\,i}$ for its homogeneous
component of degree $i$, $d_i(M):=\dim_{\mathbb R}\overline M^{\,i}$ for the
graded dimensions, and
$$\dim\overline M:=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}d_i(M)\,v^{-i}$$
for the **graded dimension** (a finite Laurent polynomial); all tensor products
below are over $S$. For a morphism $f:M\to M'$ of graded bimodules, i.e. a
degree-zero bi-$S$-linear map, the induced map
$$\overline f:\overline M\to\overline{M'},\qquad \overline f(m+MS_+):=f(m)+M'S_+ ,$$
is well defined and $k$-linear of degree zero, because $f(MS_+)\subseteq M'S_+$.
Reduction is a functor from finite right-free graded bimodules to finite
dimensional graded $k$-vector spaces; it preserves finite direct sums and
shifts, in the sense $\overline{M(d)}=\overline M(d)$ in the Elias-Williamson
shift convention $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$.

**The dominant Lefschetz operator.** Fix a strictly dominant degree-two
element
$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^nc_jx_j\in S_2,\qquad c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_n ,$$
which exists by [[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]] (for
example $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$); recall that this is exactly the condition
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot $\alpha_i^\vee$ in the
coordinate normalization of this page
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]). Let
$\rho\cdot(-):M\to M$, $m\mapsto\rho m$, denote left multiplication by $\rho$.
Since $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $\rho\,(MS_+)\subseteq MS_+$, this
operator preserves the submodule $MS_+$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$k$-linear endomorphism
$$L_0:=\rho\cdot(-):\overline M\longrightarrow\overline M,\qquad m+MS_+\longmapsto \rho m+MS_+,$$
called the **dominant Lefschetz operator** on $\overline M$. For rational
objects $B_x,B_s$ with real scalar extensions
$B_x^R=B_x\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ and $B_s^R$, the same construction
applies to the reduced tensor product
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}=\overline{(B_xB_s)^R}$, where $B_xB_s$ denotes the
tensor product over the rational polynomial ring; the operator $L_0$ on it is
the value $\zeta=0$ of the deformed operator $L_\zeta$ defined later on this
page.

**Descent detection.** For every $w\in S_n$ and every simple reflection $s_i$
one has
$$(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ell(s_iw)>\ell(w).$$
Indeed, $(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)=c_{w^{-1}(i)}-c_{w^{-1}(i+1)}$ is positive
exactly when $w^{-1}(i)<w^{-1}(i+1)$, the left-ascent criterion for inversion
length. Thus the displayed evaluation detects left descents; applied to
$w=x^{-1}$ it detects right descents of $x$, because $\ell(s_ix^{-1})=\ell(xs_i)$.

**Grading conventions.** The reduced module $\overline{B_x^R}$ has bottom degree
$-\ell(x)$ and top degree $+\ell(x)$; the unreduced bimodule has nonzero
components in arbitrarily high degrees. On a reduced module the "centered" degree $-i$ is the
internal degree $-i$, and the Lefschetz operator raises internal degree by two.
All homological (complex) shifts are written $[\,j\,]$ and all internal shifts
$(d)$, as on the rest of this page; the Bruhat order used throughout is the
rank-inequality order of
[[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]].

Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every projective object
of $\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]).

More precisely, each projective cover $P(\mu)$ produced by
[[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]] is a direct summand of the
projective object $\operatorname{pr}_C(E\otimes M(\lambda))$ of
[[lem-finite-dimensional-tensors-reach-every-block-simple]], which is a

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For all weights
$\lambda$ and $\mu$,
$$(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))=[\Delta(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[M(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
where $P(\lambda)$ is the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$, the left-hand
multiplicity is the Verma-flag multiplicity of
[[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]], and the right-hand

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]], and write
$\Delta(\mu)=M(\mu)$ for the standard objects of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], i.e. the Verma modules
of [[def-verma-module]].

A **finite Verma flag** of an object $X$ of $\mathcal O$ — also called a
**standard flag** or a **$\Delta$-flag** — is a finite increasing sequence of
subobjects
$$0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$$
such that each quotient $X_i/X_{i-1}$ is isomorphic to a Verma module
$\Delta(\mu_i)=M(\mu_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,n$. An object admitting such a flag is
called **Verma-filtered**. Since the flag is exhausted by its factors, its
class in the Grothendieck group
$K_0(\mathcal O)$ of [[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]
is
$$[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n[\Delta(\mu_i)].$$

For a Verma-filtered object $X$ and a weight $\mu$, the **multiplicity**
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is the number of indices $i$ with $\mu_i=\mu$ in a Verma
flag of $X$. This number is independent of the chosen flag by
[[lem-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-independent-of-the-flag]], so the notation
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is well-defined for Verma-filtered $X$.

is zero; a nonzero Verma-filtered object has at least one factor. A one-step
flag of $X$ is exactly an isomorphism $X\cong\Delta(\mu)$ for a single weight
$\mu$, so the objects with a one-step flag are the Verma modules themselves.
The flag is a chain of subobjects of $X$ in the module category; it is not
required to split, and later examples show that it need not.

[[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]] for the Cartan
reflection representation, with its grading fixed there. Then:

shifted by $\lambda+\rho$ in the published $\operatorname{HC}_\rho$ convention,
followed by the quotient map $\rho$) and $Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$

$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P(w_0\cdot\lambda)\ \cong\ C,$$

canonically and independently of the choice of projective cover inside its
isomorphism class;

coinvariant algebra; no graded lift of category $\mathcal O$ is asserted or

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal O_\lambda$ be a regular integral block

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published items. In the
regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$ of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]] the
assignment
$$c\colon K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z[W],\qquad[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]\longmapsto w,$$
is an isomorphism of abelian groups, and for every simple reflection $s$ the
wall-crossing functor $\theta_s$ of
[[def-wall-crossing-functor-and-unit-counit]] satisfies
$$c\,[\theta_sX]=c\,[X]\cdot(1+s)\qquad\text{for all }X\in\mathcal O_\lambda,$$
right multiplication by $1+s$ in the integral group ring $\mathbb Z[W]$.
Consequently, for a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ one has
$$c\,[\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)]=(1+s_1)(1+s_2)\cdots(1+s_k),$$
the sum of all subexpression products with their actual multiplicities; its top
Bruhat term is $w$ once and all other terms have strictly smaller labels. With
the composition $\theta_{s_1}\cdots\theta_{s_k}$ instead, the factors are
multiplied in the reverse order.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The classes $[L(\lambda)]$, and separately the classes $[M(\lambda)]$, form $\mathbb Z$-bases of $K_0(\mathcal O)$. For a fixed finite central-character label set $\Lambda=W\cdot\lambda$, the transition between its standard and simple classes is unitriangular in any linear order extending $\leq$. This remains true on a downward-closed subset of that finite poset. It is not a claim about finite downward ideals of all of $\mathfrak h^*$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]], and write
$\Delta(\mu)=M(\mu)$ for the standard objects of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], i.e. the Verma modules
of [[def-verma-module]].

A **finite Verma flag** of an object $X$ of $\mathcal O$ — also called a
**standard flag** or a **$\Delta$-flag** — is a finite increasing sequence of
subobjects
$$0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$$
such that each quotient $X_i/X_{i-1}$ is isomorphic to a Verma module
$\Delta(\mu_i)=M(\mu_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,n$. An object admitting such a flag is
called **Verma-filtered**. Since the flag is exhausted by its factors, its
class in the Grothendieck group
$K_0(\mathcal O)$ of [[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]
is
$$[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n[\Delta(\mu_i)].$$

For a Verma-filtered object $X$ and a weight $\mu$, the **multiplicity**
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is the number of indices $i$ with $\mu_i=\mu$ in a Verma
flag of $X$. This number is independent of the chosen flag by
[[lem-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-independent-of-the-flag]], so the notation
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is well-defined for Verma-filtered $X$.

The zero object has the empty flag, and every multiplicity of the zero object
is zero; a nonzero Verma-filtered object has at least one factor. A one-step
flag of $X$ is exactly an isomorphism $X\cong\Delta(\mu)$ for a single weight
$\mu$, so the objects with a one-step flag are the Verma modules themselves.
The flag is a chain of subobjects of $X$ in the module category; it is not

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral block with dominant
representative $\lambda$:

1. Projective functors form a Krull-Schmidt category.
2. Their indecomposables are indexed by $W$, with $\Theta_w$ characterized by
$\Theta_w\Delta(\lambda)\cong P(w\cdot\lambda)$. For a reduced word
$w=s_1\cdots s_k$, the functor $\Theta_w$ is a multiplicity-one summand of
$\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}$, and every other indecomposable summand has a
label $x<w$. In particular every indecomposable projective functor is generated
as a summand by wall crossings.
3. Two projective functors are naturally equivalent exactly when their induced
operators on the Grothendieck group agree.

The characterization concerns evaluation on the dominant projective Verma; no
faithfulness of that evaluation on all natural maps of arbitrary
endofunctors is asserted.

derivations.claim: The two class computations are $c[\theta_t\theta_s\Delta(\lambda)]=(1+s)(1+t)=1+s+t+st$ and $c[\theta_s\theta_t\Delta(\lambda)]=(1+t)(1+s)=1+t+s+ts$, that is $[\theta_t\theta_s\Delta(\lambda)]=[\Delta(\lambda)]+[\Delta(s\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(t\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(st\cdot\lambda)]$ and $[\theta_s\theta_t\Delta(\lambda)]=[\Delta(\lambda)]+[\Delta(t\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(s\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(ts\cdot\lambda)]$.

The two products of [F1], $(1+s)(1+t)$ and $(1+t)(1+s)$, differ: the coefficient of the length-two element $st$ is one in the first and zero in the second, and vice versa for $ts$, while $st\ne ts$ in $S_3$ and the standard classes form a $\mathbb Z$-basis, so the induced class operators on $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$ are different and already differ on the single class $[\Delta(\lambda)]$.
By the determination theorem, two projective functors whose class operators on $K_0$ differ are not naturally equivalent; hence $\theta_s\theta_t\not\cong\theta_t\theta_s$.

Feeding one factor at a time gives $c[\theta_s^2X]=c[X](1+s)^2=2c[X](1+s)=2c[\theta_sX]$ for every $X$, so the class operators of $\theta_s^2$ and of $\theta_s\oplus\theta_s$ agree and the determination theorem gives $\theta_s^2\cong\theta_s\oplus\theta_s\not\cong\operatorname{id}$, since $\theta_s\Delta(\lambda)$ has nonzero class $1+s$; hence $s\mapsto\theta_s$ is not a representation of $W$, the wall-crossing classes are the specialized self-dual Hecke generators $1+s$, whose square is $2(1+s)$; the group generator is recovered on classes by $s=[\theta_s]-1$, and 'generated by wall-crossing' cannot be read as the assignment $s\mapsto\theta_s$ being a representation of $W$.

For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, the **Verma module** is the induced
$\mathfrak g$-module

$$M(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}\mathbb C_\lambda,$$

where $U(\mathfrak g)$ is the quotient algebra of
[[def-universal-enveloping-algebra-as-a-tensor-quotient]] and
$\mathbb C_\lambda$ is [[def-one-dimensional-borel-module-of-weight-lambda]].
Write $v_\lambda:=1\otimes c_\lambda$.  Thus $M(\lambda)$ is the quotient of
$U(\mathfrak g)$ by the left ideal generated by $x$ for $x\in\mathfrak n^+$
and $h-\lambda(h)$ for $h\in\mathfrak h$; in particular,
$\mathfrak n^+v_\lambda=0$ and $hv_\lambda=\lambda(h)v_\lambda$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The simple objects of $\mathcal O$ are exactly the modules $L(\lambda)$, $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, and $L(\lambda)\cong L(\mu)$ if and only if $\lambda=\mu$. Simplicity here excludes zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For all weights
$\lambda$ and $\mu$,
$$(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))=[\Delta(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[M(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
where $P(\lambda)$ is the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$, the left-hand
multiplicity is the Verma-flag multiplicity of
[[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]], and the right-hand
multiplicity is the simple composition multiplicity of the Verma module
$M(\mu)$ ([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published items. Let
$\theta_s$ be the wall-crossing functor of
[[def-wall-crossing-functor-and-unit-counit]] attached to the simple reflection
$s$ in the regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$. For every $w\in W$ the
object $\theta_s\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ has a finite Verma flag with exactly two
factors, namely $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ and $\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)$, each with
multiplicity one; in the Grothendieck group
$$[\theta_s\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]=[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)].$$
Moreover $\theta_s$ is exact and preserves Verma-filtered objects with finite
Verma flags: if $X$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities
$(X:\Delta(v\cdot\lambda))$, then $\theta_sX$ has one with multiplicities
$(\theta_sX:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))=(X:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))+(X:\Delta(us\cdot\lambda))$,
and the same formula holds in $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$. The resulting flag is
not in general split; splitting is neither asserted nor used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a dominant regular integral representative
$\lambda$ and a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$, set
$\theta_{\underline w}=\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}$, so that the standards
follow right multiplication in word order. Then
$$\theta_{\underline w}\Delta(\lambda)\cong P(w\cdot\lambda)\oplus\bigoplus_{x<w}P(x\cdot\lambda)^{m_x},\qquad m_x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.$$
Its class is $(1+s_1)\cdots(1+s_k)$ under the standard class map, with actual
subexpression multiplicities. The BGG matrix satisfies
$(P(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=[\Delta(y\cdot\lambda):L(x\cdot\lambda)]$,
vanishes unless $y\le x$ in the Bruhat order, and has diagonal entries one.
Hence the top summand $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ occurs once and is the only summand
whose flag contains $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$; the remaining multiplicities are
determined by this triangular matrix and the product class. Consequently every
indecomposable projective is a summand of a word of wall crossings applied to
$\Delta(\lambda)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be finite-dimensional complex
semisimple, $\lambda$ the dominant regular integral representative of a block
and $\mathcal O_\lambda$ its block with antidominant weight $w_0\cdot\lambda$.
Let $C$ be the coinvariant algebra of
[[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]] for the Cartan
reflection representation, with its grading fixed there. Then:

(1) the natural maps $Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to C$ (Harish-Chandra isomorphism,
shifted by $\lambda+\rho$ in the published $\operatorname{HC}_\rho$ convention,
followed by the quotient map $\rho$) and $Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$
(multiplication) are surjective with the same kernel;

(2) consequently the multiplication map induces a canonical algebra isomorphism
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P(w_0\cdot\lambda)\ \cong\ C,$$
identifying $C$ with the endomorphism ring of the antidominant projective,
canonically and independently of the choice of projective cover inside its
isomorphism class;

(3) the grading on the right-hand side is the internal grading of the
coinvariant algebra; no graded lift of category $\mathcal O$ is asserted or
used.

This is Soergel's Endomorphismensatz [Soe90, Theorem 7], in the regular integral
case; the companion general form for singular blocks replaces $C$ by the
invariants $C^{W_\lambda}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block theory
([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]]).

In the regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$ of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]] fix the
antidominant weight $w_0\cdot\lambda$ and let
$$P:=P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$$ be a projective cover of $L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]); it is unique up to isomorphism and
indecomposable ([[prop-projective-covers-in-o-are-indecomposable-and-unique]],
[[def-projective-object]]), and it is an injective object of
$\mathcal O_\lambda$. The **Soergel functor** is
$$V:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,-)\colon\mathcal O_\lambda\longrightarrow \operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}\text{-}\mathbf{mod},\qquad M\longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,M),$$
with the left action of $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}$ on
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,M)$ induced by composition on the right of
the source: $a\cdot f=f\circ a$
([[def-projective-functors-on-a-regular-integral-category-o-block]]). Its
values on the standard objects and on the indecomposable projectives are
written $V\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):=V(\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))$ and
$VP(w\cdot\lambda):=V(P(w\cdot\lambda))$. The functor $V$ is exact, because
$P$ is projective, and hence left exact; the identity
$VP\cong\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)$ with its regular module structure
is the Yoneda identification. Replacing the chosen projective cover $P$ by an
isomorphic one changes $V$ by a natural equivalence of functors compatible
with the endomorphism-ring identification, so the construction depends only
on the isomorphism class of $P$.

**Well-definedness: $P$ is injective.** We prove that $P$ is an injective
object of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ using only the listed suppliers, following the
argument of [Soe90, Sections 1.2 and 2.1] in its algebraic form. Put
$\eta:=-\rho$; then $W\cdot\eta=\{\eta\}$, because $w\cdot\eta=w(\eta+\rho)-\rho=-\rho$
for every $w$ ([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]). By
[[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]] the simple
objects are the $L(\mu)$ with $L(\mu)$ determined by $\mu$, and the composition
factors of $M(\eta)$ have highest weights in $W\cdot\eta\cap(\eta-Q^+)=\{\eta\}$;
hence $M(\eta)=L(\eta)$ is simple. By BGG reciprocity
([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]) applied to the single-label block, and the existence
of Verma flags for projectives ([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]]),
the projective cover $P(\eta)$ has a Verma flag with the single factor
$\Delta(\eta)=M(\eta)=L(\eta)$, so $P(\eta)\cong L(\eta)$; the block
$\mathcal O_\eta$ has a single simple object, which is projective, hence is
semisimple by enough projectives ([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]),
and therefore every object of $\mathcal O_\eta$, in particular $L(\eta)$, is
injective as well as projective in $\mathcal O_\eta$
([[def-injective-object]]). A projective object of a block is projective in
$\mathcal O$ ([[lem-block-projection-preserves-projectives]]), and an
injective object of a block is injective in $\mathcal O$ because the block
decomposition is a direct sum of abelian subcategories and the exact
projections restrict split exactness blockwise. Second, we identify a
projective-injective object
in the block $\mathcal O_\lambda$: let $E=L(\lambda+\rho)$ be the
finite-dimensional simple module of highest weight $\lambda+\rho$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]])
and set
$$Q:=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}\bigl(E\otimes L(\eta)\bigr)\in\mathcal O_\lambda,$$
the exact central projection of [[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]].
Since $L(\eta)$ is projective and injective in $\mathcal O$, the tensor product
$E\otimes L(\eta)$ is projective and injective
([[lem-tensoring-a-projective-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-is-projective]]),
and its direct summand $Q$ is projective and injective in $\mathcal O$; the
general exact tensor-block biadjunction of
[[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]] gives the
same conclusion with all adjoints and, by
[[lem-tensoring-a-projective-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-is-projective]],
injectivity (equivalently, $Q$ is a direct summand of a projective-injective
object, and injectivity passes to summands). Third, we compute a
one-dimensional Hom space: since $M(a)$ with $a=w_0\cdot\lambda$ is simple by
the same top-weight argument as for $\eta$ (every other highest weight in
$W\cdot a$ lies strictly above $a$ in the root order), the tensor product
$E^{*}\otimes M(a)$ has a finite Verma flag whose factors are the
$\Delta(a+\nu)$ with $\nu$ running through the weights of the dual module
$E^{*}$, by
[[lem-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-verma-flags]]; here
$E^{*}=L(-w_0(\lambda+\rho))$ ([[prop-highest-weight-of-the-dual-representation]]).
Projecting to the central character $\chi_\eta$ retains exactly the factors
with $a+\nu\in W\cdot\eta=\{\eta\}$, that is $\nu=-w_0(\lambda+\rho)$, the
highest weight of $E^{*}$ of multiplicity one, so
$$\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\eta}\bigl(E^{*}\otimes M(a)\bigr)=L(\eta).$$
The tensor-hom adjunction and the tensor-block adjunction now give
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(Q,L(a))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(L(\eta),E^{*}\otimes M(a))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(L(\eta),L(\eta))\cong\mathbb C,$$
because every homomorphism from the block-$\eta$ simple lands in the
$\chi_\eta$-summand and $L(\eta)$ is simple. Choose the nonzero, hence
surjective, element $q:Q\to L(a)$ and lift it through the projective cover
$P(a)\to L(a)$ to a map $Q\to P(a)$; its image is a submodule of $P(a)$
surjecting onto the head $L(a)$, hence is all of $P(a)$ by essentiality of a
projective cover, so the lift is surjective and splits by projectivity of
$P(a)$. Therefore $P(a)$ is a direct summand of the injective object $Q$
([[def-injective-object]]), and direct summands of injective objects are
injective, so $P=P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ is injective. This argument uses
[[thm-bgg-verma-homomorphism-criterion]] only through the standard embedding
criterion implicit in the top-weight computations, and it does not assume the
Endomorphismensatz.

**The once-each flag.** The tensor flag of $E\otimes M(-\rho)$ has labels
$-\rho+\gamma$ for weights $\gamma$ of $E=L(\lambda+\rho)$. Projection to
$\chi_\lambda$ keeps precisely $\gamma\in W(\lambda+\rho)$, each of
multiplicity one by [[lem-weight-norm-bound-for-finite-dimensional-simple-modules]].
Thus $Q$ has each $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ once. Every such Verma contains
$M(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(a)$ by
[[lem-dominant-integral-dot-translates-embed-in-the-verma-module]]. BGG
reciprocity gives $(P(a):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))\ge1$; the splitting
$Q=P(a)\oplus Q'$ and
[[lem-direct-summands-of-verma-filtered-objects-are-verma-filtered]] give the
opposite bound one. Hence all these multiplicities equal one, $Q'$ has
an empty flag and is zero, and $Q=P(a)$. Since $P(a)$ is projective,
$V$ is exact and $\dim VX=[X:L(a)]$ for finite-length $X$: on simples its
values are $\mathbb C$ at the head label and zero otherwise. Consequently
$\dim V\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)=1$ for every $x$. Every simple submodule of a
Verma is itself a simple Verma: its universal Verma map into that Verma is
injective. Thus the unique simple standard $L(a)$ is its only possible
socle label, and [[thm-verma-homomorphism-spaces-have-dimension-at-most-one]]
makes this socle a single copy of $L(a)$.

For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, the **Verma module** is the induced
$\mathfrak g$-module

$$M(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}\mathbb C_\lambda,$$

where $U(\mathfrak g)$ is the quotient algebra of
[[def-universal-enveloping-algebra-as-a-tensor-quotient]] and
$\mathbb C_\lambda$ is [[def-one-dimensional-borel-module-of-weight-lambda]].
Write $v_\lambda:=1\otimes c_\lambda$.  Thus $M(\lambda)$ is the quotient of
$U(\mathfrak g)$ by the left ideal generated by $x$ for $x\in\mathfrak n^+$
and $h-\lambda(h)$ for $h\in\mathfrak h$; in particular,
$\mathfrak n^+v_\lambda=0$ and $hv_\lambda=\lambda(h)v_\lambda$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The simple objects of $\mathcal O$ are exactly the modules $L(\lambda)$, $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, and $L(\lambda)\cong L(\mu)$ if and only if $\lambda=\mu$. Simplicity here excludes zero.

derivations.claim: Exactness of $V$ applied to $0\to L(-2)\to M(0)\to L(0)\to0$ gives $0\to V(L(-2))\to V(M(0))\to V(L(0))\to0$, that is $0\to\mathbb k\to V(M(0))\to0$, so $V(M(0))\cong\mathbb k$, and $V(P(-2))\cong C$; also $P(-2)$ has indecomposable head $L(-2)$ so $V(L(0))=\operatorname{Hom}(P(-2),L(0))=0$ and $V(L(-2))=\mathbb k$.

Non-faithfulness: $L(0)$ is a nonzero object with one-dimensional endomorphism ring, and $\operatorname{id}_{L(0)}\ne0$ is a nonzero element of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(L(0),L(0))=\mathbb k$, while $V(L(0))=0$ forces its image in $\operatorname{Hom}_C(0,0)=0$ to be zero; so $V$ is not faithful.

Failure of fullness: $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(M(0),L(-2))=0$ while $V(M(0))\cong V(L(-2))\cong\mathbb k$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_C(\mathbb k,\mathbb k)=\mathbb k\ne0$, so the induced map between these Hom spaces is the zero map on a nonzero target and is not surjective.

The two failures use a nonprojective target: $L(0)$ is nonprojective because the nonsplit surjection $M(0)\to L(0)$ would otherwise split, and $L(-2)$ is nonprojective because the nonsplit surjection $P(-2)\to L(-2)$ would otherwise split, with $P(-2)$ indecomposable; hence they do not contradict the Struktursatz [[thm-soergels-struktursatz-full-faithfulness-on-projectives]], whose target hypothesis is exactly that $Q$ be projective (the source may be arbitrary), and they do not refute the separate assertion of faithfulness on the quotient by the $V$-killed Serre subcategory, since $L(0)$ is precisely an object killed by $V$.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of type
$A_{n-1}$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$, positive system $\Phi^+$, Weyl vector
$\rho$, Weyl group $W$ (identified with $S_n$) and dot action
$w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Fix a dominant regular integral weight
$\lambda$, i.e. $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$ for every root and
$\lambda$ integral, and let $\mathcal O_\lambda$ be the corresponding regular
integral block in the conventions of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]]: standard
objects $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)=M(w\cdot\lambda)$, simples $L(w\cdot\lambda)$,
indecomposable projectives $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ for $w\in W$, with
$\lambda=e\cdot\lambda$ the unique dominant and $w_0\cdot\lambda$ the unique
antidominant element and $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$.

This item freezes the following conventions, each inherited from the cited
suppliers and used verbatim below.

(i) **Multiplicity conventions.** $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ is
the Verma-flag multiplicity of [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]] and
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$ the composition multiplicity, and
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$$
by BGG reciprocity ([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]).

(ii) **Bruhat reversal convention.** Along the bijection
$W\ni w\mapsto w\cdot\lambda$ the Bruhat order runs opposite to the dominance
order, in the two exact senses used on this page: $y\le w$ implies
$w\cdot\lambda\le y\cdot\lambda$ in the dominance order, and every nonzero
multiplicity forces the index direction, i.e.
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]\neq0$ implies $y\le w$ in the Bruhat
order. The first sense is the inclusion direction of
[[lem-dominant-integral-dot-translates-embed-in-the-verma-module]] (for
$w\ge y$ one has $M(w\cdot\lambda)\subseteq M(y\cdot\lambda)$, so the highest
weight of the submodule is the lower one), and the second is
[[lem-jordan-holder-factors-of-verma-modules-lie-above-the-head]], which
confines every composition factor of $M(y\cdot\lambda)$ to labels
$w\ge y$. The full statement that the two orders are isomorphic as posets is
not needed here and is not asserted; only these two directions, together with
the finiteness of intervals of the Bruhat order
([[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]), are used.

(iii) **Hecke and Kazhdan–Lusztig normalization.** The Kazhdan–Lusztig basis
$\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ of the normalized type-$A$ Hecke
algebra ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]), with
$$p_{y,w}=v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})$$
in the classical $q=v^{-2}$ normalization
([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), support
$p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, diagonal $p_{w,w}=1$, and simultaneous inversion
symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$.

(iv) **Soergel label and character dictionary.** Write $R_x$ for the
polynomial standard graph bimodule supported at $x$, and $B_x$ for the
normalized indecomposable polynomial Soergel bimodule, which is generally not a
standard graph bimodule. With right reduction $\bar B=B\otimes_S\mathbb C$
and left coinvariant-module values of $V$, the projective dictionary is
$$V(P(w\cdot\lambda))\cong\bar B_{w^{-1}}$$
([[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]]).
The graph label $x$ corresponds to the standard
$\Delta(x^{-1}\cdot\lambda)$. The individual support ranks are measured on the
polynomial lift before reduction, as in
[[prop-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-standard-filtration-ranks-under-v]];
no separated graph-support filtration of the reduced module is asserted.

For degree bookkeeping use precisely the standard-generator normalization of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]:
$\Delta_x(d)=R_x(d-\ell(x))$, and $r_{x,d}(B)$ counts these normalized polynomial
standard layers. Thus the coefficient polynomial is
$$m_x(B;v):=\sum_d r_{x,d}(B)v^d,\qquad h_\Delta(B)=\sum_xm_x(B;v)\widetilde T_x,\qquad\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x.$$
Here $\widetilde T_x$ is the normalized **standard** Hecke element $H_x$ used
in clause (iii) and
[[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]. The published
Soergel split-Grothendieck-ring convention instead names its simple
Kazhdan--Lusztig generators $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_{s_i}+v$; these must not
be confused with the standard element $H_{s_i}=vT_i$
([[thm-split-grothendieck-group-of-the-soergel-category-is-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).
The standard-character supplier
[[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]] identifies $h_\Delta$
with that split-Grothendieck-ring isomorphism. This records the coefficient
normalization, and does not infer the image of a general indecomposable $B_x$
by multiplying simple generators. In particular the character theorem must be
used to identify $h_\Delta(B_x)$ with $\underline H_x$; a product of simple
Soergel classes is a Bott--Samelson class and need not be $[B_x]$.
The inverse labels and all rank comparisons above use auxiliary polynomial
gradings only; forgetting them gives the ordinary projective dictionary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If a projective object
$P$ of $\mathcal O$ admits an epimorphism $P\twoheadrightarrow L$ onto a
simple object $L$, then some indecomposable direct summand of $P$ maps onto
$L$, and that summand is a projective cover of $L$ (an essential epimorphism
with projective source, [[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]).
Any two projective covers of $L$ are isomorphic, although not canonically so,
and the endomorphism ring of a projective cover is local. In particular, for
every simple $L$ there is at most one isomorphism class of indecomposable
projectives with head $L$; when such a cover exists it is written $P(L)$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category in which every object has finite
length, and define an object to be **indecomposable** when it is nonzero and
every decomposition $X\cong Y\oplus Z$ has $Y=0$ or $Z=0$. Then:

1. every object of $\mathcal A$ is a finite direct sum of indecomposable
   objects;
2. the endomorphism ring of an indecomposable object is local, and for an
   endomorphism $f$ of an indecomposable object either $f$ is an isomorphism
   or $f$ is nilpotent;
3. the decomposition is unique up to isomorphism and permutation of the
   summands;
4. an indecomposable projective object $P$ of $\mathcal A$ has a unique
   maximal proper subobject $J(P)$, its quotient $P/J(P)$ is simple, and $P$
   is a projective cover of $P/J(P)$
   ([[def-projective-object]], [[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]];
   projectivity here is relative to $\mathcal A$. In a full subcategory closed
   under submodules, essentiality is the superfluous-kernel condition of the
   cited module definition; projectivity in the ambient module category is
   not asserted).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]], and write
$\Delta(\mu)=M(\mu)$ for the standard objects of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], i.e. the Verma modules
of [[def-verma-module]].

A **finite Verma flag** of an object $X$ of $\mathcal O$ — also called a
**standard flag** or a **$\Delta$-flag** — is a finite increasing sequence of
subobjects
$$0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$$
such that each quotient $X_i/X_{i-1}$ is isomorphic to a Verma module
$\Delta(\mu_i)=M(\mu_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,n$. An object admitting such a flag is
called **Verma-filtered**. Since the flag is exhausted by its factors, its
class in the Grothendieck group
$K_0(\mathcal O)$ of [[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]
is
$$[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n[\Delta(\mu_i)].$$

For a Verma-filtered object $X$ and a weight $\mu$, the **multiplicity**
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is the number of indices $i$ with $\mu_i=\mu$ in a Verma
flag of $X$. This number is independent of the chosen flag by
[[lem-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-independent-of-the-flag]], so the notation
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is well-defined for Verma-filtered $X$.

The zero object has the empty flag, and every multiplicity of the zero object
is zero; a nonzero Verma-filtered object has at least one factor. A one-step
flag of $X$ is exactly an isomorphism $X\cong\Delta(\mu)$ for a single weight
$\mu$, so the objects with a one-step flag are the Verma modules themselves.
The flag is a chain of subobjects of $X$ in the module category; it is not
required to split, and later examples show that it need not.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and work in a regular integral type-A block over
$\mathbb C$. With the page's right wall-crossing convention and left
$C$-module values of $V$, there is an equivalence
$$V\colon\operatorname{Proj}(\mathcal O_\lambda)\xrightarrow{\sim}\{\text{ungraded Soergel modules }B\otimes_S\mathbb C\},\qquad P(w\cdot\lambda)\longmapsto\bar B_{w^{-1}}.$$

of polynomial Bott-Samelson bimodules, or equivalently of iterated
$C\otimes_{C^s}(-)$ applied to the trivial module $\mathbb C$, not to the
regular module $C$. For a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$, the projective is the unique new
top-label summand of $\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)$; applying
$V$ gives the new summand of $\overline{B_{s_k}\cdots B_{s_1}}$, thus the
inverse label. These normalized indecomposable polynomial lifts supply
self-dual auxiliary gradings; in rank one the centered degrees are $-1,1$,
with degrees $0,2$ after an uncentered shift. Forgetting grading recovers the
projective dictionary. More generally the ungraded equivalence with
Weyl-group Soergel modules holds for every complex semisimple regular integral
block; the type-A diagrammatic label comparison applies only in type A.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a projective $P$ in a regular integral type-A
block, choose its polynomial Soergel lift $\mathsf B(P)$ determined by the
preceding projective dictionary: if $P=\bigoplus_wP(w\cdot\lambda)^{m_w}$, take

the graded multiplicity of the polynomial standard graph module supported at
$x$ in its standard support filtration, with the standard-generator
normalization of the polynomial Soergel category. Then
$$(P:\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=\sum_d r_{y^{-1},d}(\mathsf B(P)).$$

and with inverse labels, recovers the ordinary Verma-flag character of $P$.
These are ranks before reduction; no separated Bruhat-support filtration
intrinsic to the finite-dimensional module $V(P)$ is asserted, since the graph
supports coalesce at the origin. The same ungraded multiplicity comparison
holds with the corresponding Weyl-group polynomial/deformed lifts in other
complex semisimple types.

derivations.claim: The object $P:=P(w\cdot\lambda)$ is a nonzero indecomposable projective of $\mathcal O_\lambda$, namely a projective cover of the simple $L(w\cdot\lambda)$, and by the projective dictionary [F2] its Soergel value is $V(P)=\bar B_{w^{-1}}$, the right reduction of the single polynomial lift $B_{w^{-1}}$.

Every decomposition of $P$ into indecomposables is a one-summand decomposition. Indeed, by [F5] a decomposition $P\cong\bigoplus_v P(v\cdot\lambda)^{m_v}$ exists and any two such decompositions agree up to isomorphism and permutation of summands; since the nonzero object $P$ is an indecomposable projective cover by [F4], only one summand can be present, so the decomposition is $P\cong P(v\cdot\lambda)$ for a single label $v$. Applying the equivalence $V$ of [F2] to this isomorphism gives $\bar B_{w^{-1}}\cong\bar B_{v^{-1}}$; as $V$ is a bijection on isomorphism classes of indecomposables, $v=w$. Hence in the dictionary of [F3] the polynomial lift assigned to $P$ is the single term $\mathsf B(P)=B_{w^{-1}}$, with no further summands.

Substitute $\mathsf B(P)=B_{w^{-1}}$ from step 1.2 into the general rank comparison [F3] applied to the projective $P=P(w\cdot\lambda)$: its left side is the Verma-flag multiplicity $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ of [F1] and [F6], and its right side is $\sum_d r_{y^{-1},d}(B_{w^{-1}})$, the sum of the graded standard-support multiplicities of the polynomial lift $B_{w^{-1}}$. type-$A$ block with $W=S_n$, and for $w\in W$ let $B_{w^{-1}}$ be the polynomial

$V(P(w\cdot\lambda))=\bar B_{w^{-1}}$ is its right reduction. Write
$r_{x,d}(B)$ for the graded multiplicity of the polynomial standard graph
module supported at $x$ in the standard support filtration of a polynomial
Soergel bimodule $B$, in the standard-generator normalization of the polynomial
Soergel category. Then for all $y,w\in W$
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=\sum_d r_{y^{-1},d}(B_{w^{-1}}).$$
These are ranks before reduction: the right side sums the graded standard
support multiplicities of the polynomial lift, not multiplicities in any
separated filtration of the finite-dimensional module $V(P(w\cdot\lambda))$.

from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of
the upper support submodule by the part supported strictly above $Gr(y)$.

which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$

[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and

quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each

filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable

graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols

$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

characters of

which by [[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] are
well-defined functions of the bimodule and additive on direct sums, so that
they descend to $\mathbb Z$-linear maps on $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$
with values in the Hecke algebra $H_{S_n}$ of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] whose normalized
generators are $H_i=v(T_i+1)$. Then:

2. $h_\nabla$ is multiplicative, $h_\nabla(XY)=h_\nabla(X)h_\nabla(Y)$, and

([[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]), are used.

symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$.

([[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]]).

$\Delta(x^{-1}\cdot\lambda)$. The individual support ranks are measured on the
polynomial lift before reduction, as in
[[prop-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-standard-filtration-ranks-under-v]];

e0$ when $y

e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

derivations.claim: The comparison of [F1] expresses the Verma-flag multiplicity of the indecomposable projective $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ as the total graded standard-support rank of the polynomial lift $B_{w^{-1}}$: $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=\sum_d r_{y^{-1},d}(B_{w^{-1}})$.

The character theorem [F2] gives $h_\Delta(B_{w^{-1}})=\underline H_{w^{-1}}=\sum_xp_{x,w^{-1}}H_x$. By the coefficient formula of [F3], the left side is $\sum_xm_x(B_{w^{-1}};v)H_x$, where $m_x(B_{w^{-1}};v)=\sum_dr_{x,d}(B_{w^{-1}})v^d$ uses the normalized polynomial standard layers before reduction. Comparing coefficients in the standard Hecke basis of [F4] yields $m_x(B_{w^{-1}};v)=p_{x,w^{-1}}(v)$ for every $x$, as an identity of Laurent polynomials. This comparison uses the character formula; it does not identify an indecomposable class with a product of simple classes.

Evaluate step 1.2 at the label $x=y^{-1}$ and at $v=1$: the left side becomes $\sum_d r_{y^{-1},d}(B_{w^{-1}})$, which equals the multiplicity by step 1.1, and the right side becomes $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}(1)$; the inversion symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$ of [F4] and the specialization $p_{y,w}(1)=P_{y,w}(1)$ of [F5] turn this into $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=P_{y,w}(1)$ for all $y,w\in W$. The vanishing clause is the support statement $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$ of [F4] and [F5], and only the total value at one is used: no individual coefficient of $P_{y,w}$ is interpreted as a category-$\mathcal O$ multiplicity, and no grading on $\mathcal O$ is constructed — the grading in play is the auxiliary grading of the polynomial lift, normalized on the Soergel side.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 evaluates the identity at the label x = y^{-1}; when y is not below w the support clause p_{y,w} = 0 makes both sides the empty-sum value 0, which is the stated vanishing.
Zero multiplicities are an instance of the displayed equality in step 2.1, not an exception: for incomparable pairs the theorem asserts (P(w.lambda):Delta(y.lambda)) = P_{y,w}(1) = 0.
The diagonal case y = w is included: [F4] fixes p_{w,w} = 1 and the step 2.1 evaluation gives multiplicity P_{w,w}(1) = 1 at the unit label.

boundaries.reason: The Theorem is stated only for regular integral type-A blocks; singular or non-integral blocks are excluded by its hypothesis and are handled on other pages.

boundaries.evidence: The endpoint labels are included in step 2.1's quantifier: at y = e the support condition is automatic for every w, and at w = e the sum collapses to the diagonal term.
The Statement assumes AC; step 1.1 consumes it only through the rank comparison [F1], whose choice content is inherited from the block and projective theory.

boundaries.reason: The Theorem is an equality of two multiplicities; its only directional content is the support statement already disposed as the zero case, and no implication requires a separate discharge.
No converse is asserted. The Theorem does not claim that the value P_{y,w}(1) computes anything outside the regular integral block regime.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For all weights
$\lambda$ and $\mu$,
$$(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))=[\Delta(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[M(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
where $P(\lambda)$ is the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$, the left-hand
multiplicity is the Verma-flag multiplicity of
[[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]], and the right-hand
multiplicity is the simple composition multiplicity of the Verma module
$M(\mu)$ ([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral type-$A$ block
$\mathcal O_\lambda$, for all $y,w\in W$
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=P_{y,w}(1),$$
the value at $q=1$ of the classical Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial of the pair
$y\le w$; the multiplicity is the total value at one, not an individual
coefficient of $P_{y,w}$, and it vanishes unless $y\le w$ in the Bruhat order.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, define the **standard** and **costandard** weight modules by

$$\Delta(\lambda)=M(\lambda),\qquad\nabla(\lambda)=D(M(\lambda)).$$

The Verma module is defined in [[def-verma-module]], and its restricted dual is defined in [[def-restricted-dual-of-a-weight-module]]. Under the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), [[prop-restricted-duality-is-an-exact-involution-on-category-o]] places $\nabla(\lambda)$ in $\mathcal O$, so both displayed modules are objects of that category. These symbols impose no projectivity or highest-weight-category axiom.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]], and write
$\Delta(\mu)=M(\mu)$ for the standard objects of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], i.e. the Verma modules
of [[def-verma-module]].

A **finite Verma flag** of an object $X$ of $\mathcal O$ — also called a
**standard flag** or a **$\Delta$-flag** — is a finite increasing sequence of
subobjects
$$0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]], and write
$\Delta(\mu)=M(\mu)$ for the standard objects of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], i.e. the Verma modules
of [[def-verma-module]].

A **finite Verma flag** of an object $X$ of $\mathcal O$ — also called a
**standard flag** or a **$\Delta$-flag** — is a finite increasing sequence of
subobjects
$$0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$$
such that each quotient $X_i/X_{i-1}$ is isomorphic to a Verma module
$\Delta(\mu_i)=M(\mu_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,n$. An object admitting such a flag is
called **Verma-filtered**. Since the flag is exhausted by its factors, its
class in the Grothendieck group
$K_0(\mathcal O)$ of [[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]
is
$$[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n[\Delta(\mu_i)].$$

For a Verma-filtered object $X$ and a weight $\mu$, the **multiplicity**
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is the number of indices $i$ with $\mu_i=\mu$ in a Verma
flag of $X$. This number is independent of the chosen flag by
[[lem-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-independent-of-the-flag]], so the notation
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is well-defined for Verma-filtered $X$.

The zero object has the empty flag, and every multiplicity of the zero object
is zero; a nonzero Verma-filtered object has at least one factor. A one-step
flag of $X$ is exactly an isomorphism $X\cong\Delta(\mu)$ for a single weight
$\mu$, so the objects with a one-step flag are the Verma modules themselves.
The flag is a chain of subobjects of $X$ in the module category; it is not
required to split, and later examples show that it need not.

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection, $w\in S_n$ with $sw<w$, and $y\le w$. With $P_{x,z}:=0$ whenever $x\not\le z$, $$P_{y,w}(q)=q^{1-c}P_{sy,sw}(q)+q^{c}P_{y,sw}(q)-\!\!\!\sum_{\substack{y\le z\le sw\\ sz<z,\ \mu(z,sw)\ne0}}\!\!\!\mu(z,sw)\,q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(z))/2}P_{y,z}(q),$$ where $c=1$ if $sy<y$ and $c=0$ if $sy>y$; here $\mu$ is the coefficient defined in [[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]] (so the summand only occurs for $\ell(sw)-\ell(z)$ odd, and $(\ell(w)-\ell(z))/2$ is then an integer).
