For any finite sequence of based integrable modules in the finite-weight-space category $O_{\mathrm{int}}$, the field tensor bar $\Psi=\Theta(\text{composite factor bars})$, built from the normalized intertwiner $\Theta$ of [[thm-the-weightwise-quasi-r-intertwiner-exists-and-is-unique]], is well defined, semilinear, $U$- and bar-compatible, involutive and independent of all parenthesizations; all root-height sums are vectorwise finite.

For arbitrary four-axiom based integrable factors in finite Cartan type, the same field assertion and integral lattice preservation hold without multiplicity or global weight bounds, by the finite-action and universal integral-coefficient clauses of [[lem-quasi-r-divided-power-integrality-on-based-lattices]]. Their actual bar is weight-transfer triangular with diagonal $1$. Finite action and integrality do not imply finite supported normalized global lifts: the periodic rank-one construction of [[lem-periodic-cyclotomic-based-sl-two-tensor-corrections-escape-every-finite-cut]] refutes that additional unrestricted assertion and the natural integral balanced tensor triple.

The full based and globalization assertion holds for bounded $O_{\mathrm{int}}$ pairs with independently established integral action (in particular for finite Cartan type), and for the supported construction cases of the supplier: highest-first or first $C_{\mathrm{high}}$ with arbitrary based second; arbitrary based first with lowest or $C_{\mathrm{low}}$ second; finite highest products and exact based subquotients and weight-admissible direct sums of their tensor constructions; and ordered highest-prefix, based-middle, lowest-suffix products with their explicit support bounds. This includes the full finite-dimensional tensor product, with every constituent, in finite Cartan type. For any further class, the globalization assertion requires independently proved integral action and finite raw-basis correction closure in the strict weight-transfer order.

In these supported cases the actual tensor global vectors are uniquely corrected bar-fixed lifts of the raw tensor residue vectors, with corrections in $q\mathbb Z[q]$; the transition and its inverse have finite columns, the corrected vectors form an $A$-basis, and the integral tensor triple is balanced. The $q=0$ tensor crystal lattice is supplied separately by [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]], and its actual infinity chart is $\Psi(L_0^{\mathrm{tensor}})$. Exact based integral bar-compatible subquotient maps preserve corrected global bases by balanced uniqueness, within these supported constructions. Raw tensor lower vectors need not be bar fixed. The affine boundary of the integral-action supplier still disproves arbitrary based-pair integral action in general type. No universal-$R$ braiding or uncontrolled semi-infinite evaluation is asserted.

Let $M_1,M_2$ be integrable chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight modules with crystal bases $(L_1,B_1)$, $(L_2,B_2)$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]), and let $M_1\otimes M_2$ be the integrable module of [[lem-tensor-products-of-integrable-weight-modules-are-integrable]].

Then $(L_1\otimes_{A_0}L_2,\,B_1\otimes B_2)$ is a crystal basis of $M_1\otimes M_2$, and its crystal is the tensor product crystal $B_1\otimes B_2$ of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]]: for all $b_1\in B_1$, $b_2\in B_2$ and $i\in I$,

$$\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\begin{cases}\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2),\\ b_1\otimes\tilde f_ib_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2),\end{cases}\qquad \tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\begin{cases}\tilde e_ib_1\otimes b_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2),\\ b_1\otimes\tilde e_ib_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)<\varepsilon_i(b_2),\end{cases}$$

with value $0$ as soon as the selected factor maps to $0$. In particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ map $B_1\otimes B_2$ into $(B_1\otimes B_2)\cup\{0\}$, and for all $b,b'\in B_1\otimes B_2$ one has $\tilde f_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde e_ib'$, so the partial-inverse axiom holds. The equality case $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ is resolved as in the definition: $\tilde f_i$ acts on the second factor and $\tilde e_i$ on the first.

No finite dimensionality, bounded support or uniform nilpotence is assumed, and no choice principle is used.

Let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of an integrable weight module $M$ in the sense of [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]], let $i\in I$, $\lambda\in P$ and $u\in L_\lambda$, and let $u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n$ be the admissible $i$-string decomposition of $u$: the sum is finite, $u_n\in\ker E_i\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$, and $u_n=0$ whenever $n>\langle h_i,\lambda+n\alpha_i\rangle$ ([[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]]). Then:

(a) **Components lie in the lattice.** $u_n\in L\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ for every $n$.

(b) **Lattice string decomposition.** $L_\lambda=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\tilde f_i^{\,n}\bigl(L_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}\cap\ker E_i\bigr)$, the sum being direct because admissible decompositions are unique; equivalently $L=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\tilde f_i^{\,n}(L\cap\ker E_i)$.

(c) **Single surviving component.** If $u+qL=0$ in $L_\lambda/qL_\lambda$, then $u_n\in qL$ for every $n$. If $u+qL\in B_\lambda$, then there is exactly one index $n_0$ with $u_{n_0}\notin qL$, and for it $u_{n_0}+qL\in B_{\lambda+n_0\alpha_i}$, $u\equiv F_i^{(n_0)}u_{n_0}\pmod{qL}$ and $u_{n_0}+qL=\tilde e_i^{\,n_0}(u+qL)$; in particular $n_0=\varepsilon_i(u+qL)$ ([[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]), and $\tilde e_iu$ and $\tilde f_iu$ are the residues of $F_i^{(n_0-1)}u_{n_0}$ and $F_i^{(n_0+1)}u_{n_0}$.

Everything is a statement about the fixed lattice $L$ and the operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$; no finite-dimensionality, bounded support, uniform nilpotence or choice principle is assumed. Here $F_i^{(-1)}u$ is interpreted as $0$, and $F_i^{(a+1)}u=0$ for a top of coroot weight $a$, so the final formulas include both finite-string endpoints.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$, an index $i\in I$, and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. Let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra and let $A_i$ be the subalgebra generated by $E_i,F_i,K_i^{\pm1}$ ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]); write $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$ for the divided powers of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]].

(i) The assignment $e\mapsto E_i$, $f\mapsto F_i$, $k\mapsto K_i$, $k^{-1}\mapsto K_i^{-1}$ defines an algebra isomorphism from the standard rank-one algebra $\mathbb A$ over $\mathbb Q(q)$, presented by $e,f,k^{\pm1}$ with $kek^{-1}=q_i^2e$, $kfk^{-1}=q_i^{-2}f$ and $[e,f]=(k-k^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ onto $A_i$; the images of the monomials $F_i^aK_i^mE_i^b$ ($a,b\ge0$, $m\in\mathbb Z$) are linearly independent in $U_q(\mathfrak g)$, being images of the PBW monomials of the triangular decomposition ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]).

(ii) For all $a,b\ge0$, $K_iE_i^{(a)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{2a}E_i^{(a)}$ and $K_iF_i^{(b)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{-2b}F_i^{(b)}$, and for $b\ge1$ the divided powers satisfy the exact commutation formula
$$E_iF_i^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}E_i+\frac{F_i^{(b-1)}}{q_i^{b}-q_i^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}\bigl(q_i^{-2s}K_i-q_i^{2s}K_i^{-1}\bigr);$$
iterating it computes $E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}$ as a finite sum of monomials $F_i^{(b-t)}K_i^{m}E_i^{(a-t)}$ ($0\le t\le\min(a,b)$) with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$.

(iii) For every $N\ge0$ there is a simple $A_i$-module $L_i(N)$ of dimension $N+1$: it is the quotient of the cyclic module $\widetilde M(N):=A_i/\bigl(A_iE_i+A_i(K_i-q_i^N)\bigr)$ by the submodule generated by $F_i^{(N+1)}w_N$, where $w_N$ is the image of $1$, with basis the images $v_t$ of $F_i^{(t)}w_N$, $0\le t\le N$, on which $K_iv_t=q_i^{N-2t}v_t$, $F_iv_t=[t+1]_iv_{t+1}$ and $E_iv_t=[N-t+1]_iv_{t-1}$ (with $v_{-1}=v_{N+1}=0$); $L_i(N)$ is the unique simple $A_i$-module generated by a vector $v\ne0$ with $E_iv=0$, $K_iv=q_i^Nv$ and $F_i^{N+1}v=0$.

Assume inherited AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]] for the invoked quantum based/global lattice and normalized quasi-$R$ suppliers.

Work in the conventions of
[[def-higher-level-wedge-tensor-fock-module]] and
[[def-the-fock-convention-dictionary-for-finite-type-a-quantum-modules]]: the
**source parameter** is $s$, the **library parameter** is $t=s^{-1}$, the
monomial basis of the Fock module is $\{M_A\}$, and $\psi$ is the ordinary
compatible bar of
[[thm-the-qg-tensor-product-bar-is-triangular-and-compatible-with-fock-truncations]],
which is triangular and integral on the monomial basis.

The **source dual-canonical family** $(L_A)$ is the unique $\psi$-fixed family
with
$$L_A=M_A+\sum_{B<A}s\,\mathbb Z[s]\,M_B,$$
and the **canonical family** $(T_A)$ is the unique $\psi$-fixed family with
$$T_A=M_A+\sum_{B<A}s^{-1}\mathbb Z[s^{-1}]\,M_B .$$

Let $d_{A,B}(s)$ and $p_{A,B}(-s)$ be the transition coefficients defined by
$$M_B=\sum_A d_{A,B}(s)\,L_A,\qquad L_B=\sum_A p_{A,B}(-s)\,M_A,$$
and define the **quasi-canonical family** by
$$P_A:=\sum_B d_{A,B}(s)\,M_B,\qquad\text{so that}\qquad M_A=\sum_B p_{A,B}(-s)\,P_B .$$
The families $L$ and $T$ are ordinary-bar fixed; $P$ generally is not.

The **reverse-factor monomials** $\widetilde M_A$ use the reverse-column
reading of the tableau $A$; the corresponding bar-fixed families
$\widetilde L_A,\widetilde T_A$ are defined by the same triangular conditions
with respect to $\widetilde M_A$, so that $\widetilde L_A$ is supported on
$B>A$. **Rectification** is the weight-preserving combinatorial identification
of the original lower ground component $\mathrm{Rev}^\Lambda$ with the
reverse-factor lower ground component $\mathrm{Std}^\Lambda$, given by reading
down columns and reverse row insertion.

The **source sesquilinear form** is the $\mathbb C$-antilinear-in-the-first
argument pairing with
$$\langle M_A,\psi M_B\rangle=\delta_{AB},$$
and the **bilinear reverse-factor form** is
$$C(\widetilde M_A,\psi M_B)=\delta_{AB}.$$
Thus the labelled monomial Gram matrices of the two forms are the inverse
ordinary-bar matrix, not the identity. Transition duality gives
$$\langle P_A,L_B\rangle=\delta_{AB},\qquad C(\widetilde L_A,T_B)=\delta_{AB},\qquad C(\widetilde T_A,L_B)=\delta_{AB}.$$

All four families are Laurent-integral bases of the finite Fock cuts and
commute with the upper-cut and common-bottom-tail embeddings. On a highest
constituent, the source bilinear normalization $C_0$ and the library
polarization of [[def-upper-global-basis-by-the-contravariant-form]] differ by
an explicit weight power, proved in the global-basis comparison later in this
pair; no unqualified library-upper/ordinary-bar identification is asserted.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb Q(q)$, let $M\subseteq V$ be an $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-submodule spanning $V$, and let $L_0,L_\infty$ be free full rational chart lattices over $A_0,A_\infty$ (as for a based module in [[def-the-bar-lattice-and-integral-lattice-of-a-based-module]]). Put
$$L_{\mathbb Z}:=M\cap L_0,\qquad L_{\mathbb Z}^-:=M\cap L_\infty,\qquad E_{\mathbb Z}:=M\cap L_0\cap L_\infty.$$
The **integral triple** $(M,L_0,L_\infty)$ is **balanced** if the canonical $\mathbb Z$-linear map
$$E_{\mathbb Z}\longrightarrow L_{\mathbb Z}/qL_{\mathbb Z}=(M\cap L_0)/(M\cap qL_0)$$
is an isomorphism. Its inverse is the **integral globalization map** on the integral residue subgroup. **Rational balancedness** is the corresponding isomorphism $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}E_{\mathbb Z}\to L_0/qL_0$, after extending the integral subgroup by $\mathbb Q$. In the applications of this page the integral subgroup is $\mathbb Z B$ for the lower global family $B$, and its globalization gives the lower lifts $G(b)$.

For a balanced triple, the two-chart lemma of this page proves $M\cong A\otimes_{\mathbb Z}E_{\mathbb Z}$, $L_{\mathbb Z}\cong\mathbb Z[q]\otimes_{\mathbb Z}E_{\mathbb Z}$ and $L_{\mathbb Z}^-\cong\mathbb Z[q^{-1}]\otimes_{\mathbb Z}E_{\mathbb Z}$. If the triple is balanced and $E_{\mathbb Z}$ has a finite $\mathbb Z$-basis $B_E$ whose rational residue classes are a basis of $L_0/qL_0$, these lifts give bases of $M,L_0,L_\infty$ over $A,A_0,A_\infty$ respectively. Thus $A$-freeness of $M$ is a conclusion from integral balancedness together with a proved free integral residue basis; it is not automatic for an arbitrary not-finitely-generated $\mathbb Z$-submodule. All definitions apply componentwise to the finite root or label spaces.

derivations.claim: **All reverse lower constituents.** Put $q=s^{-1}$ and use the reverse ordered tensor. Each elementary wedge subset factor is minuscule: for each root its nontrivial strings have length two, coefficients one, and its basis is its lower global basis at $q=0$ in the dictionary's toral convention $K_i=D_i^{-1}D_{i+1}$. The ground vector generates it. Apply [F1] to the finite product, not to just the ground constituent. Its raw reverse monomial $A_0(q)$-span is the lower tensor chart by [F2]; finite triangular correction produces the negative-source family $\widetilde T_A$ by uniqueness. Thus the reverse Laurent lattice and the zero/infinity charts have the simultaneous global basis $\widetilde T_A$.

**The actual sesquilinear dual and exchanged coefficient rings.** Define $H(x,y)=C(\widetilde\psi x,y)$ on reverse/original factors. It is coefficient-antilinear in $x$ and linear in $y$. From [F3], $H(\widetilde M_A,M_B)=\overline{C(\widetilde M_A,\psi M_B)}=\delta_{AB}$, so its raw monomial Gram matrix is exactly $I$. Therefore the conjugate dual of the reverse $A_0(q)$-raw chart is exactly the original $A_0(s)$-raw chart: a coefficient $a(q)$ is conjugated to $a(q^{-1})=a(s)$, including denominators. Similarly the reverse infinity chart dualizes to the original infinity chart. On the global families $H(\widetilde T_A,L_B)=\delta_{AB}$ because $\widetilde T_A$ is fixed. Hence the dual integral, zero and infinity lattices have respectively bases $L_A$ over $\mathbb Z[s^{\pm1}]$, $A_0(s)$ and $A_\infty(s)$, and their common intersection is $\bigoplus_A\mathbb ZL_A$. This proves balancedness and identifies its ordinary bar with $\psi$ using the conjugate-bar identity of [F3]. It does not equate the two ordinary global bases.

**Upper operators and full tableau residues.** The matrix adjoints of [F3], with the conjugation in $H$, give $H(\widetilde F_ix,y)=H(x,E_iy)$ and $H(\widetilde E_ix,y)=H(x,F_iy)$. On a reverse divided string $v_k=F_i^{(k)}v_0$, $0\le k\le a$, let $u_k$ be its $H$-dual basis, retaining the full pairing on its multiplicity space. Then $E_iu_k=[k]_su_{k-1}$ and $F_iu_k=[a-k]_su_{k+1}$ by [F2] and $\overline{[m]_q}=[m]_s$. The upper string operators are the shifts $u_k\mapsto u_{k-1},u_{k+1}$, defined as the conjugate adjoints of the lower shifts. They preserve the dual charts from step 2.1 and their residues are the adjoints of the partial permutation matrices of the lower tensor crystal. Thus they give partial inverse tableau moves on every tensor residue, with the reverse factor order undone by the dual pairing. On a column the simultaneous $i,i+1$ occupations cancel; on the original left-to-right column word cancel $-+$, with $-$ an $i+1$-only column and $+$ an $i$-only column. The raising move takes the leftmost surviving $-$ and lowering takes the rightmost surviving $+$: this is the reverse lower tensor rule of [F2] read through the dual basis. Equalities follow from the lower rule's non-strict raising and strict lowering tests, so no equality case is changed by naming the chart upper. Both reciprocal charts have the corresponding upper operators.

**Endpoint divided powers and balanced uniqueness.** On the upper string $u_k$ of step 3.1, $E_i^{(k)}u_k=u_0$ and $E_i^{(k+1)}u_k=0$; thus if $E_i^{(n+1)}x=0$, then $E_i^{(n)}x=\tilde e_i^nx$, since all shorter components die. This is an identity on the sum of admissible strings, with its multiplicity spaces retained. If $x=L_A$ and $E_i^{(n+1)}x=0$, integrality of divided powers and preservation of both upper charts put $E_i^{(n)}x$ in their balanced intersection, with residue $\tilde e_i^nA$. Therefore it equals $L_{\tilde e_i^nA}$ when that residue is nonzero, and zero otherwise. Conversely suppose $\tilde e_i^{n+1}A=0$ but $E_i^{(n+1)}L_A\ne0$. Choose the maximal $m>n$ for which $E_i^{(m)}L_A\ne0$, possible by finite integrability. Applying the endpoint argument with $m$ gives a nonzero balanced vector with residue $\tilde e_i^mA=0$, contradicting injectivity in [F4]. Thus $E_i^{n+1}L_A=0$ iff $\varepsilon_i(A)\le n$.

**Adapted kernels, without assuming a tensor highest decomposition is based.** To exclude cancellation between global vectors outside a kernel, choose the largest $m$ occurring among the $\varepsilon_i(A)$ in a finite linear combination. Apply $E_i^{(m)}$. Step 4.1 sends its $m$-height terms to distinct top-labelled global vectors: partial inverse crystal strings imply that two labels at the same position have different top labels. Every lower-height term dies. Linear independence therefore forces all coefficients at that height to vanish if the combination is killed. Descend on $m$ to obtain the stated kernel span. The integral and chart kernels are exactly the spans of the same subset over their coefficient rings, because the global vectors are simultaneous bases. Hence all these kernel triples are balanced; quotienting by one such subset retains simultaneous bases and balancedness.

**The associated rank-one filtration.** At root weight $\lambda=\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(A)\rangle$, a string of dimension $r$ has position $k=(r-1-\lambda)/2$. Thus the sum of strings with dimension at most $r$ at that weight is precisely $\ker E_i^{k+1}$, with the natural floor when parity requires it; by step 5.1 its global labels have $\varepsilon_i\le k$, equivalently $r_i\le r$. These weightwise spaces assemble into the rank-one submodule filtration. The associated quotient of dimension $r$ has simultaneous bases indexed by the labels $r_i(A)=r$, and is a sum of actual upper strings $u_0,\ldots,u_{r-1}$. Step 4.1 identifies the top vector of the position-$k$ global residue by $E_i^{(k)}L_A=L_{\tilde e_i^kA}$, modulo the shorter-string filtration. Consequently the position-$k$ vector is the upper normalized $u_k$, whose $E_i,F_i$ coefficients are exactly $[k]_s$ and $[r-1-k]_s$ by step 3.1. Identifying the next residue by partial inverse moves proves the two asserted leading-term equations, with all errors in shorter strings. This does not require a separately selected highest-weight decomposition of the full tensor module.

**Conclusion and factor orders.** Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 construct the full source upper triple and its tableau residue crystal by conjugate duality of the entire reverse lower tensor construction; steps 4.1 and 5.1 give balanced adapted kernels; step 6.1 gives the associated-string Chevalley normalization. Reversing the initially chosen factor order repeats the same construction, and finite cuts commute with all supported subset actions and triangular global lifts. Every claim therefore concerns the full finite tensor cuts and both ordered products, without any categorical simple-label assertion.

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a set. A **permutation** of $X$ is a bijection $f : X \to X$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **symmetric group of $X$** is the
set of all permutations of $X$,

$$\operatorname{Sym}(X) \;:=\; \{\, f : X \to X \;:\; f \text{ is a bijection} \,\},$$

equipped with **composition** as its operation,

$$(f \circ g)(x) \;=\; f(g(x)) \qquad (x \in X),$$

and with the identity map $\mathrm{id}_X$, given by $\mathrm{id}_X(x) = x$, as
distinguished element.

Composition of two bijections of $X$ is again a bijection of $X$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), so $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$ is closed
under $\circ$ and $\circ$ is a binary operation on it
([[def-binary-operation]]); and $\mathrm{id}_X$ is a bijection of $X$, so it is an
element of $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, and it is a two-sided identity for
composition ([[def-identity-element]]) because
$f \circ \mathrm{id}_X = f = \mathrm{id}_X \circ f$ holds pointwise for every
$f$. That $(\operatorname{Sym}(X), \circ, \mathrm{id}_X)$ is a group is
[[lem-symmetric-group-is-a-group]].

**Cycle notation for a finite list of distinct points.** For distinct elements
$x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of $X$ with $k \ge 2$, the symbol
$(x_0\,x_1\,\cdots\,x_{k-1})$ denotes the permutation sending $x_i$ to
$x_{i+1}$ for $i < k-1$, sending $x_{k-1}$ to $x_0$, and fixing every element of
$X$ outside $\{x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}\}$. It is a bijection, because the map
described sends the set $\{x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}\}$ onto itself by a rule with an
evident inverse (send each $x_{i+1}$ back to $x_i$ and $x_0$ back to $x_{k-1}$)
and fixes the complement pointwise. A **transposition** is such a symbol with
$k = 2$, that is $(a\,b)$ with $a \ne b$: it exchanges $a$ and $b$ and fixes
everything else, and it satisfies $(a\,b) \circ (a\,b) = \mathrm{id}_X$.

A product of cycle symbols means their composite, so $(a\,b)(c\,d)$ is
$(a\,b) \circ (c\,d)$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, so that $n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). The
**symmetric group on $n$ letters** is

$$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(n)=\operatorname{Sym}(\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}),$$

the group of all bijections of $n$ under composition ([[def-symmetric-group]]),
with the composition convention

$$(\sigma\tau)(i):=(\sigma\circ\tau)(i)=\sigma(\tau(i))\qquad(i\in n),$$

so that in a product the right-hand factor acts first. An element of $S_n$ is
named by either of the two notations below.

**One-line notation.** For $\sigma\in S_n$, its **one-line form** is the list of
its values in order of their arguments,

$$\sigma=[\sigma(0),\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n-1)].$$

This list has length $n$ and its entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$, each occurring
once, because $\sigma$ is a bijection of $n$. Conversely, a list
$[b_0,b_1,\dots,b_{n-1}]$ whose entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$ each occurring once
is the one-line form of exactly one element of $S_n$, namely the map sending
each $i\in n$ to $b_i$: that map is injective because the entries are distinct,
and surjective because every element of $n$ occurs among them. So one-line
notation is a bijection from $S_n$ to the arrangements of $0,1,\dots,n-1$ in a
list. For $n=0$ the one-line form of the unique element of $S_0$ is the empty
list.

**Cycle notation.** For distinct $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{k-1}\in n$ with $k\ge2$, the
symbol $(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})$ denotes the element of $S_n$ that sends
$a_i$ to $a_{i+1}$ for each $i<k-1$, sends $a_{k-1}$ to $a_0$, and fixes every
element of $n$ outside $\{a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]); it is
called a **$k$-cycle**, and a $2$-cycle is a **transposition**. Writing cycle
symbols side by side means composing them, so $(a\,b)(c\,d)$ is
$(a\,b)\circ(c\,d)$, and the empty juxtaposition of cycle symbols is the
identity $\operatorname{id}$.

Unlike one-line notation, cycle notation does not name each permutation once:
the symbol may be started at any of its entries, so

$$(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})=(a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1}\,a_0)$$

and each $k$-cycle is written by exactly $k$ symbols of this shape. A cycle
symbol also does not record $n$, which must be supplied by the context.

For $n\ge2$, the symmetric group $S_n$ has the presentation

$$S_n=\langle s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\mid s_i^2=1,\ s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1},\ s_is_j=s_js_i\ (|i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

where, after relabelling the underlying set $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ as
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $s_i$ corresponds to the adjacent transposition
$(i\ i+1)$. For
$n=0,1$, the trivial group has the empty presentation.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $G$ be a group
([[def-group]]). The **group ring** $R[G]$ is the free left $R$-module on the
set $G$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]).

For each $g \in G$, write $[g] \in R[G]$ for the standard basis vector indexed
by $g$. Thus every element of $R[G]$ has a unique expression
$$\sum_{g \in F} r_g [g]$$
with $F \subseteq G$ finite and $r_g \in R$.

The notation is deliberately that of **formal** finite sums: at this stage
$R[G]$ is only the underlying free $R$-module with its distinguished basis. The
multiplication satisfying
$$[g][h]=[gh]$$
and the resulting $R$-algebra structure are constructed in
[[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $G$ be a group. Write $[g] \in R[G]$ for
the basis vector of [[def-group-ring]] indexed by $g \in G$.

There is a unique $R$-bilinear multiplication on $R[G]$ satisfying
$$[g][h]=[gh]\qquad(g,h\in G).$$
With this product, $R[G]$ is a unital $R$-algebra whose underlying
$R$-module has basis $\{[g]:g\in G\}$. Its identity is $[e]$, where $e$ is the
identity of $G$, and every basis element $[g]$ is a unit with inverse
$[g^{-1}]$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $I$ be a set.
The set $R[x_i:i\in I]$ consists of the functions

$$c:\mathcal M(I)\longrightarrow R$$

with finite support, where $\mathcal M(I)$ is the monoid of
[[def-monomials-on-an-index-set]]. We write such a function as the formal sum
$\sum_a c_a x^a$. Addition is pointwise. Multiplication is the convolution

$$(cd)_u:=\sum_{a+b=u}c_a d_b,$$

where only pairs in $\operatorname{supp}(c)\times\operatorname{supp}(d)$
contribute and the sum is the finite sum of
[[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]. The constant $r\in R$ is the
coefficient family supported at the zero monomial with value $r$, and the
indeterminate $x_i$ is supported at the exponent family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere.

The convolution is well defined and these operations make the displayed set a
commutative ring by [[thm-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-is-a-commutative-ring]].

A ring $R$ ([[def-ring]]) is **commutative** when its multiplication is
commutative ([[def-binary-operation]]):

$$xy \;=\; yx \qquad \text{for all } x, y \in R .$$

Addition is commutative in every ring, by axiom (R1), so the word refers to
multiplication alone.
If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x]$ is an integral domain.

If $D$ is an integral domain, then $D\setminus\{0\}$ is multiplicative. Its localisation
$$ \operatorname{Frac}(D)=(D\setminus\{0\})^{-1}D $$
is the **field of fractions** of $D$. Thus its elements are fractions $a/b$ with $a,b\in D$ and $b\ne0$, modulo the localisation equivalence relation.

For every integral domain $D$, the localisation $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ is a field. Its canonical map
$$ D\longrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}(D),\qquad d\longmapsto d/1, $$
is an injective unital ring homomorphism.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $S$ a set. There is a unital associative $R$-algebra $R\langle S\rangle$, the **free associative $R$-algebra on $S$**, whose underlying $R$-module is free on the set of finite words in $S$ (including the empty word), with product given on words by concatenation and extended $R$-bilinearly.

1. **Universal property.** For every $R$-algebra $A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and every map $S\to A$ there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $R\langle S\rangle\to A$ extending it. When $R=k$ is a field and $S$ indexes a basis of a vector space $V$, $R\langle S\rangle$ reproduces the published tensor algebra $T(V)$ ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]], [[thm-universal-property-of-the-tensor-algebra]]).
2. **Two-sided ideal description.** For $E\subseteq R\langle S\rangle$ the two-sided ideal $(E)$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]) is the set of finite sums $\sum_sa_se_sb_s$ with $a_s,b_s\in R\langle S\rangle$ and $e_s\in E$.
3. **Quotient universal property.** If $\varphi:R\langle S\rangle\to A$ is an $R$-algebra homomorphism killing $E$, then $\varphi$ factors uniquely through the quotient $R\langle S\rangle/(E)$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-universal-property]]); the quotient is the presented $R$-algebra with generators $S$ and relations $E$.

Left, right and two-sided ideals.

Let $R$ be a ring. An additive subgroup $I\le(R,+)$ is a **left ideal** when
$r i\in I$ for every $r\in R$ and $i\in I$, and a **right ideal** when
$i r\in I$ for every such $r,i$.  A **two-sided ideal**, written
$I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, is both a left and a right ideal.  In a
commutative ring these three notions agree.

The ideal generated by a subset and principal ideals.

For $S\subseteq R$, define $(S)$ to be the intersection of all two-sided ideals
of $R$ containing $S$.  This family is nonempty because it contains $R$, and
[[lem-ideal-criterion-and-intersections]] shows that $(S)$ is an ideal.  For
$a\in R$, the ideal $(\{a\})$ is written $(a)$ and is called **principal**.

A ring homomorphism whose kernel contains a two-sided ideal factors uniquely through the quotient ring.

If $I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, $f:R\to S$ is a ring homomorphism, and
$I\subseteq\ker f$, there is a unique ring homomorphism $\bar f:R/I\to S$ such
that $\bar f(r+I)=f(r)$.
For a two-sided ideal $I$, the additive cosets form a ring $R/I$ with identity $1+I$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A,B$ be $R$-algebras. The $R$-module $A\otimes_RB$ has a unique $R$-algebra structure satisfying

$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$$

and

$$1_{A\otimes_RB}=1_A\otimes1_B,\qquad r\longmapsto r(1_A\otimes1_B).$$

If $A$ and $B$ are commutative, then $A\otimes_RB$ is commutative.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

Let $R$ and $S$ be rings ([[def-ring]]). A **ring homomorphism** from $R$ to $S$
is a function $f : R \to S$ such that, for all $x, y \in R$,

- **(RH1)** $f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y)$;
- **(RH2)** $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$;
- **(RH3)** $f(1_R) = 1_S$.

A ring homomorphism from a ring to itself is a **ring endomorphism**; a
bijective ring homomorphism is a **ring isomorphism**.

**(RH3) is imposed, not derived, and the reason is exactly the reason
[[def-group-homomorphism]] treats monoids and groups differently.** Condition
(RH1) says that $f$ is a homomorphism of the additive groups
$(R,+,0_R) \to (S,+,0_S)$, and for groups preservation of the identity is *free*:
it follows from (RH1) by cancellation
([[lem-group-homomorphism-basic-properties]]). Condition (RH2) says only that
$f$ is a homomorphism of the multiplicative *semigroups*, and $(R,\cdot,1_R)$ is
a monoid that need not be a group ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]); for monoids preservation
of the identity does **not** follow and must be assumed, which is precisely why
[[def-group-homomorphism]] puts the clause $f(e) = e'$ into the definition of a
monoid homomorphism and leaves it out of the definition of a group homomorphism
([[def-identity-element]]).

So a ring homomorphism is: a homomorphism of additive groups that is also a
homomorphism of multiplicative monoids. The clause is not redundant: the
companion page exhibits a map $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$
satisfying (RH1) and (RH2) and failing (RH3).

derivations.claim: The cases $d=0,1$. For $d=0$ there are no symbols, so $\mathcal F_0=\mathbb C$ and $I_0=0$, giving $H_0=\mathbb C$. For $d=1$ the only symbol is $x_1$ and the list of relations is empty; the words in $x_1$ are $1,x_1,x_1^2,\dots$, a $\mathbb C$-basis of $\mathcal F_1$ by [F4], so $H_1$ is the polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[x_1]$ with basis $x_1^r$, $r\ge0$.

The rational-function model. On the $\mathbb C$-vector space $\Omega$ of [F3] let $m_f$ denote multiplication by $f\in\Omega$, and for $1\le i<d$ let $\sigma_i$ be the operator $(\sigma_if)(y_1,\dots,y_d)=f(y_1,\dots,y_{i+1},y_i,\dots,y_d)$ interchanging the $i$-th and $(i+1)$-st arguments. Put $a_i:=d_i^{-1}\in\Omega$ (invertible by [F3]), $\delta_i:=a_i(1+\sigma_i)$ and $T_i:=\sigma_i-\delta_i$. For a word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ in the generators of $S_d$ set $\sigma_w:=\sigma_{i_1}\!\circ\cdots\circ\sigma_{i_k}$ and $T_w:=T_{i_1}\!\cdots T_{i_k}$. The operators $\sigma_w$ are well defined by the Coxeter presentation [F1], because the $\sigma_i$ satisfy those relations and the presentation says that any two words for the same $w$ are related by them.

The skew algebra. Let $D:=\{\sum_{w\in S_d}m_{f_w}\sigma_w:f_w\in\Omega\}\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\Omega)$, a $\mathbb C$-subspace. For $f,g\in\Omega$ and $u,v\in S_d$ the identities $\sigma_um_g=m_{\sigma_u(g)}\sigma_u$ and $\sigma_u\sigma_v=\sigma_{uv}$ hold (the first expresses the substitution action on functions, the second is word concatenation), so $(m_f\sigma_u)(m_g\sigma_v)=m_{f\,\sigma_u(g)}\sigma_{uv}$; hence $D$ is a subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\Omega)$. The set $\{\sigma_w\}$ is $\Omega$-linearly independent: suppose $\sum_wf_w\sigma_w=0$ with $f_w\in\Omega$ not all zero; multiplying the resulting identity of functions by a common denominator of the $f_w$, we may assume $f_w\in\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]$. Fix integers $N_1>\cdots>N_d$ whose consecutive gaps exceed the total degree of every $f_w$, and order the finitely many $w$ with $f_w\ne0$ by the lexicographic order of the vectors $w\cdot N:=(N_{w^{-1}(1)},\dots,N_{w^{-1}(d)})$; let $w$ be maximal and let $e$ be the exponent of a top monomial of $f_w$. Applying the sum to the monomial $y^N$ gives $\sum_{w'}f_{w'}(y)\,y^{w'\cdot N}$, because $\sigma_{w'}y^N=y^{w'\cdot N}$; the vectors $w'\cdot N$ are distinct, and at the first coordinate where $w'\cdot N$ differs from $w\cdot N$ the gap exceeds the degree bound, so the monomial $y^{w\cdot N+e}$ occurs exactly once, in the summand $f_wy^{w\cdot N}$, with nonzero coefficient. This contradicts the vanishing of the sum, proving the claim.

Spanning of $H_d$ by ordered monomials. We show that every element of $H_d$ is a $\mathbb C$-linear combination of the images of ordered monomials $x^rw$; since words span $\mathcal F_d$ by [F4], it suffices to treat the image of a word $W$ in the symbols. Use strong induction on the pair $(n,\iota)$ ordered lexicographically, where $n$ is the number of $x$-symbols in $W$ and $\iota$ is the number of pairs of positions $(p<q)$ such that the $p$-th symbol is some $s_i$ and the $q$-th symbol is some $x_j$. If $n=0$, then $W$ is a word in the $s_i$; by the Coxeter presentation [F1] the subalgebra generated by the $s_i$ is spanned by the images of the elements $w\in S_d$, so the claim holds. If $n>0$ and every $x$-symbol precedes every $s$-symbol in $W$, then $W$ is of the form (word in $x$'s)(word in $s$'s), and the claim follows from commutativity of the $x$'s and the case $n=0$. Otherwise $W=W_1s_ix_jW_2$ with adjacent symbols; use $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ if $j=i+1$, $s_ix_i=x_{i+1}s_i-1$ if $j=i$ (the relation $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$ solved for $s_ix_i$), and $s_ix_j=x_js_i$ if $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$. In every case $W\equiv W_1x_{j'}s_iW_2\pm W_1W_2$, where the first word has the same $n$ and one fewer $(s,x)$-inversion pair, while the second has $n-1$ $x$-symbols; both fall under the induction hypothesis. Hence the images of ordered monomials span $H_d$.

Jucys-Murphy elements. For $1\le j\le d$ put $J_j:=\sum_{k<j}(k\ j)\in\mathbb C[S_d]$, so $J_1=0$. Then (i) $J_iJ_j=J_jJ_i$ for all $i,j$; (ii) $s_iJ_j=J_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$; and (iii) $s_iJ_{i+1}=J_is_i+1$. For (i) with $i<j$ write $\Omega_m:=\sum_{1\le k<l\le m}(k\ l)$ for the sum of all transpositions in $S_m$; $\Omega_m$ is central in $\mathbb C[S_m]$ because conjugation permutes the transpositions, and $J_m=\Omega_m-\Omega_{m-1}$. Since $J_i\in\mathbb C[S_i]\subseteq\mathbb C[S_{m-1}]\subset\mathbb C[S_m]$ for $i<m$, centrality of $\Omega_m$ in $\mathbb C[S_m]$ and of $\Omega_{m-1}$ in $\mathbb C[S_{m-1}]$ gives $[J_i,J_m]=[J_i,\Omega_m]-[J_i,\Omega_{m-1}]=0$. For (ii), conjugation by $s_i$ sends each transposition $(k\ j)$ to $(s_i(k)\ s_i(j))$; if $j<i$ both entries are fixed, and if $j>i+1$ the sum over $k<j$ contains the pairs with $k=i$ and $k=i+1$, whose images are interchanged, so the sum is preserved. For (iii), conjugation sends $(k\ i+1)$ to $(k\ i)$ for $k<i$ and fixes $(i\ i+1)$, so $s_iJ_{i+1}s_i=J_i+s_i$; multiplying on the right by $s_i$ and using $s_i^2=1$ gives (iii).

The model satisfies the relations. Since $\sigma_im_{a_i}=m_{\sigma_i(a_i)}\sigma_i=m_{-a_i}\sigma_i$, the operator identity $(1+\sigma_i)m_{a_i}=m_{a_i}(1-\sigma_i)$ and the rules $\sigma_i\delta_i=-\delta_i$, $\delta_i\sigma_i=\delta_i$ hold; hence $\delta_i^2=m_{a_i}(1+\sigma_i)m_{a_i}(1+\sigma_i)=m_{a_i^2}(1-\sigma_i)(1+\sigma_i)=0$ and $T_i^2=\sigma_i^2-\sigma_i\delta_i-\delta_i\sigma_i+\delta_i^2=1+\delta_i-\delta_i+0=1$. For $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$ both $\sigma_i$ and $\delta_i$ commute with $m_{x_j}$, so $T_im_{x_j}=m_{x_j}T_i$. For the cross relations, use $\sigma_im_{x_{i+1}}=m_{x_i}\sigma_i$, $\sigma_im_{x_i}=m_{x_{i+1}}\sigma_i$ and the two identities $m_{x_i}\delta_i-\delta_im_{x_{i+1}}=1$ and $\delta_im_{x_i}-m_{x_{i+1}}\delta_i=1$: for the first, $m_{x_i}\delta_i=m_{a_ix_i}(1+\sigma_i)$ while $\delta_im_{x_{i+1}}=m_{a_ix_{i+1}}+m_{a_ix_i}\sigma_i$, and their difference is $m_{a_i(x_i-x_{i+1})}=1$; the second is the same computation with the roles of $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$ interchanged. Therefore $T_im_{x_{i+1}}-m_{x_i}T_i=(m_{x_i}\sigma_i-m_{x_i}\sigma_i)+(m_{x_i}\delta_i-\delta_im_{x_{i+1}})=1$ and $m_{x_{i+1}}T_i-T_im_{x_i}=1$. For $|i-j|>1$, the variables and swaps in $T_i,T_j$ are disjoint, so they commute. For the braid relation put $A=(x_i-x_{i+1})^{-1}$, $B=(x_{i+1}-x_{i+2})^{-1}$, $C=(x_i-x_{i+2})^{-1}$, so $AB=C(A+B)$. The product rule of step 1.3 expands both $T_iT_{i+1}T_i$ and $T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}$ with coefficients, in the order $1,\sigma_i,\sigma_{i+1},\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1},\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i,\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i$, equal to $(-C(1+AB),BC(1-A),AC(1-B),-B(1-A)(1-C),-A(1-B)(1-C),(1-A)(1-B)(1-C))$. Here $A(B-C)=BC$ and $B(A-C)=AC$, both consequences of $AB=C(A+B)$, give the two shorter-swap coefficients and the common identity coefficient. Thus the braid relation holds. Hence the assignment $x_i\mapsto m_{x_i}$, $s_i\mapsto T_i$ preserves all the relations of the Definition, and by the universal properties [F4] it defines an algebra homomorphism $\Phi\colon H_d\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\Omega)$.

Triangular expansion. Fix $w\in S_d$ with a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, and put $c:=\prod_{t=1}^k(\sigma_{i_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_{t-1}})(1-a_{i_t})\ne0$ in $\Omega$, with the empty prefix acting as the identity. Every transported factor is nonzero because the prefix is a field automorphism. In the expansion of $T_w=\prod_t\bigl((1-a_{i_t})\sigma_{i_t}-a_{i_t}\bigr)$ by the product rule of step 1.3, the term choosing the factor $(1-a_{i_t})\sigma_{i_t}$ for every $t$ contributes $c\,\sigma_w$ after the scalar coefficients are moved left, while every other term is $m_g\sigma_v$ with $v$ the product of a proper subword of $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ in the induced order. If $\ell$ denotes the minimal number of generators needed to express a permutation, then such a proper subword $J$ has $\ell(v)\le|J|<k=\ell(w)$, using subadditivity of $\ell$ and reducedness. Collecting the expansion in the $\Omega$-basis $\{\sigma_v\}$ therefore gives $T_w=c\,\sigma_w+\sum_{\ell(v)<\ell(w)}c_v\sigma_v$ with $c\ne0$ and $c_v\in\Omega$.

The evaluation homomorphism. Assume $d\ge1$. The assignment $x_j\mapsto a+J_j$, $s_i\mapsto s_i$ defines an algebra homomorphism $\varphi\colon\mathcal F_d\to\mathbb C[S_d]$: the images of the $x$'s commute by step 1.5(i); the images of the $s_i$ satisfy the Coxeter relations by [F1]; and the cross relations follow from step 1.5(ii) and from $s_i(a+J_{i+1})=(a+J_i)s_i+1$, $(a+J_{i+1})s_i=s_i(a+J_i)+1$, which are step 1.5(iii) read in both directions. Since $\varphi(x_1-a)=a+J_1-a=0$, the quotient universal property [F4] yields an algebra homomorphism $\bar\varphi\colon H_d/(x_1-a)\to\mathbb C[S_d]$, which is surjective because the $s_i$ generate $S_d$.

Independence of the monomials in the model. By step 2.2 the change-of-basis matrix from $\{T_w\}$ to $\{\sigma_w\}$ inside $D$ is triangular with nonzero diagonal when permutations are ordered by length, hence invertible over the field $\Omega$; thus $\{T_w:w\in S_d\}$ is an $\Omega$-basis of $D$. Suppose $\sum_{r,w}c_{r,w}m_{x^r}T_w=0$ in $D$ with $c_{r,w}\in\mathbb C$ finitely supported. Grouping by $w$ gives $\sum_wP_wT_w=0$ with $P_w=\sum_rc_{r,w}x^r\in\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\subseteq\Omega$; $\Omega$-independence of the $T_w$ forces $P_w=0$ for every $w$, and linear independence of the monomials [F3] then forces $c_{r,w}=0$. Hence the elements $\Phi(x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w)$ are $\mathbb C$-linearly independent.

Basis theorem. Let $h\in H_d$ and write $h=\sum c_{r,w}x^rw$ using step 1.4. If $h=0$, applying the homomorphism $\Phi$ of step 2.1 gives $\sum c_{r,w}m_{x^r}T_w=0$, and step 3.1 yields $c_{r,w}=0$. Hence the ordered monomials form a $\mathbb C$-basis of $H_d$, and the $\mathbb C$-linear map $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_d]\to H_d$, $f\otimes w\mapsto fw$, is an isomorphism by [F5]; in particular $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ and $\mathbb C[S_d]$ are subalgebras of $H_d$ and the cross relations hold. The elementary cases $H_0=\mathbb C$, $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$ were recorded in step 1.1.

The inverse map. Assume $d\ge1$. In $H_d$ the relation $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ gives, after left multiplication by $s_i$ and use of $s_i^2=1$, the recursion $x_{i+1}=s_ix_is_i+s_i$. Hence in $H_d/(x_1-a)$ one has $x_1\equiv a$ and inductively $x_j\equiv a+u_j$ with $u_j$ in the subalgebra generated by the images of the $s_i$, namely $u_1=0$ and $u_{j+1}=s_ju_js_j+s_j$. By the basis theorem of step 4.1 every element of $H_d$ is a combination of monomials $x^rw$, and replacing each $x_j$ by $a+u_j$ expresses its image in $H_d/(x_1-a)$ as an element of the image of the subalgebra generated by the $s_i$; by [F1] and [F2] that image is the $\mathbb C$-span of $\{w:w\in S_d\}$. Therefore the canonical map $\rho\colon\mathbb C[S_d]\to H_d/(x_1-a)$, $w\mapsto w+(x_1-a)$, has image equal to the whole quotient, and it is injective because $\bar\varphi\circ\rho=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C[S_d]}$ by construction; hence $\rho$ is an isomorphism. Under it $x_j$ corresponds to $a+u_j$, and $\bar\varphi(a+u_j)=a+J_j$ by step 2.3, so $\bar\varphi(x_j)=a+\sum_{k<j}(k\ j)$; in particular $x_1$ corresponds to the scalar $a$, while for $j\ge2$ the image is not the scalar $a$. The specified images of both the $x_j$ and the $s_i$ determine the homomorphism uniquely because these elements generate the quotient.

The degree filtration. For $k\ge0$ let $F_k\subseteq H_d$ be the image of the $\mathbb C$-span of all words in the symbols containing at most $k$ of the symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d$. Steps 1.4 and 4.1 identify $F_k$ with the span of the monomials $x^rw$ with $|r|\le k$. The substitution rules of step 1.4 replace an adjacent pair $s_ix_j$ by terms containing at most one $x$-symbol each, so a product of a word with $k$ $x$-symbols and a word with $m$ $x$-symbols rewrites into words with at most $k+m$ $x$-symbols; hence $F_kF_m\subseteq F_{k+m}$ and $(F_k)_{k\ge0}$ is an algebra filtration with $1\in F_0$.

The associated graded is a semidirect product. Let $S:=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ be the algebra with $\mathbb C$-basis $x^rw$ and product $x^rw\cdot x^{r'}w'=x^{r+w\cdot r'}ww'$, where $(w\cdot r')_j=r'_{w^{-1}(j)}$; equivalently, $S$ is generated by the symbols $x_i$ and $w$ subject to the relations obtained from those of $H_d$ by deleting the inhomogeneous term $1$ from both cross relations, i.e. $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i$ and $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i$. In $\mathrm{gr}\,H_d$ the defining relations of $H_d$ project to these relations: the commutativity, Coxeter and distant-commutation relations are homogeneous of the stated degrees, while the two cross relations have the form (degree $1$ element) $=1$ (degree $0$ element), so their degree-$1$ parts are exactly $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i$ and $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i$. Consequently there is a surjective graded algebra homomorphism $S\to\mathrm{gr}\,H_d$ sending $x_i$ and $w$ to the symbols of $x_i$ and $w$. In degree $k$ both sides are $\mathbb C$-spanned by the symbols $x^rw$ with $|r|=k$: these form a spanning set of $\mathrm{gr}_kH_d$ by step 5.2 together with the basis theorem of step 4.1, and they form the basis of the degree-$k$ part of $S$ by construction; a surjection between $\mathbb C$-vector spaces with a spanning set of the same finite cardinality as a basis of the target is an isomorphism. Hence $\mathrm{gr}\,H_d\cong S$ in every degree, and the associated graded is the semidirect product $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ in which $s_i$ swaps $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$, as claimed.

Polynomial grading boundaries. For $d=0$, step 1.1 gives $H_0=\mathbb C$ with its degree-zero grading; for $d=1$, it gives $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$ with the usual polynomial grading. For $d\ge2$, suppose there were an algebra grading $H_d=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}H_d^{(k)}$ with $x_i$ in degree $1$ and $s_i$ in degree $0$. Then the relation $s_ix_{i+1}-x_is_i=1$ would have its left-hand side in degree $1$ and its right-hand side in degree $0$, forcing $1=0$, which is impossible. Hence for $d\ge2$ the polynomial-degree filtration of step 5.2 does not arise from that generator grading; its cross relation is inhomogeneous.

citations.quote: Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.

An endomorphism $N:V\to V$ is **nilpotent** if $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$. Its **nilpotency index** is the least positive integer $r$ such that $N^r=0$; this least exponent exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, let $G$
be a connected smooth algebraic group scheme of finite type over $k$ (such a
$G$ is separated by Milne 1.22 and geometrically reduced, hence a classical
variety of finite type over $k$) acting on a classical variety $X$ over $k$
([[def-dimension-classical-variety]],
[[cor-smooth-variety-classical-scheme-conventions-agree]]), and let
$x\in X(k)$ be a closed point. Then: (a) every fibre over a closed $k$-point of
the orbit map $\varrho_x:G\to O_x$ is a left translate of the stabilizer $G_x$
([[lem-action-map-fibres-and-stabilizer-subscheme]]), hence has underlying
topological dimension $\dim G_x$, equivalently the dimension of its reduction;
$G_x$ may be nonreduced ([[def-dimension-noetherian-topological-space]]);
(b) $\dim G=\dim G_x+\dim O_x$; (c) the orbit closure $\overline{O_x}$ is the
union of $O_x$ and of orbits of strictly smaller dimension; consequently every
orbit of minimal dimension in $X$ is closed, and $\overline{O_x}$ contains a
closed orbit. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the generic-fibre and
constructibility inputs.

Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, let $G$
be a connected smooth algebraic group scheme of finite type over $k$ (such a
$G$ is separated by Milne 1.22 and geometrically reduced, hence a classical
variety of finite type over $k$) acting on a classical variety $X$ over $k$
([[def-dimension-classical-variety]],
[[cor-smooth-variety-classical-scheme-conventions-agree]]), and let
$x\in X(k)$ be a closed point. Then: (a) every fibre over a closed $k$-point of
the orbit map $\varrho_x:G\to O_x$ is a left translate of the stabilizer $G_x$
([[lem-action-map-fibres-and-stabilizer-subscheme]]), hence has underlying
topological dimension $\dim G_x$, equivalently the dimension of its reduction;
$G_x$ may be nonreduced ([[def-dimension-noetherian-topological-space]]);
(b) $\dim G=\dim G_x+\dim O_x$; (c) the orbit closure $\overline{O_x}$ is the
union of $O_x$ and of orbits of strictly smaller dimension; consequently every
orbit of minimal dimension in $X$ is closed, and $\overline{O_x}$ contains a
closed orbit. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the generic-fibre and
constructibility inputs.

An endomorphism $N:V\to V$ is **nilpotent** if $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$. Its **nilpotency index** is the least positive integer $r$ such that $N^r=0$; this least exponent exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

Let $k$ be a field, let $n\geq 0$ be finite, put $P=k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and let
$A=P/I$ with a specified finite generating list $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ for the
actual ideal defining the affine scheme. For a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset
A$, write $L=A/\mathfrak m$. Let $J(\mathfrak m)$ be the $r\times n$ matrix over
$L$ obtained by mapping the formal partial derivatives $\partial f_i/\partial
t_j$ through $P\to A\to L$.

If $k$ is perfect, then $L/k$ is finite separable and
$$
\operatorname{rank}_L J(\mathfrak m)=n-\dim A_{\mathfrak m}
$$
if and only if $A_{\mathfrak m}$ is a regular local ring. For any field $k$,
the same equivalence holds at a $k$-rational point, where $L=k$, without a
perfectness assumption. If $I=I(X)$ for a reduced classical affine algebraic
set $X$ over an algebraically closed field and $\mathfrak m$ corresponds to a
closed point $x$, then, assuming AC,
$$
\dim A_{\mathfrak m}=\dim_xX=\max_{x\in X_i}\dim X_i,
$$
where $X_i$ ranges over the irreducible components through $x$. The finite
generating list need not be minimal, and $I$ need not be radical in the first
two assertions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let
$$ I=(x_1,\ldots,x_n) $$
be an ideal generated by $n\ge1$ elements, and let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal minimal over $I$. Then $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)\le n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $R$ is a Noetherian Cohen--Macaulay ring, then
$R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$ is Cohen--Macaulay for every $n\ge0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, let $0\ne M$ be finite, and let
$x_1,\ldots,x_r$ be both $M$-regular and an initial segment of a system of
parameters for $M$. Then $M$ is Cohen--Macaulay if and only if
$M/(x_1,\ldots,x_r)M$ is Cohen--Macaulay.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

For a finite module $M$ over a commutative Noetherian ring, $(S_1)$ is equivalent to every associated prime being minimal in $\operatorname{Supp}M$. For the ring itself, this means no embedded associated primes. A commutative Noetherian ring is reduced if and only if it satisfies $(R_0)$ and $(S_1)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

For every commutative Noetherian ring $R$, including rings with zero divisors and the zero ring, $R$ is normal if and only if it satisfies $(R_1)$ and $(S_2)$.

Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple
Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, let $n\ge0$, and let
$E:=V^{\otimes n}$ carry the left place action of $S_n$
([[def-commuting-symmetric-and-linear-actions-on-tensor-power]]). Let $A$ be
the image of the algebra homomorphism $\mathbb C[S_n]\to\operatorname{End}(E)$
extending the place action, and let
$B:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{g^{\otimes n}:g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\}$
be the linear span of the diagonal operators
$g^{\otimes n}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=gv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_n$.
Then:

1. **(Mutual centralizers.)** $B=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F a=aF\text{ for
   all }a\in A\}$ and $A=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F b=bF\text{ for all
   }b\in B\}$.
2. **(Uniqueness of the identification.)** $B$ is a unital
   $\mathbb C$-subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}(E)$ and equals the image of
   the diagonal action of the universal enveloping algebra
   $U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$, that is the unital subalgebra generated by the
   operators $\Delta(T)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes
   \mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}$, $T\in\operatorname{End}(V)$
   ([[lem-tensor-place-operators-span-the-symmetric-centralizer]]).

All statements include $n=0$, where $E=\mathbb C$.

derivations.claim: **Empty chains.** If $V=0$, take $t=0$; if $e=0$ on a nonzero space, its Jordan diagram has a single column and $t=1$. In either case there are no chain variables or equations, $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$, $H$ is trivial and $\theta=0$. Its image is the point orbit closure, its coordinate ring is a normal domain, and the empty equation sequence is regular. The boundary is empty and has codimension $+\infty$. All conclusions follow in these cases. Henceforth $t\ge2$.

**The open chain locus.** Put $c=\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$ and $D=2\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-c$. The differential of the chain equations is $Y_iA_i+B_iX_i-X_{i-1}B_{i-1}-A_{i-1}Y_{i-1}$, with the index-zero terms zero. If each $A_i$ is injective or $B_i$ is surjective, these equations can be solved successively for any prescribed right-hand sides: use a left inverse of $A_i$ to choose $Y_i$, or a right inverse of $B_i$ to choose $X_i$, after the preceding pair is fixed. Thus the open locus $Z^\circ$ with this condition is smooth of dimension $D$ by [F4]. It is nonempty: use $U_i=\operatorname{im}e^{t-i}$, inclusions $A_i$, and restrictions $B_i=e|_{U_{i+1}}$, transported to the fixed spaces. These maps satisfy the equations and have end map $e$.

**Alternating strings and their stabilizers.** For a nilpotent pair $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, the odd operator $T$ on $U\oplus W$ with these components has a homogeneous Jordan-string decomposition: kernels and images of its powers are graded, so the complements in the Jordan construction may be chosen homogeneous. Every string alternates letters $a$ from $U$ and $b$ from $W$. Removing all $b$ letters gives the Jordan rows of $BA$, and removing all $a$ letters gives those of $AB$. The ranks of alternating composites recover the numbers of strings of each length and starting letter, so a diagram determines one pair orbit and there are finitely many diagrams in fixed dimensions. The pair stabilizer is the unit group of its even endomorphism algebra, an open subset of a vector space and hence smooth and irreducible. On a string $A$ kills exactly a terminal $a$ and $B$ misses exactly an initial $a$; consequently $A$ is injective iff every string ends in $b$, and $B$ is surjective iff every string begins in $b$.

**Even orbit drops.** Distinct dominated types have strictly smaller orbit dimension. One can move from a dominating partition to a dominated one by repeatedly moving a box from an earlier row to a later allowable row: choose an excess row and a subsequent deficit row, taking the last row of the source plateau and the first allowed destination to preserve the partition inequalities, and repeat until the target is reached. A move from row $i$ to row $j>i$ increases $\sum_r(2r-1)\mu_r$ by $2(j-i)$ and therefore decreases the orbit dimension by that positive even number. Each allowable unit move from row lengths $a,b$ with $a\ge b+2$ is realized by a one-parameter degeneration. On chains $u_1,\ldots,u_{a-1}$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_{b+1}$ of the destination type, keep the usual lowering maps except send $v_{b+1}$ to $v_b+z u_{a-1}$, with $v_0=0$. At $z=0$ the type is $(a-1,b+1)$; for $z\ne0$ the ranks of powers are those of $(a,b)$ (the chain generated by $v_{b+1}$ has length $a$, and the remaining chain has length $b$). Keeping other strings fixed proves that dominated types belong to the top orbit closure. Hence a drop of exactly two consists of one box moved to the next row; any other drop is at least four. Equivalently, parity also follows from $\sum_j(\mu'_j)^2\equiv\sum_j\mu'_j=N\pmod2$ for the total sum; individual summands in a difference of square sums need not be even.

**The pair-orbit dimension.** Write $m=\dim U$, $n=\dim W$, and let $E,O$ be the dimensions of the even and odd centralizers of $T$. A homomorphism between Jordan strings of lengths $L,L'$ has $\min(L,L')$ possible shifts. Counting the parity of those shifts, odd strings of the same endpoint type contribute $+1$ to the even-minus-odd count, and odd strings of opposite type contribute $-1$; the two opposite Hom directions for an odd/even pair cancel, and even/even pairs contribute zero. Summing gives $E-O=(m-n)^2$, because the difference between the numbers of odd $a$-type and odd $b$-type strings is $m-n$. The pair orbit therefore has dimension $m^2+n^2-E=\tfrac12((m+n)^2-E-O)$, half the dimension of the ordinary orbit of $T$. If a string has $r_j$ letters $a$ and $s_j$ letters $b$, then $\min(r_j+s_j,r_k+s_k)=\min(r_j,r_k)+\min(s_j,s_k)$ except for equal odd lengths with opposite endpoint types, where the left side is larger by one. Let $a_l,b_l$ count the odd strings of length $l$ beginning with the two respective letters, and put $\Delta=\sum_{l\text{ odd}}a_lb_l$. Writing $C_{BA}$ and $C_{AB}$ for the ordinary conjugacy orbits, the ordinary Jordan centralizer counts now give $\dim O_{(A,B)}=mn+\tfrac12(\dim C_{BA}+\dim C_{AB})-\Delta$. This is a dimension identity for the orbit, not for the full matrix space minus the pair orbit.

**Chain strata.** Stratify $Z$ by its compatible alternating-string diagrams at every link. Compatibility means that the $b$-diagram of one link equals the $a$-diagram of the next. These are finitely many locally closed strata. For a link $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, projection of its pair orbit to the orbit of $BA$ has fiber $(Z_{\mathrm{GL}(U)}(BA)\times\mathrm{GL}(W))/G_{(A,B)}$; projection to the orbit of $AB$ instead has fiber $(\mathrm{GL}(U)\times Z_{\mathrm{GL}(W)}(AB))/G_{(A,B)}$. Indeed the numerator is the stabilizer of the specified endomorphism in the full acting group, and the denominator is the pair stabilizer. These are smooth homogeneous fibrations. Each numerator is connected and smooth, being a product of unit groups of finite-dimensional endomorphism algebras, and the pair stabilizer is smooth by step 1.3; hence the fibers are smooth and irreducible. Iterating these fibrations proves each nonempty chain stratum $Z_\delta$ smooth and irreducible. The dimension at each fiber-product step is the preceding dimension plus the pair-orbit dimension minus the shared Jordan-orbit dimension. The intermediate orbit dimensions cancel in the formula of step 2.1, giving $\dim Z_\delta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12\dim C_\sigma-\sum_{i<t}\Delta_i$, where $\sigma$ is the type of its final end map.

**Dominance and the top stratum.** The chain equations make $\theta^k$ factor through $U_{t-k}$, so $\operatorname{rank}\theta^k\le n_{t-k}$ and $\theta^t=0$. Thus its type $\sigma$ is dominated by $\eta$ by [F3]. For a $b$-diagram $\sigma$, every row must first be filled internally by alternating $a$ letters; this requires exactly $|\sigma|-\ell(\sigma)$ letters, the size of the diagram obtained by deleting its first column. Over the top diagram $\eta$, this equals $n_{t-1}$, leaving no extra letters: every string starts and ends in $b$ and the lower diagram is exactly the first-column deletion of $\eta$. Repeat down the chain. There is exactly one top stratum; it has both maximal-rank maps at every link, lies in $Z^\circ$, and has every $\Delta_i=0$. Finally, expanding $q_j=n_{t-j+1}-n_{t-j}$ gives $\tfrac12\dim C_\eta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$, so its dimension is $D$.

**Drops of at least four.** By the stratum formula and the nonnegativity of all $\Delta_i$, a final orbit drop of at least four gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-4)=D-2$. Every non-top stratum has dimension at most $D-1$. This latter estimate establishes uniqueness of the dense top stratum but does not assert that every non-top stratum has codimension two: some are smooth divisors inside $Z^\circ$.

**Drops of two and the nonsmooth-locus bound.** Suppose $\sigma$ is obtained from $\eta$ by moving a box to the next row. Let $\eta'$ and $\sigma'$ denote first-column deletions and let $m=|\eta'|$, $m'=|\sigma'|$. At the last link the available number of $a$ letters is $m$ and its $a$-diagram must be dominated by $\eta'$, since its powers factor through the shorter chain. If the receiving row was nonempty, $m=m'$: internal filling consumes every $a$, all strings begin and end in $b$, and the same next-row degeneration passes to the shorter chain. If a new singleton row is created, $m=m'+1$. After internal filling there is one extra $a$. It can be attached at either end of the shortened last row, at either end of the new singleton $b$ row, or placed in a new singleton $a$ row. No earlier row can receive it: its $a$-diagram would gain a box earlier than the removed last-row box and violate dominance by $\eta'$. In the first four placements one map is maximal rank; the lower diagram is either $\eta'$ or its next-row degeneration. In the fifth placement both maps fail maximal rank, and singleton strings of both types occur, giving $\Delta_i\ge1$. This remains valid when the shortened row is itself a singleton, when there can be more than one singleton $b$. Inducting through the shorter chain shows that either every link has a maximal-rank map and $Z_\delta\subseteq Z^\circ$, or some $\Delta_i\ge1$. In the latter case the dimension formula gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-2)-1=D-2$. Together with step 5.1, this proves $\dim(Z\setminus Z^\circ)\le D-2$.

**Complete intersection and reducedness.** Every irreducible component of the scheme cut out by its $c$ equations has dimension at least $\dim M-c=D$ by [F4]. The top stratum has dimension $D$ and all other strata have smaller dimension by step 5.1, so every component has dimension $D$. Thus the equation ideal has height $c$. Its homogeneous generators form a regular sequence in the polynomial ring: at the homogeneous maximal ideal, every prefix of length $k$ has height at least $k$, since adjoining the remaining $c-k$ equations raises height by at most $c-k$; the opposite inequality is Krull's bound. Complete the generators to a system of parameters and apply the Cohen-Macaulay parameter theorem in [F4]. Homogeneous localization detects a kernel in a multiplication map, so regularity is global. The quotient is Cohen-Macaulay, hence satisfies $S_1$ and $S_2$. Every component meets the smooth open $Z^\circ$ by step 6.1, so it satisfies $R_0$; [F5] implies reducedness.

**Irreducibility and normality of the chain.** The unique top stratum is irreducible. Its closure contains every component: otherwise a component of dimension $D$ would have a nonempty open subset outside that closure, contained in a finite union of strata of dimensions at most $D-1$, which is impossible. Thus the reduced chain ring is a domain. Its singular locus is contained in $Z\setminus Z^\circ$, of codimension at least two by step 6.1, so it satisfies $R_1$; it satisfies $S_2$ by step 7.1. Serre's criterion [F5] gives normality.

**The invariant quotient.** For one pair $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, invariants under $\mathrm{GL}(U)$ are generated by entries of $AB$: the scalar matrices force equal polynomial degrees in $A,B$, polarization turns a bihomogeneous invariant into a mixed tensor invariant, and [F6] expresses it as permutation contractions. Each contraction is a product of entries of $AB$, with possible cyclic traces also polynomials in those entries. For rational finite-dimensional $\mathrm{GL}(U)$ modules, the central scalar torus splits the space into integer weight spaces. On each weight space apply the semisimple Lie algebra complete-reducibility theorem [F6] to $\mathfrak{sl}(U)$; an invariant complement then respects the center as well. It respects the group because elementary unipotents and diagonal matrices generate $\mathrm{GL}(U)$. Thus rational quotient invariants lift by complete reducibility in bounded polynomial degree, so the same description applies to a stable closed subscheme with its induced relations. Eliminate vertices in order. At the first vertex the invariant generators are $A_1B_1$ and the remaining variables; the chain equation replaces $A_1B_1$ by $B_2A_2$. The quotient is consequently the graph over the remaining variables with the induced rank and nilpotency relations, and eliminating the next vertex applies the same one-pair calculation. Repeating leaves precisely the entries of $\theta$. Thus $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ is generated by those entries, and is the coordinate ring of the closure of $\theta(Z)$. The rank bounds of step 4.1 put the image in the orbit closure of $e$, while the inclusion/restriction construction of step 1.2, applied to every conjugate of $e$, puts its full orbit in the image. Hence that closure is $X$ and $\mathbb C[Z]^H\cong\mathbb C[X]$.

**Normality and boundary of the orbit closure.** An element of $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb C[Z]^H)$ integral over $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ is also integral over the normal domain $\mathbb C[Z]$, hence belongs to it. Being a fraction of invariant elements it is fixed by $H$, so it belongs to $\mathbb C[Z]^H$; no equality between the full invariant fraction field and the fraction field of the invariant ring is needed. Therefore $\mathbb C[X]$ is a normal domain, reduced and irreducible. The finitely many boundary nilpotent orbits have positive even dimension drops by step 1.4, so their union has codimension at least two. The point cases and their empty boundary were proved in step 1.1. This proves all chain and orbit conclusions.

citations.quote: All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of [[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in each case by the computation displayed.

For every finite-dimensional representation $\rho:\mathfrak g\to \mathfrak{gl}(V)$, the trace form is bilinear and symmetric, and it is invariant in the sense that $$B_\rho([z,x],y)+B_\rho(x,[z,y])=0.$$ Consequently the Killing form has all three properties.

If $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ is a basis and $x^1,\ldots,x^n$ is its $B$-dual basis, the **Casimir element relative to $B$** is $$\Omega_B=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x^i\in U(\mathfrak g).$$ On a representation $\rho:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$, its **Casimir operator** is $$\rho(\Omega_B)=\sum_{i=1}^n\rho(x_i)\rho(x^i).$$ The empty sums give zero when $\mathfrak g=0$.
The Casimir element $\Omega_B$ is independent of the chosen dual bases and belongs to the center of $U(\mathfrak g)$.

For any pair of $B$-dual bases $(x_i),(x^i)$, the tensor $\sum_i x_i\otimes x^i\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$, and hence its image $\sum_i x_ix^i\in U(\mathfrak g)$ under multiplication, is independent of the chosen pair.

In $T(\mathfrak g)$, regard $[x,y]\in\mathfrak g$ as an element of tensor degree one, and let $I$ be the two-sided ideal generated by $$x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y]\qquad(x,y\in\mathfrak g).$$ The **universal enveloping algebra** is $$U(\mathfrak g)=T(\mathfrak g)/I.$$ Write $$\iota_{\mathfrak g}:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow U(\mathfrak g)$$ for the composite of the degree-one inclusion with the quotient map.

A **representation** of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ on $V$ is a Lie-algebra homomorphism $$\rho:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak{gl}(V).$$ Writing $xv$ for $\rho(x)(v)$, this is equivalently a $k$-bilinear action $\mathfrak g\times V\to V$ satisfying $$[x,y]v=x(yv)-y(xv)$$ for all $x,y\in\mathfrak g$ and $v\in V$.

Let $$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$ be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements.

There is a canonical group isomorphism $$\alpha_{M,N,P}:(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP\longrightarrow M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP)$$ determined by $$\alpha_{M,N,P}((m\otimes n)\otimes p)=m\otimes(n\otimes p).$$ It respects any compatible outer module actions and is natural in $M,N,P$.

If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis $$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$ Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism.

Work over the field $\mathbb C$ and fix an integer $d\ge 0$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[def-commutative-ring]]). Let
$\mathcal F_d$ be the free associative unital $\mathbb C$-algebra on the
$d+\max(d-1,0)$ symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ (for $d=0$ there is only
the unit; for $d=1$ only $x_1$), with its word basis and universal property
([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]), and let
$I_d\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}\mathcal F_d$ be the two-sided ideal
([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]])
generated by the following elements:

- $x_ix_j-x_jx_i$ for all $1\le i,j\le d$;
- $s_i^2-1$ for $1\le i\le d-1$;
- $s_is_{i+1}s_i-s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$ for $1\le i\le d-2$;
- $s_is_j-s_js_i$ for $1\le i,j\le d-1$ with $|i-j|>1$;
- $s_ix_j-x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$, $s_ix_{i+1}-x_is_i-1$, and
  $x_{i+1}s_i-s_ix_i-1$, for $1\le i\le d-1$ and $1\le j\le d$.

The **degenerate affine Hecke algebra** is the quotient $\mathbb C$-algebra
$$H_d:=\mathcal F_d/I_d$$
with unit element written $1$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-laws]]). We keep the symbols
$x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ for their images, and for $w\in S_d$ we write
$w$ for the image in $H_d$ of any word in the $s_i$ representing $w$; this is
independent of the chosen word once the basis theorem below is proved. For
$d\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb C$, the notation $H_d/(x_1-a)$ means the quotient by the two-sided
ideal generated by $x_1-a$.

The verification below establishes exactly the structure of $H_d$ used
throughout this page: the ordered monomials
$$x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w,\qquad r_1,\dots,r_d\ge0,\ w\in S_d,$$
form a $\mathbb C$-basis, so that
$H_d\cong\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_d]$ as a vector
space with polynomial and group-algebra subalgebras
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]], [[def-group-ring]]);
$H_0=\mathbb C$ and $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$; for $d\ge1$ and every $a$ there is a unique
algebra isomorphism
$$H_d/(x_1-a)\cong\mathbb C[S_d],\qquad x_j\longmapsto a+\sum_{k<j}(k\ j),\qquad s_i\longmapsto(i\ i+1);$$
and total polynomial degree is an algebra filtration whose associated graded is
the semidirect product $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ in which
$s_i$ acts by swapping $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$. For $d\ge2$, the cross relation is
inhomogeneous, so it does not turn $H_d$ into a graded algebra with
$\deg x_i=1$ and $\deg s_i=0$. For $d=0$ the algebra $\mathbb C$ has its
degree-zero grading, and for $d=1$ the algebra $\mathbb C[x_1]$ has its
natural polynomial grading.

derivations.claim: $\Omega$ is the flip on $V\otimes V$. On the tensor basis, $\Omega(v_a\otimes v_b)=\sum_{i,j}(E_{ij}v_a)\otimes(E_{ji}v_b)=\sum_{i,j}\delta_{ja}v_i\otimes\delta_{ib}v_j=v_b\otimes v_a=P_{01}(v_a\otimes v_b)$ by [F1]. Consequently $\Omega_{ab}=P_{ab}$ whenever the two labelled factors $a,b$ are both natural factors; in particular $\Omega_{j,j+1}=s_j$ on the $V$-factors.

Naturality and commutation with $\mathfrak g$. For a $\mathfrak g$-module map $f\colon M\to M'$, the map $f\otimes1^{\otimes d}$ intertwines $x_j$ and $s_i$: it plainly intertwines the place permutations $P_{ab}$, and it intertwines $\Omega_{0j}$ because the Casimir operator on a tensor product of modules is an intertwiner by [F2]. For the same reason each $x_j$ and $s_i$ commutes with the $\mathfrak g$-action on $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$, the action on the $V$-factors being the natural one.

The $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ Casimir. The trace form restricts to a nondegenerate form on $\mathfrak{sl}_N$: $\mathfrak{sl}_N=\{X\in\mathfrak g:B(X,z)=0\}$ because $B(X,z)=\operatorname{tr}(X)$ and $B(z,z)=N\ne0$. Hence $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}=\Omega-\frac1Nz\otimes z$ is the inverse tensor of $B|_{\mathfrak{sl}_N}$: for $X\in\mathfrak{sl}_N$, contracting the second factor of $\Omega$ with $X$ gives $\sum_{ij}B(X,E_{ji})E_{ij}=X$, while contracting the second factor of $z\otimes z$ with $X$ gives $B(X,z)z=\operatorname{tr}(X)z=0$; so contraction with $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ also returns $X$, and by [F2] the dual tensor is unique. Thus $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the $\mathfrak{sl}_N$-Casimir for the restricted trace form.

The recursion. Since $s_j=P_{j,j+1}$ and $P_{ab}$ are involutions with $P_{ab}\Omega_{ab}P_{ab}=\Omega_{ab}$ and conjugation by $P_{j,j+1}$ replaces the label $j$ by $j+1$ in every operator supported on labels $\{0,1,\dots,j\}$, one has $s_j\Omega_{0j}s_j=\Omega_{0,j+1}$, $s_jP_{kj}s_j=P_{k,j+1}$ for $k<j$, and $s_js_j=1$. Hence $s_jx_js_j+s_j=\Omega_{0,j+1}+\sum_{k<j}P_{k,j+1}+P_{j,j+1}=x_{j+1}$, using $x_{j+1}=\Omega_{0,j+1}+\sum_{k<j+1}P_{k,j+1}$ and $P_{j,j+1}=s_j$. Thus the operators satisfy the recursion of [F4]. The remaining Hecke relations require the independent commutator check in [[thm-the-casimir-and-place-permutation-operators-satisfy-degenerate-affine-hecke-relations]].

The source dictionary. Let $\Omega$ now denote the $\mathfrak{sl}_N$-Casimir in the formula (2.2.1) of the source [F5], so that on two natural factors $\Omega_{ij}=P_{ij}-1/N$ by steps 1.1 and 1.3, i.e. $P_{ij}=\Omega_{ij}+1/N$, which is exactly [AS, (2.2.1)]. On $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ the library $\mathfrak{gl}_N$-Casimir satisfies $\Omega^{\mathfrak{gl}_N}_{0j}=\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}_{0j}+z_M/N$ (the extra term $\frac1Nz\otimes z$ acts on factor $0$ as $z_M/N$ and on factor $j$ as the identity on $V$), while $\Omega^{\mathfrak{gl}_N}_{kj}=\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}_{kj}+1/N$ for two natural factors; therefore $y_j=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2}=\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}(\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}_{kj}+\tfrac1N)+\tfrac{N-1}{2}$, which is precisely the source formula (2.2.2) in [F5].

Special cases. For $d=0$ there are no labels $j\ge1$, so the family $(x_j)$ and $(s_i)$ is empty and the Definition records only the module $M$; the recursion and the dictionary are vacuous. For the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ the action of $\mathfrak g$ is zero, so $\Omega_{0j}=0$ and $z_M=0$; hence $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$, with the empty sum $x_1=0$.
