citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_N(\mathbb C)$,
with upper-triangular Borel, and represent $a=\lambda+\rho$ by coordinates
of sum zero. For every $i<j$ with $a_i-a_j\in\mathbb Z$, require
$a_i-a_j\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$. Thus $a$ is regular and strictly decreasing
inside each coordinate coset modulo $\mathbb Z$; there is no ordering of
complex numbers from different cosets. Write $P$ for the weight lattice,
$U_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_\lambda$, and
$\mathcal O_{\lambda+P}$ for objects of genuine $\mathcal O$ whose weights
belong to $\lambda+P$.

Let $\mathcal H_\chi$ consist of finitely generated $U$-bimodules $B$ with
$B\ker\chi_\lambda=0$ and locally finite adjoint $\mathfrak g$-action.
For finite-dimensional $E$ let $\Phi_E=E\otimes U_\chi$, with diagonal
left action and ordinary right action. Then
$$T_\lambda(B)=B\otimes_U\Delta(\lambda)$$
is an exact equivalence $\mathcal H_\chi\simeq\mathcal O_{\lambda+P}$.
Every object on either side has a finite presentation by the respective
projective generators $\Phi_E$ and $E\otimes\Delta(\lambda)$. The induced
map is the natural, composition-preserving identification
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal H_\chi}(\Phi_E,\Phi_F)\ \cong\ (E^*\otimes F\otimes U_\chi)^{\mathfrak g}\ \cong\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E\otimes\Delta(\lambda),F\otimes\Delta(\lambda)).$$
The comparison commutes naturally with finite-dimensional tensoring.

For $\mathfrak{gl}_N$ the corresponding statement uses
$\mathcal O_{\lambda+\mathbb Z^N}$ and finite-dimensional modules with
integral coordinate weights; $\mathcal H_\chi$ additionally requires its
adjoint Cartan weights to be integral and its adjoint scalar centre to act
semisimply. No assertion here supplies standard-label transport, a
parabolic restriction, or this equivalence for a nonprojective source
Verma or a singular source weight.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

Every object of $\mathcal O$ has a finite composition series and is both Noetherian and Artinian. The length of zero is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every simple object
$L(\mu)$ of $\mathcal O$ admits a projective cover
$P(\mu)\twoheadrightarrow L(\mu)$
([[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]), which may be chosen
inside the linkage class of $\mu$; the cover is unique up to isomorphism and
indecomposable. Consequently $\mathcal O$ has enough projectives: every object
of $\mathcal O$ is a quotient of a finite direct sum of such projective
covers, because objects of $\mathcal O$ have finite length and each composition
factor is a quotient of its projective cover.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be an ordered basis of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Then the monomials

$$x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_r^{a_r} \qquad (a_i\in \mathbb N_0)$$

form a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$. In particular, multiplication identifies $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ with the symmetric algebra $S(\mathfrak g)$ on the symbols of the $x_i$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

For a linkage class $C=W_\lambda\cdot\lambda$, let $\mathcal O_C$ be the full subcategory of objects all of whose simple composition factors have labels in $C$. Then $\mathcal O=\bigoplus_C\mathcal O_C$, and each nonzero $\mathcal O_C$ is indecomposable as a categorical direct summand. These are precisely the blocks. Each $\mathcal O_C$ lies in $\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda}$; a central-character summand can contain several blocks. Independently, grouping weights by cosets of the root lattice $Q$ gives a canonical coarser decomposition by weight cosets.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

If $[M(\lambda):L(\mu)]\ne0$, then $\mu\uparrow\lambda$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The set $\Phi_\lambda$ is preserved by its root reflections. If $\mu\in W_\lambda\cdot\lambda$, then $\Phi_\mu=\Phi_\lambda$ and $W_\mu=W_\lambda$. The equivalence classes generated by moves $\eta\mapsto s_\alpha\cdot\eta$ with $\alpha\in\Phi_\eta$ are exactly $W_\lambda\cdot\lambda$. Every strong-linkage chain stays in one such class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
published category-$\mathcal O$ theory. Let
$\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_J=\mathfrak l_J\oplus\mathfrak u_J$ be the standard
parabolic of
[[def-standard-parabolic-and-levi-subalgebras-from-simple-roots]], with
reductive parabolic Levi $\mathfrak l_J$, nilradical $\mathfrak u_J$ and Weyl
group $W_J$; the ambient category is $\mathcal O$ of [[def-bgg-category-o]]
with standard objects the Verma modules [[def-verma-module]].

**(1) Dominance for the Levi.** A weight $\lambda$ is **$\mathfrak p$-dominant**
if $\langle\lambda,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for all
$\alpha\in\Phi_J^+$ (this is dominance for the Levi root system; in particular
$\lambda$ is integral for $\Phi_J$; see
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]] for the ambient
notion). No integrality condition is imposed on the simple coroots outside
$J$, or on the central part $\mathfrak z_J$ of the Levi.

**(2) Generalized Verma modules.** For a $\mathfrak p$-dominant $\lambda$ let
$E(\lambda)$ be the finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak p$-module obtained
from the finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak l_J$-module of highest weight
$\lambda$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]])
by letting $\mathfrak u_J$ act by zero. Define the **generalized Verma module**

$$M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak p)}E(\lambda).$$

**(3) The parabolic category.** The **parabolic category** $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$
is the full subcategory of $\mathcal O$ whose objects are the finitely
generated $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-modules on which
$U(\mathfrak p)$ acts locally finitely, that is, on which every vector lies
in a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak p$-submodule; equivalently, every vector
lies in a finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak l_J$-submodule and is annihilated by a power of $\mathfrak u_J$
(local finiteness for the nilpotent $\mathfrak u_J$).

The following structural facts are part of the definition; the arguments are
given in the Remarks.

**(4) Generalized Vermas lie in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$.** For each
$\mathfrak p$-dominant $\lambda$, $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ is an
object of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ with highest weight $\lambda$, and the
natural surjection $M(\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$
exhibits $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ as the largest quotient of the Verma
module $M(\lambda)$ that lies in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$.

**(5) Simples.** The simple objects of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ are exactly
the simple highest-weight modules $L(\lambda)$ with $\lambda$
$\mathfrak p$-dominant
([[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]]).

**(6) Serre property.** $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ is closed under subobjects,
quotients and extensions in $\mathcal O$; in particular it is an abelian
subcategory of $\mathcal O$ stable under finite direct sums.

**(7) Costandard objects.** For $\mathfrak p$-dominant $\lambda$ put
$\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=D M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$, the restricted
dual of [[prop-restricted-duality-is-an-exact-involution-on-category-o]].
These are the **costandard objects** of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$; each is
naturally a submodule of the ordinary dual Verma $D M(\lambda)$. They need not
be quotients of ordinary dual Vermas.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and that $I$ is bounded
below, so $n_j=m_j+1-\inf(I)$ and $n=\sum_jn_j$ are finite; the upper end of
$I$ may remain unbounded. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)$ and let
the standard parabolic $\mathfrak p$ have Levi
$\mathfrak{gl}_{n_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{n_l}$
([[def-standard-parabolic-and-levi-subalgebras-from-simple-roots]]).
For a tableau $A$ let $a_1,\dots,a_n$ be its ordinary highest-weight
reading: read columns from left to right and each column from top to bottom,
so its entries are strictly decreasing. This is also the normally ordered column reading of
[[def-higher-level-wedge-tensor-fock-module]]. Put
$$\lambda_A=\sum_{j=1}^{n}(a_j+j-1)\,\varepsilon_j .$$
Strict columns make $\lambda_A$ Levi-dominant, so that the simple highest weight
module $L(A)$ of [[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]]
and the induced generalized standard
$M(A)=M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda_A)$ of
[[def-parabolic-category-o-for-a-standard-parabolic]] belong to the genuine
parabolic category $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ of
[[thm-parabolic-category-o-is-a-highest-weight-category]].

Use the published **half-sum convention**
$\rho_j=(n+1-2j)/2$; then
$$\lambda_{A,j}+\rho_j=a_j+\frac{n-1}{2},$$
so the $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ Harish-Chandra shifted-coordinate multiset of the
block is the tableau-entry multiset plus the common scalar $(n-1)/2$, and this
multiset together with the displayed scalar $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ centre labels the
central character ([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]). The Fock
weight $\sum_j\delta_{a_j}=\Lambda-\alpha$ of the Fock item belongs to the
different $\mathfrak{gl}_{I^+}$ weight lattice and indexes that entry multiset;
it is **not** a literal $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ highest weight.

For an entry multiset $\alpha$ the corresponding **finite parabolic central
block** $\mathcal O^\Lambda_\alpha$ has labels
$\mathrm{Col}^\Lambda_\alpha$, generalized standards $M(A)$, simples $L(A)$,
projective covers $P(A)$ and costandards $\nabla(A)$, with the BGG reciprocity,
restricted duality and highest-weight structure inherited from
[[thm-parabolic-category-o-is-a-highest-weight-category]]; by
[[lem-type-a-tableau-central-summands-are-single-linkage-blocks]] it is a single
linkage block. Its simple and standard classes form bases of its Grothendieck
group, and its numerical multiplicities include repeated-entry singular central
characters. The direct sum over the admitted entry multisets is
$\mathcal O^\Lambda$. **Opposite blocks** use the reversed Levi order and the
reverse-column reading, with the correspondingly reversed label order
([[lem-the-parabolic-semi-regular-duality-and-reverse-column-label-map]]).

Every finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak g$-module is a cyclic highest-weight module whose highest weight is dominant integral, and for each dominant integral weight

$$\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^r m_i\omega_i \qquad (m_i\in \mathbb N_0),$$

there exists, up to isomorphism, a unique finite-dimensional simple module $L(\lambda)$ with highest weight $\lambda$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Every $H$-weight in the relevant weight-coset category is nonintegral when the adjacent shifted coordinates belong to different entry cosets: $\eta(H)=(\eta+\rho)_i-(\eta+\rho)_{i+1}-1$, and weight changes are integral. This holds in every subquotient. If $Fv=0$ for a weight vector of weight $h$, choose $r\ge0$ maximal with $E^rv\ne0$, using positive-root local nilpotence in $\mathcal O$. The $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ relation gives $FE^{r+1}v=-(r+1)(h+r)E^rv$, a contradiction. Thus $F$ is injective on every object and subquotient of that category.

Powers of $F$ satisfy both Ore conditions in $U(\mathfrak g)$: iterating $Fu=uF+[F,u]$ gives the finite binomial commutation formula, since $\operatorname{ad}F$ is locally nilpotent on each enveloping element. PBW makes $U$ a domain. Its localization $U_F=\bigcup_{k\ge0}F^{-k}U$ is a directed union of free right $U$-modules; consequently localization $M_F=U_F\otimes_U M$ is exact. Step 1.1 makes $M\to M_F$ injective, and the diagram of short exact sequences $0\to M\to M_F\to M_F/M\to0$ proves exactness of $C_F(M)=M_F/M$. Therefore $T_s(M)={}^{\phi}C_F(M)$ is exact. The adjoint exponentials defining $\phi$ are finite on every $u\in U$; they send $E,F,H$ to $-F,-E,-H$ and act as the adjacent permutation on the Cartan.

Let $v$ be the normalized highest vector of $\Delta_\eta$. The class $F^{-1}v$ becomes a highest vector of weight $s\cdot\eta$: its new $E$ is $-F$, whose value lies in $\Delta_\eta$; the other transformed positive roots are positive roots distinct from $\alpha_i$, and commuting them through $F^{-1}$ leaves positive-root terms killing $v$. The new $F$ sends $F^{-r}v$ to $r(\eta(H)+r+1)F^{-r-1}v$, with every scalar nonzero. PBW, ordered with $F$ first, gives the basis of the localized quotient with $F$-powers $-1,-2,\ldots$; reflection permutes the remaining positive roots. Hence the displayed vector generates the quotient. Its character is $s(e^\eta\sum_{r\ge1}e^{r\alpha_i}\prod_{\beta>0,\beta\ne\alpha_i}(1-e^{-\beta})^{-1})=\operatorname{ch}\Delta_{s\cdot\eta}$. The highest-vector surjection is an isomorphism by equality of each finite weight dimension. This fixes its scalar by $v_{s\cdot\eta}\mapsto[F^{-1}v_\eta]$.

For finite-dimensional $X$, localization commutes with tensoring. On $M_F\otimes X$ the total operator $F_M+F_X$ has inverse $F_M^{-1}\sum_{k\ge0}(-F_M^{-1}F_X)^k$; the sum is finite since $F_X$ is nilpotent. The localization universal property identifies $(M\otimes X)_F$ with $M_F\otimes X$ and identifies the embedded $M\otimes X$. Quotienting and the Weyl matrix $W_X=\exp(E_X)\exp(-F_X)\exp(E_X)$ identify $T_s(M\otimes X)$ naturally with $T_s(M)\otimes X$. For two finite tensor factors, $W_{X\otimes Y}=W_X\otimes W_Y$, so associativity and the tensor-unit diagrams commute. The diagonal Weyl action fixes the invariant Casimir and commutes with flips, proving their compatibility as actual operators.

Choose regular coset-dominant $\lambda$ in the weight-coset category. Crossing distinct cosets preserves each coset's internal order, so $s\cdot\lambda$ meets the same regular coset-dominance hypotheses; its central character equals $\chi_\lambda$. For a generator map encoded by $t\in(E^*\otimes F\otimes U_\chi)^{\mathfrak g}$, its action is the finite sum of finite-tensor matrix entries followed by enveloping operators on $\Delta_\lambda$. The invariant matrix map commutes with the total $F$ on the tensor modules, so its unique localized extension agrees with the same enveloping-operator formula under the tensor localization of step 4.1. Passing to the quotient, twisting and applying the matrices of step 4.1 transforms $t$ by simultaneous Weyl conjugation in its three factors. Each $t$ lies in a finite adjoint submodule, so that conjugation is $\exp(E_{\mathrm{diag}})\exp(-F_{\mathrm{diag}})\exp(E_{\mathrm{diag}})$ and fixes $t$, since its diagonal $\mathfrak g$-action is zero. Thus $T_s$ induces exactly the common Hom identification of [F1], respecting composition and identity. The scalar from step 3.1 is the same on all generators $X\otimes\Delta_\lambda$, so it cancels on every generator Hom space; an arbitrary unnormalized scalar is not treated as a literal equality of highest vectors.

Every object has a finite presentation by finite direct sums and summands of the generators in [F1]. Exactness and steps 3.1–4.1 show that its $T_s$ image is the cokernel of a map between target generators, hence belongs to the target category $\mathcal O$. Step 5.1 identifies all generator maps. Every target presentation therefore lifts, proving essential surjectivity. Applying Hom from a generator to a source presentation and its target presentation gives identical cokernel diagrams, since those generators are projective; applying Hom from a presented object gives identical kernel diagrams. This proves full faithfulness on all objects. Idempotents are preserved and reflected by the generator Hom identification, so summands cause no gap. Consequently $T_s$ is an exact category equivalence, established on actual maps and presentations.

Compose these swaps in a stable bubble sort by the fixed coset order. Each swap crosses different cosets; none permutes indices inside a coset. The composite sends $\Delta_\eta$ to $\Delta_{w\cdot\eta}$ and therefore sends its unique simple head to $L(w\cdot\eta)$. It transports projective covers by exact equivalence and essentiality. Every original column consists entirely of one coset; stable sorting retains its coordinates as a consecutive block and retains their internal order. At the end, the original Levi simple roots are therefore positive simple roots of the sorted column Levi. Their highest-weight integral-dominance pairings are unchanged. By the actual Levi simple criterion and Serre property of [F4], the composite and its inverse restrict to the full parabolic subcategories. Because generalized Vermas are the largest parabolic-finite quotients of ordinary Vermas, their quotient universal property is transported, giving the claimed generalized-standard labels as modules. No intermediate swap is asserted to preserve an intermediate parabolic subcategory.

The coherent comparison of two sorting paths can be made on tensor-projective generators. Each path has the common [F1] Hom matrix identification of step 5.1; their final Weyl representatives differ at most by a diagonal torus matrix when they induce the same coordinate permutation. Diagonal simultaneous action again fixes invariant matrices. Their reference-standard highest lines admit a unique comparison after fixing its nonzero scalar; tensor it with $X$ for every generator and summand. The equality on generator Hom matrices makes these comparisons natural, and taking presentation cokernels extends them uniquely to all objects, independently of a presentation by full faithfulness. Comparisons for three paths compose because they coincide on the normalized reference generator and its tensor presentations. This proves the stated normalization and coherence, without asserting an unnormalized inverse-twist or braid identity.

After sorting let $\mathfrak q$ have contiguous coset Levi $\mathfrak l=\bigoplus_\kappa\mathfrak{gl}_{N_\kappa}$ and positive outside radical $\mathfrak u$. In a fixed linkage block $C$, [F3] says exactly that highest labels are obtained by permutations within the coset blocks, including when entries repeat. Hence all highest labels have the same block-centre values $z_\kappa$. For each initial union of coset blocks, write $Z_r$ for its diagonal trace and $b_r$ for the common highest-label value. Every module weight satisfies $b_r-\mu(Z_r)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$: this holds on simple highest-weight modules by their negative-root weights and on all finite-length objects by their composition series. An outside negative root strictly lowers at least one prefix; an inside root leaves every prefix fixed. The simultaneous top section $S(M)=\{v:Z_rv=b_rv\ \forall r\}$ is therefore a Levi module and is annihilated by $\mathfrak u$. It is exact, since it is a direct sum of Cartan weight spaces and the Cartan acts semisimply. These are integer differences from fixed complex values, not inequalities on complex numbers.

In fact $M^{\mathfrak u}=S(M)$. If a nonzero homogeneous radical-invariant vector lies in a lower prefix section, its Levi cyclic module has a highest vector: its positive Levi orbit is finite-dimensional and a maximal weight therein is killed by every positive Levi root. Radical invariants are Levi-stable because $[\mathfrak l,\mathfrak u]\subset\mathfrak u$. That Levi highest vector is thus a full $\mathfrak g$ highest vector. Its cyclic module has a simple highest-weight quotient of the same weight and the same strictly lower prefix, contradicting the actual label restriction in [F3]. Decomposing a general invariant into centre weights gives the same contradiction componentwise. Moreover $S$ detects nonzero objects: every simple of $C$ has a nonzero highest vector in its top section, and exactness plus a composition series proves the assertion for every nonzero finite-length object.

Let $C_{\mathfrak l}$ be the product integral-reflection orbit for the Levi highest weights with these fixed scalar centres, and define $R(X)=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak q)}X$, with $\mathfrak u$ acting by zero. PBW makes $R$ exact and identifies $S(R(X))=X$ naturally: every outside negative PBW monomial lowers some prefix, so only its degree-zero term contributes. For a Levi simple $L_{\mathfrak l}(\eta)$, induction is a quotient of the ordinary $\mathfrak g$ Verma of label $\eta$, hence lies in $C$ by [F3] and has finite length by [F2]. Every composition factor has nonzero top section by step 10.1; exactness and $S(R(L_{\mathfrak l}(\eta)))=L_{\mathfrak l}(\eta)$ imply that there is only one factor. Thus $R(L_{\mathfrak l}(\eta))=L_{\mathfrak g}(\eta)$ is simple. Exactness extends block membership and finite length to $R(X)$ for every finite-length $X$ by a Levi composition series.

Induction and radical invariants are adjoint, and step 10.1 identifies the latter with $S$. Their unit is PBW's top-section isomorphism $X\to S(R(X))$. For the counit $R(S(M))\to M$, applying exact $S$ gives this identity, so its kernel and cokernel have zero top section; both are finite-length objects of $C$ and vanish by detection in step 10.1. Hence $R$ and $S$ are inverse exact category equivalences. This argument proves full faithfulness from the actual unit and counit. It does not deduce it from composition matrices. By induction transitivity, ordinary Levi Vermas go to ordinary $\mathfrak g$ Vermas; the corresponding column-generalized Vermas go to their genuine column-parabolic inductions. The Levi integrability criterion restricts the equivalence to the column-parabolic subcategories just as in step 7.1; projective covers again follow by exact equivalence.

Each finite Levi factor block has a finite projective generator (finite label orbit and [F2], or its parabolic reflector). For two outer tensor projectives, their Hom is the tensor product of their factor Homs, by tensor-Hom and the finite-dimensional factor Hom spaces; applying a factor-projective Hom successively is exact: a fixed weight for the other factors cuts a finite-generated factor-$\mathcal O$ module, since PBW bounds the negative monomials in those fixed coordinates; factor projectivity therefore applies weight by weight. The resulting multiplicity module is in the remaining factor $\mathcal O$, by the same PBW finiteness with the finitely many generator weights of the projective. Their outer tensor sum therefore is projective, and its simple quotients cover all factor tuples. Those tuples exhaust the simple labels of the direct-sum Lie algebra: the outer tensor of the factor simples is cyclic on the tensor of their highest vectors. Any nonzero submodule has a highest vector by positive-root local finiteness and bounded highest-weight support; taking invariants successively in the separate positive root algebras leaves only that tensor highest line, because a simple highest-weight factor has no other highest vector. The submodule thus contains the cyclic generator, proving simplicity and identifying the unique simple quotient of the direct-sum Verma. Thus the outer tensor generator gives finite presentations of every object and has the tensor-product endomorphism algebra. Applying the generator Hom and its presentation inverse proves the product description in the Statement. This also proves standard/simple/projective tensor labels as objects, not just as classes.

The original tableau convention gives $\eta_i+\rho_i=a_i+(N-1)/2$, so dot sorting is literally stable sorting of the $a_i$. In the sorted $\kappa$ block the Levi coordinate is $a_t+B_\kappa+t-1$. The integral coordinate from the Statement is $a_t-c_\kappa+n-n_\kappa+t-1$; their difference is exactly $\delta_\kappa$. Tensoring with the one-dimensional Lie algebra representation $x\mapsto\delta_\kappa\operatorname{tr}(x)$ is an exact inverse equivalence with inverse shift $-\delta_\kappa$, and its tensor associativity is ordinary scalar multiplication. It carries highest vectors, induced standards, simple heads and projective covers. Since a ground entry in global row $r$ is $c_\kappa+1-r$, its integral image is $1-(r-n+n_\kappa)$; these are the actual bottom-aligned integral ground rows. The retained heights give $m_j=q_j-n_\kappa$ nonincreasing and $m_j+1-(1-n_\kappa)=q_j$. For an admitted-ground label, subtracting its original ground entry gives a nonnegative integer; the displayed dictionary preserves that difference. Its integral entry is therefore at least the corresponding bottom-aligned integral ground entry and lies in the fixed admitted alphabet of [F4]. For an arbitrary genuine label the scalar shift still gives an integral parabolic highest weight, but no fixed-cut membership follows. Thus the height/charge dictionary holds generally and the fixed admitted component hypotheses of [F4] hold on the stated admitted-ground subcategories, without treating a nonintegral scalar trace character as an algebraic determinant character.

For clarity about tensor transport, the ordinary induction tensor identity is $R(X)\otimes V\cong U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak q)}(X\otimes\operatorname{Res}_{\mathfrak q}V)$; it follows from the coproduct and antipode and is natural in $X,V$. The restricted vector representation has its actual prefix-$\mathfrak q$ filtration whose sections are the coset vector modules $V_\kappa$ with outside radical zero. Exact induction therefore gives a filtration of $R(X)\otimes V$ with sections $R(X\otimes V_\kappa)$. A projected linkage/entry-multiset tensor summand admitting an entry change in coset $\kappa$ kills the other sections: their highest labels change a different coset multiset, so their central characters or linkage classes differ by [F3]. Only the $\kappa$ section survives, giving its natural component comparison; the dual vector representation has the reversed filtration and the same argument. Thus the residue-projected operators transport to the appropriate integral factor. Iterated tensor comparisons use the same actual filtrations and the associative tensor identity, so their diagrams commute; no unrestricted tensor-product assertion is inferred.

The trace-character shift changes the relevant vector Casimir eigenvalue by its scalar: for $\Omega=\sum_{i,j}E_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}$, replacing the first-factor action by $E_{ij}+\delta_{ij}\delta$ adds $\delta\sum_i1\otimes E_{ii}=\delta$ on a vector representation; the dual gives the corresponding opposite shift. The offset can be computed explicitly: on a vector-tensor Verma section of highest label $\eta+\varepsilon_i$, the quadratic central element has value $\sum_k\eta_k(\eta_k+N+1-2k)$, while its value on the vector is $N$. Taking half the difference gives the global tensor-Casimir eigenvalue $\eta_i+1-i$. For the Levi coordinate $t=i-B_\kappa$, the same calculation gives $\eta_i+1-t$, greater by $B_\kappa$. Hence the trace shift contributes $\delta_\kappa-B_\kappa=c_\kappa-n+n_\kappa$ to the original residue: $(c_\kappa+q_j-n)-(q_j-n_\kappa)=c_\kappa-n+n_\kappa$. This computes the parameter dictionary and the block projections of step 15.1; no integer residue is silently equated with its complex original. It does not replace a proof of the full affine-Hecke natural-transformation presentation. Together with steps 4.1 and 15.1 this proves the claimed normalized compatibility, and steps 7.1, 12.1–13.1 and 14.1 prove the typed category equivalence with all stated labels and hypotheses.

Steps 7.1 and 14.1: the zero-degree admitted label is ground and the scalar shift sends its rows to the exact integral ground rows; zero modules are preserved by localization and top sections.
Steps 7.1 and 14.1: with one coset there are no sorting swaps, the product has one Levi factor and only the explicit scalar-character shift remains.

citations.quote:
A finite geometric simplicial complex $K$ is considered with its Euclidean
realization and induced metric; subcomplex, closure, star and link terminology
follows [[def-simplicial-subcomplex-star-closure-and-link]]. For $b\in|K|$ the
**tangent star** is the union of the tangent cones at $b$ of all simplices
containing $b$, that is, the rays locally contained in the closed star.

A map $f:|K|\to M$ is **piecewise smooth** when every restriction $f|\sigma$ to
a closed simplex extends smoothly to a neighbourhood in its affine hull and the
extensions agree on common faces. In a target coordinate chart the differential
$df_b$ is then the well-defined continuous piecewise linear map on the tangent
star that equals $D(f|\sigma)(b)$ on the cone of each simplex $\sigma$
containing $b$; agreement on common faces makes it independent of the chosen
containing simplex. A **smooth immersion of a complex** requires $df_b$
injective on the entire tangent star at every point, not merely on each simplex
tangent space; a **smooth embedding** requires in addition that $f$ be a
homeomorphism onto its image, and a **finite smooth triangulation** of $M$ is
such an embedding onto $M$. A corner-adapted triangulation must be face
compatible: the inverse image of each local corner face is locally the restriction of a
subcomplex, and the
differential fan maps the source tangent star homeomorphically onto the
appropriate tangent orthant, or its specified face sector. This last local
orthant condition is the corner-adapted triangulation contract.

After an ambient Euclidean realization of the target, or in a fixed finite
family of compact target chart patches, $g:K'\to M$ on a finite subdivision
$K'$ of $K$ is a **strong $C^1$ $\delta$-approximation** to $f$, for $\delta>0$, if
$\sup_b|g(b)-f(b)|<\delta$ and $|dg_b(v)-df_b(v)|<\delta|v|$ for all $b$ and
all nonzero tangent-star vectors $v$. A relative approximation **fixed on $L$** means
$g|_{|L|}=f|_{|L|}$, subdivision of $L$ permitted unless explicitly prohibited.
**Shape control** means a positive lower bound on
$r(\sigma)/\operatorname{diam}\sigma$ for every positive-dimensional simplex,
where $r(\sigma)$ is the distance from the barycentre to the relative boundary;
it is not asserted for arbitrary iterated barycentric subdivisions.

Two embeddings $f_i:K_i\to M$ **fit in a subcomplex** if the inverse images of
$f_1(|K_1|)\cap f_2(|K_2|)$ are subcomplexes $L_i$ and
$f_2^{-1}f_1:L_1\to L_2$ is a simplexwise affine isomorphism; the fit is
**full** if every simplex all of whose vertices belong to $L_i$ belongs to
$L_i$. For a full fit, gluing along that isomorphism gives a finite simplicial
complex and its union map: simplices from opposite sides can share only
vertices of the glued full subcomplex, so their common vertices span a common
face. For a fit that is not full, first barycentrically subdivide both sides
compatibly to make the common subcomplex full, then glue. The union map is
well defined because the maps agree on the identified points.

For a smooth bundle $\pi:E\to B$ and a supplied base triangulation $h:D\to B$,
a **projection-preserving diagram** consists of $F:K\to E$ and a map $r:K\to D$
that is affine on each simplex into a simplex of the original $D$ and satisfies
$\pi F=hr$; the affine/PL requirement does not require domain vertices to map
to vertices of the original fixed base complex. Fitting preserves the
projection when all modified maps satisfy the same equality with the original
$h$ and the original affine $r$ restricted to their subdivisions; a fixed
relative bundle piece must already carry such a diagram. A projection-preserving
diagram is determined by the pair $(F,r)$ together with its restrictions to
subdivisions, so a modification supported away from a piece leaves the original
diagram there exactly on the nose. No generic smooth map is called a bundle
merely because it is proper.

For relative extension on a compact manifold with corners, supplied boundary
data are admissible only when they are compatible on all corner-face
intersections and satisfy the tangent-orthant condition above; the extension
keeps their pointwise parametrization, with compatible subdivisions permitted,
and no extension of arbitrary incompatible boundary data is asserted.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $F \subseteq X$ be closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$: the metric
subspace $(F, d_F)$ is a compact metric space
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be a
continuous bijection ([[def-metric-continuity]],
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). Then:

1. $f[U]$ is open in $Y$ for every $U$ open in $X$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]);
2. the inverse function $f^{-1} : Y \to X$ is continuous.

The words used are deliberately those of open sets and of the inverse map: a
single name for a continuous bijection with continuous inverse is not available
at this point in the reading order. No choice principle is used.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

derivations.claim: Uniform rank bound. If $K$ has only vertices, immersion is automatic and a sufficiently small value error preserves the finite separation of distinct embedded vertices; the empty case is vacuous. Otherwise, for each positive-dimensional original simplex $\sigma$ let $D_\sigma$ be its direction space. Its tangent cone at $b\in\sigma$ spans $D_\sigma$ and every vector of $D_\sigma$ is a difference of two cone vectors, so whole-star injectivity makes $A_{b,\sigma}:=D(f|\sigma)(b)$ injective on $D_\sigma$. Compactness of $\sigma$ times its unit sphere gives a common least singular value $\mu>0$ over all original simplices. The strong derivative bound also holds, with $\le\delta$, on the entire direction space of each refined simplex: apply the bound at its relative interior points, where every direction is tangent, then pass to its boundary by continuity. Thus $D(g|s)(b)$ has least singular value at least $\mu-\delta$ on every refined simplex $s$, and derivative errors less than $\mu/2$ give angle errors at most $4\delta/\mu$ by [F4].

Two-segment separation. Suppose two segments have common endpoint $x$ and a simplexwise affine injective map $H$ carries their outward directions to nonzero vectors making angle $\beta>0$. In their image plane project onto the oriented line perpendicular to the internal bisector, or onto the image line when $\beta=\pi$. The two projected directions have opposite signs. Any nonzero derivative making angle less than $\beta/2$ with its corresponding image direction has the same strict projection sign. Segment integration then makes the projected map strictly monotone along each segment and puts their open images on opposite sides of the image of $x$, so the map is injective on their union. This also applies to a finite piecewise smooth subdivision of the segments: integrate on each subsegment and add.

Geometric separation. For two geometric simplices $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ with common face $\tau$ proper in both, let $c$ be the barycentre of $\tau$ and $\eta$ the opposite face of $\sigma_1$. For $p=(1-t)x+ty$, $x\in\tau$, $y\in\eta$, set $X(p)=(1-t)x+tc$, taking $X(p)=c$ when $t=1$ and $X(p)=p$ on $\tau$. This is a continuous projection fixing $\tau$, and $p-X(p)=t(y-c)$. The unit directions of $\sigma_2-c$ form a compact set: in barycentric direction coordinates the cone is given by zero sum and nonnegative coordinates at vertices outside $\tau$, hence is closed. No ray $y-c$ with $y\in\eta$ has a direction in this cone, since a common ray would either put $y$ in $\tau$ or put $y$ in $\operatorname{aff}(\tau)$, contrary to [F5]. Therefore the angle between those directions has a positive minimum. For $q\in\sigma_2$ the vector $q-X(p)$ belongs to that cone, because $c-X(p)$ lies in the direction space of $\tau$, the lineality space of the cone. This proves the same lower angle bound for the two rays from $X(p)$ to $p$ and $q$, when both are nonzero. The projection formula is preserved by separate affine injections of the two simplices agreeing on $\tau$, provided their image intersection is exactly the image of $\tau$.

Uniform frozen angles. For $b\in\tau$ define the frozen map on each simplex containing $b$ by $H_b(x)=A_{b,\sigma}(x-b)$. This is simplexwise affine, agrees on common faces, and is injective on their union by the whole-star hypothesis. Its image simplices therefore intersect exactly in $H_b(\tau)$. Apply step 1.3 to these image simplices. Their separation angle has a positive minimum uniformly over $b\in\tau$: use the fixed compact sets $y\in\eta$ and unit directions $z$ of $\sigma_2-c$, and minimize the continuous angle between $A_{b,\sigma_1}(y-c)$ and $A_{b,\sigma_2}z$ on their product with $\tau$. Neither vector vanishes by step 1.1, and a zero angle is excluded by the image intersection property. The finite minimum over all ordered original simplex pairs, capped at $\pi/2$, gives $\alpha>0$; take $\alpha=\pi/2$ if there are no such pairs. No single linear extension of $H_b$ to the span of two simplices is asserted.

Local estimates independent of the subdivision. Choose $\delta<\mu/2$ with $4\delta/\mu<\alpha/8$. For each $b$, choose a small relative ball $U_b$ meeting only original simplices containing $b$. Continuity of their finitely many derivative fields makes the angle between $D(f|\sigma)(c)h$ and $A_{b,\sigma}h$ less than $\alpha/8$ for $c\in U_b\cap\sigma$ and every nonzero direction $h\in D_\sigma$. Step 1.1 and [F4] give angle less than $\alpha/4$ between each refined derivative of $g$ along $h$ and $A_{b,\sigma}h$. This bound holds on subdivided segments, including their one-sided derivatives. Shrink to a ball $V_b$ so that for any two original simplices containing $b$, the projection in step 1.3 sends $V_b\cap\sigma_1$ into $U_b$; there are only finitely many projections and each fixes $b$. The two segments joining points of $V_b$ through that projection lie in $U_b$, since its intersections with simplices are convex. These neighbourhoods depend on $f$ and $K$, not on $g$ or its subdivision.

Local injectivity and immersion. For distinct $p,q\in V_b$ in one original simplex, join them through their midpoint; their frozen outward rays are antiparallel. Otherwise use their minimal original carriers and the projection of step 1.3 onto their common face; both carriers contain $b$, and their frozen rays make angle at least $\alpha$ by step 2.1. If one segment is trivial, the other alone has a strictly monotone projection. In all cases steps 1.2 and 3.1 give $g(p)\ne g(q)$. To check immersion at $b$, apply the same argument to the frozen piecewise linear map $J_b(x)=dg_b(x-b)$ on the refined tangent fan. Scale any two star vectors until their endpoints lie in $V_b$ and in the closed star of $b$ in the subdivision. On every refined cone the derivative of $J_b$ is $D(g|s)(b)$, whose angle from the appropriate $A_{b,\sigma}$ is less than $\alpha/8$ by step 1.1; the projected paths stay in the original cones containing $b$ and may be split across the finitely many refined cones. Step 1.2 separates their endpoints exactly as above. Hence $dg_b$ is injective on the entire tangent star, for every $b$, proving immersion.

Global embedding. If $f$ is an embedding, take a finite subcover $V_{b_1},\ldots,V_{b_m}$ of $|K|$ and put $C=|K|^2\setminus\bigcup_i(V_{b_i}\times V_{b_i})$. This compact set misses the diagonal, so $|f(p)-f(q)|$ has a positive minimum $\eta$ on it; if it is empty omit this bound. Require also $\delta<\eta/3$. On $C$, $|g(p)-g(q)|>\eta-2\delta>0$, and outside $C$ distinct points are separated by step 4.1. Thus $g$ is continuous and injective on a compact space, hence a homeomorphism onto its image by [F2]; together with immersion this is an embedding. The same $\delta$ works for every finite subdivision, with no shape or mesh restriction.

citations.quote: Every finite convex cell complex has a compatible finite simplicial triangulation. Choose one relative interior point in each nonempty cell; triangulate the boundary in increasing dimension and cone from that point. This construction agrees on every common face and preserves each cell as a subpolyhedron.

The **barycentric subdivision** of $K$ is $\operatorname{sd}K=\Delta F(K)$, using [[def-face-poset-and-order-complex]]. Thus its vertices are the nonempty faces $\sigma$ of $K$, and its nonempty simplices are strict chains $\sigma_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\sigma_q$.

A subcomplex $A\subseteq K$ gives $F(A)\subseteq F(K)$ with the induced order; hence every chain in $F(A)$ is a chain in $F(K)$ and $\operatorname{sd}A$ is a subcomplex. The vertex associated to $\{v\}$ is distinct as a label from $v$, though its geometric position will be the same. There is no vertex for the empty face; the complex with no vertices subdivides to itself.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

A finite geometric simplicial complex $K$ is considered with its Euclidean
realization and induced metric; subcomplex, closure, star and link terminology
follows [[def-simplicial-subcomplex-star-closure-and-link]]. For $b\in|K|$ the
**tangent star** is the union of the tangent cones at $b$ of all simplices
containing $b$, that is, the rays locally contained in the closed star.

A map $f:|K|\to M$ is **piecewise smooth** when every restriction $f|\sigma$ to
a closed simplex extends smoothly to a neighbourhood in its affine hull and the
extensions agree on common faces. In a target coordinate chart the differential
$df_b$ is then the well-defined continuous piecewise linear map on the tangent
star that equals $D(f|\sigma)(b)$ on the cone of each simplex $\sigma$
containing $b$; agreement on common faces makes it independent of the chosen
containing simplex. A **smooth immersion of a complex** requires $df_b$
injective on the entire tangent star at every point, not merely on each simplex
tangent space; a **smooth embedding** requires in addition that $f$ be a
homeomorphism onto its image, and a **finite smooth triangulation** of $M$ is
such an embedding onto $M$. A corner-adapted triangulation must be face
compatible: the inverse image of each local corner face is locally the restriction of a
subcomplex, and the
differential fan maps the source tangent star homeomorphically onto the
appropriate tangent orthant, or its specified face sector. This last local
orthant condition is the corner-adapted triangulation contract.

After an ambient Euclidean realization of the target, or in a fixed finite
family of compact target chart patches, $g:K'\to M$ on a finite subdivision
$K'$ of $K$ is a **strong $C^1$ $\delta$-approximation** to $f$, for $\delta>0$, if
$\sup_b|g(b)-f(b)|<\delta$ and $|dg_b(v)-df_b(v)|<\delta|v|$ for all $b$ and
all nonzero tangent-star vectors $v$. A relative approximation **fixed on $L$** means
$g|_{|L|}=f|_{|L|}$, subdivision of $L$ permitted unless explicitly prohibited.
**Shape control** means a positive lower bound on
$r(\sigma)/\operatorname{diam}\sigma$ for every positive-dimensional simplex,
where $r(\sigma)$ is the distance from the barycentre to the relative boundary;
it is not asserted for arbitrary iterated barycentric subdivisions.

Two embeddings $f_i:K_i\to M$ **fit in a subcomplex** if the inverse images of
$f_1(|K_1|)\cap f_2(|K_2|)$ are subcomplexes $L_i$ and
$f_2^{-1}f_1:L_1\to L_2$ is a simplexwise affine isomorphism; the fit is
**full** if every simplex all of whose vertices belong to $L_i$ belongs to
$L_i$. For a full fit, gluing along that isomorphism gives a finite simplicial
complex and its union map: simplices from opposite sides can share only
vertices of the glued full subcomplex, so their common vertices span a common
face. For a fit that is not full, first barycentrically subdivide both sides
compatibly to make the common subcomplex full, then glue. The union map is
well defined because the maps agree on the identified points.

For a smooth bundle $\pi:E\to B$ and a supplied base triangulation $h:D\to B$,
a **projection-preserving diagram** consists of $F:K\to E$ and a map $r:K\to D$
that is affine on each simplex into a simplex of the original $D$ and satisfies
$\pi F=hr$; the affine/PL requirement does not require domain vertices to map
to vertices of the original fixed base complex. Fitting preserves the
projection when all modified maps satisfy the same equality with the original
$h$ and the original affine $r$ restricted to their subdivisions; a fixed
relative bundle piece must already carry such a diagram. A projection-preserving
diagram is determined by the pair $(F,r)$ together with its restrictions to
subdivisions, so a modification supported away from a piece leaves the original
diagram there exactly on the nose. No generic smooth map is called a bundle
merely because it is proper.

For relative extension on a compact manifold with corners, supplied boundary
data are admissible only when they are compatible on all corner-face
intersections and satisfy the tangent-orthant condition above; the extension
keeps their pointwise parametrization, with compatible subdivisions permitted,
and no extension of arbitrary incompatible boundary data is asserted.

derivations.claim: Lattice subdivisions with a uniform thickness bound. If $K$ has no positive-dimensional simplices, its unchanged complex and secant $f$ prove the approximation assertions with the thickness condition vacuous. Otherwise give the finitely many vertices a total order and realize the abstract complex as a union of faces of one standard simplex $\Delta\subset\mathbb R^N$ with vertices $0,e_1,\dots,e_N$. The original geometric realization is related to this one by a linear isomorphism on each simplex, and finitely many such isomorphisms have uniformly bounded operator norms and inverse norms on their affine spans. In $\mathbb R^N$ cut the unit lattice cubes by the hyperplanes $\sum_i x_i=j$, $j\in\mathbb Z$, and all their faces; these cuts form a locally finite convex cell complex, since intersections arise by activating the shared supporting equalities. After translating a cube to $[0,1]^N$ only the cuts with $j=0,\dots,N$ occur, so there are finitely many cell shapes up to translation; triangulating every cell compatibly by [F1] with the translation-invariant choice of the average of its vertices gives finitely many simplex shapes, with maximal diameter $D$ and positive minimum thickness $\theta_0$ in positive dimensions. The simplex $m\Delta=\{x_i\ge0,\ \sum_i x_i\le m\}$ and each of its faces are unions of these cells, so scaling by $1/m$ gives subdivisions of $\Delta$, hence of the embedded abstract complex, with mesh at most $D/m$ and thickness at least $\theta_0$; restrictions to all faces agree because one global cell complex is used. Transporting back to the original realization multiplies diameter and inradius by the finitely many bounded factors of the linear isomorphisms, leaving the claimed mesh bound and one positive thickness $\theta$. Iterated barycentric subdivision has no such bound and is not used.

Combinatorial extension of a subdivision, and coned corrections. For the extension statement, extend the given subdivision of $A$ combinatorially in increasing dimension: keep every original simplex outside the closed star of $A$, and for each affected simplex whose boundary has already been subdivided, cone that boundary subdivision from the original barycentre. Each cone over a face simplex from the barycentre of the ambient simplex is a simplex, and the cones agree on common faces by the ray description of a simplex, so this produces a subdivision of $K$ containing the given subdivision of $A$. Suppose a correction $e=g-f$ is already defined and piecewise smooth on the subdivided boundary of an original simplex $\sigma$ with barycentre $c$; every $x\ne c$ in $\sigma$ has the unique expression $x=c+t(y-c)$ with $0<t\le1$ and $y\in\partial\sigma$. The function $b(s)=\exp(-1/s)$ for $s>0$ and $b(s)=0$ for $s\le0$ is smooth, since every right derivative is a polynomial in $1/s$ times $\exp(-1/s)$ and tends to zero at $0$. Thus $a(t)=b(t-1/3)/(b(t-1/3)+b(2/3-t))$ is a smooth scalar taper with $a(t)=0$ for $t\le1/3$ and $a(t)=1$ for $t\ge2/3$ and define $G(x)=f(x)+a(t)e(y)$ on $\sigma\setminus\{c\}$ and $G(c)=f(c)$. On each coned simplex this is smooth across $c$, because $a=0$ near $c$ forces $G=f$ there, and it assumes the prescribed values on the boundary; faces agree because $t$ and $y$ are determined by $x$ and $e$ is one function on the subdivided boundary.

Secant estimate on a shape-controlled simplex. A zero-dimensional refined simplex has secant value $f$ and zero tangent space, so contributes zero error. Let $s$ be a positive-dimensional refined simplex inside an original simplex $\sigma$, with incenter $b$, diameter $h$ and inradius $r\ge\theta h$, and put $T_b(x)=f(b)+Df(b)(x-b)$. On the compact simplex $\sigma$ the derivative of $f$ has a modulus of continuity $\omega_\sigma(h)\to0$ as $h\to0$, uniformly in the base point. To justify uniformity, for any $\varepsilon>0$ continuity supplies balls about each base point on which its derivative differs from the centre value by less than $\varepsilon/2$. The balls of half those radii cover $\sigma$; a finite subcover and the minimum of their half-radii ensure that any two sufficiently close points have derivative difference less than $\varepsilon$ by the triangle inequality. Define $\omega_\sigma(h)$ as the supremum of those differences at distance at most $h$; boundedness follows from the same finite-cover argument. Segment integration along $[b,x]$ gives $|f(x)-T_b(x)|\le h\,\omega_\sigma(h)$ for $x\in s$. The affine map $S_m-T_b$ interpolates the vertex errors $f(v)-T_b(v)$, each of modulus at most $h\,\omega_\sigma(h)$, and an affine function on a simplex attains its supremum at a vertex, so $\sup_s|S_m-T_b|\le h\,\omega_\sigma(h)$. For an affine map $A$ on $s$ with $\sup_s|A|\le E$ and a unit vector $v$ in the affine span of $s$, the point $b+rv$ lies in $s$ by the definition of incenter and inradius, so $|DA(v)|=|A(b+rv)-A(b)|/r\le2E/r$. Applying this to $S_m-T_b$ gives $\|DS_m-Df(b)\|\le2\omega_\sigma(h)/\theta$, and adding the continuity term $\|Df(b)-Df(x)\|\le\omega_\sigma(h)$ gives $\|DS_m-Df(x)\|\le(2/\theta+1)\omega_\sigma(h)$ for all $x\in s$. As the mesh tends to zero, both the value and the derivative errors tend to zero uniformly over all base points and all vectors of the refined tangent cones of $\sigma$; taking the maximum of the finitely many moduli $\omega_\sigma$ over the original simplices proves strong piecewise $C^1$ convergence.

Extension error bounds. On a cone over a boundary simplex, $x=c+t(y-c)$; writing the barycentric coordinates of $x$ in $\sigma$ and summing those outside the face carrying $y$ shows that $t$ is an affine function of $x$ divided by the fixed barycentre-to-face height, and $y=c+(x-c)/t$. On the region $t\ge1/3$ the bounds $|Dt|\le C_1(\sigma)$ and $\|Dy\|\le C_2(\sigma)$ depend only on the original simplex, not on the subdivision of the boundary. The strong bound on $De$ controls its operator norm on the entire direction space of each refined boundary simplex: apply it at relative interior points, where every direction is tangent, and pass to the boundary by continuity. The correction of step 1.2 has value $a(t)e(y)$ and derivative $a'(t)e(y)Dt+a(t)De(y)Dy$ by the chain rule, so its supremum norm and derivative norm are bounded by $C_\sigma\|e\|_{C^1}$ with $C_\sigma$ depending only on $\sigma$; near $c$ the correction vanishes identically. Hence, for finitely many affected simplices handled in increasing dimension, the product of the finitely many constants $C_\sigma$ converts any requested final error into a sufficient bound on the initial error, uniformly over all subdivisions of $A$; a zero correction on an already fixed subcomplex is retained, and the correction is zero outside the closed star of $A$ by construction. If $p$ is affine and its linear part is $P$, then $p(g)=p(f)$ is equivalent to $P(e)=0$ on $A$. The formula gives $P(a(t)e(y))=a(t)P(e(y))=0$ on every newly extended simplex, so induction preserves $p(G)=p(f)$ everywhere.

Relative approximation with plane preservation. For the relative statement, barycentrically subdivide once if necessary so that $L$ is full: a face chain all of whose barycentric vertices lie in $L$ lies in $L$ by [F1]. Then let $d$ be the sum of the barycentric coordinates at vertices outside $L$; on each subdivision simplex the coordinates are affine, so $d$ is a global continuous piecewise affine nonnegative function, and its zero set is exactly $|L|$: a point of $|L|$ lies in a subdivision simplex all of whose vertices lie in $L$ because $L$ is full, so all coordinates outside $L$ vanish, while $d(x)=0$ forces $x$ into the hull of vertices lying in $L$, hence into $|L|$. The zero set of $d$ is closed and the complement of $U$ is compact, so, when $|K|\setminus U$ is nonempty, a positive lower bound $d_0$ exists: continuity and positivity give neighbourhoods on which $d$ is at least half its value at the centre, and a finite subcover gives the minimum of finitely many positive half-values. If $|K|\setminus U$ is empty, take $g_m=f$ and the assertion outside $U$ is vacuous. Otherwise take the cutoff $\chi(s)=a(s/d_0)$ using step 1.2, so $\chi=0$ on $[0,d_0/3]$ and $\chi=1$ on $[2d_0/3,\infty)$ and its values lie in $[0,1]$; its derivative is bounded, and the piecewise affine function $d$ has bounded derivative on the fixed finite subdivision. Setting $g_m=f+\chi(d)(S_m-f)$ gives, near $|L|$, $g_m=f$; outside $U$, $g_m=S_m$; and the derivative error is bounded by the derivative error of $S_m$ plus a fixed constant times its value error, both of which tend to zero by step 2.1. Each simplex restriction is smooth and face values agree. If $f$ maps an original simplex into an affine plane, then so do its vertex interpolants and every affine combination of $f$ with them, so all affine target-plane constraints are preserved, and the preliminary subdivision still admits the uniformly controlled subdivisions of step 1.1.

Assembly. The subdivisions of step 1.1 have mesh tending to zero and one positive thickness bound and, by step 2.1, their secant maps converge strongly in piecewise $C^1$ to $f$; step 3.1 provides the relative version, fixing $f$ near $L$, agreeing with a secant map outside $U$ and preserving affine target-plane constraints. For the extension statement, step 1.2 extends the subdivision and defines the coned correction, and step 2.2 bounds its $C^1$ norm by a constant depending only on the original simplices times the $C^1$ norm of the boundary correction, uniformly over all subdivisions of $A$; choosing the initial error small enough, in the finitely many affected simplices in increasing dimension, therefore realises any prescribed final strong-approximation error, keeps the correction zero outside the closed star of $A$, and preserves a vanishing affine-linear component. This proves all three assertions.

Let $K$ be finite and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ a whole-star smooth immersion in the
sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]].
There is $\delta>0$ such that every strong piecewise $C^1$
$\delta$-approximation $g:K'\to\mathbb R^q$, on any finite subdivision $K'$,
is a whole-star immersion. If $f$ is also an embedding, $\delta$ may be chosen
so that $g$ is an embedding. The subdivision need not have a mesh or shape
bound.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

all nonzero tangent-star vectors $v$. A relative approximation **fixed on $L$** means
$g|_{|L|}=f|_{|L|}$, subdivision of $L$ permitted unless explicitly prohibited.
**Shape control** means a positive lower bound on

where $r(\sigma)$ is the distance from the barycentre to the relative boundary;

**full** if every simplex all of whose vertices belong to $L_i$ belongs to

complex and its union map: simplices from opposite sides can share only
vertices of the glued full subcomplex, so their common vertices span a common
face. For a fit that is not full, first barycentrically subdivide both sides

well defined because the maps agree on the identified points.

to vertices of the original fixed base complex. Fitting preserves the
projection when all modified maps satisfy the same equality with the original

relative bundle piece must already carry such a diagram. A projection-preserving
diagram is determined by the pair $(F,r)$ together with its restrictions to
subdivisions, so a modification supported away from a piece leaves the original
diagram there exactly on the nose. No generic smooth map is called a bundle
merely because it is proper.

data are admissible only when they are compatible on all corner-face
intersections and satisfy the tangent-orthant condition above; the extension
keeps their pointwise parametrization, with compatible subdivisions permitted,
and no extension of arbitrary incompatible boundary data is asserted.

derivations.claim: Structure of a zero set. Fix a coordinate and an original simplex, writing $u=\rho_iF$ and $Z=u^{-1}(0)\cap\sigma$. The zero set is a finite union of faces. Its maximal faces are pairwise disjoint: if two met at $b$, the hypothesis would identify their union of tangent cones with the zero face of the convex cone $C_b$ under the supporting form $du_b$. This zero face is convex and corresponds to a face $\tau$ of $\sigma$ containing $b$: the supporting form vanishes on the direction space of the minimal face containing $b$, is nonnegative on every vertex direction $v-b$, and its zero cone is generated by that direction space and precisely the zero-valued vertex directions. A relative interior direction of that face must belong to one of the finitely many zero-face cones, forcing that face to contain $\tau$; hence $\tau\subset Z$, contrary to maximality of two distinct intersecting faces. Thus, near any maximal zero face $\tau$, the only zero face is $\tau$ itself. If $Z=\sigma$, plane preservation already forces $\rho_iG=0$ throughout $\sigma$; assume otherwise that $Z$ is nonempty and proper. For every $z\in\tau$ and every vertex $v$ outside $\tau$, the tangent hypothesis gives $du_z(v-z)>0$. Their finite minimum over the compact face $\tau$ is a number $\kappa_\tau>0$. This is a bound on those transverse vertex directions, not on all unit directions outside the zero cone.

Distance lower bound. Near a proper maximal zero face $\tau$, write $x=(1-t)z+ty$ by barycentric projection, with $z\in\tau$, $y$ in the opposite face and $t$ the sum of coordinates outside $\tau$. For $x$ sufficiently near $\tau$, $t<1/2$ and $|x-z|\le t\operatorname{diam}\sigma$ is arbitrarily small, uniformly along $\tau$. Step 1.1 gives $du_z(y-z)\ge\kappa_\tau$ by expressing $y$ as a convex combination of outside vertices. Uniform continuity of $du$ on $\sigma$ follows directly by covering it with half-radius continuity balls, taking a finite subcover, and using the triangle inequality on each corresponding full-radius ball. It gives $du_{z+s(x-z)}(y-z)\ge\kappa_\tau/2$ for $0\le s\le1$, after choosing the neighbourhood small enough. Segment integration yields $u(x)\ge t\kappa_\tau/2\ge[\kappa_\tau/(2\operatorname{diam}\sigma)]\operatorname{dist}(x,Z)$, since $z\in Z$ and $|x-z|\le t\operatorname{diam}\sigma$. Take the finite minimum of these positive constants over the maximal zero faces. If the compact remainder outside their neighbourhoods is nonempty, the continuous positive ratio $u(x)/\operatorname{dist}(x,Z)$ has a positive minimum there by [F2]; if it is empty, omit this bound. Consequently there is $a>0$ with $u(x)\ge a\operatorname{dist}(x,Z)$ on the whole simplex. No such bound is needed when $Z$ is empty or the whole simplex.

Perturbing the coordinate functions. For $x\in\sigma$ choose a closest point $z\in Z_{i,\sigma}$ when the zero set is nonempty and proper; it exists by compactness of $Z_{i,\sigma}$ and the segment $[z,x]$ lies in the convex simplex. Since $\rho_iG(z)=\rho_iF(z)=0$ on the zero subcomplex, segment integration of the piecewise smooth difference along $[z,x]$, split into the finitely many refined pieces and added, gives $|\rho_iG(x)-\rho_iF(x)|\le\delta|x-z|=\delta\operatorname{dist}(x,Z_{i,\sigma})$, using the derivative bound of the strong approximation. Choose $\delta<a/2$ with $a$ from step 2.1. Then $\rho_iG(x)\ge(a/2)\operatorname{dist}(x,Z_{i,\sigma})$, so $\rho_iG\ge0$ on $\sigma$ with equality exactly on $Z_{i,\sigma}$. If $Z_{i,\sigma}=\sigma$, plane preservation gives $\rho_iG=0$ there. If $Z_{i,\sigma}$ is empty, then $\rho_iF$ has a positive minimum $m_\sigma$ on the compact simplex by [F2], and the value error $|G-F|<\delta$ with $\delta<m_\sigma/2$ keeps $\rho_iG$ positive on all of $\sigma$.

Conclusion. Choose $\delta>0$ below $\delta_0$ of [F1], every $a/2$ for a proper nonempty zero set, and every $m_\sigma/2$ for an empty zero set, omitting nonexistent cases. Every strong $\delta$-approximation $G$ preserving the zero subcomplexes then has $\rho_iG\ge0$ with zero set exactly $Z_{i,\sigma}$ on every simplex, for every $i$: all coordinate functions are nonnegative and the coordinate zero sets are exactly the prescribed ones, so $G$ maps $K$ into the same closed orthant with the same boundary structure. By [F1] $G$ is again a whole-star embedding. This supplies the side control that affine-plane preservation alone does not give, as the half-plane warning in the cited Munkres exercise requires.

Let $K$ be a finite geometric complex and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ piecewise smooth in
the sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]].
There are subdivisions $K_m$ agreeing on every original face, with mesh
tending to zero and a single lower thickness bound $\theta>0$ for every
positive-dimensional simplex, whose secant maps $S_m$, defined by affine
interpolation of the values of $f$ at vertices, converge strongly in piecewise

If $L\subset K$ is a subcomplex and $U$ an open neighbourhood of $|L|$, the
approximation can instead be chosen pointwise equal to $f$ on a neighbourhood
of $|L|$ and equal to a secant map outside $U$, on shape-controlled
subdivisions; subdivision of $L$ is permitted and does not alter $f$ there, and
every affine target-plane constraint already satisfied by $f$ on original

$A\subset K$, a sufficiently small strong approximation $g$ to $f|_A$ on any
subdivision extends to a prescribed small strong approximation $G$ to $f$ on a
subdivision of $K$, with $G=f$ and with the original simplices unchanged
outside the closed star of $A$. The permitted error of $g$ depends on the
requested error and the finite original simplices, not on the shape of the

bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) and a subset of a bounded
set is bounded. No choice principle is used.

intersections and satisfy the tangent-orthant condition above; the extension

Let $F:K\to[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$ be a finite whole-star smooth
embedding, and write $\rho_iF$ for its first $c$ coordinate functions. Assume
for each original simplex $\sigma$ and each $i$ that
$Z_{i,\sigma}=\{x\in\sigma:\rho_iF(x)=0\}$ is a union of faces and that, at
every $b\in Z_{i,\sigma}$, the linear form $d(\rho_iF)_b$ on the tangent cone of
$\sigma$ is nonnegative with zero set precisely the tangent cone of
$Z_{i,\sigma}$. These are the adapted face/tangent conditions, not merely
simplex rank conditions.

There is $\delta>0$ such that every strong $\delta$-approximation $G$ preserving
each of these coordinate planes on the specified zero subcomplexes maps all of
