Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. We use cochains as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], with $X[k]^n=X^{n+k}$ and $d_{X[k]}^n=(-1)^kd_X^{n+k}$. Thus $H^n(X[k])=H^{n+k}(X)$. The cochain category $K(\mathcal A)$ is the reindexed published homotopy category. Put

$$D(\mathcal A)=K(\mathcal A)[\mathrm{qis}^{-1}],\qquad Q:K(\mathcal A)\longrightarrow D(\mathcal A).$$

Likewise $D^-,D^+,D^b$ initially mean the localizations of the termwise bounded variants of [[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]. Roof morphisms exist by [[lem-quasi-isomorphisms-admit-the-roof-calculus-in-the-homotopy-category]] and [[thm-the-calculus-of-fractions-constructs-the-localization]] under its standing size hypothesis: a small category of complexes, or supplied small cofinal denominator families. Every assertion of Hom sets is under that hypothesis. In the bounded module models, supplied replacements will separately exhibit those Hom sets. No general local-smallness theorem for unbounded $D(\mathcal A)$ is asserted.

The cone convention is $\operatorname{Cone}(f)^n=Y^n\oplus X^{n+1}$, $d(y,x)=(d_Yy+fx,-d_Xx)$, and its triangle ends in $X[1]$.

Let
$$0\to A^\bullet\to B^\bullet\to C^\bullet\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of cochain complexes in an abelian category. Then
there is a natural exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n(A)\to H^n(B)\to H^n(C)\xrightarrow{\partial^n}H^{n+1}(A)\to H^{n+1}(B)\to H^{n+1}(C)\to\cdots.$$

Let $K^{p,q}$ be a first-quadrant double cochain complex whose signed total
complex uses finite direct sums on every diagonal. Suppose a cochain complex
$C^\bullet$ maps to the bottom edge so that, for every $p$, the augmented
column
$$0\longrightarrow C^p\longrightarrow K^{p,0}\xrightarrow{v}K^{p,1}\xrightarrow{v}K^{p,2}\longrightarrow\cdots$$
is exact and the augmentations commute with the horizontal maps. Then the
induced cochain map $C^\bullet\to\operatorname{Tot}K$ is a quasi-isomorphism.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $X$ be a topological space and let
$\mathcal F$ be a flasque sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-flasque-sheaf]]). Then for every open subspace $U\subseteq X$ and every
integer $q>0$,
$$H^q(U,\mathcal F|_U)=0,$$
where $H^q(U,-)$ denotes sheaf cohomology on the space $U$
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]) computed with the global
sections functor of $U$, and $\mathcal F|_U$ is the restriction of $\mathcal F$
to $U$. Equivalently, every restriction $\mathcal F|_U$ is $\Gamma$-acyclic
([[def-acyclic-sheaf-global-sections]]).

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum on a class $\mathcal D$, let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor, and let
$$0\to A\to J^0\to J^1\to J^2\to\cdots$$
be an $F$-acyclic resolution of $A$ relative to $I$. Assume moreover that
$A\in\mathcal D$ and that, for $Z^0:=A$ and
$$0\to Z^q\to J^q\to Z^{q+1}\to0\qquad(q\ge0),$$
each $Z^q$ lies in $\mathcal D$. Then for every $n\ge 0$ there is a canonical
isomorphism
$$R_I^nF(A)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(F(J^\bullet_{\mathrm{del}})).$$

derivations.claim: The inverse image $f^*=f^{-1}$ is exact and $f^*\dashv f_*$, and $f_*$ preserves injective objects. By [F4] there is a natural isomorphism $(f^{-1}G)_x\cong G_{f(x)}$ under which the stalk of $f^{-1}\varphi$ is $\varphi_{f(x)}$; since exactness is tested stalkwise, $f^{-1}$ preserves kernels, images and cokernels and is exact. The adjunction bijection of [F4] is $k$-linear, its two directions being given on sections by the canonical $k$-linear maps $G\to f_*f^{-1}G$ and $f^{-1}f_*F\to F$; hence $f^*$ is left adjoint to $f_*$ in $\operatorname{Sh}_k$. If $I$ is injective, then $\operatorname{Hom}_Y(-,f_*I)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_X(f^*(-),I)$ is a composite of the exact functor $f^*$ and the exact representable functor $\operatorname{Hom}_X(-,I)$, so $f_*I$ is injective.

The tensor product has the expected stalks, and tensoring is exact in each variable. Define $A\otimes_kB$ as the sheafification of the sectionwise tensor presheaf of [F5]. By [F5] sheafification preserves stalks, so $(A\otimes_kB)_x$ is the filtered colimit $\varinjlim_U A(U)\otimes_kB(U)$ over the open neighbourhoods of $x$; since tensor products of vector spaces commute with filtered colimits, this is $A_x\otimes_kB_x$, and the stalk of $A\otimes\varphi$ is $\operatorname{id}\otimes\varphi_x$. For fixed $B$, the functor $A\mapsto A\otimes_kB$ is therefore stalkwise $A_x\mapsto A_x\otimes_kB_x$, which is exact because every $k$-vector space is flat, and exactness is stalkwise by [F4]; the same holds in the other variable. The restriction to opens is the evident one, so all these maps are compatible with restriction, and no choice is used in this step.

Injective $k$-sheaves are flasque. Let $I$ be injective and let $U\subseteq V$ be open. The canonical map $j_{U!}k_U\to j_{V!}k_V$ of [F6] is a monomorphism of $k$-sheaves: on stalks it is the identity $k\to k$ on $U$, the monomorphism $0\to k$ on $V\setminus U$, and $0\to0$ elsewhere. By [F6], $\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_{U!}k_U,I)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_U(k_U,I|_U)\cong I(U)$ and similarly with $V$. Injectivity of $I$ extends every morphism $j_{U!}k_U\to I$, that is, every section over $U$, along this monomorphism to a morphism $j_{V!}k_V\to I$, that is, a section over $V$ restricting to it. Hence the restriction $I(V)\to I(U)$ is surjective, and $I$ is flasque by [F8].

The adjunction $f^*\dashv Rf_*$ holds on bounded-below derived categories. Let $F$ be a bounded-below complex on $X$ and let $j:F\to I_F$ be a bounded-below termwise injective replacement, supplied under DC by [F3]; declare $Rf_*F:=f_*I_F$, well defined up to canonical isomorphism because any two such replacements are homotopy equivalent by [F3] and $f_*$ preserves homotopy equivalences. Since $f_*$ preserves zero objects in each degree, $f_*I_F$ is bounded below, and it is termwise injective by step 1.1; hence it is K-injective by [F3], and for every bounded-below complex $G$ on $Y$ the localization identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(Y)}(G,f_*I_F)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{K(Y)}(G,f_*I_F)$. The levelwise adjunction of [F4] identifies this with $\operatorname{Hom}_{K(X)}(f^*G,I_F)$, and because $I_F$ is K-injective and quasi-isomorphic to $F$, this is $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(X)}(f^*G,F)$. All identifications are natural and $k$-linear, and the triangle identities are the triangle identities of the levelwise adjunction, so $f^*\dashv Rf_*$ on $D^+$.

Flasque $k$-sheaves are acyclic for sections on every open set. Let $F$ be flasque and embed it into an injective $I$ using [F2], with quotient $Q$. Viewed as a short exact sequence of underlying abelian sheaves, the sequence $0\to F\to I\to Q\to0$ has flasque kernel $F$ and flasque middle term $I$ by step 1.3, so [F8] gives that $I(U)\to Q(U)$ is surjective for every open $U$ and that $Q$ is flasque. Write $H^q(U,-)$ for the right derived functors of the $k$-linear sections functor at $U$ formed with the functorial datum of [F2]; no comparison with abelian sheaf cohomology is yet assumed. By [F7] the family $(H^q(U,-))_{q\ge0}$ is a cohomological delta functor, so the displayed short exact sequence yields a long exact sequence; by [F7] again $H^q(U,I)=0$ for $q>0$ because $I$ is injective. Hence $H^1(U,F)=0$ and, for every $n\ge1$, $H^{n+1}(U,F)\cong H^n(U,Q)$. Since $Q$ is again flasque, the same argument applies to $Q$, and induction on $n$ gives $H^n(U,F)=0$ for all $n\ge1$ and every open $U$, uniformly over all flasque $k$-sheaves. To establish the comparison, resolve any $k$-sheaf $G$ by the functorial $k$-injective resolution of [F2]. Forgetting scalars and restricting to $U$ preserves exactness by the stalk criterion [F4]; each resolution term is flasque by step 1.3, so its underlying abelian sheaf on $U$ is acyclic by [F10]. The abelian resolution datum in [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]] is defined on all of $\mathrm{Ab}(U)$, hence includes every kernel in this resolution. The acyclic-resolution theorem of [F10] therefore identifies the cohomology of this section complex naturally with the published $H^q(U,G|_U)$. The same section complex computes the $k$-linear derived functors, giving their natural comparison as underlying abelian groups. This uses flasqueness, not injectivity after forgetting scalars; for example $\mathbb F_p$ is injective as a vector space on a point but not as an abelian group.

Bounded complexes are K-flat. Filter a bounded complex $A$ by its finitely many descending stupid truncations; each successive quotient is one sheaf $A^p$ placed in degree $p$. For any acyclic complex $C$, tensoring this quotient with $C$ gives a shift of $A^p\otimes_k C$, acyclic by the exactness proved in step 1.2. The filtration sequences are split in each degree, so tensoring preserves them; their long exact cohomology sequences prove by finite induction that $\operatorname{Tot}(A\otimes_k C)$ is acyclic. This argument permits unbounded $C$, since only finitely many $A$-degrees occur in each total degree. For a quasi-isomorphism $B\to B'$ its cone is acyclic by [F9], and its tensor with $A$ is the cone of the tensor map, with the signed total differential. Hence tensor with $A$ preserves quasi-isomorphisms. Applying this in both variables shows that the signed total tensor of bounded representatives computes $A\otimes_k^LB$, independently of the representatives.

The sheaf tensor–Hom adjunction holds on sections over each open. For $k_X$-modules $H,A,G$ there is a natural bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_X(H\otimes_kA,G)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_X(H,\mathcal Hom(A,G))$: on sections over an open $U$ it is the vector-space tensor–Hom transposition $g\mapsto(h\mapsto g(h\otimes-))$, with inverse $s\mapsto(h\otimes a\mapsto s(h)(a))$, and these sectionwise bijections are compatible with restriction to smaller opens and with the $k_X$-module structures because both constructions are built from restriction maps and scalar multiplication. Hence for fixed $A$ the functor $\mathcal Hom(A,-)$ is right adjoint to the exact functor $-\otimes_kA$ of step 1.2; consequently $\mathcal Hom(A,J)$ is injective whenever $J$ is injective, its representable functor being the composite of $-\otimes_kA$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_X(-,J)$. The bijection is natural in all three variables.

The internal derived Hom has the injective model. For bounded $A$ and a bounded-below injective replacement $B\to I_B$, put $R\mathcal Hom(A,B)=\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I_B)$, with degree-$n$ term $\prod_p\mathcal Hom(A^p,I_B^{p+n})$ and differential $d\varphi=d_I\varphi-(-1)^n\varphi d_A$. The product is finite. Its terms are injective by step 2.4 and it is bounded below, hence K-injective by [F3]. Restriction of an injective sheaf to any open $U$ remains injective, because restriction is right adjoint to exact extension by zero [F6]. Thus the same model over $U$ computes $R\operatorname{Hom}_U(A|_U,B|_U)$ after taking sections. In particular the object represents the tensor–Hom functor $C\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_D(C\otimes_k^LA,B)$, rather than $C\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_D(C,B)$; it is a sheaf-valued internal Hom, not Hom of stalks.

Bounded-below flasque complexes are acyclic for derived sections. Let $C^\bullet$ be a bounded-below complex of flasque $k$-sheaves, with $C^n=0$ for $n<b$, let $\varphi:C^\bullet\to J^\bullet$ be a bounded-below termwise injective replacement supplied by [F3], and fix an open $U$. I first record a lemma: if $K^\bullet$ is an acyclic bounded-below complex whose every term is acyclic for the sections functor at $U$, then $\Gamma(U,K^\bullet)$ is acyclic. Indeed, put $Z^n=\ker(K^n\to K^{n+1})$; the complex is acyclic, so $0\to Z^n\to K^n\to Z^{n+1}\to0$ is a short exact sequence for every $n$, and $Z^n=0$ for $n<b$. If $Z^n$ is acyclic for sections at $U$, then the long exact sequence of [F7] for this sequence, together with the acyclicity of $K^n$, shows that $Z^{n+1}$ is again acyclic for sections at $U$; inducting on $n$ upward from $n<b$, every $Z^n$ is acyclic. With all $Z^n$ acyclic, the same sequences give short exact sequences $0\to\Gamma(U,Z^n)\to\Gamma(U,K^n)\to\Gamma(U,Z^{n+1})\to0$ on sections, so the kernel of $\Gamma(U,K^n)\to\Gamma(U,K^{n+1})$ equals the image of $\Gamma(U,K^{n-1})\to\Gamma(U,K^n)$: the former is the kernel of $\Gamma(U,K^n)\to\Gamma(U,Z^{n+1})$, which is the image of $\Gamma(U,Z^n)$ because $\Gamma$ of a short exact sequence is left exact and the sequence is right exact at the quotient, and $\Gamma(U,K^{n-1})\to\Gamma(U,Z^n)$ is surjective, so the two images agree. Hence $H^n(\Gamma(U,K^\bullet))=0$ for every $n$. Now apply this lemma to the cone $K^\bullet=\operatorname{Cone}(\varphi)$ of the cochain map $\varphi$ in the convention of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]. Its terms $J^n\oplus C^{n+1}$ are direct sums of an injective term, acyclic for sections at $U$ by [F7], and a flasque term, acyclic by step 2.2; a direct sum of two acyclic objects is acyclic by the long exact sequence [F7] applied to $0\to J^n\to J^n\oplus C^{n+1}\to C^{n+1}\to0$. The cone is acyclic and bounded below, so the lemma gives that $\Gamma(U,\operatorname{Cone}(\varphi))$ is acyclic. The canonical identification of complexes $\Gamma(U,\operatorname{Cone}(\varphi))\cong\operatorname{Cone}(\Gamma(U,\varphi))$ holds because sections over $U$ preserve finite direct sums and the differentials are those of $\varphi$; by the cone criterion [F9] the map $\Gamma(U,C^\bullet)\to\Gamma(U,J^\bullet)$ is therefore a quasi-isomorphism for every open $U$. Since any two bounded-below injective replacements of $C^\bullet$ are homotopy equivalent by [F3], the ordinary section complex $\Gamma(U,C^\bullet)$ represents the derived sections $R\Gamma(U,C^\bullet)$ of the bounded-below flasque complex.

The internal model is independent of representatives. For a quasi-isomorphism $g:A\to A'$ of bounded complexes, put $C=\operatorname{Cone}(g)$. On every open $U$, the restriction $I|_U$ of a bounded-below injective complex is K-injective by step 3.1 and [F3], so $\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_U(C|_U,I|_U)$ is acyclic. These are the sections of $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(C,I)$; taking exact filtered stalk colimits shows that this sheaf complex is acyclic. The cone of $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A',I)\to\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I)$ is isomorphic, with the usual Hom signs, to $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(C,I)[1]$, so the map is a quasi-isomorphism by [F9]. In the second variable, any homotopy equivalence between injective replacements is carried by $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,-)$ to a homotopy equivalence. The injective-model comparison of [F3] therefore makes the construction a natural bifunctor of the derived objects, compatible with restriction to opens.

The tensor–Hom adjunction and its coherence identities hold on the derived category. For a bounded complex $C$ and a bounded-below complex $I$ of injectives, the currying map $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A\otimes_kC,I)\to\mathcal Hom^\bullet(C,\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I))$, which sends a morphism $\varphi$ to $c\mapsto(a\mapsto(-1)^{|c||a|}\varphi(a\otimes c))$ on pure tensor sections and extends by linearity and gluing, is an isomorphism of complexes: over each open it is the vector-space tensor–Hom transposition of step 2.4, bijective on sections, and the Koszul sign makes both sides carry the single differential rule $d\psi=d_I\psi-(-1)^n\psi d_{\text{source}}$ of [[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]], so it commutes with differentials and with restriction. Taking $I$ to be an injective replacement of the bounded-below complex $B$ and using that $C$ is K-flat and $I$, $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I)$ are K-injective, the $H^0$ transposition identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_D(C\otimes_k^LA,B)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_D(C,R\mathcal Hom(A,B))$ naturally in the bounded $C,A$ and bounded-below $B$; this is the tensor–Hom adjunction, with unit and counit the canonical currying maps. The associativity isomorphism $(A\otimes_kB)\otimes_kC\cong A\otimes_k(B\otimes_kC)$, the symmetry isomorphism $A\otimes_kB\cong B\otimes_kA$ with its Koszul sign, the evaluation morphism $R\mathcal Hom(A,B)\otimes_k^LA\to B$, and the currying bijection all hold on pure tensor sections, where they are the usual vector-space identities, and extend by linearity, gluing and the comparison maps of step 4.1; being defined on sections they are natural and compatible with restriction to opens, hence internal. The triangle identities are those of step 2.4 at chain level.

The claims are now assembled. Inverse image is exact and $f^*\dashv Rf_*$ on $D^+$ is step 2.1; the derived tensor of bounded complexes is the signed total tensor by step 2.3; the internal derived Hom is the injective model of step 3.1, well defined by step 4.1; flasque sheaves are acyclic for sections on every open set by step 2.2, and bounded-below flasque complexes compute their derived sections by step 3.2; the tensor–Hom adjunction and the dg associativity, symmetry, evaluation and currying identities are step 5.1. AC is assumed and consumed exactly as follows: AC yields DC by [F1], DC is used by the injective replacement suppliers of [F3] and the delta-functor and injective-acyclicity statements of [F7], the functorial injective resolutions of [F2] use the Grothendieck embedding theorem under AC, and the flasque section lifting of [F8] uses Zorn's lemma under AC; the stalk, tensor, Hom and adjunction verifications are choice-free. No bounded-constructibility claim for the internal Hom is made: that is supplied later on this page by the geometric finite conical and incidence models, which are not prerequisites of this lemma.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 covers empty open sets and zero objects in the flasque-resolution argument, and step 1.1 covers the empty space in the stalk and adjunction computations.
Step 2.3 treats the zero and acyclic complexes in the K-flatness assembly, and step 3.1 the vanishing of the Hom complex in low degrees; the zero section is used throughout.
Step 1.2 computes the tensor of a single sheaf with the constant sheaf, and step 2.4 verifies the adjunction on a single open, which is the one-generator case.
The boundedness hypotheses include complexes concentrated in a single degree and the zero complex; steps 2.3 and 3.1 treat these degenerate ranges explicitly.

boundaries.reason: No interval endpoints occur; cohomological degrees are arbitrary integers and the bounded-below bounds are handled in steps 2.3 and 3.1.

boundaries.evidence: Step 6.1 records the exact AC uses: the AC to DC derivation, the injective replacement and enough-injectives data, the delta-functor and injective-acyclicity statements, and the flasque section lifting, while the stalk, tensor, Hom and adjunction verifications are choice-free.

boundaries.reason: The lemma states exactness, adjunction and acyclicity assertions; no equivalence between two conditions is part of the claim.
The converse statements, such as reconstructing exactness from the adjunction, are not part of the claim and are not used.

risk_review.notes: All twelve steps and cited supplier statements checked. Exact pullback and field tensor follow stalkwise; injectives restrict to opens via exact j!. Finite stupid filtration gives K-flatness for arbitrary acyclic inputs; finite Hom products preserve injectivity. Internal Hom independence is tested on every open, not inferred from global K-injectivity, and contravariant cone has shift [1]. Flasque acyclicity and bounded-below acyclic assembly use cycle induction with the lower bound. The currying signs agree with cochain Hom and symmetry. Zero complexes and empty opens cause no exception; arbitrary field allowed. AC supplies injective data, DC and Zorn section lifting, as explicitly declared. No bounded-constructibility claim inferred.

citations.quote:
Every classical variety is Noetherian and has finitely many irreducible components. Every open or closed subvariety has a finite affine cover.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

If $U$ is a nonempty open of an irreducible classical variety $X$, then $\dim U=\dim X$. Every proper closed subvariety $Z\subsetneq X$ has $\dim Z<\dim X$.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a perfect field
([[def-perfect-field]]) and let $X$ be a reduced $k$-scheme of finite type over
$k$. Then:

1. the regular locus $X_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in|X|:\mathcal O_{X,x}\text{ is a regular local ring}\}$
   ([[def-singular-and-regular-loci-variety]]) is open in $X$;
2. for every irreducible component $Z$ of $X$
   ([[def-irreducible-component-of-a-topological-space]]) the intersection
   $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap Z$ is a dense open subset of $Z$; in particular every
   irreducible component contains a nonempty dense open subset of points
   regular on $X$;
3. if $X\ne\varnothing$, then $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\ne\varnothing$.

No separatedness, irreducibility or equidimensionality hypothesis is imposed,
and $X$ may be empty, in which case the second clause is vacuous and the third
is not asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a perfect
field and let $X$ be a finite-type $k$-scheme. Here **regular** means that $X$
is locally Noetherian and every local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is regular local;
**smooth over $k$** means that $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth under the
local-standard-smooth convention of
[[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]. Then
$$X\text{ is regular}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\to\operatorname{Spec}k\text{ is smooth}.$$
No reducedness, irreducibility, or closed-point restriction is imposed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field and
$f:X\to Y$ a morphism of finite-type $k$-schemes. The morphism $f$ is
**smooth** if every point $x\in X$ has affine neighborhoods
$x\in V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ and $f(x)\in U=\operatorname{Spec}A$, with
$f(V)\subseteq U$, for which the induced map $A\to B$ is standard smooth at
the prime corresponding to $x$ ([[def-ag-standard-smooth-algebra]]). Thus the
condition is imposed at every source point, including nonclosed points; it is
local on the source and target. In this condition, standard smoothness at a
prime means that after a further principal shrinking around that prime the
ring map has a standard smooth presentation.

The pointwise and global equivalences in
[[thm-ag-standard-smooth-geometric-regularity]] identify standard smoothness
for finite-presentation affine charts with flatness and geometrically regular
scheme-theoretic fibres. Applied after the local shrinkings above, this gives
the corresponding local criterion for $f$. The local-presentation clause
itself is choice-free; AC is assumed here for that proved equivalence, through
the cited theorem.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A **standard smooth presentation** of an
$R$-algebra $S$ consists of integers $n\ge c\ge0$, elements
$f_1,\dots,f_c$ of the polynomial ring $P=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]) and an element $g\in P$
such that
$$S\cong\bigl(R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(f_1,\dots,f_c)\bigr)_g$$
as $R$-algebras, and such that the Jacobian matrix of
([[lem-ag-polynomial-quotient-differentials]])
$$\Bigl(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial x_i}\Bigr)_{\substack{1\le j\le c\\1\le i\le n}}$$
has a $c\times c$ minor whose image in $S$ is a unit, that is, an invertible
element. The integer $n-c\ge0$ is the **relative dimension** of the
presentation. The case $c=0$ is allowed and is exactly a localisation of a
polynomial ring, $S\cong(R[x_1,\dots,x_n])_g$; the case $n=c=0$ presents
$S=R[\,]_g$ for $g\in R$, that is a localisation of $R$ itself.

For a homomorphism $R\to S$ of commutative rings that is finitely presented as
an $R$-algebra ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]) and a prime
$\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$, the map is **standard smooth at
$\mathfrak q$**, or has a standard smooth presentation at $\mathfrak q$, when
there is $h\in S\smallsetminus\mathfrak q$ such that $S_h$ admits a standard
smooth presentation over $R$. It is **locally standard smooth** when this holds
at every prime of $S$; equivalently, when every point of $\operatorname{Spec}S$
has an affine open neighbourhood on which $S$ is presented by a single
standard smooth presentation.

Two conventions are part of the definition. First, the invertible minor may be
assumed to sit in the first $c$ columns: if a minor on columns
$i_1<\dots<i_c$ is a unit, the automorphism of $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ permuting the
variables so that these become the first $c$ variables carries the presentation
to one whose minor in the first $c$ columns is that unit, and the relative
dimension $n-c$ is unchanged. Second, a further principal localisation can be
absorbed into the presentation: adjoining a variable $z$ with the single
equation $zg-1$ to a presentation produces a standard smooth presentation of
the localisation, the new equation contributing a diagonal entry that keeps a
block minor invertible, and it changes $n$ and $c$ by the same amount, so that
the relative dimension is again unchanged.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be an algebraically
closed field of characteristic $0$, let $X$ and $Y$ be irreducible classical
varieties over $k$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), and let
$f\colon X\to Y$ be a morphism of classical varieties. Assume $X$ is smooth
over $k$, that is, the structure morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth
in the locally-standard-smooth sense of [[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]
(equivalently, since $k$ is perfect, $X$ is regular). Then:

1. there is a dense open subvariety $U\subseteq Y$ such that the restriction
   $$f^{-1}(U)\longrightarrow U$$
   is a smooth morphism of finite-type $k$-schemes; when $f$ is not dominant
   one may take $U$ with $f^{-1}(U)=\varnothing$, the empty morphism being
   smooth;
2. if in addition $f$ is dominant, there is a nonempty open (hence dense)
   $V\subseteq U$ such that for every closed point $y\in V$ the
   scheme-theoretic fibre
   $$X_y=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}k(y)$$
   ([[def-scheme-theoretic-fibre]]) is nonempty, smooth over $k$, and of pure
   dimension $r=\dim X-\dim Y$.

Neither $Y$ nor $f$ is required to be smooth or flat, the fibres are not
required to be irreducible or connected, and no statement is made about the
size of $U$ or $V$. The characteristic-$0$ hypothesis enters through the
critical-locus dimension bound of
[[lem-critical-locus-image-dimension-bound]] in claim 1 and through the
perfectness of $k$; the failure of the target-open statement for a
non-smooth source and the positive-characteristic failure of the
corresponding source-side statement are recorded on the counterexample page of
this pair.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be algebraically closed and let $X,Y$ be
smooth classical varieties over $k$, with their finite-type $k$-scheme
structures. Assume their structure morphisms are smooth in the sense of
[[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]. Let $f:X\to Y$ be a finite-type morphism
of these $k$-schemes ([[def-locally-finite-type-and-finite-type-morphism]])
and let $x\in X$ be a classical
closed point with $y=f(x)$. All such points have residue field $k$. Here
“smooth at $x$” means that the induced scheme morphism is locally standard
smooth at $x$ ([[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]); the structural morphisms
$X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ are locally
standard smooth at $x$ and $y$, respectively. Then $f$ is smooth at $x$ if
and only if its differential
$$d_xf:T_xX\longrightarrow T_yY$$
is surjective. If these equivalent conditions hold, the scheme-theoretic
fibre $X_y=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}k$ has a regular local ring at $x$
of dimension $\dim_xX-\dim_yY$.
For every such $f$ (whether or not it is smooth at $x$), its fibre tangent
space is canonically
$$T_x(X_y)=\ker(d_xf).$$

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A **standard smooth presentation** of an
$R$-algebra $S$ consists of integers $n\ge c\ge0$, elements
$f_1,\dots,f_c$ of the polynomial ring $P=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]) and an element $g\in P$
such that
$$S\cong\bigl(R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(f_1,\dots,f_c)\bigr)_g$$
as $R$-algebras, and such that the Jacobian matrix of
([[lem-ag-polynomial-quotient-differentials]])
$$\Bigl(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial x_i}\Bigr)_{\substack{1\le j\le c\\1\le i\le n}}$$
has a $c\times c$ minor whose image in $S$ is a unit, that is, an invertible
element. The integer $n-c\ge0$ is the **relative dimension** of the
presentation. The case $c=0$ is allowed and is exactly a localisation of a
polynomial ring, $S\cong(R[x_1,\dots,x_n])_g$; the case $n=c=0$ presents
$S=R[\,]_g$ for $g\in R$, that is a localisation of $R$ itself.

For a homomorphism $R\to S$ of commutative rings that is finitely presented as
an $R$-algebra ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]) and a prime
$\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$, the map is **standard smooth at
$\mathfrak q$**, or has a standard smooth presentation at $\mathfrak q$, when
there is $h\in S\smallsetminus\mathfrak q$ such that $S_h$ admits a standard
smooth presentation over $R$. It is **locally standard smooth** when this holds
at every prime of $S$; equivalently, when every point of $\operatorname{Spec}S$
has an affine open neighbourhood on which $S$ is presented by a single
standard smooth presentation.

Two conventions are part of the definition. First, the invertible minor may be
assumed to sit in the first $c$ columns: if a minor on columns
$i_1<\dots<i_c$ is a unit, the automorphism of $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ permuting the
variables so that these become the first $c$ variables carries the presentation
to one whose minor in the first $c$ columns is that unit, and the relative
dimension $n-c$ is unchanged. Second, a further principal localisation can be
absorbed into the presentation: adjoining a variable $z$ with the single
equation $zg-1$ to a presentation produces a standard smooth presentation of
the localisation, the new equation contributing a diagonal entry that keeps a
block minor invertible, and it changes $n$ and $c$ by the same amount, so that
the relative dimension is again unchanged.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be
holomorphic, and suppose the complex rank of $DF$ is the constant value $r$ on a
neighbourhood of $a\in U$. Then there are biholomorphic coordinate changes
$\alpha$ near $a$ and $\beta$ near $F(a)$ such that

$$\beta\circ F\circ \alpha^{-1}(u,v)=(u,0)$$

for $(u,v)\in\mathbb C^r\times\mathbb C^{m-r}$ near $0$. Empty blocks are
omitted when $r=0$, $r=m$, or $r=n$.

Assume AC. Every nonempty irreducible separated complex algebraic variety of
finite type is connected in its analytic topology. For every locally closed
algebraic subset $A$ of a separated finite-type complex variety $X$, the closure
of $A$ in the analytic topology equals its Zariski closure as a set of classical
complex points. In particular smooth irreducible algebraic strata are connected
complex manifolds once their holomorphic charts have been supplied.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: We record a partition construction. Let $Z$ be a reduced separated complex algebraic variety of finite type and let $\mathcal C$ be a finite list of closed subsets of $Z$. There is a finite partition of $Z$ into irreducible smooth locally closed strata such that every member of $\mathcal C$ is a union of strata and every stratum is open dense in its own irreducible closure. If $Z=\varnothing$ take the empty partition. Otherwise let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m$ be the irreducible components of $Z$, finitely many by [F1]. Remove from $Z_i$ its nonsmooth locus, the other components $Z_j$, and every $C\cap Z_i$ with $C\in\mathcal C$ and $C\nsupseteq Z_i$. Each removed set is closed, and each is proper in the irreducible $Z_i$; by [F3] and [F2] the nonsmooth locus has smaller dimension, and by [F2] the other removed sets do too, so the result $U_i$ is a nonempty dense open subset of $Z_i$ and is contained in or disjoint from every $C\in\mathcal C$. The $U_i$ are pairwise disjoint and open in $Z$, because their complement is the finite union of the removed closed sets and the sets $Z_j$ with $j\ne i$. The remainder $Z':=Z\setminus\bigcup_iU_i$ is closed and meets each $Z_i$ in a proper closed subset, so $\dim Z'<\dim Z$ by [F2]. Partition $Z'$ by the same construction with $\mathcal C$ replaced by the restrictions of all members of $\mathcal C$ and of all $Z_i$ to $Z'$, and iterate. The dimension of the remainder strictly decreases at every round, so the recursion terminates; because each round respects the restricted lists, every member of $\mathcal C$ is a union of strata and every stratum is open dense in its irreducible closure. The closure of a stratum emitted in a recursion round is a component of that round's closed remainder; it meets no earlier stratum and no other stratum emitted in that round, and the added component restrictions make it a union of subsequent strata. Thus this partition also has the frontier property.

Now construct the target strata in rounds on a closed residual subvariety $R\subseteq Y$, starting with $R=Y$; at each stage keep finite lists of prescribed closed subsets of $R$ and of $f^{-1}(R)$, initially the given lists and later those lists enlarged by the restrictions of the closures of all previously emitted strata. Apply step 1.1 to $f^{-1}(R)$ with the maintained source list, obtaining a finite partition into irreducible smooth locally closed strata $Z_\alpha$. Fix an irreducible component $R_i$ of $R$ and remove from it its nonsmooth locus, the other components of $R$, and every maintained target prescribed closed subset not containing $R_i$; by [F1] this leaves a nonempty dense open subset $V_i^0\subseteq R_i$. For each $\alpha$ the image $f(Z_\alpha)$ is irreducible and lies in a component of $R$, so its closure in $R$ is an irreducible closed subset of some component. If that closure is not $R_i$, then its intersection with $R_i$ is a proper closed subset, and we remove it from $V_i^0$; if the closure equals $R_i$, then $f|_{Z_\alpha}$ is dominant, $Z_\alpha$ is smooth and irreducible, and [F4] supplies a dense open subset of $R_i$ over which $Z_\alpha\to R_i$ is smooth, with nonempty fibres over the closed points after shrinking to lie in the image. There are finitely many $\alpha$, so intersecting $V_i^0$ with all the supplied dense opens contained in the images produces a nonempty dense open $V_i\subseteq R_i$ such that every $Z_\alpha$ whose image closure is not $R_i$ has no point over $V_i$, while every $Z_\alpha$ whose image closure is $R_i$ maps smoothly and onto $V_i$.

Emit the target strata $V_i$ of this round and, for every $\alpha$ whose image closure $\overline{f(Z_\alpha)}$ in $R$ equals $R_i$, the source stratum $S_{\alpha,i}:=Z_\alpha\cap f^{-1}(V_i)$, which is nonempty. It is open in $Z_\alpha$ because $V_i$ is open in $R_i$ and $Z_\alpha\subseteq f^{-1}(R_i)$, hence it is an irreducible smooth locally closed subvariety of $X$, and it maps smoothly and onto $V_i$ as the restriction of the map of step 2.1. Every source point over $V_i$ lies in exactly one such stratum, because the $Z_\alpha$ partition $f^{-1}(R)$ and their intersections with $f^{-1}(V_i)$ are exactly the emitted pieces; those with other image closures have empty intersection by step 2.1. Within the round, closures behave as in step 1.1: the closure of $S_{\alpha,i}$ meets $f^{-1}(V_i)$ in the union of the strata $S_{\beta,i}$ with $Z_\beta\subseteq\overline{Z_\alpha}$, since $f^{-1}(V_i)$ is open in the closed set $f^{-1}(R_i)$.

Put $R':=R\setminus\bigcup_iV_i$; it is closed and has $\dim R'<\dim R$ by [F2], since each component of $R$ lost a dense open subset. Enlarge both lists by the closures of the emitted strata, restrict to $R'$ and $f^{-1}(R')$, and repeat steps 2.1 and 3.1. The target dimension strictly decreases each round, so after finitely many rounds the emitted strata partition $Y$ and $X$. Every emitted stratum $S$ is open dense in its irreducible closure: a target stratum $V_i$ is open dense in $R_i$, while a source stratum $S_{\alpha,i}$ is a nonempty open subset of $Z_\alpha$ and has the same irreducible closure. For source strata the within-round frontier property follows from steps 1.1 and 3.1; closures lie in $f^{-1}(R_i)$ and meet no source stratum over another $V_j$. Target closures likewise meet no other target stratum of the round. Each closure lies in the current closed residual and hence meets no earlier stratum. Finally the maintained lists contain these closures in every later round, forcing every later stratum to be contained in or disjoint from each closure. Consequently $\overline S$ is a union of strata, and every stratum $P\subseteq\overline S\setminus S$ has $\dim P<\dim S$: indeed $\overline P$ is an irreducible closed subset of $\overline S$ with $\dim\overline P\le\dim S$, equality would give $\overline P=\overline S$, and then $P$ and $S$, being dense opens of the irreducible $\overline P=\overline S$, would meet, contradicting disjointness of strata. Thus every stratum closure is a union of strata of no larger dimension and its boundary has strictly smaller dimension. Every prescribed subset is a union of strata by the invariance maintained in steps 1.1 and 2.1, and the empty source contributes no source strata.

Finally let $S\to T$ be one emitted restriction onto a target stratum. Zero-dimensional smooth strata are locally single points: they are zero-dimensional Noetherian varieties, hence finite sets of closed points, so their analytic charts and maps to a zero-dimensional target require no implicit-function or constant-rank theorem. A standard smooth presentation with no equations already gives open coordinate charts. In the remaining positive-dimensional cases, the stratum $S$ is a smooth complex variety by construction, so by [F3] it is locally standard smooth over $\mathbb C$; the defining equations of a standard smooth presentation near a point have an invertible Jacobian minor, and [F5] turns them into holomorphic charts of $S$ near that point, with holomorphic transition maps. Similarly $T$ carries holomorphic charts. The map $S\to T$ is a morphism of classical varieties, so in these charts its components are restrictions of regular functions on affine charts, hence locally polynomial quotients with nonvanishing denominators in the ambient coordinates and therefore holomorphic in the chart parameters. At every point the differential of $S\to T$ is surjective by the smoothness of the restriction and the criterion of [F5]; since surjectivity onto a target of dimension $n$ is the nonvanishing of some $n\times n$ minor, the rank stays full on a neighbourhood, and the holomorphic constant rank theorem exhibits the map near each point as a linear projection in suitable holomorphic coordinates. Hence the restriction is a submersion of complex manifolds, in particular a submersion of the underlying real smooth manifolds. No properness or topological triviality is used, and AC is inherited exactly through the cited suppliers.

Each emitted source and target piece is nonempty and irreducible, so [F6] proves its analytic connectedness. Its analytic closure is its algebraic closure by [F6]; therefore the algebraic frontier bookkeeping of step 4.1 is the analytic frontier condition as well. Combined with step 5.1 this produces finite connected smooth analytic strata with the required frontier and submersion restrictions, while preserving all algebraic compatibility and dimension conclusions.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement explicitly allows the empty source: step 2.1 still stratifies the target, and step 3.1 emits no source stratum because no component $Z_alpha$ exists.

boundaries.reason: The rounds of step 4.1 compare dimensions and never divide by one; a zero-dimensional residual component simply contributes a last stratum rather than a special case.
No singleton or one-round hypothesis occurs; step 2.1 runs the round construction until the target residual is empty, for any finite number of rounds.
Strata are open subsets of regular loci, so there is no degenerate stratum parameter; singular points stay in the continuing residual and are stratified in later rounds.
No interval or asymptotic endpoint appears; strip closures are recorded as finite set-theoretic frontiers in steps 2.1 and 4.1.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement assumes AC, consumed through the regular-locus and dimension suppliers [F3] and [F4] in steps 1.1 and 2.1; each round selects only from finite lists of components and strata.

boundaries.reason: The theorem asserts existence of compatible partitions, not an equivalence, so no forward direction is owed.
No converse is claimed: the result does not assert that every map-compatible partition admits a smooth Whitney refinement.

citations.quote:
Let $k$ be a field and let $A$ be a nonzero finite-type $k$-algebra. Then
there exist algebraically independent elements $z_1,\ldots,z_d\in A$ such that
$A$ is a module-finite algebra over the polynomial ring
$k[z_1,\ldots,z_d]$.

For every field $K$ and every finite $d\ge0$, the ring $K[x_1,\ldots,x_d]$ is
an integrally closed domain.

Let $A$ be an integrally closed domain with field of fractions $K$, let $L/K$ be a field extension, and let $u\in L$ be integral over $A$. Then the minimal polynomial of $u$ over $K$ has coefficients in $A$.

In particular, if $f(T)\in A[T]$ is monic and factors in $K[T]$ as
$$ f(T)=(T-a)h(T) $$
with $a\in K$, then $h(T)\in A[T]$.

Every field of characteristic zero is perfect. Every finite field is perfect,
and every algebraically closed field is perfect.

Let $E=F(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r)$ be a finite extension. If all but possibly
one of the generators are separable over $F$, then $E/F$ is simple. In
particular, every finite separable extension is simple.

Let $F$ be a field and let $f,g\in F[x]$ be not both zero. Repeated polynomial division terminates at a last nonzero remainder, whose monic associate is $d=\gcd(f,g)$. There are $A,B\in F[x]$ such that

$$ Af+Bg=d. $$

Moreover, $d$ divides both $f$ and $g$, and every common divisor of $f$ and $g$ divides $d$.

Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root.

This proof uses Liouville's theorem and is independent of the minimum-modulus proof cited in the accompanying agreement remark.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be a domain, let $g:U\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic
and not identically zero, and let
$f:U\setminus Z(g)\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic. Assume that $f$ is locally
bounded near every point of $Z(g)$. Then there is a unique holomorphic
extension $F:U\to\mathbb C$ with
$F|_{U\setminus Z(g)}=f$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). Then $f$ is
continuous on $U$ and separately holomorphic on $U$
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]]). Moreover, for $a\in U$ and $k<m$ the
slice $f_{a,k}$ is complex differentiable at $a_k$ with derivative
$Df(a)e_k$, and

$$Df(a)e_k=\partial_{z_k}f(a),\qquad Df(a)h=\sum_{k<m}\bigl(\partial_{z_k}f(a)\bigr)h_k .$$

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho$, let
$f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and separately holomorphic, let $r$
be a polyradius with $r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and let
$C_k(t)=a_k+r_k\exp(it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ set

$$c_\alpha:=\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{C_0}\!\cdots\!\int_{C_{m-1}} f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta_{m-1}\cdots d\zeta_0 ,$$

an iterated integral as in the polydisc Cauchy formula. Then, with
$M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$,

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k},$$

and for every real $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
$\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ with

$$f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\qquad(z\in\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)).$$

Since every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$ lies in $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ for some
$\theta<1$, the expansion holds throughout $\Delta_r(a)$.

**The coefficients are asserted here only as those iterated integrals.** That
$c_\alpha$ equals $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ needs termwise differentiation
and is not claimed by this statement.

Let $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and let $r$ be a polyradius. Suppose
$c,c':\mathbb N^m\to\mathbb C$ both satisfy a bound
$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$ and
$|c'_\alpha|\le M'\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$, and suppose

$$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha=\sum_\alpha c'_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha \qquad\text{for every }z\in\Delta_r(a).$$

Then $c_\alpha=c'_\alpha$ for every multi-index $\alpha$. In particular a
function has at most one such power-series representation about a given centre,
and its coefficients are $\partial^\alpha_zf(a)/\alpha!$.

Assume AC. Let $V$ be an irreducible complex algebraic variety of positive
dimension ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]),
let $O\subseteq V$ be a nonempty Zariski open subset and let $z\in V$. There is
an irreducible algebraic curve $C\subseteq V$ through $z$ not contained in
$V\setminus O$. There is also a holomorphic map $\gamma:\Delta\to V$ from a
sufficiently small complex disk, with $\gamma(0)=z$ and $\gamma(s)\in O$ for
all $s\ne0$; here $\Delta$ is a disk centred at $0$ and a map into $V$ is
holomorphic when its coordinate functions in an affine model containing its
image are holomorphic. The arc can be obtained by analytically parametrizing a
point over $z$ in the finite normalization of $C$.

Every classical variety is Noetherian and has finitely many irreducible components. Every open or closed subvariety has a finite affine cover.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Fix an algebraically closed field $k$. The affine models used here are polynomial zero sets $Z\subseteq k^n$, including empty and reducible sets. Their closed subsets are common zero loci of polynomial families, relative to $Z$. Intersections combine equations, and finite unions use products of equations, so these are the closed sets of a topology.

For an open $U\subseteq Z$, let $\mathcal O_Z(U)$ consist of functions $U\to k$ locally equal to $a/b$ for polynomials $a,b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the chosen neighbourhood. Pointwise operations and restriction make these sets a sheaf of $k$-algebras: quotient expressions persist on restriction, and functions that agree locally glue uniquely with the same local quotient property. At a point z its stalk is the ring of germs of such functions. Evaluation at z maps it onto k, with kernel the germs vanishing at z. A germ nonzero at z is invertible: shrink to where its numerator and denominator are both nonzero and interchange them. Thus the kernel is the unique maximal ideal. These affine models are locally ringed spaces in the sense of [[def-locally-ringed-space]], with residue fields canonically k.

A **classical algebraic prevariety** over k is a quasi-compact locally ringed space with a structure sheaf of k-algebras, covered by open subspaces isomorphic over k to these affine models. Here quasi-compact means every open cover has a finite subcover. Equivalently it admits a finite affine-model cover. To justify the converse, each affine model is quasi-compact: polynomial principal opens $D_Z(h)=\{z:h(z)\ne0\}$ form a basis. Given an open cover, take all h whose principal opens lie in a member. Their principal opens cover Z. The ideal generated by these h in $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ is finitely generated by [[thm-hilbert-basis-theorem]], iterated from the field k. Express finitely many generators using finitely many of the original h. Those finitely many h have the same common zero locus as the whole ideal, hence their principal opens still cover Z and yield a finite subcover. The empty model has the empty subcover. A finite union of quasi-compact subspaces is quasi-compact.

A map is **regular** when it is a morphism of locally ringed spaces as in [[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]] whose sheaf maps respect k. For these function sheaves its sheaf map is necessarily pullback of functions: the local stalk map induces a k-map between residue fields k, hence the identity, so the value of a pulled-back section at x is its value at the image of x. Conversely, continuous pullback of local regular functions gives a local stalk map because a function vanishing at the image vanishes after pullback.

Regularity can therefore be checked on affine charts: near every source point choose a target affine chart containing its image and an open neighbourhood in a source affine chart mapped into it; the target coordinate functions must pull back to locally polynomial quotients. This condition also implies continuity. Indeed zero sets of locally polynomial quotients are locally polynomial zero sets, hence closed; pulling back polynomial equations consequently gives closed sets. Substitution then pulls every local quotient on the target back to a local quotient on the source, using this continuity to restrict to its domain and its nonvanishing denominator. Thus the chart condition and the locally ringed-space definition agree.

A prevariety is **separated** when the equalizer of every pair of regular maps into it, from any classical prevariety, is closed. A **classical algebraic variety** is a separated prevariety. Here varieties may be reducible or empty; an **irreducible classical variety** is nonempty and irreducible in the sense of [[def-irreducible-topological-space-and-subset]]. These definitions and the local verifications above use no Axiom of Choice.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $A\subseteq B$ be commutative rings with $A\ne0$, and let $b\in B$. The following are equivalent: $b$ is integral over $A$; $A[b]$ is finitely generated as an $A$-module; and there exists a faithful $A[b]$-module that is finitely generated over $A$, where faithful means that $rM=0$ implies $r=0$ for $r\in A[b]$. See [[def-integral-element-and-algebraic-integer]].

derivations.claim: First let $Z$ be irreducible affine with coordinate domain $B$. By [F1] choose $R=\mathbb C[z_1,\ldots,z_d]\subseteq B$ with $B$ finite over $R$. Write $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$. The localization $(R\setminus\{0\})^{-1}B$ is a finite-dimensional $K$-domain; multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and hence surjective, so this domain is a field, equal to $E=\operatorname{Frac}(B)$. If $d=0$, $B$ is a finite-dimensional complex domain and therefore a field; [F2] forces every algebraic element over $\mathbb C$ to lie in $\mathbb C$, so $B=\mathbb C$ and $Z$ is one point. Otherwise [F2] supplies a primitive element $\eta\in E$ over $K$. Write $\eta=b/s$ with $b\in B$, $0\ne s\in R$ and put $\theta=b$; then $K(\theta)=E$, and $\theta$ is integral over $R$ by [F1], using the finite faithful $R[\theta]$-module $B$ (faithfulness follows by evaluating an annihilator at $1$). By [F1] its monic minimal polynomial is $P(z,T)\in R[T]$, of degree $m=[E:K]\ge1$. It is irreducible and separable over $K$. For finitely many $R$-module generators of $B$, express each as a $K$-linear combination of $1,\theta,\ldots,\theta^{m-1}$ and clear the finitely many denominators. This gives $0\ne a\in R$ with $B_a=R_a[\theta]$. Since $P$ is monic, division by $P$ and linear independence of these powers over $K$ identify this algebra with $R_a[T]/(P)$.

By separability and [F2], there are polynomials $H,J\in K[T]$ with $HP+J\partial_TP=1$. Clear denominators to obtain $H_0,J_0\in R[T]$ and $0\ne\delta\in R$ with $H_0P+J_0\partial_TP=\delta$. Put $g=a\delta$ and $V=\mathbb C^d\setminus Z(g)$. This set is nonempty because a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish everywhere on $\mathbb C^d$ (induction on $d$ using the finiteness of roots of a nonzero one-variable polynomial). It is path connected: for distinct $v,w\in V$, the polynomial $t\mapsto g(v+t(w-v))$ is nonzero at $t=0,1$, hence has only finitely many zeros; the complex parameter plane minus those zeros has a path from $0$ to $1$, obtained from the straight segment by finitely many small circular detours. Its image connects $v$ to $w$ in $V$. The principal open $U\subseteq Z$ where $g$ does not vanish is, by step 1.1's coordinate algebra, the space $\{(z,t):z\in V,\ P(z,t)=0\}$. All its coordinate identifications and inverses are polynomial quotients, hence analytic homeomorphisms. For each $z\in V$, $P(z,T)$ is monic of degree $m$ and has exactly $m$ distinct complex roots by the Bezout identity and [F2]. The implicit-function theorem [F3] gives disjoint holomorphic graphs near these roots on one common small connected base ball. They exhaust every nearby fibre because there are already $m$ distinct roots of its degree-$m$ polynomial. Thus $U\to V$ is an actual $m$-sheeted holomorphic covering, with no appeal to an unproved normalization or covering comparison.

Suppose $U=U_1\amalg U_2$ is a nontrivial analytic clopen partition. On each connected small graph of step 2.1 its membership in $U_1$ or $U_2$ is constant. Consequently the number $m_i$ of roots over $z$ belonging to $U_i$ is locally constant on $V$, hence constant since $V$ is connected. Nonemptiness of both pieces implies $1\le m_i<m$ and $m_1+m_2=m$. Define on $V$ the monic polynomials $Q_i(z,T)$ whose roots are precisely the roots on $U_i$ over $z$. Their coefficients are elementary symmetric functions of those roots; the local holomorphic graphs make them holomorphic, and changing the enumeration changes no symmetric function, so these coefficients glue without any chosen global root functions. Pointwise on $V$ one has $P(z,T)=Q_1(z,T)Q_2(z,T)$.

Write $P(z,T)=T^m+p_1(z)T^{m-1}+\cdots+p_m(z)$. Every root satisfies $|t|\le1+\sum_j|p_j(z)|$: if $|t|$ exceeds this quantity, then $|t|>1$ and $|t|^m\le\sum_j|p_j(z)||t|^{m-j}\le(\sum_j|p_j(z)|)|t|^{m-1}<|t|^m$, a contradiction. The polynomial coefficients therefore give a bound $|t|\le C(1+\|z\|_\infty)^D$ for some integer $D\ge0$ and $C\ge1$, valid also near $z=0$. Each coefficient of $Q_i$ is a sum of finitely many products of at most $m_i$ such roots; it is locally bounded near $Z(g)$ and has a bound $C'(1+\|z\|_\infty)^{Dm_i}$ on $V$. Apply [F3] to extend each coefficient to all of $\mathbb C^d$. The same bound holds after extension by continuity: the nonzero polynomial $g$ cannot vanish on an ordinary open ball, since that ball contains a product of disks and successively restricting each variable would force all its coefficients to vanish. Hence $V$ is analytically dense in $\mathbb C^d$.

An entire function $h$ on $\mathbb C^d$ satisfying $|h(z)|\le C'(1+\|z\|_\infty)^N$ for an integer $N\ge0$ is a polynomial. Indeed [F4] on the radius-$R$ polydisc centred at zero gives $|c_\alpha|\le C'(1+R)^N/R^{|\alpha|}$; uniqueness makes the coefficients independent of $R$ by comparison on the smaller common polydisc. Letting $R\to\infty$ forces $c_\alpha=0$ for $|\alpha|>N$. Its expansion therefore is the finite polynomial $\sum_{|\alpha|\le N}c_\alpha z^\alpha$ on every polydisc, hence on all of $\mathbb C^d$. Apply this to step 4.1's coefficients: $Q_i\in R[T]$. The equality $P=Q_1Q_2$ on $V$ is a polynomial identity, since each coefficient of their difference vanishes on a nonempty ordinary open ball and the preceding one-variable restriction argument makes that coefficient the zero polynomial. Both factors have positive degree smaller than $m$, contradicting the irreducibility of $P$ in $K[T]$. Thus $U$ is analytically connected. This argument factors $P$ itself; it does not infer that one of two polynomial factors is zero from their vanishing on different analytic pieces.

The open $U$ is Zariski nonempty in the irreducible affine $Z$. If $Z$ has positive dimension, [F5] supplies at each $x\in Z$ an arc tending to $x$ with punctured image in $U$, so $U$ is analytically dense in $Z$. The zero-dimensional case was already a singleton in step 1.1. The closure of a connected set is connected: any clopen separation of its closure would restrict to a separation of the set, putting the set in one closed side and hence its closure there. Therefore $Z$ is analytically connected. For a general irreducible $X$, choose a nonempty affine open $Z\subseteq X$. It is irreducible and connected by the affine case; [F5] makes it analytically dense in $X$ when $X$ has positive dimension. If $X$ has dimension zero, its nonempty irreducible affine opens are singletons; irreducibility forces them to meet, so $X$ is one point. Again connectedness passes to the closure, proving the first assertion.

Finally let $A\subseteq X$ be locally closed algebraic, and write $C$ for its Zariski closure. Algebraic closed sets are analytically closed, because their polynomial equations are continuous on affine charts; hence the analytic closure of $A$ lies in $C$. There is a Zariski open $O\subseteq X$ with $A=C\cap O$. For each of the finitely many irreducible components $C_j$ of $C$, the set $A\cap C_j$ is a nonempty open subset: otherwise the dense set $A$ would be contained in the union of the other components, a proper closed subset of $C$. If $\dim C_j>0$, [F5] gives at every point of $C_j$ an arc with punctured image in $A\cap C_j$, proving analytic density there. If $\dim C_j=0$, it is a point by the affine argument and the finite affine-cover property, and nonemptiness of $A\cap C_j$ puts that point in $A$. Thus every $C_j$ lies in the analytic closure, which is therefore exactly $C$. The empty subset has empty closure in both topologies. The final manifold clause only combines this connectedness with supplied holomorphic charts; no chart existence is inferred from irreducibility.

boundaries.evidence: Statement connectedness assumes nonempty irreducible varieties; Proof 7.1 treats the empty locally closed subset separately.
Proof 1.1 and 6.1 treat polynomial base dimension zero as the one-point variety; no implicit function or several-variable estimate used.
Proof 2.1 works at m=1; Proof 3.1 makes a nontrivial partition impossible when 1<=m_i<m.

A1 and Proof 1.1 inherit AC for normalization and primitive-element suppliers; Proof 3.1 uses symmetric functions independent of sheet enumeration.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to S$ be a finite morphism of schemes. Then every ring map $A\to B$ induced by $f$ on an affine chart $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq S$ with $f^{-1}(U)=\operatorname{Spec}B$ is integral. Moreover $f$ is universally closed: for every morphism $T\to S$ the base-changed projection $X\times_ST\to T$ is a closed map, so the image of $X\times_ST$ and of every closed subset of it is closed in $|T|$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:A\to B$ be an integral ring map, and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ with $\ker f\subseteq\mathfrak p$. Then there exists a prime ideal $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}(B)$ such that $f^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak p$.

Let $k$ be a field and let $A$ be a nonzero finite-type $k$-algebra. Then there exist algebraically independent elements $z_1,\ldots,z_d\in A$ such that $A$ is a module-finite algebra over the polynomial ring $k[z_1,\ldots,z_d]$.

If $X$ is an irreducible classical variety, then $\dim X=\operatorname{trdeg}_k k(X)<\infty$. Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.
Let $k$ be a field, let $A$ be a finite-type $k$-domain, and let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. Then $$ \dim A=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K. $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field, let $A$ be a finite-type $k$-domain, and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(A)$. Then $$ \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)+\operatorname{trdeg}_k\operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak p)=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\operatorname{Frac}(A). $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $$ I=(x_1,\ldots,x_n) $$ be an ideal generated by $n\ge1$ elements, and let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal minimal over $I$. Then $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)\le n$.

If $U$ is a nonempty open of an irreducible classical variety $X$, then $\dim U=\dim X$. Every proper closed subvariety $Z\subsetneq X$ has $\dim Z<\dim X$. Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Let $k$ be a field and let $C$ be a reduced $k$-scheme of finite type, of pure dimension one (for example a reduced projective plane curve or an open subscheme of one). Then there exists a finite morphism $
u\colon C^{\mathrm{nu}}	o C$ with the following properties: 1. $C^{\mathrm{nu}}$ is regular of dimension one (equivalently normal: all local rings are discrete valuation rings or fields); 2. $
u$ is an isomorphism over the regular locus of $C$ and is birational on each irreducible component; 3. on an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $C$, $
u$ is the morphism corresponding to the integral closure of $A$ in its total ring of fractions; 4. $
u$ is unique up to a unique $C$-isomorphism, and $
u_*\mathcal O_{C^{\mathrm{nu}}}$ is a coherent $\mathcal O_C$-module. No separability or perfectness hypothesis on $k$ is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a perfect field and let $X$ be a finite-type $k$-scheme. Here **regular** means that $X$ is locally Noetherian and every local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is regular local; **smooth over $k$** means that $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth under the local-standard-smooth convention of [[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]. Then $$X\text{ is regular}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\to\operatorname{Spec}k\text{ is smooth}.$$ No reducedness, irreducibility, or closed-point restriction is imposed.

Let $C$ be a complex algebraic curve, meaning a one-dimensional algebraic set over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-affine-algebraic-set]]), and let $p\in C$ lie either in $\mathbb C^N$ (affine case) or in a standard affine chart of $\mathbb{CP}^N$ with its coordinates $(\zeta_1/\zeta_i,\dots)$ (projective case, [[def-projective-space-points]]). Assume that near $p$ the curve is the common zero set of holomorphic functions $f_1,\dots,f_{N-1}$ on a neighbourhood of $p$, and that their complex Jacobian matrix at $p$ has rank $N-1$. Here the matrix $J_F(p)=(\partial f_i/\partial t_j(p))$ uses the equation-row and coordinate-column convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-affine-algebraic-set]], extended directly to the stated local holomorphic functions by their complex partial derivatives; this hypothesis is the **Jacobian-rank sense** of nonsingularity used in this pair. Then there are an index $j$, a plane domain $A\subseteq\mathbb C$ and a holomorphic map $\phi:A\to\mathbb C^{N-1}$ such that, after permuting the coordinates so that the $j$-th coordinate comes first, $C$ agrees near $p$ with the graph $\{(z,\phi(z)):z\in A\}$, and the projection $(z,\phi(z))\mapsto z$ is a homeomorphism of that neighbourhood of $p$ in $C$ onto the plane domain $A$ whose inverse $z\mapsto(z,\phi(z))$ is holomorphic: one free ambient coordinate is a local parameter. Moreover, if two such local parameters $z$ and $w$ are defined on overlapping pieces, coming from the same ambient chart or from two standard affine charts, then the transition $z\mapsto w$ is holomorphic wherever both are defined.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$. Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible: $$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$ Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that $$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$ and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed, $$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $k$ be any field, let $n\geq0$ be finite, let $I$ be an ideal of $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and put $$X=\operatorname{Spec}(k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I).$$ Let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in X(k)$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ be any finite generating list of the actual ideal $I$. Then the coordinate-velocity map gives a canonical $k$-linear isomorphism $$T_aX\cong\ker\!\left(J_{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}(a):k^n\longrightarrow k^r\right).$$ The kernel is independent of the chosen finite generating list of $I$. No reducedness, perfectness, or characteristic hypothesis is needed. Finiteness of the list is available for every finite $n$ by the finite-variable polynomial Noetherian result cited below.

Let $X$ be a locally Noetherian scheme and $x\in X$. Write $R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, let $\mathfrak m_x$ be its maximal ideal, and set $\kappa(x)=R/\mathfrak m_x$. The point $x$ is **regular** when $R$ is a regular local ring, with regularity defined by $\operatorname{edim}R=\dim R$. Then the intrinsic tangent space $T_xX$ is finite-dimensional over $\kappa(x)$, and $$x\text{ is regular}\Longleftrightarrow\dim_{\kappa(x)}T_xX=\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}.$$ This is absolute regularity of the local ring; it asserts no smoothness over a base field.
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every nonzero commutative Noetherian local ring $R$ satisfies $\dim R\le\operatorname{edim}R<\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). A regular local ring $R$ of dimension $d$ is a domain and Cohen–Macaulay. For every regular system $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$, the tuple is $R$-regular and $R/(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$ is regular local of dimension $d-c$ for all $0\le c\le d$.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then the polynomial ring $R[x]$ is a Noetherian commutative ring. No hypothesis beyond Noetherianity is placed on $R$: it may have zero divisors, and it may be the zero ring.

Every classical variety is Noetherian and has finitely many irreducible components. Every open or closed subvariety has a finite affine cover. Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Choose an affine open neighbourhood $V_0$ of $z$ in $V$. Then $V_0$ is irreducible of dimension $d=\dim V\ge1$, and $V_0\cap O\ne\varnothing$ because two nonempty open subsets of the irreducible $V$ meet ([[def-irreducible-topological-space-and-subset]]). Put $B=V_0\setminus O$; it is closed in $V_0$ and proper.

By [F2] applied to the coordinate ring $A$ of $V_0$, choose a finite morphism $h:V_0\to\mathbb A^d$ induced by an injection $\mathbb C[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\hookrightarrow A$ with $A$ module-finite over the image; the integer $d$ is $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Frac}(A)=\dim V_0$ by [F3]. For every irreducible component $W$ of $B$ the image $h(W)$ is closed by [F1], and the induced map $\mathbb C[t]/I(h(W))\hookrightarrow A/I(W)$ is finite and injective; hence $\operatorname{Frac}(A/I(W))$ is algebraic over $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb C[t]/I(h(W)))$, the two function fields have the same transcendence degree, and $\dim W=\dim h(W)$ by [F3]. A finite union of closed sets has dimension the maximum of the dimensions of its irreducible components, so $\dim h(B)=\dim B<d$, the inequality by [F3] since $B$ is a proper closed subset of the irreducible $V_0$. Thus $h(B)$ is a proper closed subset of $\mathbb A^d$ and there is a nonzero polynomial $P$ vanishing on it, or $P=1$ if $B=\varnothing$.

Write $a=h(z)$. The Taylor expansion of a nonzero polynomial $P$ at $a$ has a nonzero homogeneous part, and a nonzero polynomial on $\mathbb C^d$ is not identically zero (induction on $d$ using that a nonzero one-variable polynomial has finitely many roots), so there is $w\ne0$ with $P(a+tw)$ not the zero polynomial in $t$; if $B=\varnothing$ take any $w\ne0$. The affine line $\ell=\{a+tw:t\in\mathbb C\}$ is therefore not contained in $h(B)$.

Let $g_1,\ldots,g_{d-1}$ be linear forms cutting out $\ell$ in $\mathbb A^d$ (no forms occur when $d=1$), and let $C_0$ be an irreducible component of the closed subset $h^{-1}(\ell)\subseteq V_0$ containing $z$; such a component exists because $h(z)=a\in\ell$. Every component of $h^{-1}(\ell)$ has dimension at least $1$: it is a component of the zero set of the $d-1$ pulled-back forms, so its defining prime is minimal over an ideal generated by $d-1$ elements, has height at most $d-1$ by [F3], and $\dim=\dim A-\operatorname{ht}\ge d-(d-1)=1$; for $d=1$ this reads $\dim V_0=1$. Every component has dimension at most $1$ because it maps finitely into the curve $\ell$, so its dimension equals that of its closed image by the dimension comparison of step 2.1. Hence every component is a curve, and $C_0$ is one of them.

The curve $C_0$ is not contained in $B$: otherwise $h(C_0)\subseteq h(B)$, while $h(C_0)$ is closed in $\ell$, irreducible, and of dimension $1=\dim C_0$ by step 4.1, hence equal to $\ell$, contradicting $\ell
ot\subseteq h(B)$ from step 3.1. Therefore $C_0\cap O=C_0\setminus B
e\varnothing$. The closure $C:=\overline{C_0}$ in $V$ is an irreducible curve through $z$ meeting $O$, so $C
ot\subseteq V\setminus O$.

View $C_0$ with its reduced induced structure: it is a reduced finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme of pure dimension one, so by [F4] it has a finite normalization $\nu:C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}\to C_0$, which is surjective by [F1]; choose $z_0\in C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}$ with $\nu(z_0)=z$. Then $C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}$ is regular of dimension one and, over $\mathbb C$, smooth.

Take an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}A_0$ of $C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}$ containing $z_0$ and identify it with a closed algebraic set $X=V(I)\subseteq\mathbb C^M$, $I\subseteq\mathbb C[t_1,\ldots,t_M]$. Since $\mathcal O_{X,z_0}$ is a regular local ring of dimension one, [F6] gives $\dim_{\mathbb C}T_{z_0}X=1$; for a finite generating list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ of $I$ this tangent space is the kernel of the $r\times M$ Jacobian matrix at $z_0$, so that matrix has rank $M-1$, and some $M-1$ of the $f_i$, say $f_1,\ldots,f_{M-1}$, have an invertible $(M-1)\times(M-1)$ minor at $z_0$. Put $Z=V(f_1,\ldots,f_{M-1})$ and let $J'$ be their Jacobian. Then $\dim\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}\le\operatorname{edim}\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}=\dim\ker J'(z_0)=M-(M-1)=1$ by [F6], while $\dim\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}\ge\dim\mathcal O_{X,z_0}=1$ because $X\subseteq Z$ induces a surjection of local rings and dimensions do not increase under quotients. Hence $\dim\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}=1$ and it is regular, therefore a local domain.

The inclusion $X\subseteq Z$ induces a surjection of one-dimensional local rings $\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}	woheadrightarrow\mathcal O_{X,z_0}$. Its kernel is a prime ideal, and since the source is a one-dimensional local domain, a nonzero kernel would be the maximal ideal with a zero-dimensional quotient, contradicting $\dim\mathcal O_{X,z_0}=1$; so the kernel is zero and $\mathcal O_{X,z_0}\cong\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}$. Write $I(X)=(g_1,\ldots,g_k)$ by [F7]. Each $g_i$ maps to zero in $\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}$, so for each $i$ there is $h_i
otin\mathfrak m_{z_0}$ with $h_ig_i$ vanishing on $Z$; for $h=h_1\cdots h_k
otin\mathfrak m_{z_0}$ all the $g_i$ vanish on $Z\cap\{h
e0\}$, and since $X\subseteq Z$ we get $X\cap\{h
e0\}=Z\cap\{h
e0\}$.

If $M=1$, step 8.1 identifies $X$ with an open neighbourhood of $z_0$ in $Z=\mathbb C$, so translation is the required holomorphic chart. For $M>1$, applying [F5] to $Z$ at $z_0$, whose $M-1$ defining functions have rank $M-1$ at $z_0$ by step 7.1, yields a plane domain $A'\subseteq\mathbb C$ and a holomorphic map $\gamma_0:A'\to\mathbb C^M$ whose image is a neighbourhood of $z_0$ in $Z$, with $\gamma_0$ injective and inverse holomorphic; let $c$ be the value of the free coordinate at $z_0$ and replace $\gamma_0$ by $s\mapsto\gamma_0(c+s)$ on a disk $\Delta\subseteq A'-c$ centred at $0$, so that $\gamma_0(0)=z_0$. Shrinking $\Delta$ and using step 8.1, we may assume $\gamma_0(\Delta)\subseteq X$. Composing $\gamma_0$ with the inclusion $X\subseteq C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}$ and with $\nu$ gives an arc into $C$; it is nonconstant and holomorphic, because every coordinate function of the affine model $V_0$ pulls back to a regular function on the affine set $X$, is there represented by a polynomial in $t_1,\ldots,t_M$, and substitution of the holomorphic graph coordinates gives a holomorphic function of $s$. The finite normalization of $C$ restricts over the open curve $C_0=C\cap V_0$ to the normalization of $C_0$: both affine descriptions use the same integral closure, localized at the defining open. Thus this parametrizes a point in the normalization of $C$ as stated.

It remains to make the punctured arc avoid $V\setminus O$. Since $C_0
ot\subseteq B$ and $B$ is closed in the irreducible curve $C_0$, the set $C_0\setminus O=C_0\cap B$ has dimension $0$ by [F3] and is therefore finite: a classical variety is Noetherian with finitely many irreducible components, and a zero-dimensional irreducible component is a single point. Because $
u$ is finite, each of its fibres is finite: on an affine chart the coordinate ring is a finitely generated module over the base with finite-dimensional reduction modulo a maximal ideal. Hence $F:=
u^{-1}(C_0\setminus O)$ is finite. The chart $\gamma_0$ of step 9.1 is injective, so $\gamma_0^{-1}(F)$ is finite with at most $|F|$ elements; replacing the disk by a smaller concentric disk, we may assume no nonzero parameter in $\Delta$ has $\gamma_0(s)\in F$ (if $z\in O$, the parameter $0$ is not in this preimage either). Then for every $s
e0$ the point $
u(\gamma_0(s))$ lies in $C_0\setminus
u(F)=C_0\cap O\subseteq O$. Thus $\gamma:=
u\circ\gamma_0:\Delta	o V$ is holomorphic with $\gamma(0)=z$ and $\gamma(s)\in O$ for all $s
e0$, and the arc was obtained by parametrizing the point $z_0$ over $z$ in the finite normalization $C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}$.

boundaries.reason: The hypothesis $dim Vge1$ excludes the empty variety, $O$ is required nonempty, and the proof takes no union or intersection over an unbounded family.

boundaries.evidence: The set $C_0setminus O$ is a closed subset of the irreducible curve $C_0$ not containing it, so it has dimension $0$ and step 10.1 excises its finitely many points by a smaller radius.

When $d=1$, the chosen affine line is all of $\mathbb A^1$, no cutting forms occur and $h^{-1}(\ell)=V_0$ is the required curve; it is not the finite fibre $h^{-1}(a)$. Step 9.1 separately gives translation when the normalized curve embeds in $\mathbb C$ with $M=1$.
A singular curve is exactly what step 6.1 handles by replacing $C_0$ with its finite normalization before the analytic chart of step 9.1 is taken.
Step 10.1: The arc is defined on a disk including zero. Shrinking its radius excludes all nonzero parameters mapping to the finite bad set, preserving its specified value at zero.
The Statement assumes AC; the normalisation of step 2.1 and the lying-over and height-theorem inputs cited in steps 2.1-4.1 are the exact inherited uses, as recorded in [A1].

boundaries.reason: The Statement asserts existence of a curve and of a holomorphic arc, not a biconditional, so no forward implication is owed.
No converse is claimed; the lemma does not assert that every arc through $z$ arises from a normalization of some curve $C$.
