The local-ring quotient argument uses two one-dimensional domains; the kernel cannot be nonzero. citations.quote: Let $X$ be a reduced quasi-projective complex algebraic variety, regarded as a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) with its analytic topology, its smooth points (regular local rings) and its finite smooth algebraic frontier stratifications ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). (a) **Whitney conditions.** Let $X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ be a finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification whose strata are pure-dimensional, and let $R\subseteq\overline S\setminus S$ be incident strata. In local analytic charts of an ambient smooth manifold, the pair $(S,R)$ satisfies **Whitney (a)** at $y\in R$ if for every sequence $x_n\in S$ with $x_n\to y$ whose tangent planes $T_{x_n}S$ converge to a plane $T$, one has $T_yR\subseteq T$; it satisfies **Whitney (b)** at $y$ if additionally, whenever $y_n\in R$ with $y_n\to y$ and the real secant lines through $x_n,y_n$ converge to a line $\ell$, one has $\ell\subseteq T$. A **finite complex algebraic Whitney stratification** of $X$ is a finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification satisfying (a) and (b) at every point of every incident pair. Coordinate independence of the limits and the implication (b)$\Rightarrow$(a), commonly used in the literature, are not assumed as proved here; requiring both conditions makes the intended interface explicit. (b) **Tube control data.** A system of **tube control data** on the analytic stratified space $X$ consists of an open neighbourhood $T_R$ of each stratum $R$, a continuous retraction $\pi_R:T_R\to R$ and a continuous radius $\rho_R:T_R\to[0,\infty)$ such that $\rho_R^{-1}(0)=R$, both maps are smooth on each stratum, and for every incident upper stratum $S$ the pair $(\pi_R,\rho_R)$ restricts to a submersion $S\cap T_R\to R\times(0,\infty)$. On the overlap neighbourhoods where the compositions are defined one requires $\pi_R\pi_S=\pi_R$ and $\rho_R\pi_S=\rho_R$ for $R<S$; every compatibility assertion must name the common domain on which the composition is defined. Tubes may be shrunk. For local conical constructions one requires local properness over compact base slices: sufficiently small closed radius ranges over a compact neighbourhood in $R$ have compact inverse image inside the tube. (c) **$f$-compatible tubes and controlled lifts.** Let $f:W\to B$ be a stratified submersion onto a smooth manifold. A tube system is **$f$-compatible** if $f\pi_R=f$ on the tubes used. A **controlled lift** of a smooth base field $v$ on $B$ is a field $V$ that is smooth on each stratum and satisfies $df(V)=v\circ f$, $d\pi_R(V)=V|_R\circ\pi_R$ and $d\rho_R(V)=0$ on specified controlled tube neighbourhoods. **Locally bounded** means the ambient norm is bounded on a neighbourhood of every point; this is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of the definition. **Radial controlled lifts** instead satisfy $d\rho_R(V)=\rho_R$ with fixed $\pi_R$ together with the appropriate annular overlap controls. (d) **Conical product neighbourhoods.** A **conical product neighbourhood along $R$** is a stratum-preserving homeomorphism from a neighbourhood of a point of $R$ to $B^{2\dim_{\mathbb C}R}\times c(L)$ carrying $R$ to the ball times the cone apex, with compact finitely Whitney-stratified $L$. The radial and tangential transports must be compatible with the actual coefficient data when cohomological local systems are deduced; topological existence alone does not supply canonical derived-sheaf transport. (e) **Finite triangulation of a noncompact space.** In the compactification convention used here, a **finite triangulation** of a noncompact space $X$ consists of finite simplicial complexes $D\subseteq K$ together with a homeomorphism $|K|\setminus|D|\to X$; compatibility with prescribed subsets means they are unions of interiors of retained simplices. This does not assert that algebraic morphisms become simplicial, and real simplicial dimensions do not replace the complex dimensions of the algebraic strata.

For a dominant morphism $f:X\to Y$ between irreducible classical varieties, there is a nonempty open $U\subseteq Y$, contained in $f(X)$, such that every $X_y$ with $y\in U$ is nonempty and has pure dimension $r=\dim X-\dim Y$. Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Assume AC. Let $V$ be an irreducible complex algebraic variety of positive
dimension ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]),
let $O\subseteq V$ be a nonempty Zariski open subset and let $z\in V$. There is
an irreducible algebraic curve $C\subseteq V$ through $z$ not contained in
$V\setminus O$. There is also a holomorphic map $\gamma:\Delta\to V$ from a
sufficiently small complex disk, with $\gamma(0)=z$ and $\gamma(s)\in O$ for
all $s\ne0$; here $\Delta$ is a disk centred at $0$ and a map into $V$ is
holomorphic when its coordinate functions in an affine model containing its
image are holomorphic. The arc can be obtained by analytically parametrizing a
point over $z$ in the finite normalization of $C$.

Every classical variety is Noetherian and has finitely many irreducible components. Every open or closed subvariety has a finite affine cover. Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

If $U$ is a nonempty open of an irreducible classical variety $X$, then $\dim U=\dim X$. Every proper closed subvariety $Z\subsetneq X$ has $\dim Z<\dim X$. Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Let $k$ be any field, let $n\geq0$ be finite, let $I$ be an ideal of $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and put $$X=\operatorname{Spec}(k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I).$$ Let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in X(k)$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ be any finite generating list of the actual ideal $I$. Then the coordinate-velocity map gives a canonical $k$-linear isomorphism $$T_aX\cong\ker\!\left(J_{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}(a):k^n\longrightarrow k^r\right).$$ The kernel is independent of the chosen finite generating list of $I$. No reducedness, perfectness, or characteristic hypothesis is needed. Finiteness of the list is available for every finite $n$ by the finite-variable polynomial Noetherian result cited below.

For every $r$-subset $I$ of a basis of an $n$-dimensional $V$, the locus $p_I\ne0$ in $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf A_k^{r(n-r)}$; these loci cover the Grassmannian and have regular transition maps.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A **standard smooth presentation** of an $R$-algebra $S$ consists of integers $n\ge c\ge0$, elements $f_1,\dots,f_c$ of the polynomial ring $P=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ ([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]) and an element $g\in P$ such that $$S\cong\bigl(R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(f_1,\dots,f_c)\bigr)_g$$ as $R$-algebras, and such that the Jacobian matrix of ([[lem-ag-polynomial-quotient-differentials]]) $$\Bigl(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial x_i}\Bigr)_{\substack{1\le j\le c\\1\le i\le n}}$$ has a $c\times c$ minor whose image in $S$ is a unit, that is, an invertible element. The integer $n-c\ge0$ is the **relative dimension** of the presentation. The case $c=0$ is allowed and is exactly a localisation of a polynomial ring, $S\cong(R[x_1,\dots,x_n])_g$; the case $n=c=0$ presents $S=R[\,]_g$ for $g\in R$, that is a localisation of $R$ itself. For a homomorphism $R\to S$ of commutative rings that is finitely presented as an $R$-algebra ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]) and a prime $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$, the map is **standard smooth at $\mathfrak q$**, or has a standard smooth presentation at $\mathfrak q$, when there is $h\in S\smallsetminus\mathfrak q$ such that $S_h$ admits a standard smooth presentation over $R$. It is **locally standard smooth** when this holds at every prime of $S$; equivalently, when every point of $\operatorname{Spec}S$ has an affine open neighbourhood on which $S$ is presented by a single standard smooth presentation. Two conventions are part of the definition. First, the invertible minor may be assumed to sit in the first $c$ columns: if a minor on columns $i_1<\dots<i_c$ is a unit, the automorphism of $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ permuting the variables so that these become the first $c$ variables carries the presentation to one whose minor in the first $c$ columns is that unit, and the relative dimension $n-c$ is unchanged. Second, a further principal localisation can be absorbed into the presentation: adjoining a variable $z$ with the single equation $zg-1$ to a presentation produces a standard smooth presentation of the localisation, the new equation contributing a diagonal entry that keeps a block minor invertible, and it changes $n$ and $c$ by the same amount, so that the relative dimension is again unchanged.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$. Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible: $$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$ Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that $$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$ and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed, $$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a perfect field and let $X$ be a finite-type $k$-scheme. Here **regular** means that $X$ is locally Noetherian and every local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is regular local; **smooth over $k$** means that $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth under the local-standard-smooth convention of [[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]. Then $$X\text{ is regular}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\to\operatorname{Spec}k\text{ is smooth}.$$ No reducedness, irreducibility, or closed-point restriction is imposed.

Fix an algebraically closed field $k$. The affine models used here are polynomial zero sets $Z\subseteq k^n$, including empty and reducible sets. Their closed subsets are common zero loci of polynomial families, relative to $Z$. Intersections combine equations, and finite unions use products of equations, so these are the closed sets of a topology. For an open $U\subseteq Z$, let $\mathcal O_Z(U)$ consist of functions $U\to k$ locally equal to $a/b$ for polynomials $a,b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the chosen neighbourhood. Pointwise operations and restriction make these sets a sheaf of $k$-algebras: quotient expressions persist on restriction, and functions that agree locally glue uniquely with the same local quotient property. At a point z its stalk is the ring of germs of such functions. Evaluation at z maps it onto k, with kernel the germs vanishing at z. A germ nonzero at z is invertible: shrink to where its numerator and denominator are both nonzero and interchange them. Thus the kernel is the unique maximal ideal. These affine models are locally ringed spaces in the sense of [[def-locally-ringed-space]], with residue fields canonically k. A **classical algebraic prevariety** over k is a quasi-compact locally ringed space with a structure sheaf of k-algebras, covered by open subspaces isomorphic over k to these affine models. Here quasi-compact means every open cover has a finite subcover. Equivalently it admits a finite affine-model cover. To justify the converse, each affine model is quasi-compact: polynomial principal opens $D_Z(h)=\{z:h(z)\ne0\}$ form a basis. Given an open cover, take all h whose principal opens lie in a member. Their principal opens cover Z. The ideal generated by these h in $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ is finitely generated by [[thm-hilbert-basis-theorem]], iterated from the field k. Express finitely many generators using finitely many of the original h. Those finitely many h have the same common zero locus as the whole ideal, hence their principal opens still cover Z and yield a finite subcover. The empty model has the empty subcover. A finite union of quasi-compact subspaces is quasi-compact. A map is **regular** when it is a morphism of locally ringed spaces as in [[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]] whose sheaf maps respect k. For these function sheaves its sheaf map is necessarily pullback of functions: the local stalk map induces a k-map between residue fields k, hence the identity, so the value of a pulled-back section at x is its value at the image of x. Conversely, continuous pullback of local regular functions gives a local stalk map because a function vanishing at the image vanishes after pullback. Regularity can therefore be checked on affine charts: near every source point choose a target affine chart containing its image and an open neighbourhood in a source affine chart mapped into it; the target coordinate functions must pull back to locally polynomial quotients. This condition also implies continuity. Indeed zero sets of locally polynomial quotients are locally polynomial zero sets, hence closed; pulling back polynomial equations consequently gives closed sets. Substitution then pulls every local quotient on the target back to a local quotient on the source, using this continuity to restrict to its domain and its nonvanishing denominator. Thus the chart condition and the locally ringed-space definition agree. A prevariety is **separated** when the equalizer of every pair of regular maps into it, from any classical prevariety, is closed. A **classical algebraic variety** is a separated prevariety. Here varieties may be reducible or empty; an **irreducible classical variety** is nonempty and irreducible in the sense of [[def-irreducible-topological-space-and-subset]]. These definitions and the local verifications above use no Axiom of Choice.

For every $r$-subset $I$ of a basis of an $n$-dimensional $V$, the locus $p_I\ne0$ in $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf A_k^{r(n-r)}$; these loci cover the Grassmannian and have regular transition maps.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Put $d=\dim S$ and let $G$ be the graph of the map $(x,y)\mapsto(T_xS,[x-y])$ from $S\times Y$ to $\operatorname{Gr}(d,n)\times\mathbb P^{n-1}$; it is algebraic by [F5], because on chart domains the tangent plane is the kernel of the Jacobian matrix of local equations, whose basis entries are regular ratios on each fixed nonzero-minor chart and the secant coordinates are regular since $x\ne y$. Let $Z$ be the reduced closure of $G$ in $\overline S\times Y\times\operatorname{Gr}(d,n)\times\mathbb P^{n-1}$. The graph $G$ is isomorphic to $S\times Y$, hence irreducible by [F6], and $\overline S$, $Y$, $\operatorname{Gr}(d,n)$ and $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ are irreducible; the ambient product is therefore irreducible by [F6], and its closed subset $Z$, the closure of the irreducible $G$, is irreducible as well. Let $B=Z\setminus G$, a proper closed subset, and let $g:Z\to Y$ be the projection; it is dominant because it is onto on $G$.

Apply [F2] to $g$ to obtain a dense open subset of $Y$ over which the fibres $Z_y$ are nonempty and pure of dimension $r=\dim Z-\dim Y$. This number is positive, because each fibre contains $G_y=\{(x,y,T_xS,[x-y]):x\in S\}\cong S$ of dimension $\dim S\ge1$. Each irreducible component $B_i$ of the proper closed subset $B$ has $\dim B_i<\dim Z$ by [F4]; if $B_i\to Y$ is dominant, [F2] gives a further dense open of $Y$ over which its fibres have pure dimension $\dim B_i-\dim Y\le r-1$, and if it is not dominant we remove its image closure. Intersecting the finitely many dense opens leaves a dense open $Y^0\subseteq Y$ on which $Z_y$ is pure $r$-dimensional while $B_y$ has dimension at most $r-1$; hence no irreducible component of $Z_y$ is contained in $B_y$, and for every component $V$ of $Z_y$ the set $V\cap G_y=V\setminus B_y$ is a nonempty dense open subset of the irreducible $V$.

e0$. Then $T(s)=T_{x(s)}S$ and $[u(s)]=[x(s)-y]$ for $s
e0$, so $x(s)

e0$. Choosing a projective chart containing $[u]$, the normalized representative of the arc is holomorphic, and since $x(s)-y$ is not identically zero some coordinate has finite positive vanishing order; with $m\ge1$ the minimum of these orders, $x(s)-y=s^mv(s)$ with $v$ holomorphic and $v(0)
e0$, and $[v(0)]=[u]$.

Let $p_0$ be a complex covector annihilating the complex plane $T$. In a Grassmannian matrix chart around $T$ write $T(s)$ as the graph of a holomorphic matrix $A(s)$ with $A(0)=A_0$, possible for small $s$ because $T(s)\to T$; every annihilator of the graph of $A(s)$ has the form $q(s)=(-A(s)^tb,b)$ for $b\in(\mathbb C^{n-d})^*$, and $b$ can be chosen with $(-A_0^tb,b)=p_0$ because $p_0$ annihilates $T$. The resulting $q(s)$ is holomorphic and annihilates each $T(s)$. Since $x(s)\in S$ for $s\ne0$, its derivative lies in $T_{x(s)}S=T(s)$ by [F5], so $q(s)(x'(s))=0$ for $s\ne0$. Differentiating $x(s)-y=s^mv(s)$ gives $x'(s)=s^{m-1}(mv(s)+sv'(s))$, and dividing by $s^{m-1}$ and letting $s\to0$ yields $p_0(mv(0))=0$, hence $p_0(v(0))=0$. Every annihilator of $T$ therefore kills $v(0)$, so $v(0)\in T$ and the limiting complex secant line $[u]$ lies in $T$.

Now let $x_j\in S$ and $y_j\in Y$ be sequences converging to the same point $y\in Y^0$, with tangent planes $T_{x_j}S$ converging to a plane $T$ and real secant lines through $x_j,y_j$ converging to a real line $\ell$. After choosing their signs, the secant directions normalized to unit vectors converge to a unit vector $w$ spanning $\ell$, and the complex projective points $[x_j-y_j]=[w_j]$ converge to $[w]$, the complex line spanned by $\ell$; moreover $(x_j,y_j,T_{x_j}S,[x_j-y_j])\in G\subseteq Z$ converges to $(y,y,T,[w])\in Z_y$ because $Z$ is closed. Applying steps 3.1 and 4.1 to this incidence point shows that its limiting complex secant line lies in $T$, so $w\in T$ and $\ell=\mathbb Rw\subseteq T$. This is Whitney (b) at $y$ in the full moving-point form.

For Whitney (a) at $y$, let $x_j\in S$ converge to $y$ with tangent planes converging to $T$, and let $w\in T_yY$ be a nonzero real tangent vector (the zero vector already belongs to $T$). In a holomorphic chart of the smooth manifold $Y$ near $y$ choose points $y_j\in Y$ of the form $y+\epsilon_jw+o(\epsilon_j)$ with $\epsilon_j>0$, $\epsilon_j\to0$ and $\|x_j-y\|/\epsilon_j\to0$, for instance $\epsilon_j=\sqrt{\|x_j-y\|}$ and a straight segment in the chart. Then $\|x_j-y_j\|\ge\epsilon_j\|w\|/2$ for large $j$, and the secant directions from $y_j$ to $x_j$ converge to the real line spanned by $w$. Since the tangent planes $T_{x_j}S\to T$, Whitney (b) from step 5.1 places that real line in $T$, so $w\in T$. Every real tangent vector of $T_yY$ arises in this way, so $T_yY\subseteq T$, proving Whitney (a).

Set $E=Y\setminus Y^0$; it is a proper closed algebraic subset by step 2.1, and steps 5.1 and 6.1 show that $(S,Y)$ satisfies (a) and (b) at every point of $Y\setminus E$. For finitely many prescribed incident upper strata $S_1,\ldots,S_m$ over the same irreducible $Y$, apply the construction to each and take the union of the finitely many proper closed exceptional sets; since $Y$ is irreducible, that finite union is still proper, by [F4]. For a quasi-projective ambient manifold, use the finitely many affine ambient charts $U_\alpha$ that meet $Y$; their intersections with the irreducible $Y$ are nonempty opens. Inside each chart apply the affine result to every pair of irreducible components $(S_i,Y_j)$ of $(S\cap U_\alpha,Y\cap U_\alpha)$ with $Y_j\subseteq\overline{S_i}$ and $\dim Y_j<\dim S_i$, and for each point of an irreducible component of $Y\cap U_\alpha$ one of these pairs accounts for every sequence in $S$ converging to it after passing to a subsequence in a component. Each chart exceptional set is closed in $Y\cap U_\alpha$ and has smaller dimension than $Y$, so its closure in $Y$ is proper by [F4]. The union of these finitely many closures and the proper closed complements $Y\setminus U_\alpha$ is still proper because $Y$ is irreducible. Outside this union every chart argument applies, giving the required closed $E\subsetneq Y$.

boundaries.reason: Both $S$ and $Y$ are irreducible and hence nonempty under the Statement conventions, and no union over an unbounded family occurs, so the empty case cannot arise.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 computes $r=dim Z-dim Y$ and shows it is positive because every fibre contains the graph point, so the zero-dimensional-fibre case is excluded before the arc argument begins.

boundaries.reason: No singleton hypothesis appears; the argument is uniform in $dim S,dim Y,n$, and a single incidence point is handled locally in step 3.1.

boundaries.evidence: The graph closure $Z$ is irreducible by step 1.1 and may be singular. Its fibres may be reducible; step 3.1 selects a positive-dimensional irreducible fibre component through the incidence point.

boundaries.reason: The exceptional subset $E$ is excluded wholesale and the conclusion is claimed away from it; no asymptotic value at the frontier of $E$ is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement assumes AC, inherited through the fibre-dimension supplier [F2] at step 2.1 and the curve-arc supplier [F3] at step 3.1, as recorded in [A1].

boundaries.reason: The theorem produces a proper closed exceptional set, not a characterization, so no forward implication direction is owed.
No converse is claimed; the result does not assert that Whitney regularity fails on all of $E$ or that $E$ is minimal.

risk_review.notes: Complete seven-step review: G is an irreducible algebraic graph, open in its closure Z over S, hence B=Z minus G is proper closed. Generic fibre purity of Z and lower dimensions for all dominant boundary components ensure each fibre component meets G, licensing the normalized curve arc with y fixed. A holomorphic annihilator along the Grassmannian chart kills x'(s); the leading arc coefficient lies in T. This applies to limits with moving lower points, establishes real Whitney (b), then yields (a) by choosing epsilon much larger than distance x_j-y. Finite chart and upper-stratum unions remain proper because Y is irreducible. Disjointness ensures every secant is nonzero; dim S>=1 licenses the arc. All current suppliers' hypotheses and inherited AC were checked; no unresolved defect.

The radial and tangential transports must be compatible with the actual coefficient data when cohomological local systems are deduced; topological existence alone does not supply canonical derived-sheaf transport.

(e) **Finite triangulation of a noncompact space.** In the compactification convention used here, a **finite triangulation** of a noncompact space $X$ consists of finite simplicial complexes $D\subseteq K$ together with a homeomorphism $|K|\setminus|D|\to X$; compatibility with prescribed subsets means they are unions of interiors of retained simplices. This does not assert that algebraic morphisms become simplicial, and real simplicial dimensions do not replace the complex dimensions of the algebraic strata.

Assume AC. Let $f:X\to Y$ be one morphism of reduced separated complex
algebraic varieties of finite type
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), and
prescribe finitely many closed algebraic subsets of each. There are finite
partitions of $X$ and $Y$ into irreducible smooth locally closed algebraic
strata such that every prescribed subset is a union of strata, every stratum
closure is a union of strata of no larger dimension with its boundary of
strictly smaller dimension, and each source stratum maps surjectively and
smoothly onto one target stratum. On analytic spaces each such restriction is a
submersion. The source may be empty. This assertion imposes no Whitney
condition, conical control or topological triviality.

Every classical variety is Noetherian and has finitely many irreducible components. Every open or closed subvariety has a finite affine cover.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

If $U$ is a nonempty open of an irreducible classical variety $X$, then $\dim U=\dim X$. Every proper closed subvariety $Z\subsetneq X$ has $\dim Z<\dim X$.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a perfect field
([[def-perfect-field]]) and let $X$ be a reduced $k$-scheme of finite type over
$k$. Then:

1. the regular locus $X_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in|X|:\mathcal O_{X,x}\text{ is a regular local ring}\}$
   ([[def-singular-and-regular-loci-variety]]) is open in $X$;
2. for every irreducible component $Z$ of $X$
   ([[def-irreducible-component-of-a-topological-space]]) the intersection
   $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap Z$ is a dense open subset of $Z$; in particular every
   irreducible component contains a nonempty dense open subset of points
   regular on $X$;
3. if $X\ne\varnothing$, then $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\ne\varnothing$.

No separatedness, irreducibility or equidimensionality hypothesis is imposed,
and $X$ may be empty, in which case the second clause is vacuous and the third
is not asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a perfect
field and let $X$ be a finite-type $k$-scheme. Here **regular** means that $X$
is locally Noetherian and every local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is regular local;
**smooth over $k$** means that $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth under the
local-standard-smooth convention of
[[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]. Then
$$X\text{ is regular}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\to\operatorname{Spec}k\text{ is smooth}.$$
No reducedness, irreducibility, or closed-point restriction is imposed.

Assume AC. Let $S,Y\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be disjoint irreducible smooth locally
closed complex algebraic varieties with $Y\subseteq\overline S$ and
$\dim Y<\dim S$. There is a proper closed algebraic subset $E\subsetneq Y$ such
that $(S,Y)$ satisfies Whitney (a) and (b) at every point of $Y\setminus E$.
Finite prescribed incident upper strata can be treated with one common
exceptional subset by taking a finite union. The same result holds in the
affine charts of a quasi-projective algebraic ambient manifold.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be an algebraically
closed field of characteristic $0$, let $X$ and $Y$ be irreducible classical
varieties over $k$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), and let
$f\colon X\to Y$ be a morphism of classical varieties. Assume $X$ is smooth
over $k$, that is, the structure morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth
in the locally-standard-smooth sense of [[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]
(equivalently, since $k$ is perfect, $X$ is regular). Then:

1. there is a dense open subvariety $U\subseteq Y$ such that the restriction
   $$f^{-1}(U)\longrightarrow U$$
   is a smooth morphism of finite-type $k$-schemes; when $f$ is not dominant
   one may take $U$ with $f^{-1}(U)=\varnothing$, the empty morphism being
   smooth;
2. if in addition $f$ is dominant, there is a nonempty open (hence dense)
   $V\subseteq U$ such that for every closed point $y\in V$ the
   scheme-theoretic fibre
   $$X_y=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}k(y)$$
   ([[def-scheme-theoretic-fibre]]) is nonempty, smooth over $k$, and of pure
   dimension $r=\dim X-\dim Y$.

Neither $Y$ nor $f$ is required to be smooth or flat, the fibres are not
required to be irreducible or connected, and no statement is made about the
size of $U$ or $V$. The characteristic-$0$ hypothesis enters through the
critical-locus dimension bound of
[[lem-critical-locus-image-dimension-bound]] in claim 1 and through the
perfectness of $k$; the failure of the target-open statement for a
non-smooth source and the positive-characteristic failure of the
corresponding source-side statement are recorded on the counterexample page of
this pair.

Assume AC. Let $f:X\to Y$ be one morphism of reduced separated complex
algebraic varieties of finite type
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), and
prescribe finitely many closed algebraic subsets of each. There are finite
partitions of $X$ and $Y$ into irreducible smooth locally closed algebraic
strata such that every prescribed subset is a union of strata, every stratum
closure is a union of strata of no larger dimension with its boundary of
strictly smaller dimension, and each source stratum maps surjectively and
smoothly onto one target stratum. On analytic spaces each such restriction is a
submersion. The source may be empty. This assertion imposes no Whitney
condition, conical control or topological triviality.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every nonempty irreducible separated complex algebraic variety of
finite type is connected in its analytic topology. For every locally closed
algebraic subset $A$ of a separated finite-type complex variety $X$, the closure
of $A$ in the analytic topology equals its Zariski closure as a set of classical
complex points. In particular smooth irreducible algebraic strata are connected
complex manifolds once their holomorphic charts have been supplied.

derivations.claim: Replace every prescribed locally closed subset $A$ by the two prescribed closed subsets $\overline A$ and $\overline A\setminus A$; their difference recovers $A$, and it suffices to respect the resulting finite list of closed subsets. Refine the smooth-partition construction of [F2] to construct, for a closed residual variety $R$ together with a finite list of prescribed closed subsets and finitely many previously fixed smooth strata outside $R$ whose closures must be respected, a Whitney partition of $R$ compatible with all of them: take the irreducible components $R_i$ of $R$, remove their nonsmooth loci and their intersections with the other components, and remove every prescribed closed subset not containing $R_i$, obtaining dense smooth opens $L_i$; then for every previously fixed upper stratum $S$, remove $R_i\cap\overline S$ when $R_i\not\subseteq\overline S$, and when $R_i\subseteq\overline S$ use [F3] to remove the closure in $R_i$ of the exceptional subset of [F3], which is proper because it has dimension smaller than $\dim R_i$. Finitely many upper strata leave nonempty dense smooth opens $U_i\subseteq R_i$, and [F3] makes each $U_i$ Whitney-regular with every incident previously fixed upper stratum.

Emit the $U_i$ as strata, add their closures $R_i$ to the list of closed subsets to be respected, and recurse on the closed complement $R\setminus\bigcup_iU_i$, whose dimension drops because every component lost a dense open subset. The recursion terminates by induction on dimension, producing a finite partition of $R$ into smooth irreducible locally closed strata. Strata of the same round have no frontier relation, since each $U_i$ misses all other components $R_j$. Every pair of incident strata has its upper stratum emitted earlier, and when the lower stratum was emitted step 1.1 imposed Whitney (a) and (b) with that upper stratum; boundaries have strictly smaller dimension by [F2]. The respected closures make every stratum closure a union of strata. In a quasi-projective ambient space, cover it by finitely many affine coordinate charts and apply the affine-chart version of [F3]; a sequence in $R$ converging to a point meets only finitely many components of the chart intersections, so passing to a subsequence in one component reduces the conditions to the chart version. Thus Whitney partitions compatible with a finite list of closed sets and with fixed external upper strata exist.

Construct the map-compatible partitions by decreasing target residual dimension. Start with target residual $R=Y$ and source residual $f^{-1}(R)=X$, and at each later round maintain the original closed-set lists together with the closures of all previously emitted source and target strata. Partition the source residual $f^{-1}(R)$ by step 2.1, so that it is Whitney-compatible with all previously emitted source strata. For each irreducible component $R_i$ of $R$, choose a dense smooth open $L_i\subseteq R_i$ as in step 1.1, respecting the target prescriptions and Whitney-regular with all previously emitted target strata. For every new source stratum $Z_\alpha$ compute the closure of its image in $R$; if that closure is not $R_i$, remove its intersection with $R_i$, a proper closed subset; if the closure is $R_i$, then $Z_\alpha\to R_i$ is dominant and [F4] supplies a dense open subset of $R_i$ on which the restriction is smooth and onto. Intersecting the finitely many resulting dense opens with $L_i$ gives a nonempty dense open $V_i\subseteq R_i$.

Emit the $V_i$ as target strata and the nonempty pieces $Z_\alpha\cap f^{-1}(V_i)$ as source strata. Each such piece is open in the smooth irreducible stratum $Z_\alpha$, hence smooth irreducible and locally closed, and it is Whitney-regular with every incident previously fixed upper source stratum, because Whitney conditions are local and were imposed on all of $Z_\alpha$ in step 2.1; with the pieces of the same round it has no frontier relation except through closures, which the later rounds make unions of strata because every closure is added to the respected list. Each piece maps smoothly and onto $V_i$ by its selection in step 3.1, and target strata are Whitney-regular with earlier target strata since $V_i\subseteq L_i$. Source frontier relations inside $f^{-1}(\bigcup_iV_i)$ are inherited from the source partition, and a stratum closure over $R_i$ misses every $V_j$ with $j\ne i$.

Remove $\bigcup_iV_i$ from $R$, restrict both residuals and both lists, add all newly emitted stratum closures to the respective lists, and repeat. The target dimension strictly decreases each round, so after finitely many rounds every target point and every source point has been placed: a source point lies over one emitted target stratum and is contained in one emitted piece. Future source partitions are chosen Whitney-compatible with every earlier source stratum by step 2.1, and future target opens are chosen Whitney-compatible with earlier target strata in step 3.1, so every incident pair is covered; the closure-bookkeeping makes all stratum closures unions of strata. Each emitted piece is irreducible and nonempty, so [F7] makes it analytically connected and identifies its analytic closure with the algebraic closure tracked by the construction. This yields finite smooth Whitney frontier stratifications of $X$ and $Y$, respecting all prescribed subsets (including the strata of any prescribed finite algebraic stratification, which were treated as prescribed sets in step 1.1), with each source stratum mapping smoothly and surjectively onto one target stratum.

The analytic clauses follow from [F5] and the same locally standard smooth Jacobian charts: the strata are smooth complex manifolds, and each smooth restriction is, in those charts, a holomorphic map whose differential is onto and whose rank is locally constant, hence a submersion. If $f$ is proper in the analytic topology and $T$ is a target stratum, then for every compact subset $C\subseteq T$ the inclusion $T\hookrightarrow Y$ is continuous, so $C$ is compact in $Y$, and $f^{-1}(C)\subseteq f^{-1}(T)$ is compact by properness of $f$; hence the restriction $f^{-1}(T)\to T$ is proper, although individual source strata inside $f^{-1}(T)$ may fail to be closed. Empty spaces and empty prescribed families add no strata, and no tube control, isotopy or triangulation existence is claimed.

For the projective case factor $f$ as a closed algebraic embedding $i:X\hookrightarrow Y\times\mathbb P^N(\mathbb C)$ followed by the projection $\pi:Y\times\mathbb P^N(\mathbb C)\to Y$. Complex projective space is the continuous image of the unit sphere in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ under $z\mapsto[z]$, hence compact by [F6]. A closed algebraic embedding is analytically closed, because in each chart its defining polynomial equations have continuous coefficients and their common zero set is closed. For a compact $C\subseteq Y$ the set $\pi^{-1}(C)=C\times\mathbb P^N(\mathbb C)$ is compact by [F6], and $f^{-1}(C)=i^{-1}(C\times\mathbb P^N(\mathbb C))$ is a closed subset of it, hence compact. Therefore $f$ is analytically proper, and step 6.1 applies; this is the analytic properness used by the consumers.

boundaries.evidence: An empty source is admitted; step 1.1 replaces prescribed locally closed sets and the rounds of step 2.1 emit target strata while the empty source residual stays empty.

boundaries.reason: No symbolic expression is divided and no count is reduced; zero-dimensional strata are emitted in step 4.1 by the same regular-locus mechanism as higher-dimensional ones.
There is no singleton hypothesis; a one-point variety is stratified by its single dimension-zero stratum via step 2.1, and the map clause is vacuous on it.
Prescribed sets are refined by the closed-set replacement of step 1.1 and every stratum is an open subset of a regular locus, so no degenerate stratum survives to require an argument.
No interval or asymptotic endpoint occurs; frontier relations are finite closure conditions maintained in step 5.1.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement assumes AC, consumed through the regular-locus and dimension suppliers [F2] and [F4]; each round of steps 2.1-5.1 selects only from finite lists of components and closures.

boundaries.reason: Existence of the compatible stratifications is asserted, not an equivalence, so no forward direction is owed.
No converse is claimed: the theorem does not assert that every partition with smooth restrictions is Whitney-refinable in this sense.

citations.quote: Let $X$ be a reduced quasi-projective complex algebraic variety, regarded as a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) with its analytic topology, its smooth points (regular local rings) and its finite smooth algebraic frontier stratifications ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). (a) **Whitney conditions.** Let $X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ be a finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification whose strata are pure-dimensional, and let $R\subseteq\overline S\setminus S$ be incident strata. In local analytic charts of an ambient smooth manifold, the pair $(S,R)$ satisfies **Whitney (a)** at $y\in R$ if for every sequence $x_n\in S$ with $x_n\to y$ whose tangent planes $T_{x_n}S$ converge to a plane $T$, one has $T_yR\subseteq T$; it satisfies **Whitney (b)** at $y$ if additionally, whenever $y_n\in R$ with $y_n\to y$ and the real secant lines through $x_n,y_n$ converge to a line $\ell$, one has $\ell\subseteq T$. A **finite complex algebraic Whitney stratification** of $X$ is a finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification satisfying (a) and (b) at every point of every incident pair. Coordinate independence of the limits and the implication (b)$\Rightarrow$(a), commonly used in the literature, are not assumed as proved here; requiring both conditions makes the intended interface explicit. (b) **Tube control data.** A system of **tube control data** on the analytic stratified space $X$ consists of an open neighbourhood $T_R$ of each stratum $R$, a continuous retraction $\pi_R:T_R\to R$ and a continuous radius $\rho_R:T_R\to[0,\infty)$ such that $\rho_R^{-1}(0)=R$, both maps are smooth on each stratum, and for every incident upper stratum $S$ the pair $(\pi_R,\rho_R)$ restricts to a submersion $S\cap T_R\to R\times(0,\infty)$. On the overlap neighbourhoods where the compositions are defined one requires $\pi_R\pi_S=\pi_R$ and $\rho_R\pi_S=\rho_R$ for $R<S$; every compatibility assertion must name the common domain on which the composition is defined. Tubes may be shrunk. For local conical constructions one requires local properness over compact base slices: sufficiently small closed radius ranges over a compact neighbourhood in $R$ have compact inverse image inside the tube. (c) **$f$-compatible tubes and controlled lifts.** Let $f:W\to B$ be a stratified submersion onto a smooth manifold. A tube system is **$f$-compatible** if $f\pi_R=f$ on the tubes used. A **controlled lift** of a smooth base field $v$ on $B$ is a field $V$ that is smooth on each stratum and satisfies $df(V)=v\circ f$, $d\pi_R(V)=V|_R\circ\pi_R$ and $d\rho_R(V)=0$ on specified controlled tube neighbourhoods. **Locally bounded** means the ambient norm is bounded on a neighbourhood of every point; this is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of the definition. **Radial controlled lifts** instead satisfy $d\rho_R(V)=\rho_R$ with fixed $\pi_R$ together with the appropriate annular overlap controls. (d) **Conical product neighbourhoods.** A **conical product neighbourhood along $R$** is a stratum-preserving homeomorphism from a neighbourhood of a point of $R$ to $B^{2\dim_{\mathbb C}R}\times c(L)$ carrying $R$ to the ball times the cone apex, with compact finitely Whitney-stratified $L$. The radial and tangential transports must be compatible with the actual coefficient data when cohomological local systems are deduced; topological existence alone does not supply canonical derived-sheaf transport. (e) **Finite triangulation of a noncompact space.** In the compactification convention used here, a **finite triangulation** of a noncompact space $X$ consists of finite simplicial complexes $D\subseteq K$ together with a homeomorphism $|K|\setminus|D|\to X$; compatibility with prescribed subsets means they are unions of interiors of retained simplices. This does not assert that algebraic morphisms become simplicial, and real simplicial dimensions do not replace the complex dimensions of the algebraic strata.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an embedded smooth submanifold. Then there is a positive smooth function $\delta:S\to(0,\infty)$ such that the restricted normal addition map $$E:\Omega_\delta\to\mathbb R^m,\qquad \Omega_\delta:=\{(p,v)\in N^\perp S:\|v\|<\delta(p)\},$$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open neighbourhood of $S$. In particular, $S$ has a tubular neighbourhood in $\mathbb R^m$.

In ZF, $$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$ DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Write $y=\pi(x)$ and $n=x-y$ for a point of the tube, and $r=\|n\|$. When $r>0$, differentiating the norm gives $dr_x(v)=\langle n/r,v-d\pi_x(v)\rangle=\langle n/r,v\rangle$, because $d\pi_x(v)\in T_yR$ is orthogonal to $n$; and at $y\in R$ the inverse differential of normal addition identifies $d\pi_y$ with the orthogonal projection onto $T_yR$ by [F2]. Fix a lower-stratum coordinate patch with a smooth orthonormal frame for $TR$, and use it to identify the target of $d\pi$ with $\mathbb R^m$, $m=\dim R$.

For $x$ in an incident upper stratum $S$ let $A_x:T_xS\to\mathbb R^m\oplus\mathbb R$ be the matrix of $(d\pi_x,dr_x)$ in that frame. Suppose no uniform lower bound $\|A_x^*\lambda\|\ge c\|\lambda\|$ held near a point $y_0\in R$. Then there are $x_j\to y_0$ in incident strata and unit vectors $\lambda_j=(a_j,b_j)$ with $\|A_{x_j}^*\lambda_j\|\to0$; passing to one of the finitely many strata and to subsequences, the tangent planes $T_{x_j}S$ converge to a plane $T$, the unit normal directions $n_j/r_j$ converge to a unit vector $u$, and the target vectors converge to a unit $(a,b)$. By smoothness of the tube projection, $d\pi_{x_j}$ converges to the orthogonal projection onto $T_{y_0}R$, and by step 1.1 the adjoints satisfy $A_{x_j}^*\lambda_j\to \Pi_T(a)+bu$, where $\Pi_T$ is the orthogonal projection onto $T$.

By Whitney (a), $T_{y_0}R\subseteq T$, so $\Pi_T(a)=a$; by Whitney (b) applied to the secants $x_j-\pi(x_j)$, the unit limit $u$ lies in $T$. In particular $A_x^*$ is injective, $A_x$ is surjective, and $(\pi,r)|_S$ is a submersion throughout that neighbourhood.

Set $H_x=A_x^*(A_xA_x^*)^{-1}$. Its image lies in $T_xS$ and $A_xH_x=\mathrm{id}$, and it is smooth along $S$ because the frame, the tube differentials and their coefficients are smooth; the singular-value bound gives $\|H_x\|\le1/c$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. The $z$-directions of the adapted charts give smooth local splittings $j_s:Q\to T\mathbb R^N|_S$ of the quotient map whose images are vertical for every active map. The sum is locally finite in $s$, smooth in all variables, and linear in $v$; at $x=s$ it equals $j_s(v)=\sum_\alpha\theta_\alpha(s)j_\alpha(s)(v)$, whose quotient is $v$ because every summand splits the quotient map. Whenever $s\in C_i$, every summand of nonzero weight lies in a neighbourhood carrying that constraint, so $W(s,v;\cdot)$ is vertical for $F_i$ near $x=s$.

By [F3] applied to the jointly smooth field $W$ this is defined and smooth on an open neighbourhood of the zero section: for small $v$ the field is small, and rescaling the parameter or restricting a common short-time interval gives the time-one solution. All radius requirements so far are positive local requirements on $s$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a reduced quasi-projective complex algebraic variety, regarded as a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) with its analytic topology, its smooth points (regular local rings) and its finite smooth algebraic frontier stratifications ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). (a) **Whitney conditions.** Let $X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ be a finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification whose strata are pure-dimensional, and let $R\subseteq\overline S\setminus S$ be incident strata. In local analytic charts of an ambient smooth manifold, the pair $(S,R)$ satisfies **Whitney (a)** at $y\in R$ if for every sequence $x_n\in S$ with $x_n\to y$ whose tangent planes $T_{x_n}S$ converge to a plane $T$, one has $T_yR\subseteq T$; it satisfies **Whitney (b)** at $y$ if additionally, whenever $y_n\in R$ with $y_n\to y$ and the real secant lines through $x_n,y_n$ converge to a line $\ell$, one has $\ell\subseteq T$. A **finite complex algebraic Whitney stratification** of $X$ is a finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification satisfying (a) and (b) at every point of every incident pair. Coordinate independence of the limits and the implication (b)$\Rightarrow$(a), commonly used in the literature, are not assumed as proved here; requiring both conditions makes the intended interface explicit. (b) **Tube control data.** A system of **tube control data** on the analytic stratified space $X$ consists of an open neighbourhood $T_R$ of each stratum $R$, a continuous retraction $\pi_R:T_R\to R$ and a continuous radius $\rho_R:T_R\to[0,\infty)$ such that $\rho_R^{-1}(0)=R$, both maps are smooth on each stratum, and for every incident upper stratum $S$ the pair $(\pi_R,\rho_R)$ restricts to a submersion $S\cap T_R\to R\times(0,\infty)$. On the overlap neighbourhoods where the compositions are defined one requires $\pi_R\pi_S=\pi_R$ and $\rho_R\pi_S=\rho_R$ for $R<S$; every compatibility assertion must name the common domain on which the composition is defined. Tubes may be shrunk. For local conical constructions one requires local properness over compact base slices: sufficiently small closed radius ranges over a compact neighbourhood in $R$ have compact inverse image inside the tube. (c) **$f$-compatible tubes and controlled lifts.** Let $f:W\to B$ be a stratified submersion onto a smooth manifold. A tube system is **$f$-compatible** if $f\pi_R=f$ on the tubes used. A **controlled lift** of a smooth base field $v$ on $B$ is a field $V$ that is smooth on each stratum and satisfies $df(V)=v\circ f$, $d\pi_R(V)=V|_R\circ\pi_R$ and $d\rho_R(V)=0$ on specified controlled tube neighbourhoods. **Locally bounded** means the ambient norm is bounded on a neighbourhood of every point; this is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of the definition. **Radial controlled lifts** instead satisfy $d\rho_R(V)=\rho_R$ with fixed $\pi_R$ together with the appropriate annular overlap controls. (d) **Conical product neighbourhoods.** A **conical product neighbourhood along $R$** is a stratum-preserving homeomorphism from a neighbourhood of a point of $R$ to $B^{2\dim_{\mathbb C}R}\times c(L)$ carrying $R$ to the ball times the cone apex, with compact finitely Whitney-stratified $L$. The radial and tangential transports must be compatible with the actual coefficient data when cohomological local systems are deduced; topological existence alone does not supply canonical derived-sheaf transport. (e) **Finite triangulation of a noncompact space.** In the compactification convention used here, a **finite triangulation** of a noncompact space $X$ consists of finite simplicial complexes $D\subseteq K$ together with a homeomorphism $|K|\setminus|D|\to X$; compatibility with prescribed subsets means they are unions of interiors of retained simplices. This does not assert that algebraic morphisms become simplicial, and real simplicial dimensions do not replace the complex dimensions of the algebraic strata.

derivations.claim: Induct on stratum dimension, retaining the already constructed tube maps on outer collars while shrinking their final tube domains. Give each tube map $E_R(r,v)$ the displacement bound $\|E_R(r,v)-r\|<\operatorname{dist}(r,\overline R\setminus R)/3$ when the frontier is nonempty, and cap displacement and radius by one; these are positive local bounds on the locally closed $R$ and can be enforced by [F2] and [F3]. Consequently a convergent sequence of tube points whose base points tend to the frontier has the same frontier limit, since the displacement tends to zero. In particular, the smaller closed-radius band of a tube, intersected with a stratum different from it, has relative closure inside the retained outer tube: if the base limit lies in $R$ this follows from the strict radius inequality and continuity, and if it lies on the frontier then the point limit would lie in a strictly lower-dimensional stratum, which is impossible.

Make the tubes of incomparable strata disjoint. Their ambient closures miss the other stratum by the frontier axiom $\overline R=\coprod_{Q\le R}Q$. Impose on a tube based at $r\in R$ the displacement bound $\operatorname{dist}(r,\overline S)/3$ and the symmetric bound for a tube based at $s\in S$. If a point $x$ lay in both tubes, then $\|r-s\|\le\|x-r\|+\|x-s\|<(\operatorname{dist}(r,\overline S)+\operatorname{dist}(s,\overline R))/3\le2\|r-s\|/3$, a contradiction. There are finitely many pairs, and shrinking retains every previously established identity and submersion property. Hence the active lower-stratum controllers at any point of a stratum form a chain.

Suppose all tubes of lower-dimensional strata are constructed, and consider a new stratum $S$. Inside the currently retained tube of each $R<S$ choose three variable squared-radius bands with bounds $\epsilon_R>\epsilon_R/2>\epsilon_R/4$, the outer bound smaller than the actual parameter radius squared. Let $C_R$ be the closure in $S$ of the middle band intersected with $S$; by step 1.1 it is relatively closed in $S$, contained in the outer tube, and the ambient closure $A_R$ of the inner band satisfies $A_R\cap S\subseteq\operatorname{int}_S C_R$. The map $F_R=(\pi_R,\rho_R)$ is submersive on $S$ by the induction hypothesis. On an overlap with $R<T<S$ the old identities give $F_R=F_R|_T\circ F_T$ wherever the compositions are defined, so every active lower controller factors through the maximal active one, and by step 2.1 the simultaneously active indices are totally ordered. Thus the chain hypothesis of [F2] holds. If the root map $f$ is present, treat it as an everywhere active controller: on lower tubes $f=f|_R\circ\pi_R$, and it is submersive on $S$ where no lower controller is active.

Apply [F2] to the manifold $S$, the finitely many controllers $F_R$ with constraint sets $C_R$ (and $f$ if present), obtaining $E_S$ and $\pi_S$ that preserve $F_R$ whenever the base point lies in $C_R$, and preserve $f$ in the root case. Arrange that every point of the new tube lying in an inner $R$-band has its $S$-base in $C_R$: choose by [F3] a smooth nonnegative $\psi_R$ supported in $\operatorname{int}_S C_R$ and positive on the relatively closed $A_R\cap S$, put $b_R(s)=\operatorname{dist}(s,A_R)+\psi_R(s)>0$, and impose $\|E_S(s,v)-s\|<b_R(s)/2$ for every $R$ using the size-bound clause of [F2]. If $s\notin C_R$ and $E_S(s,v)\in A_R$, then $\psi_R(s)=0$ and $\operatorname{dist}(s,A_R)\le\|E_S(s,v)-s\|<\operatorname{dist}(s,A_R)/2$, a contradiction; so $s\in C_R$ and $F_R(E_S(s,v))=F_R(s)$. Both the radius and its base-dependent bound depend only on $F_R$, so membership in the inner $R$-band is also preserved under $\pi_S$. Restricting every old final tube to its inner band keeps the compositions defined on the actual intersections and keeps $\pi_R\pi_S=\pi_R$ and $\rho_R\pi_S=\rho_R$ there.

Set $\rho_S(E_S(s,v))=\|v\|^2$ in the Euclidean quotient-bundle norm; its zero set is $S$. This map need not be the ordinary nearest-point tube, but it is related to one by a smooth ambient diffeomorphism: identify the quotient bundle with the orthogonal normal bundle, let $E_0$ be ordinary normal addition shrunk into its diffeomorphism domain, and put $\Phi=E_0E_S^{-1}$, which fixes $S$, carries $\pi_S$ to the ordinary tube projection and $\rho_S$ to squared normal distance. Whitney (a),(b) are preserved by the ambient diffeomorphism: derivatives transform tangent limits, and the integral mean-value formula gives $\Phi(x_j)-\Phi(y_j)=D\Phi(y)(x_j-y_j)+o(\|x_j-y_j\|)$ for sequences tending to $y$, so secant limits transform by the same invertible differential. Applying [F1] to the transformed incident upper strata and shrinking the new tube makes $(\pi_S,\rho_S)$ submersive on every incident upper stratum, since squaring the positive radius does not change the rank; no prior control identity is lost.

This completes the finite induction over strata. At each stage one may again impose the incomparable-displacement bounds of step 2.1 on the new tube and shrink the finitely many old tubes accordingly; the proved identities are retained, and the smaller old radius bands are preserved because their $F_R$-values are. Every shrink leaves a positive radius at every base point, so each final tube is a neighbourhood of its stratum. For local properness fix a compact base slice in a sufficiently small neighbourhood where $W$ is closed in the ambient open set; such a neighbourhood exists because $W$ is locally closed. A sufficiently small uniform closed fiber-radius ball over that slice is compact inside the tube parameter domain and this ambient open set. Its image under the tube embedding is compact, and its intersection with the relatively closed $W$ is compact. This intersection is exactly the closed-radius inverse image in the stratified tube, proving local properness. All imposed size bounds are continuous positive functions, or admit local positive lower bounds before choosing their smooth minorants. The optional root-controller construction yields $f\pi_S=f$ throughout each final tube. Thus the stated compatible tube control data exist; continuous stratified flows are not supplied by this construction.

control data $(T_S,\pi_S,\rho_S)$, with $\rho_S$ a squared bundle radius, such

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

These are locally positive restrictions because $R$ is locally closed; [F3] supplies smooth positive radius minorants, chosen below half the original radius. Shrinking preserves $f\pi_R=f$ and the control identities: a smaller radius bound depends only on the base and is preserved by every higher projection preserving $(\pi_R,\rho_R)$. Construct the lift in increasing stratum dimension. On a stratum $R$ with no active lower tube, the adjoint right inverse of $df|_{TR}$ gives a smooth lift of $v$. Suppose lifts $V_R$ are fixed on all lower-dimensional strata and are controlled and locally bounded there. On an upper stratum $S$ inside a lower tube, use the smooth minimum-norm right inverse of $(d\pi_R,dr_R)|_{TS}$, where $r_R=\sqrt{\rho_R}>0$, to lift $(V_R(\pi_Rx),0)$; it lifts $v$ because $f\pi_R=f$. These minimum-norm lifts are bounded by $\|V_R(\pi_Rx)\|+1$ after shrinking the $R$-tube. Near $y\in R$, a contrary sequence of unit-normalized violations has a limiting upper tangent plane containing $T_yR$ and the limiting normal secant direction in it, by Whitney (a),(b); the normalized pair differential stays surjective by [F2]. Its limiting linear equation with target $(V_R(y),0)$ has $V_R(y)$ itself as a solution, so its minimum-norm solution has norm at most $\|V_R(y)\|$, and continuity of the minimum-norm matrix inverse on these surjective limit matrices contradicts the violation. The same argument holds in an adapted tube using its smooth normal-model diffeomorphism or its transverse quotient splitting. Finitely many incident strata give one positive local bound, and [F3] chooses a variable tube radius imposing it at every base point.

For patching on $S$ use middle bands with radius bound half that of each outer lower tube, and strictly smaller inner bands. Their relative closures in $S$ stay in the outer domains: for convergent band points, step 1.1 bounds the bases; a frontier base limit would equal the point limit and lie below the controller stratum, hence cannot lie in $S$, while a base limit in the controller stratum leaves the limiting normal parameter strictly inside the outer domain. Thus the middle bands are relatively closed in $S$. At a point the active middle-band indices form a chain; take a neighbourhood avoiding every closed middle band not active at its centre and lying in the domains of all active controllers, choose there the lift through the maximal active controller, and use the lift of $df$ where none is active. A subordinate smooth partition from [F3] gives a convex sum of these fields. At every point of an inner $R$-band all contributing patches carry the $R$-constraint, so the sum satisfies $d\pi_R(V_S)=V_R\circ\pi_R$ and $d\rho_R(V_S)=0$ there, and it satisfies $df(V_S)=v\circ f$ everywhere. Shrink each actual control domain into the inner band; no derivative of a partition coefficient enters these linear vector-field equations.

The patched fields are locally bounded across lower strata. In each patch controlled by $T$ the norms are bounded by $\|V_T(\pi_Tx)\|+1$ from step 2.1. For any sequence of tube points converging in $W$, the displacement cap of step 1.1 makes their bases bounded. Pass to a convergent base subsequence in $\overline T$. If its limit belongs to $T$, smoothness bounds $V_T$ there; if it belongs to $\partial T$, step 1.1 forces the displacement to tend to zero, so that base limit is the original point limit in $W$, where $V_T$ is locally bounded by induction. An unbounded sequence of lift norms would therefore have a bounded subsequence, a contradiction. Only finitely many lower strata occur, so the finite maximum bounds all contributing lifts. Away from their tubes the ordinary smooth lifts are locally bounded, and a sequence tending to a lower stratum is eventually in its inner tube, so uncontrolled patches do not contribute there. Convex sums retain these bounds, finishing the finite dimension induction of locally bounded controlled lifts.

Solve the ODE within each stratum using [F4]. In a small relatively compact ambient ball where $W$ is closed and the constructed field has bound $M$, solutions starting in a smaller ball cannot leave the larger ball before a fixed positive time, by $\|x(t)-x(0)\|\le M|t|$. If a maximal solution had a shorter finite endpoint, this bound makes it Cauchy with a limit in the compact closed piece of $W$. A limit in the same stratum permits ordinary ODE continuation. A limit in a smaller incident stratum $R$ is impossible: on a terminal segment inside its controlled tube $\rho_R$ is constant and positive, but continuity at the limit in $R$ forces it to tend to zero. The argument works backward in time as well, so a common short flow interval exists for all nearby initial points, including points in different strata.

Take locally bounded controlled lifts of each coordinate field on a base box; their flows exist on a common source neighbourhood by step 5.1. Starting in the centre fibre, flow successively for the coordinate increments; each flow changes only its own base coordinate, and reversing the flows in reverse order supplies a continuous inverse. Restricting the centre fibre to a relatively open neighbourhood of the point and choosing a sufficiently small box and flow domain, the image is open: the inverse-coordinate conditions are an open base-box condition together with an open condition on the continuous return-to-centre-fibre map. The result is a stratum-preserving product neighbourhood over the box; commutation of the different lifts is unnecessary.

If $f$ is proper, cut off the base coordinate fields outside a slightly larger coordinate box. Over every finite time interval a base path has compact image, whose full proper inverse image is compact; the lift is bounded on that compact inverse image by step 4.1, so the endpoint and constant-radius arguments of step 5.1 give complete lifted flows for these base paths. The coordinate-flow construction of step 7.1 therefore applies at every point of the whole centre fibre and produces a bundle trivialization of the full inverse image of the smaller box. All constructions are smooth on each stratum and jointly continuous on $W$.

derivations.claim: Work in an affine ambient chart about $y$ and shrink it so that $X$ is closed there. Only finitely many strata have closures not containing $y$; discard a small neighbourhood meeting none of those closures, so that only $R$ and its incident upper strata remain and $R$ is the lowest local stratum. Choose the ordinary normal tube of $R$ with projection $\pi$ and distance $r$, and a relatively compact coordinate ball $B\subseteq R$ about $y$. By [F4], after shrinking over a slightly larger compact base ball, $(\pi,r)$, and hence $(\pi,r^2)$, is submersive on all remaining upper strata for $0<r<\epsilon$.

Put $W^\circ=X\cap\pi^{-1}(B)\cap\{0<r<\epsilon\}$ and $g=(\pi,r):W^\circ\to B\times(0,\epsilon)$. This is a locally closed Whitney-stratified subset of the punctured ambient ordinary tube, and $g$ extends smoothly there and is submersive on all its strata by step 1.1. Apply the optional submersion-preserving clause of [F2] directly to $(W^\circ,g)$: its upper-stratum tubes satisfy $g\pi_S=g$, hence preserve the already chosen ordinary $\pi$ and $r$. Together with the lowest triple $(T_R,\pi,r^2)$, these give compatible local data on the retained overlaps; only the upper tubes have been constructed, and the lowest maps have not been replaced. The map $g$ is proper: a compact target subset lies over a compact base subset and a closed radial interval bounded away from zero and $\epsilon$, and its inverse image is a closed subset of a compact normal disk-bundle slice inside the chart where $X$ is closed. Fix $0<r_0<\epsilon/3$; the reference fibre $L_y=g^{-1}(y,r_0)$ is compact, being the intersection of $X$ with the affine normal space $y+N_yR$ and the radius-$r_0$ sphere. It is real semialgebraic: in this affine chart $X$ and its algebraic strata are described by finitely many real polynomial equalities and inequalities, and the normal plane and sphere have linear and quadratic equations.

By [F3] lift coordinate fields on $B$ preserving the radial coordinate; their flows trivialize the whole reference-radius link family over a smaller base box, identifying $g^{-1}(B\times\{r_0\})$ with $B\times L_y$. Separately lift the radial base field $r\partial_r$, cut off only near the upper radial endpoint so that it equals $r\partial_r$ for $r\le r_0$; properness of $g$ supplies all lifted finite-time transports between any two positive radii in $(0,r_0]$, with time $\log(r/r_0)$ and inverse of opposite time. These flows keep $\pi$ fixed, so combining horizontal reference-radius transport with radial transport gives a stratum-preserving homeomorphism $B\times L_y\times(0,r_0)\to X\cap\pi^{-1}(B)\cap\{0<r<r_0\}$ with continuous inverse. Commutation between different chosen lifts is unnecessary because the flows are applied and reversed in a fixed order.

Extend the map of step 3.1 over cone apex points by sending $(b,\mathrm{apex})$ to $b\in R$. The distance from a transported point to its base point is exactly its ordinary normal radius $r$, so convergence to the apex is uniform over the compact link and compact base subboxes independently of the speed of the radial field; conversely, $x_j\to b\in R$ gives $\pi(x_j)\to b$ and $r(x_j)\to0$, and compactness of $L_y$ means the radial parameters converge to the apex in its quotient cone topology regardless of the link direction. Hence both the extended map and its inverse are continuous, and the image $U_y=X\cap\pi^{-1}(B)\cap\{r<r_0\}$ is open in $X$. Rescaling $r$ identifies its radial interval with $[0,1)$, yielding the displayed ball times cone; if there are no upper strata the link is empty and its cone is the single apex.

The link strata are the intersections of the upper strata with the normal plane and sphere, and they are smooth by submersivity of $g$. They satisfy the frontier and Whitney conditions. For the frontier assertion, [F3] gives a source-local product for $g$ at each lower fibre point, so taking a stratum closure commutes locally with taking that fixed fibre, and the original frontier relations restrict with the same dimension drop in each stratum. For the Whitney assertion, if limiting upper tangent planes are $T$ and $K=\ker dg$ is the common fibre kernel, Whitney (a) includes the lower tangent plane in $T$, on which $dg$ is still onto, so the fibre tangent planes converge to $T\cap K$ with the expected dimension; fibre secants lie in $K$ in the limit by the first-order Taylor formula for constant $g$-values, and they lie in $T$ by Whitney (b), so they lie in $T\cap K$. This proves both conditions on the fibre, and the horizontal transport of step 3.1 identifies these finite link strata over every nearby base point, establishing local constancy of stratified homeomorphism type along $R$.

The tube-data assertion follows from [F2] in ambient charts; for quasi-projective spaces one may use a smooth Euclidean ambient embedding of projective space by the rank-one Hermitian projector $[z]\mapsto zz^*/\|z\|^2$, whose chart inverses are coordinate ratios, and apply the same smooth construction. For an algebraic morphism over a target stratum coordinate box the smooth ambient-extension hypothesis of [F3] is supplied explicitly: regular coordinate functions of the algebraic map extend in source affine embedding charts as polynomial or localized polynomial functions, and target-stratum smooth coordinate functions extend to a target ambient neighbourhood using an ordinary tube retraction; their composites give local smooth coordinate extensions of the restricted map. Patch these Euclidean coordinate functions with [F5] on a source ambient neighbourhood; on the stratified space they all equal the original map, so their convex sum equals it and has the same tangential derivatives, and shrinking the ambient neighbourhood keeps its values in the chosen base box. Thus it is a smooth ambient extension submersive on every source stratum, and the proper whole-fibre and local source-product assertions follow from [F3] applied to these actual extensions. The complex stratum $R$ has real dimension $2\dim_{\mathbb C}R$, so the product factor has the claimed dimension, and real link or simplex dimensions do not replace it. All constructions are local or use the stated actual analytic properness.
