To check their relative closures in a higher stratum $Z$, take band points $p_j\to p\in Z$. Their bases $x_j$ are bounded by the displacement cap, so a subsequence converges in compact $\overline X$. A frontier base limit would force $p_j-x_j\to0$, putting $p$ in a stratum below $X$, contrary to $Z>X$. A base limit in $X$ gives a convergent normal-parameter subsequence with $\|v\|^2/b_X(x)^2\le1/2$, hence a limit inside the outer tube. Thus the bands have relative closure there, and shrinking preserves disjointness of incomparable tubes.

Fix $X$. On $W\cap T_X\setminus X$ the map $g_X=(\pi_X,\rho_X)$ is submersive on each stratum. Construct a field lifting the target field $(0,r)$ in increasing dimension of incident strata: on a minimal stratum use a smooth right inverse of $dg_X$ given by the adjoint minimum-norm matrix inverse; on a higher stratum inside a lower incident $Z$-tube lift $(V_Z\pi_Z,0)$ through $(d\pi_Z,d\rho_Z)$, which also lifts $(0,r)$ because $g_X\pi_Z=g_X$. The active middle-band controllers at any point form a chain by [F1], and the maximal one implies all lower constraints by differentiating the control factorizations. Patches avoiding inactive closed middle bands and lying inside the active outer domains, combined with a smooth subordinate partition (whose derivatives do not enter, since the equations in the field are linear), give a smooth field $V_X$ with $dg_XV_X=(0,\rho_X)$ and with $d\pi_ZV_X=V_Z\pi_Z$, $d\rho_ZV_X=0$ in every inner $Z$-band. Doing this for the finitely many $X$ with the same constant bands, then retaining only inner tubes and multiplying all radii by four, restores $\rho_Z<1$ on every retained tube by a constant rescaling that preserves all equations. For $Y<X$ the field also preserves $\pi_Y$ and $\rho_Y$ wherever defined, because both factor through $\pi_X$ and $d\pi_XV_X=0$.

Establish compact trapping for these fields, without assuming ambient boundedness on open strata, by induction on stratum dimension. Near a point $q$ of a lower stratum $Z$ choose a compact base slice $C\subseteq Z$ containing its trajectory for a common short time, and a closed small radius band whose inverse image $K$ is compact and lies inside the retained tube. For initial upper points close enough to $q$ the projected trajectory follows the smooth $Z$-flow and its radius stays constant, so while the upper ODE exists it remains in the interior of $K$: a first exit would have a compact limit with base in the interior of $C$ and radius strictly below the outer boundary, a contradiction. If an upper trajectory had a finite maximal endpoint within the common interval, compactness gives a cluster point; a cluster point in its own stratum allows ordinary ODE extension because the smooth field is bounded on a relatively compact coordinate ball and a sufficiently late visit cannot leave during the remaining short time, making the path Cauchy; a cluster point $q'$ in a lower stratum $Z'$ admits the same base-flow trap on a short interval covering the remaining time, and a sufficiently late visit to that trap cannot leave it, with $\rho_{Z'}$ a fixed positive value on the terminal segment, contradicting that the visits converge to $q'$ and force that value to zero; only incident lower strata can be cluster strata by the frontier condition. This gives a common short flow interval near each lower point, and the same argument backward gives inverse flows. Joint continuity follows from the compact tube slice estimate that the distance to the projection tends uniformly to zero as the radius tends to zero together with continuity of the projected lower flow, so incident-stratum sequences approaching a lower initial point have the correct flow limit; finite stratification and time subdivision complete the induction.

Obtain the initial radial family by flowing the field $V_X$ for time $\log(s/\rho_X(p))$, since $\dot\rho_X=\rho_X$ and $\dot\pi_X=0$; this time is finite (negative, zero or positive) for positive source and target levels inside the retained domain, and existence over the fixed base $\pi_X(p)$ with radii in a closed positive interval follows because the full inverse image in compact $W$ is compact in normal-bundle coordinates, so step 3.1's endpoint argument applies. Ordinary uniqueness gives the semigroup identity and inverse transport between levels; the control equations give preservation of every other incident radius and projection, and of the higher-projection equivariance. A trajectory starting in a retained higher tube cannot leave it during a finite radial transport, because its normalized radius there is constant and a first exit is excluded by local properness over the compact projected trajectory; the same holds for transport in a lower tube across a higher tube. Consequently all transports used below stay in their actual normalized tube domains, which is the purpose of step 1.1's normalization.

Construct the final families in increasing dimension of $X$. Suppose the lower families are fixed and modify the current $X$-family by a decreasing induction on $Y<X$. For the currently processed $Y$ retain a small outer $Y$-band $0<\rho_Y<c$ lying inside all previously needed $Y$-commutation domains, possible with a positive constant by the finitely many earlier corrections, and put $a=c/2$. Writing $F^Y_{u\to v}$ for transport along the fixed $Y$-family between radius levels, choose a smooth $\phi$ with $\phi(t)=a$ for $t\le a$, $\phi(t)=t$ for $t\ge2c/3$, and $a\le\phi(t)<c$ for $0<t<c$. For a point $p$ with $t=\rho_Y(p)<c$ replace the current $X$-family by $\widetilde R_X(s)(p)=F^Y_{\phi(t)\to t}R_X(s)F^Y_{t\to\phi(t)}(p)$; all terms are defined by step 4.1, the intermediate $X$-operation preserves the $Y$-radius, the modification is conjugation on each fixed $Y$-slice and equals the old family near the outer boundary where $\phi(t)=t$, so it patches continuously and stratumwise smoothly with the old family outside the $Y$-band.

The correction preserves the $X$-semigroup law because both $X$-operations preserve $t$ and the middle $Y$-transports cancel; it preserves $\rho_X\widetilde R_X(s)=s$ because the $Y$-transports preserve $\rho_X$; it preserves $\pi_X$ because higher-projection equivariance of the $Y$-transports moves the $X$-base forward and back around an $X$-operation that fixes its base. For any other incident radius $\rho_Z$ each $Y$-transport preserves it and the middle $X$-operation preserves it, while for $Z=Y$ the two transports cancel its change. Lower-projection preservation and higher-projection equivariance survive by the same composition calculation: a $Y$-transport that moves such a projection has its equivariance move it forward and back around an $X$-operation fixing it, or produces the identical corrected operation on the projected higher stratum. Hence all domain statements and actual controls of step 4.1 remain true after the correction.

For $t<a$ the correction transports to the common reference level $a$, performs the same $X$-operation there and transports back, so in $Y$-coordinates $(q,t)=(R_Y(a)p,\rho_Y(p))$ it has the form $(q,t)\mapsto(A_s(q),t)$ independent of $t$; it therefore commutes with every $Y$-transport whose source and target lie in this inner band. Shrink the final $Y$-commutation domain to $t<a$ (retaining the outer maps for the next correction, and rescaling by the constant $a$ if desired). For a previously treated $Z$ with $Y<Z<X$ the $Z$-family commutes with the $Y$-transports by the fixed lower-family construction, preserves $t$, and commutes with the current $X$-family by the inner induction, so moving it through the three factors of step 5.1 shows it commutes with the corrected $X$-family. Incomparable strata have disjoint tubes and equal-dimensional strata are incomparable, so all previously imposed commutations survive; the finite nested induction terminates with every incident pair commuting, and all further rescalings are by constants that preserve radius equalities and controls.

Fix a retained normalized reference $a$. The inverse of $p\mapsto(R_X(a)p,\rho_X(p))$ is $(q,t)\mapsto R_X(t)q$, by the semigroup law and the invertible level transport of step 4.1; both maps are continuous and smooth on each incident stratum. Adjoining the zero end by $(q,0)\mapsto\pi_X(q)$ is continuous: locally on compact base slices the parameter-vector norm is $b_X(\pi_X(p))\sqrt{\rho_X(p)}$, the smooth tube embedding has bounded fibre derivative on a smaller compact parameter slice, so the physical displacement is at most a fixed constant times this norm, and transport to radius zero converges uniformly to the base projection; the same estimate gives inverse continuity at the adjoined stratum, and compactness of each closed link fibre supplies the uniform quotient neighbourhoods. This yields the claimed open mapping-cylinder model and completes all assertions.

risk_review.notes: Complete eight-step review: normalized squared-radius control is preserved by base-dependent scaling. Linear lifts are constructed on chain overlaps; compact traps and constant lower radii prevent finite-time escape into a lower stratum and give continuous stratified flows without assuming ambient smoothness. At fixed base, every compact positive radial interval lies in a compact tube slice. Conjugation by previously fixed lower radial transports yields common-reference-level independence and commuting collars, preserves all other radii and projection equivariance, and patches where phi(t)=t. Finite nested induction preserves earlier commutations. The mapping-cylinder inverse is level transport; zero-end continuity follows uniform tube-displacement estimates on compact base slices and compact link fibres. Compact W is closed, so it meets the repaired control-data hypothesis. No semialgebraic or globally ambient-smooth flow is claimed; AC is inherited through partitions/tubes.

citations.quote: Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex. Its **geometric realization** $|K|$ is the set of functions $\alpha:V \to [0,1]$ such that: 1. $\alpha(v)=0$ for all but finitely many $v \in V$; 2. $\sum_{v \in V}\alpha(v)=1$; 3. the support $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha):=\{v \in V:\alpha(v)\neq 0\}$ is a simplex of $K$. For each simplex $\sigma=\{v_0,\dots,v_n\}$ of $K$, write $$|\sigma|:=\{\alpha \in |K| : \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\subseteq \sigma\}.$$ Sending $\alpha$ to the barycentric tuple $(\alpha(v_0),\dots,\alpha(v_n))$ identifies $|\sigma|$ with the geometric simplex spanned by the standard basis vectors indexed by $v_0,\dots,v_n$, so $|\sigma|$ carries its Euclidean simplex topology. We give $|K|$ the **weak topology** with respect to these simplex inclusions: a subset $U\subseteq |K|$ is declared open exactly when $U\cap|\sigma|$ is open in $|\sigma|$ for every simplex $\sigma$ of $K$.

For finite $K$, the weak topology on $|K|$ equals the Euclidean subspace topology in $\mathbb R^{V(K)}$; $|K|$ is compact, metrizable and Hausdorff. If $P$ is a finite subcomplex of any $K$, then $|P|\hookrightarrow|K|$ is a closed embedding, with that same finite Euclidean topology.
If $K$ is a finite abstract simplicial complex, then its geometric realization $|K|$ is compact and Hausdorff.

**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on $Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$ ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]): $$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$ That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]], where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually, $C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$. **Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a **quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the quotient topology of $q$, that is when $$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$ The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$ ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause (b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$. **Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is **saturated** with respect to $q$ when $$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$ equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when $x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the **saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are saturated. **Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation** on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric ($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$ imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the **equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is $X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the **canonical projection** is $$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$ which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an **identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it is a union of equivalence classes. **A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$ let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons $\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in \{\varnothing, B\}$. **Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map *together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

Two constructions are defined here, one for maps *into* spaces and one for maps *out of* spaces. Every further construction on this page is an instance of one of them. **Initial topology.** Let $X$ be a set, let $I$ be an index set, let $(Y_i, \mathcal{T}_i)$ be a topological space for each $i \in I$ ([[def-topological-space]]), and let $f_i : X \to Y_i$ be a function for each $i$. The **initial topology** on $X$ induced by the family $(f_i)_{i \in I}$ is $$\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{in}} \;:=\; \big\langle\, \{\, f_i^{-1}[V] : i \in I,\ V \in \mathcal{T}_i \,\} \,\big\rangle ,$$ the topology generated by the preimages of the open sets of the $Y_i$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]). *This is well posed, and the obligation is discharged by the item cited.* For an arbitrary family $\mathcal{S}$ of subsets of $X$, the family $\langle \mathcal{S} \rangle$ is a topology on $X$, contains $\mathcal{S}$, and is contained in every topology on $X$ containing $\mathcal{S}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]); no further verification is needed here. By [[thm-basis-criterion]] a **basis** for $\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{in}}$ is the family of intersections of finitely many sets $f_i^{-1}[V]$, the intersection of none being $X$. **Final topology.** Let $X$ be a set, let $(Z_i, \mathcal{S}_i)$ be a topological space for each $i \in I$, and let $g_i : Z_i \to X$ be a function for each $i$. The **final topology** on $X$ induced by the family $(g_i)_{i \in I}$ is $$\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{fin}} \;:=\; \{\, U \subseteq X : g_i^{-1}[U] \in \mathcal{S}_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\} .$$ *This is a topology, and the verification is carried out here rather than assumed.* Preimage commutes with the three set operations named in the axioms: $g_i^{-1}[\varnothing] = \varnothing$ and $g_i^{-1}[X] = Z_i$, which gives (T1); $g_i^{-1}[\bigcup \mathcal{U}] = \bigcup \{\, g_i^{-1}[U] : U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$ for every family $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{fin}}$, which with (T2) in $Z_i$ gives (T2); and $g_i^{-1}[U \cap V] = g_i^{-1}[U] \cap g_i^{-1}[V]$, which with (T3) in $Z_i$ gives (T3) ([[def-topological-space]]). **Two degenerate cases, stated because they are used.** For $I = \varnothing$ the initial topology is $\langle \varnothing \rangle = \{\varnothing, X\}$, the indiscrete topology, and the final topology is $\mathcal{P}(X)$, the discrete topology, the defining condition being vacuous ([[def-standard-topologies]], [[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]). For a family consisting of a single map the definitions read the same way with the index dropped. **The subspace topology is the model initial topology.** Let $(X,\mathcal{T})$ be a space, let $S \subseteq X$ and let $\iota : S \to X$ be the inclusion. Then $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$, so the generating family for the initial topology of the one-element family $(\iota)$ is exactly $\mathcal{T}_S = \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\}$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). That family is already a topology, so generating adds nothing and the initial topology of $\iota$ **is** the subspace topology. Everything [[def-subspace-topology-top]] proves about it is therefore quoted here and not reproved: its closed sets are the traces of the closed sets, a basis of $X$ traces to a basis of $S$, the inclusion is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]), $\mathcal{T}_S$ is the coarsest topology making $\iota$ continuous, and a map $g : Z \to S$ is continuous if and only if $\iota \circ g$ is. **Terminology.** A family $(f_i)$ as above is the *defining family* of the initial topology, and likewise for the final one; both topologies depend on the whole family and not on any one member. The characteristic properties that make these two constructions worth naming are the subject of the next item.

Let $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ be topological spaces, with subspaces carrying the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Then: 1. **Composites.** If $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Y \to Z$ are continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) then $g \circ f : X \to Z$ is continuous. 2. **Open cover.** Let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $\{\, U_i : i \in I \,\}$ be a family of open subsets of $X$ with $\bigcup_{i \in I} U_i = X$. If $f|_{U_i} : U_i \to Y$ is continuous for every $i \in I$, then $f$ is continuous. 3. **Finite closed cover.** Let $f : X \to Y$ be a function, let $n \ge 1$ and let $F_1, \dots, F_n$ be closed subsets of $X$ with $F_1 \cup \dots \cup F_n = X$. If $f|_{F_k} : F_k \to Y$ is continuous for every $k$, then $f$ is continuous. The converses of claims 2 and 3 hold with no hypothesis on the cover at all: every restriction of a continuous map to a subspace is continuous ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). The finiteness in claim 3 is not removable; see the remarks.

Let $f,g:X\to\mathbb R$ be continuous maps from a topological space. Then $f+g$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max(f,g)$, and $\min(f,g)$ are continuous. On the open cozero set $\operatorname{coz}(g)$, the quotient $f/g$ is continuous. The same holds for every finite sum, product, maximum, or minimum of continuous real-valued maps.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces ([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$. Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]]. $f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$. $f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$. **The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open $U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of $f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$, which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the same statement written twice. **Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$ is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later item, which are different notions.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let $S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is $$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$ the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair $(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in $\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the ambient space needs emphasis. **$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1): $\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if $\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of $\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since $U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying $U' \cap S = W$ — and then $\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in $X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T3) in $X$. **Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set $C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed $F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and $S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$ matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing. **Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for $\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then $\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for $\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$ and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence $x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$ shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for $\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with unions. **The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$, $\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$, so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous ([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover $\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$. **Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then $$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$ *Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has $(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous; conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous. Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]. **Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and $S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since $(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$ ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]). **When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$ is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$ contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

derivations.claim: Write $x_v$ for the barycentric coordinates of a point of $|K|$ and put $f_i(x)=\sum_{f(v)=i}x_v$, so that $f(x)=(f_i(x))_i$ is a convex combination. In every simplex of $K$ cut by the finitely many hyperplanes $f_i=f_j$ and take the resulting closed convex cells and all their faces; the same arrangement intersected with a simplex gives intersections as faces, so these cells form a finite polytopal subdivision of $K$. For a cell $C$ let $I(C)$ be the set of vertices $i$ such that $f_i$ is maximal on $C$; it is nonempty, and $I(C)\subseteq I(C')$ whenever $C'$ is a face of $C$. For every $i\in I(C)$ the image of $C$ under $f$ lies in the star of $i$, and the set $I(C)$ spans a simplex of $L$ contained in the image simplex. For every nonempty simplex $A$ on vertices in $I(C)$ include the join cell $A*C$ in the Euclidean join of $|L|$ and $|K|$, and include $|L|$ itself and every face of every such join. The join identities $(A*C)\cap(A'*C')=(A\cap A')*(C\cap C')$ and the face structure of the underlying cells make this a finite polytopal complex $T_f$ whose upper boundary is $|K|$ and whose lower boundary is $|L|$. A point of its relative interior has unique join coordinates $(1-t)y+tx$ with $0<t<1$, $y\in|L|$, $x\in|K|$, and lies in $T_f$ exactly when the support of $y$ consists of vertices where $f_i(x)$ attains its maximum.

Any finite polytopal complex $P$ is triangulated by induction on dimension: for each cell choose a point in its relative interior, having already chosen one for every proper face, and cone the already triangulated boundary from that point. Each ray from the interior point meets the boundary in exactly one point, the cones over cells have disjoint relative interiors and meet along the cones over their intersections, and the constructions agree on common faces, so this is a finite simplicial complex with the same underlying subset and the same dimension. Applied to the finite list of cells of $T_f$ (and to any finite sublist, coning subcomplexes first) it also respects unions of cells. Its dimension is at most $\max(\dim K+1,\dim L)$: if $C$ lies in a source simplex $\sigma$ with image simplex $\tau$, then $f|_\sigma$ is the affine surjection onto $\tau$, and the $k-1$ equations $f_i=f_j$ with $i,j\in I(C)$ (where $k=|I(C)|$) are independent on $\tau$; hence $\dim C\le\dim\sigma-(k-1)$ and $\dim(A*C)=k+\dim C\le\dim\sigma+1$ for every join cell, while the remaining lower cells have dimension at most $\dim L$. For each pair $(K_j,L_j)$ the cells with $C\subseteq|K_j|$ and $A\subseteq|L_j|$, together with $|L_j|$, form a subcomplex: faces of such cells again satisfy those inclusions, because $K_j$ and $L_j$ are subcomplexes and $f(K_j)\subseteq L_j$. The top preimage $f^{-1}(|L_j|)$ is a union of source faces, since $f$ is simplicial, hence a union of cells of the subdivision. One further barycentric subdivision makes all these subcomplexes full: its vertices are cells, and a chain all of whose vertices lie in a selected subcomplex is a chain of cells of that subcomplex.

For $x\in C$ and $i\in I(C)$ put $P_i(x)_v=x_v/f_i(x)$ when $f(v)=i$ and $P_i(x)_v=0$ otherwise. Since $f(x)$ is a point of the simplex $\tau\subseteq L$, some coordinate $f_i(x)$ is at least $1/N$ with $N$ the number of vertices of $L$, so the denominators are bounded below on every cell and $P_i$ is continuous on $C$ with values in the face of the source simplex over $i$. Define $H$ on the join cell $A*C$ by $H((1-t)y+tx)=[u,t]$, where $u=t\,x+(1-t)\sum_{i\in A}y_iP_i(x)$ and the bracket denotes the class in $M_f$ of the point $(u,t)\in|K|\times[0,1]$. The vector $u$ is a convex combination of points of the source simplex, so it lies in $|K|$, and $f(u)=t\,f(x)+(1-t)y$. For $0<t<1$ the join coordinates of a point are unique, and on intersections $A*C\cap A'*C'$ the representation has $y\in A\cap A'$, $x\in C\cap C'$, so the values agree; at $t=1$ the value is $[x,1]$ and at $t=0$ it is $[u,0]=f(u)=y$, the lower point itself, so the formula is well defined and fixes both boundary copies. It is continuous on each closed cell, because the $P_i$ are continuous and the map $(u,t)\mapsto[u,t]$ is the composite of a continuous map with the quotient projection; by the finite closed-cover form of [F2] it is continuous on all of $T_f$.

Define a map $\Psi$ on $|K|\times[0,1]\sqcup|L|$ as follows: $\Psi$ is the identity on $|L|$; for $u\in|K|$ and $0<t<1$ put $z=f(u)$ and let $m=m(u,t)>0$ be the unique number with $\sum_i\min(z_i,m)=t$ (unique because the left side is continuous, vanishes at $m=0$, is strictly increasing while below $\sum_iz_i=1$, and $t<1$), and set $v_i=\min(z_i,m)/t$ for $t>0$, $y_i=(z_i-m)_+/(1-t)$, and $x_w=(v_{f(w)}/z_{f(w)})u_w$ when $z_{f(w)}>0$ and $x_w=0$ otherwise; at $t=0$ define $\Psi(u,0)=f(u)$ directly, and at $t=1$ define $\Psi(u,1)=u$ on the upper copy. Then $z=t\,v+(1-t)y$ with $v,y$ probability vectors, $f(x)=v$, and $x$ lies in every source simplex containing $u$; moreover $x_w=u_w/t$ when $z_{f(w)}\le m$ and $x_w=m\,u_w/(t\,z_{f(w)})$ when $z_{f(w)}\ge m$, so the formulas are continuous on their finitely many closed regions with denominators bounded below by $t/N$ on each collar $t\ge t_0>0$ and extend continuously to $t=0$ with value $y=f(u)$ and to $t=1$ with value $x=u$. Hence $\Psi$ is continuous and satisfies $\Psi(u,0)=f(u)=\Psi(f(u))$, so it respects the equivalence relation and descends to a continuous map $\Phi:M_f\to T_f$. The two constructions are inverse: substituting $H$'s formula into the threshold equations recovers $\sum_i\min(z_i,m)=t$ and returns the given $[u,t]$, while for a join point $(1-t)y+tx\in T_f$ and $u=t\,x+(1-t)\sum y_iP_i(x)$ one computes $z_i=t f_i(x)+(1-t)y_i\le t\max_jf_j(x)=:m$ when $y_i=0$, and $z_i=m+(1-t)y_i$ with $f_i(x)=\max_jf_j(x)$ when $y_i>0$; the threshold equation then determines $m=t\max_jf_j(x)$, and the normalized coordinates of $u$ recover $x$ and $y$ as $(t+(1-t)y_i/f_i(x))x_w=u_w$. So $H\circ\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Phi\circ H=\mathrm{id}$, and the continuous bijection $H$ is a homeomorphism with inverse $\Phi$.

The retraction $R$ of the cylinder onto $|L|$, read through $H$, is $R((1-t)y+tx)=(1-t)y+t\,f(x)$ on each join cell, an affine map that is piecewise linear after step 2.1. For a pair $(K_j,L_j)$, if $x\in|K_j|$ then each $P_i(x)$ has support in the same source simplex, hence $u\in|K_j|$. Conversely the inverse formula has $\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(u)$, so $u\in|K_j|$ implies $x\in|K_j|$; the collapsed end is precisely the chosen $|L_j|$. Thus the preimage of the mapping cylinder of $f|_{K_j}:K_j\to L_j$ is exactly the subcomplex described in step 2.1. Separately, $f^{-1}(|L_j|)$ is a source subcomplex and is retained on the top boundary, as proved in step 2.1. Finally, on each join cell with $t$ bounded away from zero the map $H$ is given by rational functions of the affine coordinates with denominators bounded away from zero, hence is smooth there in the ambient affine coordinates; nothing is asserted about differentiability at the collapsed end $t=0$, where the quotient is not a manifold chart. This proves all asserted clauses.

boundaries.evidence: The collection of pairs $(K_j,L_j)$ in the Statement may be empty, and step 5.1 attaches the corresponding subpolyhedra one at a time, so the empty list imposes no cell and no subdivision.

boundaries.reason: Step 3.1 divides only by the weights $f_i(x)$, which are bounded below by $1/N$ on each cell before the division, so no zero denominator is reached.

boundaries.evidence: A one-vertex source is the case $dim K=0$ of step 1.1: the hyperplane arrangement is trivial and the join formulas of step 4.1 triangulate the resulting cone on a point.

Vertex identifications are explicitly allowed, so collapsings are not excluded; steps 3.1 and 4.1 index cells by the fibres of $f$ and define the threshold $m$ whenever the collapsed weights are positive.
The two ends are $t=0$, where the identification $xsim f(x)$ is imposed, and $t=1$; step 4.1 defines the map separately there and verifies both inverse identities at these ends.

boundaries.reason: Neither the Statement nor the proof assumes AC; the subdivision points of step 2.1 are chosen by explicit recursion on dimension over a finite complex.
The lemma asserts the existence of a triangulation with listed properties rather than a characterization, so no implication direction is owed.
No converse is claimed: the lemma does not assert that only mapping cylinders admit such finite triangulations.

risk_review.notes: Complete review of polytopal cells, dimension, forward and inverse formulas: max-coordinate ties add k-1 independent equations, bounding join dimension by dim K+1. Threshold m is unique for interior t, has m>=t/N, and its normalized source coordinates preserve simplex support. At t=0 the join's source coefficient tends to zero and y tends to f(u); at t=1 x tends to u. Both formulas recover each other. Collapsed source vertices and constant maps are allowed. K empty leaves L alone; L empty forces K empty, so no denominator involving N is used. Every K_j cylinder and top f^{-1}(L_j) is retained by cells and simultaneous subdivision. Finite interior-point choices require no AC. No differentiability is claimed at the collapsed end.

citations.quote: Assume AC. Let $W$ be a compact finite smooth Whitney-stratified subset of a smooth Euclidean ambient space, with the frontier condition. After shrinking compatible tube data and smoothly rescaling their squared radii by positive functions of their base projections, there are normalized tubes $T_X=\{\rho_X<1\}$ and stratum-preserving radial projections $R_X(s):T_X\setminus X\to\{\rho_X=s\}$ for $0<s<1$. On every incident overlap $Y<X$ they satisfy $$R_X(s)R_Y(t)=R_Y(t)R_X(s),\qquad \rho_YR_X(s)=\rho_Y,\qquad \rho_XR_Y(t)=\rho_X,$$ whenever the source and target points lie in the indicated retained tubes. They also satisfy $\pi_XR_X(s)=\pi_X$, $R_X(s)R_X(t)=R_X(s)$, and $\pi_ZR_X(s)=R_X(s)|_Z\pi_Z$ for $X<Z$ on overlaps. They are continuous on their stratified domains and smooth on individual strata. For a fixed reference $a\in(0,1)$, $(R_X(a),\rho_X)$ identifies the punctured tube with $S_X(a)\times(0,1)$, where $S_X(a)=W\cap\{\rho_X=a\}$; adjoining $X$ identifies it with the corresponding open mapping cylinder of $\pi_X:S_X(a)\to X$. This is a controlled topological collar; no semialgebraicity of the resulting flows is asserted.

Let $f:K\to L$ be a simplicial map of finite complexes; vertex identifications
are allowed. Its topological mapping cylinder
$$M_f=(|K|\times[0,1]\sqcup|L|)/((x,0)\sim f(x))$$
has a finite triangulation of dimension at most $\max(\dim K+1,\dim L)$ and a
homeomorphism $H$ to $M_f$ fixing both boundary copies. The triangulated
cylinder retraction to $|L|$ is piecewise linear. Before triangulating, its
cells and $H$ have the explicit formulas in the proof. For every finite
collection of pairs of subcomplexes $(K_j,L_j)$ with $f(K_j)\subseteq L_j$, the
corresponding cylinders are subpolyhedra; one simultaneous subdivision makes
them subcomplexes. The construction also retains the top subpolyhedron
$f^{-1}(|L_j|)$ for each $L_j$. On each cell away from the collapsed end, $H$
is smooth in affine coordinates; no immersion or smooth tangent-star claim is
made at a collapsed end. All boundaries may be subdivided: the lemma does not
promise an extension of an arbitrarily fixed boundary triangulation without
subdivision.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\pi:E\to B$ be a smooth bundle with compact
total space, compact smooth base and compact smooth fibre, permitting corners.
A bundle here comes with finite smooth local product trivializations, whose
transition maps preserve all local source/target corner faces; a boundary face
in a product chart is either a base face or a fibre face. Let $h:D\to B$ be a
supplied finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.

Then there is a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation $F:K\to E$
and a piecewise affine map $r:K\to D$ with $\pi F=hr$. Thus the actual bundle
projection is PL over the fixed base parametrization. Refining base pieces for
local construction does not change $h$ or the original complex $D$ in the final
diagram: $r$ on a domain simplex is affine into a simplex of the original $D$.

The construction is relative to any supplied finite diagram $C:J\to E$,
$\pi C=hr_J$, corner-adapted and embedding onto a closed neighbourhood of a protected subpolyhedron
$R$ contained in its relative interior, provided the fitting supports of the
remaining pieces can be chosen disjoint from $R$. In particular this applies
when $C$ is an already triangulated collar neighbourhood of the entire boundary
and $R$ is a smaller collar: the original boundary and all its corner-face
intersections are kept pointwise, with compatible subdivisions allowed. All
union intersections are full subcomplexes.

This relative contract requires the **collar diagram**, not just an arbitrary
triangulation of the boundary without any projection-preserving neighbourhood
extension. Nor does proper smoothness of $\pi$ alone replace the supplied bundle
trivializations.

Let $F:K\to M$ and $G:L\to M$ be whole-star smooth embeddings of finite complexes into a smooth manifold without boundary. Given any positive strong $C^1$ tolerance, there are approximations on finite subdivisions fitting in a full subcomplex whose union is a whole-star smooth embedding. The same conclusion holds for bundle diagrams $\pi F=hr_K$, $\pi G=hr_L$ over a fixed whole-star smooth base embedding $h:D\to B$, when all relevant images are in a smooth bundle with product trivializations. The final approximations satisfy these **same** diagrams with $h$ and $r_K,r_L$ unchanged as point maps, so the bundle projection is preserved exactly. The union map has the induced affine map to $D$. The construction may be supported in a prescribed open neighbourhood $V$ of the new piece being fitted, including only the old pieces whose images meet that neighbourhood. In particular it fixes a closed protected region $R$ pointwise whenever all newly processed pieces and their required closed stars have images in $V$, with $\overline V\cap R=\varnothing$, and the maps already fit on the pieces outside this support. This is the fixed-collar relative interface: it does not assert arbitrary pointwise fixed-side fitting without the neighbourhood/separation hypotheses. Additional local affine plane constraints are preserved if the chosen charts make them coordinate planes and the already supplied diagrams respect them. For corner targets the same construction applies when all pieces satisfy the adapted face/tangent hypotheses of [[lem-corner-adapted-strong-approximations-remain-in-the-same-orthant]] in these charts; that lemma proves every altered piece remains in its original orthant.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth, let $p\in M$, and suppose $F$ has constant rank $r$ on a neighbourhood of $p$. Then there are smooth charts $\varphi:U\to\mathbb R^m$ at $p$ and $\psi:V\to\mathbb R^n$ at $F(p)$ such that $$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}(u,v)=(u,0)$$ for $(u,v)\in\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb R^{m-r}$ near $\varphi(p)$, with the zero in $\mathbb R^{n-r}$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every $(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of $$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$ is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair $(y,\lambda)$.

In ZF, $$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$ DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $W$ be compact with finite compatible tube data and the actual commuting radial collars of [F1]. Retain outer maps while using inner normalized domains. Fix a stratum $X$ and a level $0<a<1$; write $A=\{p\in T_X:\rho_X(p)=a\}$ and $L=\overline A$ in $W$, which is compact. A limit of points of $A$ leaving $T_X$ must land on the frontier of $X$: in tube parameters either the bases have an interior limit, which retains the tube because the normalized radius is the fixed $a<1$, or the bases approach the frontier, where the imposed displacement bound forces the point and its base to have the same limit. Consequently $L$ meets only upper incident strata, where it is the smooth hypersurface $\rho_X=a$, and lower frontier strata of $X$; it misses $X$ itself and incomparable strata.

Membership in $L$ on a lower frontier stratum $Y<X$ is locally constant along $Y$, by transport rather than by an appeal to a Whitney property of $L$. On a small $Y$-base coordinate box construct smooth lifts of each base coordinate field in increasing dimension, with the maximal incident tube controller as in [F1]; the field on $Y$ is the given coordinate field and upper fields satisfy $d\pi_ZV=V_Z\pi_Z$ and $d\rho_ZV=0$ on the retained tube of every lower $Z$. On the $X$-tube the lift therefore preserves $\rho_X=a$. The compact-trapping proof of [F1] gives a jointly continuous short flow even without ambient boundedness on an entire outer tube, and it maps $A$ to itself wherever defined, hence maps its closure $L$ to itself, as does the inverse flow. Ordered coordinate transports along $Y$ prove local constancy of membership, so $L\cap Y$ is an open and closed union of components of $Y$.

The same horizontal-lift construction, with the level constraints imposed in the chain of controllers, shows that the closure-incidence label of an upper level piece is locally constant on each lower level piece. If a disconnected level piece has different incidence labels, split it by the finitely many Boolean labels recording membership in the closures of the finitely many upper pieces; these subsets are open and closed smooth pieces, and since there are at most finitely many labels this makes a finite frontier stratification without assuming finitely many connected components. The maps and collars below restrict to these pieces, because the transports preserve each closure and hence its incidence labels.

For a lower frontier $Y<X$ the restricted $Y$-tube retracts $L$ into $L\cap Y$: radial $Y$-transport preserves $\rho_X$ on $A$ by the commuting collar identities, and its limit as $\rho_Y\to0$ is $\pi_Y$, so $\pi_Y(A\cap T_Y)\subseteq L$ and continuity gives the same inclusion for $L\cap T_Y$. For an upper $Y>X$ the identity $\rho_X\pi_Y=\rho_X$ shows directly that $\pi_Y$ preserves the level hypersurface. Therefore all inherited projections have their actual target in the corresponding stratum of $L$.

The inherited radius/projection maps are submersive on the smooth strata of $L$. If $Y<X<Z$, then on $Z$ the map $(\pi_X,\rho_X)$ is submersive and $(\pi_Y,\rho_Y)$ factors through $\pi_X$, while the latter pair is submersive on $X$; hence the joint map $(\pi_Y,\rho_Y,\rho_X)$ is submersive on $Z$, and restricting to $\rho_X=a$ gives the full rank of $(\pi_Y,\rho_Y)$ there. If $X<Y<Z$, then $(\pi_Y,\rho_Y)$ is submersive on $Z$ and $\rho_X$ factors through $\pi_Y$; its restriction to the kernel of $d\rho_X$ surjects onto the tangent space of $(Y\cap\{\rho_X=a\})\times(0,1)$, because lifting a target vector with $d\rho_X=0$ through the original pair and using the factorization forces the lift to satisfy the same equation. This is precisely the needed level-pair submersion.

All control equations and incomparable-domain disjointness restrict, and local properness restricts because $L$ is closed in compact $W$. The radial families restrict too: they preserve $A$ where defined, preserve its closure by continuity, and preserve the new incidence labels; their semigroup, commutation and projection equations are the original equations on actual retained domains, and zero-end convergence still follows from the compact tube estimate. Thus $L$ is a compact finite smooth controlled stratified space with commuting collars. Its maximal stratum dimension is at most $\dim(W)-1$, since upper level strata lose one dimension and lower frontier strata have dimension strictly less than $\dim X\le\dim W$; this is the dimension drop needed by the interior triangulation induction. Nothing here identifies $L$ with an algebraic or semialgebraic set.

For each stratum $Z$ define its core by removing the small open tubes of lower-dimensional strata; compactness is literal. A sequence in this core tending to the frontier of $Z$ would eventually lie in the open tube of its limiting lower stratum, contradicting the definition, so the core is a closed subset of $W$ contained in $Z$, hence compact; the same argument applies to a level link after lower-stratum tubes are removed.

At a core point the active lower controllers form a chain and the differentials of their radius functions are independent on the stratum. For a chain $Y_1<\cdots<Y_k<Z$, the submersion $(\pi_{Y_k},\rho_{Y_k})$ on $Z$ and the factorizations of the earlier radius functions through $\pi_{Y_k}$ let one lift first through the earlier joint radius map and then through the maximal pair, proving surjectivity of the joint radius map on $Z$. In constant-rank coordinates the inequalities $\rho_{Y_j}\ge d_j$ are independent half-space coordinates, so the core is a smooth compact manifold with corners and every designated face or face intersection is a genuine corner face, which checks the corner-face compatibility premise of [F3] and [F4].

The normal level-core map to a fixed base core, $\pi_X:Z\cap S_X(a)\to X$, is a proper corner submersion with compatible faces. For $Y<X$ the boundary coordinate $\rho_Y-d_Y$ is the pullback of the same base boundary coordinate under $\pi_X$, and for $X<Y<Z$ it is an extra source face coordinate; the pair-map factorization proves surjectivity of the joint differential $(d\pi_X,d\rho_{Y_1},\ldots,d\rho_{Y_k})$ for the extra source faces, and the preceding kernel argument also applies to the fixed equation $\rho_X=a$. Thus local smooth constant-rank charts put the map and all active faces in the form $(b,u)\mapsto b$, with base inequalities in the coordinates $b$, the corresponding source inequalities equal to those base inequalities, and extra source inequalities in the coordinates $u$; properness follows from the proved compactness of the truncated cores.

To obtain bundle charts choose a sufficiently small corner box in the base. For each base coordinate $b_i$ choose local smooth horizontal fields satisfying $d\pi_XV_i=\partial/\partial b_i$ and $dh_jV_i=0$ for every active extra source face-defining coordinate $h_j$; the joint differential just proved has a smooth right inverse giving these fields. Choose patches avoiding every inactive closed face and retaining every active one; a smooth subordinate partition preserves all these linear equations, and no derivative of a partition coefficient enters. A source face pulled back from the base automatically has the prescribed derivative of that base coordinate, so it must not incorrectly be required tangent to an outward base field.

On a compact inverse image finitely many extended smooth corner charts give a common short flow time. Flow each coordinate in a fixed order from a selected base point, possibly on a boundary face; the coordinate segment remains in the base orthant, extra source faces are invariant, and corresponding source faces follow the nonnegative base coordinates, so the source path remains in the corner manifold. Extend the smooth field temporarily across the coordinate hyperplanes in its chart to define the one-sided boundary flow and retain only the part with nonnegative base and fibre face coordinates. Compactness and the face constraints exclude finite-time exit, and reversing the coordinate flows returns to the selected fibre and supplies the smooth inverse. These products preserve every named face and the projection exactly, and a finite base cover gives genuine finite smooth bundle product trivializations, which are the additional hypothesis required by the relative smooth bundle-fitting author [F4].

For a finite controlled space $W$ let $W^{(p)}$ be its union of strata of real dimension at most $p$, closed by the frontier axiom. Put $T_p(d)=\bigcup_{\dim Y\le p}\{\rho_Y<d\}$, and for a stratum $X$ of dimension $i$ put $X_d^0=X\setminus T_{i-1}(d)$. Every such core is a compact manifold with corners by step 8.1. For a top stratum $Z$ of dimension $n$ put $S_d^p(Z)=Z_d^0\cap\bigcup_{\dim Y\le p}\{\rho_Y=d\}$; intersections of these sets are genuine corner faces because incomparable tube domains are disjoint and the joint rank of the radii in every active chain has been proved.

An interior $d$-triangulation triangulates all cores $X_d^0$, retains every intersection with a lower normal level as a subpolyhedron, and makes the level-to-base projections PL. A partial $(d,p)$-triangulation does the same on all lower-dimensional cores and only on $S_d^p(Z)$ for each top stratum. At every stage the prescribed faces and their intersections are full subcomplexes after one common barycentric subdivision. Smooth-core pieces and positive-width collar pieces carry the nondegenerate local inverse and tangent-star contract of [F3] and [F4]; this is not asserted at a singular collapsed end, and singular ends arise only in the final topological gluing.

The induction retains buffers: if $d'<d$, choose $d'<d''<d$, retain the prescribed pieces on a closed collar, and fit within the larger open collar. All objects are compact and there are finitely many strata and flags, so each supplier's local fine-approximation bounds have positive minima on each of the finitely many compact pieces and a finite subdivision satisfies them. There is no infinite process, and no claim that an arbitrary preassigned incompatible smooth boundary triangulation can be extended.

Given an already triangulated level $J=f^{-1}(S_X(d))$, attach the product $J\times[d',d]$ along $J\times\{d\}$ and map $(q,t)\mapsto R_X(t)f(q)$; this is an embedding onto the annular $X$-collar whose inverse records the outer level point and $\rho_X$. The product has a finite triangulation, for instance by ordering simplex vertices and decomposing each simplex prism into finitely many monotone staircase simplices, with the same vertex order on shared faces; restrict this subdivision to every marked face. If several collars are extended, the radial commutation identity makes their two product parameterizations agree on overlap, including their corner parameters, so a common subdivision of the finitely many product faces glues them without changing their maps. Every radius preserved by a transport has the same marked level set before and after extension, and every lower projection transported equivariantly retains its induced PL coordinate expression; this is the precise sense in which extension is independent of the order of incidence of collar operations.

The mutually inductive assertions are $B_n$: extend an interior triangulation of the lower skeleton to an interior triangulation of an $n$-dimensional space after decreasing $d$; and $C_{(n,p)}$: extend a partial top-boundary triangulation through the faces whose lower controlling stratum has dimension $p$, after decreasing $d$. The order is $B_{n-1}$, then $C_{(n,0)},\ldots,C_{(n,n-1)}$, then $B_n$. The base consists of compact zero-dimensional cores, which are finite because each point is open in its zero-manifold and compactness gives a finite subcover by singleton neighbourhoods. The relative strengthening retains the prescribed finite collar faces and their inherited projections, and every application below is to boundary data produced by the preceding collar and core construction, with the star contract and compatible corners; it is not an unrestricted relative triangulation theorem for arbitrary subsets.

For $C_{(n,p)}$ process the $p$-dimensional lower strata $X$ separately; their tubes are disjoint. Work at the original outer level $S_X(d)$, reserving $d'<d''<d$. The already triangulated portion consists of its intersections with the lower skeleton and the top boundary faces previously handled by $C_{(n,q)}$ for $q<p$. Extend those prescribed portions along every other lower collar to the intermediate parameter $d''$; their intersections with $S_X(d)$ are still subpolyhedra by radius preservation. Pass to the compact closure of the level link, whose controlled structure and strict dimension drop were proved in steps 6.1 and 7.1, and apply the already completed dimension-$(n-1)$ interior and partial extension induction to that link, retaining the prescribed collar intersections. This triangulates all lower link pieces and every required boundary of the still untriangulated top link core.

The map to the fixed triangulated $X$-core is PL on this prescribed portion. On a portion controlled by a higher stratum $Y>X$ it factors as the inherited link projection to $Y\cap S_X(d)$ followed by the already triangulated map to $X$, and both factors are PL by the induction data. On portions near a lower $Y<X$ it is equivariant with the previously defined collar transports, so the product coordinate maps are the transported old PL maps. All these factorizations hold on actual tube overlaps, and the radius equations keep their source and target in the retained cores.

The relative bundle prerequisite is a diagram on an entire closed collar, not merely on its boundary; it is supplied before fitting. Extend every already triangulated boundary face by a positive-width radial product collar. For a controller $Y>X$ one has $\pi_XR_Y=\pi_X$, so the affine diagram map ignores that collar coordinate; for $Y<X$ one has $\pi_XR_Y=R_Y|_X\pi_X$, and the fixed target triangulation is extended by the identical $Y$-collar operation, so the diagram map carries that collar coordinate identically to the base. On multiple-face intersections the radial families commute and give the same product coordinate maps in either order. Thus $\pi_XF=hr$ holds throughout the closed collar and $r$ is PL after a common product subdivision; a smaller collar is protected and the positive-width buffer separates every later fitting support from it. This is the actual collar-neighbourhood hypothesis of [F4], not an assertion that a manifold boundary-extension theorem automatically preserves a bundle projection.

What remains in the top link stratum is a smooth compact manifold-with-corners core whose map to the fixed $X$-core has the actual finite face-compatible bundle charts proved in steps 9.1-11.1. The relative smooth bundle theorem [F4] triangulates it over that fixed base, making the projection PL; the projection-preserving fitting supplier fits it to the retained positive-width boundary collar, fixes the prescribed subcomplex and retains the projection exactly. The nondegenerate local star premise holds on both pieces, being supplied for the smooth core by [F3] and for the collar by the product construction. Full-subcomplex intersections follow from the fitting contract and a common subdivision. Transport the resulting entire link triangulation radially from $\rho_X=d$ to $\rho_X=d'$; its projection to $X$ does not change and its intersections with all previously treated collar faces agree with the previous partial extension, because the $X$-radial transport commutes with those transports and preserves their radii. Glue along those common full subcomplexes. This constructs $C_{(n,p)}$ using only smaller-dimensional induction and the proved smooth bundle-fitting interface.

For $B_n$ use the completed $C_{(n,p)}$ to triangulate every top-stratum boundary at an intermediate parameter $d''$, and extend this boundary triangulation to parameter $d'$ by the collar operator. The remaining portion of each top stratum is a smooth compact manifold with corners; apply the relative manifold triangulation theorem of [F3] and the ordinary finite-fitting clause of [F4] to that core, retaining its already triangulated closed boundary collar, so no bundle structure on the generic top core is required. The shared collar has the star contract and a buffer, and every face intersection is a genuine corner face; a finite simultaneous subdivision makes the overlaps full subcomplexes. Gluing the finite core and collar complexes gives the interior triangulation, the already lower-dimensional pieces and their boundary projections retain their maps, and only finitely many $(n,p)$ assertions occur, so finitely many decreases of $d$ leave a positive final parameter.

Fix the resulting interior triangulation $g_n:J_n\to W$; its image is the disjoint union of all stratum cores. Descend in $i$, with the invariant that the image of $g_i$ is this union plus $W\setminus T_{i-1}(d)$, that all stratum portions and future lower level sets are subpolyhedra, and that the projection from every future lower level to its current base portion is PL. Only these future projections need be retained; no claim is made that every old higher projection becomes a PL map on the completed space.

For a stratum $X$ of dimension $i-1$ let $A_X=g_i^{-1}(S_X(d))$ and $B_X=g_i^{-1}(X)$; the base portion is precisely $X_d^0$ because the smaller-dimensional frontier tubes have not yet been filled, and the normal level portion is correspondingly truncated over this base, hence compact, with PL projection $f_X:A_X\to B_X$ by the invariant. Finite subdivision makes it simplicial by an explicit finite polytope construction: cut the target by the affine-hull and facet hyperplanes of the images of every face of every source simplex on which the map is affine, so every such image is a union of resulting target cells; cut each source simplex by the inverse images of these target cells. Every face of a source cell is a source face intersected with the inverse image of a target face, so its image is one target cell or empty, because the target refinement has already made every original source-face image a union of cells. For each nonempty source cell choose an interior point mapping to the chosen interior point of its image target cell, which exists because an affine surjection of a convex polytope onto its image sends relative interior onto relative interior. Cone the face subdivisions using these points and barycentrically cone the target cells; nested source faces have nested image target faces, with repetitions allowed, so the resulting map is simplicial. Mark all intersections with future lower levels and stratum closures, and apply one further barycentric subdivision to make all these marked subcomplexes full.

Use the mapping-cylinder helper [F2] for $f_X$, allowing simplex vertex identifications; its finite domain and explicit homeomorphism with threshold inverse have already been constructed. Map its topological cylinder to $W$ by $(q,t)\mapsto R_X(td)g_i(q)$ for $t>0$, with the zero end mapped to $\pi_Xg_i(q)$. [F1] supplies continuity at that zero end and the homeomorphism onto the closed $X$-collar over $X_d^0$. The new collar meets the old image only in its outer level $A_X$ and base $B_X$: every old higher collar began at a core with $\rho_X\ge d$ and its radial transports preserve $\rho_X$, so no old point has $0<\rho_X<d$ over this base; two distinct same-dimensional $X$-collars are disjoint because their tubes are incomparable. Thus gluing along the two boundary copies is injective; the domain is finite compact, the target $W$ is Hausdorff, and the radial inverse proves surjectivity onto exactly the newly filled collar, so the map onto the new image is a homeomorphism.

For a future lower stratum $Y<X$ the functions $\rho_Y$ and $\pi_Y$ factor through $\pi_X$ on the $X$-collar, so the part of $S_Y(d)$ inside this new cylinder is exactly the cylinder over the corresponding marked source and base subcomplex pair; the mapping-cylinder helper makes it a subpolyhedron, and its projection to the future $Y$-base is the cylinder retraction followed by the existing base projection $\pi_Y|_X$, both PL. This proves the descending invariant. Stratum-closure intersections are retained by the same subcylinder compatibility, because the radial maps preserve strata, so an upper stratum or its closure contributes its marked top subset together with the appropriate zero-end base subset. No dimension used here is a complex perversity dimension.

After all $i$ have been processed the image is $W$, and all strata and prescribed unions of strata are unions of open simplices. The complex dimension is at most the maximal real stratum dimension: smooth core complexes have their manifold dimension, link dimensions drop by one, and the mapping-cylinder dimension bound of [F2] adds at most one to the source-link dimension while retaining the smaller base dimension. The finite simplicial cylinder maps are smooth inside positive-height cells, and radial transport is smooth on each smooth stratum; at a zero end the lower stratum already has its smooth core triangulation, and no ambient smooth immersion through a singular end is asserted. The finite list of glued complexes therefore supplies the claimed finite compatible stratified triangulation by the preceding interior construction and the exact relative-supplier premises.

Zero-dimensional strata enter the skeleton filtration of step 12.1 first, and step 13.1 triangulates the resulting cores; the collar levels used throughout are positive, so no zero radius is evaluated.
