citations.quote:
Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex. Its **geometric realization**
$|K|$ is the set of functions $\alpha:V \to [0,1]$ such that:

1. $\alpha(v)=0$ for all but finitely many $v \in V$;
2. $\sum_{v \in V}\alpha(v)=1$;
3. the support $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha):=\{v \in V:\alpha(v)\neq 0\}$ is a simplex of $K$.

For each simplex $\sigma=\{v_0,\dots,v_n\}$ of $K$, write
$$|\sigma|:=\{\alpha \in |K| : \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\subseteq \sigma\}.$$
Sending $\alpha$ to the barycentric tuple
$(\alpha(v_0),\dots,\alpha(v_n))$ identifies $|\sigma|$ with the geometric
simplex spanned by the standard basis vectors indexed by $v_0,\dots,v_n$, so
$|\sigma|$ carries its Euclidean simplex topology.

We give $|K|$ the **weak topology** with respect to these simplex inclusions:
a subset $U\subseteq |K|$ is declared open exactly when $U\cap|\sigma|$ is open
in $|\sigma|$ for every simplex $\sigma$ of $K$.

Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex.

A **subcomplex** of $K$ is a subfamily $L \subseteq K$ that is itself closed
under taking subsets.

If $\sigma \in K$, its **closure** is the subcomplex
$$\overline{\sigma}:=\{\tau \in K : \tau \subseteq \sigma\}.$$
More generally, if $A \subseteq K$, its closure is
$$\overline{A}:=\{\tau \in K : \tau \subseteq \sigma \text{ for some } \sigma \in A\}.$$

For a simplex $\sigma \in K$, the **closed star** of $\sigma$ in $K$ is
$$\operatorname{St}_K(\sigma):=\{\tau \in K : \sigma \cup \tau \in K\},$$
and the **open star** is the union, after realization, of the relative
interiors of simplices $\rho\in K$ with $\sigma\subseteq\rho$.

The **link** of $\sigma$ in $K$ is
$$\operatorname{Lk}_K(\sigma):=\{\tau \in K : \tau \cap \sigma=\varnothing \text{ and } \sigma \cup \tau \in K\}.$$

For finite $K$, the weak topology on $|K|$ equals the Euclidean subspace topology in $\mathbb R^{V(K)}$; $|K|$ is compact, metrizable and Hausdorff. If $P$ is a finite subcomplex of any $K$, then $|P|\hookrightarrow|K|$ is a closed embedding, with that same finite Euclidean topology.

If $K$ is a finite abstract simplicial complex, then its geometric realization
$|K|$ is compact and Hausdorff.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$.
Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]].

$f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the
preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$.

$f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$.

**The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only
if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open
$U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is
continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of
$f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$,
which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and
a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and
then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$,
so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the
same statement written twice.

**Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$
is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is
defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being
asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the
corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later
item, which are different notions.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

derivations.claim: Put $L=|\operatorname{lk}_K\sigma|$ and let $E=\{rq:0\le r<1,\ q\in L\}$ inside the Euclidean coordinate space on the vertices of the link, with the subspace topology. For an empty link both the cone by convention and $E=\{0\}$ are a single apex, so assume $L\ne\varnothing$. The continuous map $L\times[0,1)\to E$, $(q,r)\mapsto rq$, identifies exactly $L\times\{0\}$ with the apex: if $rq=r'q'$ with $r,r'>0$, coordinate sums give $r=r'$ and then $q=q'$. It therefore descends to a continuous bijection $\varphi:c_{<1}(L)\to E$. For each $0<t<1$, the closed radial cone $(L\times[0,t])/(L\times\{0\})$ is compact by [F2], and its continuous bijection onto $E_t=\{rq:0\le r\le t,\ q\in L\}$ is a homeomorphism because $E_t$ is Hausdorff. Away from the apex the inverse on the full open cone is continuous by $r=\sum_vz_v$, $q=z/r$, followed by the quotient projection. At the apex, the preimage of any quotient-open neighbourhood is an open set containing $L\times\{0\}$. Product neighbourhoods of its points, a finite cover of the compact link $L$, and the minimum of their positive radii give an $\epsilon>0$ with $L\times[0,\epsilon)$ in that preimage. The relatively open set $\{z\in E:\sum_vz_v<\epsilon\}$ is consequently mapped by $\varphi^{-1}$ into the given neighbourhood. Thus the inverse is continuous at the apex too, and $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism of the full open cone.

For a point $x$ of the open star put $a=\sum_{v\in\sigma}x_v>0$, set $p_v=x_v/a$ for $v\in\sigma$ and $z_v=x_v$ for $v\notin\sigma$. Then $p\in\operatorname{relint}|\sigma|$, $r:=\sum_vz_v=1-a<1$, and the support of $x$ is $\sigma\cup\operatorname{supp}(z)$, so $\operatorname{supp}(z)$, if nonempty, is a simplex of the link. Conversely, given $p\in\operatorname{relint}|\sigma|$ and $z\in E$ with $r=\sum_vz_v$, define a coordinate family by $x_v=(1-r)p_v$ on $\sigma$ and $x_v=z_v$ off $\sigma$; it is nonnegative with sum one, and its support is $\sigma\cup\operatorname{supp}(z)$, a simplex of $K$ because $\operatorname{supp}(z)$ is a simplex of the link. The two constructions are mutually inverse: from $x$ one recovers $a=1-r$ and $z$, hence $x$; from $(p,z)$ one recovers $p$ from the normalized $\sigma$-coordinates and $z$ from the outside coordinates. Both are continuous, the only division being by $a>0$ on the open star for the forward map, while the inverse is a polynomial expression in $(p,z)$ and the continuous function $r=\sum_vz_v$. By step 1.1 the second factor is the cone $c_{<1}(L)$, and since $\operatorname{supp}(z)$ records exactly which link simplex the radial coordinate lies over, each simplex interior containing $\sigma$ is carried to the product of the corresponding link-simplex interior with $(0,1)$, while points with $z=0$ map to $\operatorname{relint}|\sigma|\times\{\mathrm{apex}\}$ and the simplex $\sigma$ itself to the apex. Thus the star is homeomorphic to the stated product.

The open star is open in $|K|$ because it is the finite intersection, over the vertices of $\sigma$, of the sets on which one barycentric coordinate is positive, each open in the weak topology by definition. The link is a subcomplex of the finite complex $K$, hence it has finitely many simplices and compact realization by [F2]. Finally, if a point $x$ of the star lay in $|D|$, its support would be a simplex $\rho$ of $D$ with $\sigma\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(x)=\rho$; the subcomplex $D$ is closed under taking faces, so $\sigma\in D$, contradicting $\sigma\notin D$. Hence the star is disjoint from $|D|$.

boundaries.evidence: When the link is empty the Statement declares the cone to be a single apex, and step 1.1 realizes this directly as the one-point space ${0}$ with the subspace topology.
The radial coordinate $r=1-a$ vanishes exactly at the apex; step 2.1 defines the inverse there and the quotient presentation of $c_{<1}$ is what makes the zero-radius point well defined.
If $sigma$ is a single vertex whose link is empty, step 1.1 identifies the cone factor with the apex and the chart is the identity on the interior of $|sigma|$.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate simplex is admitted: $sigma$ is required nonempty and the link uses only simplices disjoint from it, so no face-containment parameter degenerates.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 proves inverse continuity at radius zero by a uniform positive radius obtained from compactness of the link; compactness is used only on each closed radial subcone with radius t<1. Step 2.1 gives the inverse formula on the full half-open radial range.

boundaries.reason: No choice principle is used; the barycentric splitting of step 2.1 is an explicit formula and the simplex incidences are read off from the finite complex $K$.
The Statement displays a homeomorphism and lists its properties; it states no biconditional, so there is no forward direction to discharge.
No converse classification is claimed; the lemma does not characterize which open subsets of $|K|$ arise as open stars.

risk_review.notes: Complete review: a=sum sigma coordinates is positive on the star, and the inverse x=((1-r)p,z) gives mutually inverse continuous coordinates. Compactness of the link supplies a uniform small radius for every quotient-open apex neighbourhood, proving the inverse's continuity there. Empty links give a singleton by the declared convention; nonempty sigma excludes a zero denominator. The apex factor corresponds to relint sigma in the star, and any D containing a support simplex would contain sigma as a face, proving deletion compatibility. Finiteness and compactness are supplied; no AC, complex-stratum chart or triangulation existence claim is used.

citations.quote: Let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on an arbitrary space $X$. For a singular simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$, write $v_i=\sigma(e_i)$ and $\gamma_{01}^\sigma(t)=\sigma(1-t,t,0,\ldots,0)$. The **intrinsic singular local chain group** is $$C_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\bigoplus_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0}.$$ Write an element of the $\sigma$-summand as $m\sigma$. Its boundary is $$\partial(m\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}(m)(\sigma\delta_0)+\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^im(\sigma\delta_i),$$ and the boundary of a zero-simplex is zero. The exceptional zeroth face transports its coefficient from the old first vertex $v_0$ to the new first vertex $v_1$; all other faces keep $v_0$. The **intrinsic singular local cochain group** is the product $$C^n_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\prod_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0},$$ so a cochain $\varphi$ assigns $\varphi(\sigma)\in\mathcal L_{v_0}$ to every simplex, with no finite-support requirement. Its positive coboundary, consistent with [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]], is $$(\delta\varphi)(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(\sigma\delta_0)\bigr)+\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}(-1)^i\varphi(\sigma\delta_i).$$ Now the exceptional face value is transported back from $v_1$ to $v_0$. For $A\subseteq X$, restrict $\mathcal L$ along the inclusion and set $$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)/C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L),\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=\ker\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)\to C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L)\bigr).$$ For a connected CW complex with chosen basepoint $x$, universal cover $\widetilde X$, $\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$, and base fiber $M=\mathcal L_x$ carrying $g m=T_{\bar g}m$, the equivalent universal-cover models are $$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$ The first tensor product is the balanced construction of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] using the right action of [[def-right-group-ring-action-on-the-chains-of-a-universal-cover]]. For the second, convert that right chain module to a left one by $$g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}.$$ Thus an equivariant cochain has the correctly typed rule $$\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c),$$ not a module-Hom between one right and one left module. The intrinsic/tensor identification sends $\widetilde\sigma\otimes m$ to the simplex $\sigma=p\widetilde\sigma$ with coefficient obtained by transporting $m$ along the path represented by $\widetilde\sigma(e_0)$. If $\widetilde\sigma$ is replaced by $\widetilde\sigma\cdot g$, that path is changed by the loop $g^{-1}$ and the coefficient becomes the transport of $gm$, exactly the balanced relation. The analogous statement for cochains proves the displayed equivariance rule. These maps respect the two boundary formulas term by term. The **cellular local chain and cochain groups** of a connected CW complex are $$C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=\operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$ For a CW pair, quotient by the lifted subcomplex before tensoring and use the corresponding relative cellular complex before applying equivariant Hom. For a disconnected CW complex, take the direct sum of chain complexes and the degreewise product of cochain complexes over its components. Universal-cover coordinates of this componentwise description require a supplied basepoint in each component; the intrinsic complexes require no simultaneous basepoint choice and remain the definition when no such family is supplied. The next lemma proves square-zero and independence of supplied lift bases. Empty spaces and negative degrees give zero groups, the zero local system gives the zero complexes, and constant systems reduce to the ordinary formulas because every transport is the identity.

Let $X$ be a nonempty connected finite CW complex with supplied characteristic maps, let $x\in X$ be a basepoint, put $\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$, and let $$p:\widetilde X\longrightarrow X$$ be a chosen universal cover, which exists for the spaces considered here because a finite CW complex is locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected ([[thm-universal-cover-existence]]). Write $R=\mathbb Z[\pi]$ for the integral group ring, a unital ring with basis the classes $[g]$ of the group elements ([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]). **Lifted CW structure.** Every open cell $e\subseteq X$ is contractible, so $p^{-1}(e)$ splits into components each mapped homeomorphically onto $e$; such a component is an **open cell of $\widetilde X$ over $e$**. To obtain its **lifted characteristic map**, choose a point above the image of one interior point of the characteristic disk and lift the entire characteristic map $D^n\to X$ through $p$; this is possible because $D^n$ is simply connected ([[thm-covering-space-lifting-criterion]]), and its interior maps homeomorphically onto the chosen component over $e$. The inverse $e\to p^{-1}(e)$ alone cannot be composed with the characteristic map on its boundary, where that inverse is undefined. These lifted characteristic maps give the standard lifted CW structure ([[def-cell-attachment-by-a-characteristic-map]], [[def-skeleta-cw-subcomplex-and-relative-cw-complex]]). Its $n$-skeleton is $$\widetilde X^n:=p^{-1}(X^n),$$ the union of the closed lifted cells over the cells of $X$ of dimension at most $n$; for a CW pair $(X,A)$ the preimage $p^{-1}(A)$ is a CW subcomplex of $\widetilde X$ and $p^{-1}(X^n\cup A)=p^{-1}(X^n)\cup p^{-1}(A)$ is the $n$-skeleton of the relative lifted structure. **Deck action.** Identify $\pi$ with the deck group of $p$ by the no-reversal isomorphism of [[thm-deck-group-of-a-universal-cover-is-the-fundamental-group]], writing $T_g$ for the covering homeomorphism attached to $g\in\pi$; thus $T_1=\mathrm{id}$, $T_{gh}=T_g\circ T_h$, and every $T_g$ carries lifted cells onto lifted cells of the same dimension. A deck transformation is determined by its value at one point and acts freely, so the lifts of a single cell $e$ are exactly the cells $T_g\widetilde e$ for one chosen lift $\widetilde e$. **Right group-ring action.** The action of the deck group on the singular and cellular chains of $\widetilde X$ is written on the left and the length-preserving insertion of inverses makes it a right action of $R$ by $$c\cdot g:=T_g^{-1}(c)=T_{g^{-1}}(c),\qquad g\in\pi,$$ extended $\mathbb Z$-bilinearly in $c$ and the group-ring coefficient ([[def-relative-singular-homology]], [[def-oriented-cellular-chain-group]]); in particular $(c\cdot g)\cdot h=c\cdot gh$. Each $T_{g^{-1}}$ is a homeomorphism of pairs $(\widetilde X^n,\widetilde X^{n-1})\to(\widetilde X^n,\widetilde X^{n-1})$ and of pairs $(\widetilde X^n\cup p^{-1}A,\widetilde X^{n-1}\cup p^{-1}A)$, so the action passes to the homology of those pairs. **Based cellular chains.** For each cell $e$ of $X$ choose an orientation of $e$, that is, an orientation of the disk of its characteristic map, and choose one oriented lift $\widetilde e$ carrying that orientation. Put $$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R):=H_n(\widetilde X^n,\widetilde X^{n-1};\mathbb Z),$$ $$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X,p^{-1}(A);R):=H_n\bigl(\widetilde X^n\cup p^{-1}(A),\,\widetilde X^{n-1}\cup p^{-1}(A);\mathbb Z\bigr).$$ The notation after the semicolon records the **deck-induced $R$-module structure**; the homology coefficients are integral. By [[thm-relative-homology-of-consecutive-cw-skeleta]] these integral homology groups are free abelian on the lifted cells. The right action above makes them finite free right $R$-modules on one chosen oriented lift of each cell of $X$ (respectively each relative cell of $(X,A)$): the lifts of one cell form the $\pi$-orbit $\{T_g\widetilde e\}$, and $[g]\mapsto T_{g^{-1}}\widetilde e$ bijects $\pi$ with that orbit. Using $R$ as a second homology coefficient group here would duplicate the lift-indexed generators and would not yield the claimed rank. Degrees without relative cells give the zero module, and for a disconnected finite $X$ the construction is applied componentwise with its component group ring.

Assume AC. For a CW pair $(X,A)$ and local system $\mathcal L$, the cellular cochain complex obtained from the skeletal filtration computes singular cohomology with local coefficients: $$H^n\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H^n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$ For a connected pair, it is the equivariant-Hom complex on cellular chains after the published right chain action is converted to the left action $g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}$; equivalently its cochains satisfy $\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c)$. The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology: $$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$ The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically, $$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$ If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice**, through [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]. Then every vector space $V$ over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) has a basis ([[def-linear-basis]]). In particular the zero space has a basis, namely $\varnothing$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $F$ be a free $R$-module with basis indexed by $X$. 1. Assuming the Axiom of Choice, $F$ is projective and therefore flat. 2. If $X$ is finite, only finite choice is needed for projectivity; if $X=\varnothing$, no choice is needed. 3. Regardless of choice, $F$ is flat, because tensoring with $F$ is a direct sum of copies of the identity tensor functor.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M$ be an $R$-module. The module $M$ is **flat** if the functor $-\otimes_RM$ preserves exact sequences: whenever $A\to B\to C$ is exact, so is $$A\otimes_RM\longrightarrow B\otimes_RM\longrightarrow C\otimes_RM.$$ Since tensoring is always right exact ([[thm-right-exactness-of-tensor-products]], [[def-exact-and-short-exact-sequences-of-modules]]), the definition asks for the remaining left-hand exactness. Its equivalent formulation as preservation of injections is proved separately rather than built into the definition. The module $M$ is **faithfully flat** if a sequence of $R$-modules is exact exactly when its tensor with $M$ is exact. For a unital ring homomorphism $f:R\to S$ ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) between commutative rings, $S$ is an $R$-module by $r\cdot s=f(r)s$. The map $f$ is **flat**, respectively **faithfully flat**, when this $R$-module is flat, respectively faithfully flat.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Work first on one component, with basepoint $x$, group $\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$ and fibre $M=L_x$. By [F1] the degree-$q$ term of the cellular local cochain complex is $\operatorname{Hom}_{k[\pi]}(P_q,M)$ with $P_q$ free over $k[\pi]$ on the finitely many relative $q$-cells of the component, so choosing that finite basis identifies it with the finite product $M^{n_q}$; since $M$ is finite-dimensional, the term is finite-dimensional, and it is zero for $q<0$ and for $q>d$. By [F2] the cohomology $H^q(X,A;L)$ is the cohomology of this complex, so it is finite-dimensional as a kernel, image or quotient of finite-dimensional spaces and vanishes outside $[0,d]$. For a disconnected pair the cochain complex is the degreewise product of the complexes of the finitely many components, and the same conclusions hold componentwise; the empty pair has the zero complex.

Let $k'$ be a field extension and give $M\otimes_kk'$ the induced $k'[\pi]$-module structure; these fibres with the extended transport maps form the local system $L\otimes_kk'$. The termwise map $\operatorname{Hom}_{k[\pi]}(P_q,M)\otimes_kk'\to\operatorname{Hom}_{k'[\pi]}(P_q\otimes_kk',M\otimes_kk')$, defined on a basis of the free module $P_q$, is an isomorphism, because both sides identify with $(M\otimes_kk')^{n_q}$; it is natural in the second variable and therefore intertwines the differentials, which are obtained by dualizing the same $k[\pi]$-linear cellular boundary of [F2]. Hence $C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;L)\otimes_kk'$ is isomorphic, as a complex, to $C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;L\otimes_kk')$.

By [F3] the field $k'$, viewed as a $k$-vector space, is free and hence flat, so tensoring over $k$ with $k'$ preserves exact sequences. Applying this to the kernel-image sequences of the complex of step 1.1 gives a canonical isomorphism $H^q\bigl(C^*\otimes_kk'\bigr)\cong H^q(C^*)\otimes_kk'$, which by step 2.1 and [F2] is the stated map $H^q(X,A;L)\otimes_kk'\to H^q(X,A;L\otimes_kk')$, natural in the coefficients. The finiteness, the vanishing outside $[0,d]$, and the isomorphism all hold separately on each component and for the empty pair, where both complexes vanish.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement includes the empty pair and the zero local system; the componentwise computation of step 1.1 then has no components, and finiteness and the tensor comparison hold vacuously.
The vanishing range $q<0$ and $q>d$ includes the zero-dimensional case $d=0$, where the tensor comparison of step 3.1 is applied to the single nonzero term.
A one-point component is the case of step 1.1 with trivial $pi$, where the cellular complex is $M$ in degree zero and both finiteness and scalar extension are immediate.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate parameter occurs; the local system has finite-dimensional fibres and the CW pair is an arbitrary finite pair, with no nondegeneracy hypothesis beyond finiteness.
The cutoff outside $[0,d]$ is a degree range, not a limiting endpoint: no boundary value or one-sided limit of a family is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 3.1: AC is inherited from the cellular cohomology supplier [F2] and the vector-space basis supplier [F3]; the termwise scalar comparison and all component products are finite.

boundaries.reason: Finiteness, vanishing and the isomorphism are asserted separately; the lemma states no biconditional, so no forward direction is owed.
There is no converse claim, for instance no assertion that finite-dimensionality of the groups characterizes finite CW pairs.

risk_review.notes: Complete three-step review: converted left action g.c=c.g^{-1} matches the equivariant Hom supplier, and monodromy is the reversed-path left convention. Finitely many components/cells and finite-dimensional fibres give bounded finite terms. Empty pair, zero coefficients, degree zero and d endpoints give the advertised bounds. The natural scalar-extension map respects transports; flatness preserves the kernel/image short exact sequences. AC is explicitly inherited from cellular cohomology and a basis for k' over k. No claim about arbitrary sheaf cohomology or compact support is made.

citations.quote:
Assume AC. Let $X$ be a reduced quasi-projective complex algebraic variety with
a finite smooth complex algebraic Whitney stratification. Its analytic
stratified space admits compatible tube control data. At every point $y$ of a
stratum $R$ there is a stratum-preserving neighborhood homeomorphism
$$U_y\cong B^{2\dim_{\mathbb C}R}\times c_{<1}(L_y),$$
where $L_y$ is a compact finitely Whitney-stratified real semialgebraic normal
link. The ball times cone apex is $R\cap U_y$, and upper strata correspond to
their link strata times positive radius and the ball. The local construction
can preserve a chosen ordinary normal projection and radius at $R$. Links are
locally constant in stratified homeomorphism type along $R$. Proper stratified
algebraic submersions, with their actual analytic properness, have whole-fiber
local stratified bundle trivializations; local submersions have
source-neighborhood products. No compatible triangulation or finite
sheaf-cochain model is assumed or asserted here.

Assume AC. A compact finite controlled Whitney-stratified subset of a smooth
ambient space admits a finite triangulation of dimension at most the largest
real stratum dimension, compatible with every stratum closure and any
prescribed union of strata. Each open stratum is a union of open simplices. The
homeomorphism is smooth on the pieces within each stratum. The construction may
make the finitely many normal link-bundle projections between triangulated
compact stratum cores piecewise linear. It does not make an arbitrary algebraic
map globally simplicial. In particular it applies individually to
compactifications of quasi-projective complex varieties and to their compact
controlled links, once the stated Whitney/control hypotheses have been
supplied.

Let $K$ be a finite simplicial complex and let $\sigma$ be a nonempty simplex.
Let $\operatorname{lk}_K\sigma$ be the subcomplex of simplices $\tau$ disjoint
from $\sigma$ with $\sigma\cup\tau\in K$, and let $\operatorname{st}_K(\sigma)$
be the open star of $\sigma$
([[def-simplicial-subcomplex-star-closure-and-link]]). Then
$$\operatorname{st}_K(\sigma)\cong\operatorname{relint}|\sigma|\times c_{<1}(|\operatorname{lk}_K\sigma|),$$
where $c_{<1}(L)=(L\times[0,1))/(L\times\{0\})$ with the quotient topology, and
the cone on the empty space means a single apex. The homeomorphism takes each
simplex interior containing $\sigma$ to the product with the corresponding
link-simplex interior and positive radial coordinate; the simplex $\sigma$
itself maps to the apex. The link is compact and has finitely many simplices.
If $D\subseteq K$ is a subcomplex and $\sigma\notin D$, this star lies in
$|K|\setminus|D|$.

Assume AC. Let $(X,A)$ be a finite CW pair of dimension $d$, let $k$ be a field
and let $L$ be a $k$-vector-space local system with finite-dimensional fibres
([[def-local-system-of-r-modules-and-its-pullback]]). Then $H^q(X,A;L)$ is
finite-dimensional, vanishes for $q<0$ and $q>d$, and for every field extension
$k\subseteq k'$ the natural map is an isomorphism:
$$H^q(X,A;L)\otimes_k k'\cong H^q(X,A;L\otimes_k k').$$
The assertion holds separately on every component, including the empty pair.

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a finite simplicial complex, $D$ a subcomplex and $X=|K|\setminus|D|$. Let $P$ be the face poset of the open simplices of $K$ not in $D$, ordered by inclusion of faces. The exact realization of finite-dimensional covariant $k$-diagrams on $P$ induces a fully faithful functor into $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$, with essential image the complexes having bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on each open simplex. Ordinary and compact-support cohomology, ordinary Hom and internal derived Hom have bounded finite cochain models and commute with every coefficient field extension. For a local product projection $\operatorname{pr}:V\times F\to V$ with supplied finite deleted-boundary models and $B$ in the stated constructible subcategory on the base, there is a natural local comparison $R\operatorname{pr}_*\operatorname{pr}^*B\simeq B\otimes_k C^*(F;k)$, taking the unit to $B\otimes(k\to C^*(F;k))$. This does not assert that an arbitrary algebraic map is simplicial.

Let $P$ be a finite nonempty poset, regarded as a category with one arrow $p\to q$ exactly when $p\le q$, and let $h$ be the largest number of strict inequalities in a chain of $P$. Let $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ be the abelian category of covariant diagrams of $k$-vector spaces on $P$, i.e. the functor category of $k$-vector spaces indexed by $P$, with its cochain complexes as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]. If $M$ is a bounded complex of diagrams in $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ whose vector spaces are finite-dimensional and vanish outside internal degrees $[a,b]$, then the derived inverse limit $\mathbf R\lim M:=\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(\underline k,M)$ ([[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]]) has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[a,b+h]$. If $A,B$ are such complexes, concentrated in $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$ respectively, then their derived Hom has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[c-b,d-a+h]$. These models commute with every field extension. For the empty poset, the diagram sections and the derived Hom model are zero by convention.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $f:X\to Y$ be one morphism of reduced quasi-projective complex
algebraic varieties, and prescribe finitely many closed or locally closed
algebraic subsets in source and target. There exist finite smooth complex
algebraic Whitney (a),(b) stratifications with frontier on $X$ and $Y$
respecting all prescribed subsets, such that each source stratum maps
surjectively and smoothly onto one target stratum. A further finite algebraic
stratification may be prescribed and refined. The analytic strata are smooth
complex manifolds and the restrictions are smooth submersions. If $f$ is proper
in the analytic topology, in particular if it is a projective algebraic
morphism, the whole restriction $f^{-1}(T)\to T$ over any target stratum is
proper; no restriction of $f$ to a nonclosed individual source stratum is
asserted proper.

derivations.claim: By quasi-projectivity choose an algebraic locally closed embedding $X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N$. Its reduced projective closure $\overline X$ has $X$ as an open subset, and $B=\overline X\setminus X$ is closed algebraic. Take closures of the finitely many marked supports and the pieces of the given constructibility stratification. Apply [F1]'s connected finite Whitney stratification construction to the identity morphism of $\overline X$, respecting these closed algebraic subsets and their finite locally closed differences. This gives a complex Whitney refinement on which every cohomology sheaf of $F$ stays finite-rank locally constant; passing to smaller smooth strata preserves local constancy. The compact analytic space $\overline X^{\mathrm{an}}$ embeds smoothly in a finite Euclidean space: send a projective line represented by $z\ne0$ to its Hermitian rank-one projector $zz^*/(z^*z)$. This is well-defined, injective, and smooth in the projective coordinate charts; its chart inverse recovers the ratios of the projector's nonzero column, so it is a smooth embedding. It is compact because it is the continuous image of the unit sphere. Its restricted algebraic Whitney strata satisfy the real smooth Whitney conditions used by [F2]. Apply [F2], including all chosen stratum unions. Let $K$ be the resulting finite complex and $D$ the subcomplex mapping onto $B$; one barycentric subdivision makes every marked subcomplex full if needed. Restricting the homeomorphism yields $X^{\mathrm{an}}\cong |K|\setminus|D|$ as claimed.

Every retained open simplex is contained in one original complex stratum. The cohomology of $F$ on it is finite-rank locally constant, so $F$ belongs to the actual essential image of [F4]. It therefore has a bounded finite-dimensional diagram representative on the face poset of the retained simplices, with no assertion that the analytic sheaf category itself is finite. The finite bar construction of [F5] computes actual ordinary derived global sections and actual derived Hom because [F4] proves full faithfulness against the analytic sheaf category by independently established star acyclicity. Its compact-support clause identifies the actual support functor with finite relative cochains on the compactification pair; this uses the c-soft acyclicity and open extension by zero declared in [F4]. Finite simplicial stars and their closed subcomplex complements admit the explicit finite product/cone models of [F3]. Thus local support cohomology is computed by the finite cone of restriction from such a neighborhood to its complement of the marked support, with the conventional shift determined by the support triangle. These restrictions and their maps are the actual sheaf restrictions under [F4], not merely vector spaces with matching dimensions. For the constant sheaf on a compact model the ordinary cellular model has no cochain terms above the simplicial dimension, which is at most twice the complex dimension by [F2]. All face-chain lengths and cohomology amplitudes are finite, so the models are uniformly bounded for the finitely many chosen strata and supports.

The ordinary incidence calculation alone gives constructibility on real simplices. To obtain local constancy along a complex stratum $S$, use [F1]'s actual local chart $U\cong V\times cL$, where $V$ is a small contractible ball in $S$ and the chart preserves the complex strata. The compact link $L$ has a finite inherited controlled stratification and a finite triangulation by [F2], and $cL$ truncated to a finite radius has a finite deleted-boundary model. Each product stratum is a product of the contractible $V$ with a link stratum. The restriction of the cohomology sheaves of $F$ is locally constant there. On a link simplex, therefore, its restriction to $V$ times that simplex is represented by a finite coefficient complex independent of the $V$ direction. This last derived assertion follows from [F4], rather than assuming a sheaf is invariant under every stratum-preserving homeomorphism: pullback along the projection to the link is fully faithful on the relevant finite incidence categories because [F4]'s product comparison has fibre $V$ and $C^*(V;k)\simeq k$ by [F3]. Filter the finitely many link simplices by closed skeleta. On a simplex piece the object is a pullback: finite-rank constant sheaves on the contractible product have no positive Ext between them by [F4] and its constant-sheaf comparison. The finite ordinary truncation triangles therefore split there, expressing its locally constant bounded complex by a finite coefficient complex. The ordinary exact open/closed extension-by-zero triangles in [F4] build the object through this finite filtration. Full faithfulness lifts the connecting morphisms between pullbacks, so their finite cones are again pullbacks. Induction proves that the restriction of $F$ to this chart is pulled back from a finite link-cone object. The same argument applies simultaneously to the chosen finite collection of input objects and marked support strata.

In step 3.1's chart, ordinary local sections, punctured-neighborhood sections and sections with a marked support are therefore the corresponding finite link/cone cochains, constant in the $V$ direction. Their restriction morphisms are the product/incidence morphisms, so their support cones are locally constant too. Applying this also to two input complexes shows that their internal derived Hom is locally constant in the $V$ direction, with bounded finite-dimensional stalks computed by [F4] and [F5]. Finitely many complex Whitney strata give a uniform amplitude bound. Hence the result is constructible for the complex stratification (or its finite simultaneous support refinement), not merely for the real simplex partition. This is the local constructibility and finite local cohomology assertion required for the later open/closed and perverse gluing constructions. It does not substitute the real simplex dimension for the complex dimension of $S$.

Finally every displayed incidence, bar, relative support and link-cone model is a finite matrix complex of finite-dimensional $k$-spaces. Tensor with a field extension $k\subset k'$ is exact, carries its kernels and images to the corresponding kernels and images, and commutes with every finite sum, differential, restriction map and cone. The comparisons of [F4] and the finite local-system comparison of [F3] therefore identify these scalar-extended complexes with the actual corresponding sheaf constructions over $k'$. The constructions and comparisons are locally coherent through their actual incidence morphisms. This proves all claimed finite cohomology and coefficient-extension assertions.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and steps 1.1-2.1: An empty marking collection imposes no extra support constraints. The zero input complex, or the empty variety, yields zero cochain models; an empty marking collection alone does not force the input complex to vanish.
The vanishing above the dimension bound is the zero statement in high degree: the cellular model of step 2.1 has no cochain terms above the simplicial dimension of the triangulation.
A point is the base instance of step 1.1: the triangulation supplies a single vertex, so $dim K=0$ and the bound is an equality.
Marked supports may repeat or nest; step 1.1 closes and differences the finitely many marks, so degeneracies of the support collection need no separate treatment.
The deleted boundary is the noncompact endpoint of the model: step 1.1 realizes the boundary by the subcomplex $D$, and the compact-support clause of step 2.1 is the relative model on the pair.
AC is assumed and inherited exactly through [F1] and [F2] in step 1.1; the finite matrix constructions of steps 2.1-5.1 make no further selections.

No converse is claimed: the theorem does not assert that finite-dimensional local cohomology forces constructibility on the given stratification.
