The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

derivations.claim: Closure of a quasi-compact immersion. Let $f:W\to P$ be a quasi-compact immersion from a reduced finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme into a Noetherian scheme, factored as a closed immersion $W\hookrightarrow V$ followed by an open immersion $V\hookrightarrow P$. By [F2] its scheme-theoretic image $Z=V(\mathcal K)$, $\mathcal K=\ker(\mathcal O_P\to f_*\mathcal O_W)$, restricts on $V$ to $W$, so $W$ is open in $Z$ with the same local rings. On an affine open $T=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq P$, the kernel $\mathcal K(T)$ is radical: if $g^r$ restricts to zero on $f^{-1}(T)$, then $g$ restricts to zero because $W$ is reduced. Thus $A/\mathcal K(T)$ is reduced, proving that $Z$ is reduced. If $W$ were not dense in $Z$, its proper reduced closed closure in $Z$ would receive $f$: its defining sections restrict to functions zero at every point of the reduced scheme $W$, hence zero on every affine open of $W$. This contradicts minimality of the scheme-theoretic image, so $W$ is dense. Every irreducible component meets $W$: the complement of the finitely many other components is a nonempty open subset of $Z$ contained in that component, since an irreducible component cannot be contained in their finite union; density forces this open to meet $W$.

Blowups of integral projective schemes are projective. Let $Y$ be an integral finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme whose structure morphism is H-projective, and let $\mathcal I$ be a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf of finite type. If $\mathcal I=0$ then $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y=\operatorname{Proj}_Y(\mathcal O_Y\oplus0\oplus\cdots)=\varnothing$, which is projective as the empty closed subscheme of $\mathbb P^0_{\mathbb C}$; assume $\mathcal I\ne0$. Fix a closed immersion $Y\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}$ and let $L=\mathcal O_Y(1)$ be the pullback of $\mathcal O(1)$, which is H-very ample by construction and ample over the affine base $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$; $Y$ is Noetherian and $\mathcal I$ is coherent, so for some $m\ge0$ the twist $\mathcal I(m)=\mathcal I\otimes L^{\otimes m}$ is globally generated. Its evaluation map $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal I(m))\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathcal O_Y\to\mathcal I(m)$ is surjective and $Y$ is quasi-compact with $\mathcal I(m)$ of finite type, so finitely many global sections $s_0,\dots,s_n$ already generate $\mathcal I(m)$: on a finite affine cover, a finitely generated module generated by the image of the global sections is generated by finitely many of them. Put $L'=L^{\otimes m}$, view the $s_i$ as meromorphic sections of the invertible sheaf $L'$, and set $F=\sum_i\mathcal O_Ys_i=\mathcal I(m)$ and $I=F\otimes L'^{-1}=\mathcal I$, so the ratio map of the $s_i$ is $Y\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$. The graph-closure corollary gives $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y=\operatorname{Proj}_Y(\bigoplus_{d\ge0}I^d)=B$ with a closed immersion $(\pi,\psi):B\hookrightarrow Y\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$. Composing with the closed immersion $Y\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ obtained by base change of $Y\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}$ and then with the Segre embedding, itself a closed immersion, exhibits $B$ as a closed subscheme of $\mathbb P^{(N+1)(n+1)-1}_{\mathbb C}$; hence the structure morphism of $B$ is H-projective.

Disjoint unions of projective schemes are projective. Let $Z_1,\dots,Z_t\subseteq\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$ be closed subschemes with pairwise disjoint underlying sets and ideals $\mathcal I_\alpha$. The product ideal $\mathcal J=\mathcal I_1\cdots\mathcal I_t$ equals the intersection $\bigcap_\alpha\mathcal I_\alpha$: on an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}A$ the ideals $J_\alpha$ of the $Z_\alpha$ satisfy $V(J_\alpha)\cap V(J_\beta)=\varnothing$ for $\alpha\ne\beta$, so $J_\alpha+J_\beta=A$ and the product of pairwise comaximal ideals is their intersection. At a point $x\in Z_\alpha$ one has $\mathcal I_{\beta,x}=\mathcal O_x$ for $\beta\ne\alpha$, so $\mathcal J_x=\mathcal I_{\alpha,x}$; therefore $V(\mathcal J)=\bigsqcup_\alpha Z_\alpha$ as subschemes of $\mathbb P^M$, and the natural morphism $\bigsqcup_\alpha Z_\alpha\to\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$ is a closed immersion. Now let $X_1,\dots,X_t$ be projective $\mathbb C$-schemes, say $X_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb P^{M_\alpha}_{\mathbb C}$ closed. The coordinate-block maps $\mathbb P^{M_\alpha}_{\mathbb C}\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$, $M=\sum_\alpha(M_\alpha+1)-1$, identify the projective spaces with pairwise disjoint linear subspaces (vanishing of all coordinates outside one block), and are closed immersions; the images of the $X_\alpha$ are closed subschemes with pairwise disjoint underlying sets, so the preceding paragraph realizes $\bigsqcup_\alpha X_\alpha$ as a closed subscheme of $\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$. Hence a finite disjoint union of projective $\mathbb C$-schemes is projective over $\mathbb C$.

Local reduction to pure dimensions and constant codimension. Let $Y$ be a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme and $C\subseteq Y$ a regular closed subscheme with ideal sheaf $\mathcal I$, a coherent ideal. Fix $x\in C$; if $C=\varnothing$ there is nothing to prove. Since smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-schemes and regular finite-type $\mathbb C$-schemes are smooth over $\mathbb C$ in characteristic zero, $C$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$ and, being regular Noetherian and reduced, each of its points lies on exactly one irreducible component; the components of $C$ are therefore pairwise disjoint, finitely many, and each is a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme of pure dimension $n$, with local rings equal to those of $C$ at its points. Let $C_0$ be the component through $x$ and let $Y^\circ$ be the connected component of $Y$ containing $x$; it is a single irreducible component, hence pure of dimension $m$, and open in $Y$. Choose an affine open $U\subseteq Y^\circ$ containing $x$ and disjoint from $C\smallsetminus C_0$ (a finite union of closed sets missing $x$). Then $U$ is smooth of pure dimension $m$, $C\cap U=C_0\cap U$ is closed in $U$, smooth, irreducible of dimension $n$, and the closed immersion $C\cap U\hookrightarrow U$ has constant codimension $d=m-n$.

Regularity and components. A point $w\in W$ is a regular point of $Z$: the local rings of $Z$ and $W$ at $w$ coincide by step 1.1, and a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme has regular local rings. Every irreducible component of $Z$ meets $W$: for a component $Z_\alpha$ of the reduced Noetherian $Z$, the complement of the union of the finitely many other components is a nonempty open subset of $Z$ contained in $Z_\alpha$, nonemptiness holding because otherwise irreducibility of $Z_\alpha$ would place it inside one of the other components, contradicting maximality; and the dense open $W$ meets every nonempty open subset. If $Z$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$, as the schemes $P$, $P_i$ and $Z'$ below are, then its irreducible components are pairwise disjoint: a common point of two components would give the local ring there two distinct minimal primes and hence a non-domain, whereas a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme has regular local rings, which are domains. Consequently, for smooth $Z$, the components are finitely many pairwise disjoint integral closed subschemes, open and closed in $Z$.

Blowups preserve finite disjoint unions of integral projective schemes. Let $X=\bigsqcup_\alpha X_\alpha$ with each $X_\alpha$ integral, finite type and H-projective over $\mathbb C$, and let $\mathcal I$ be a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf of finite type on $X$; write $\mathcal I_\alpha=\mathcal I|_{X_\alpha}$. Since the pieces are open and closed, the blowup restricts: $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X\cong\bigsqcup_\alpha\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I_\alpha}X_\alpha$. If $\mathcal I_\alpha=0$ then that piece is empty; if $\mathcal I_\alpha\ne0$ then $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I_\alpha}X_\alpha$ is integral, finite type and H-projective by step 1.2. So the blowup is again a finite disjoint union of integral projective $\mathbb C$-schemes, and it is projective over $\mathbb C$ by step 1.3; the relevant ideals are quasi-coherent of finite type, as ideals of closed subschemes of finite-type $\mathbb C$-schemes (affine-locally the kernel of a surjection of Noetherian rings, hence finitely generated).

Smoothness of the blowup along a regular center. Keep the notation of step 1.4 and first blow up the coordinate subspace: for $A=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_m]$ and $I=(x_{n+1},\dots,x_m)$, the chart of $\operatorname{Bl}_I\operatorname{Spec}A$ indexed by $x_j$ ($n<j\le m$) is $\operatorname{Spec}A[I/x_j]$, and $A[I/x_j]$ is generated over $A$ by the fractions $x_l/x_j$ ($n<l\le m$, $l\ne j$); substituting $x_l=y_lx_j$ exhibits it as the polynomial ring $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n,x_j,\ y_l\ (n<l\le m,\ l\ne j)]$, the two presentations agreeing inside $A_{x_j}$ because the $y_l$ are algebraically independent over $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n,x_j]$ (clearing denominators uses only that $x_j$ is a nonzerodivisor). Hence $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathbb A^n}\mathbb A^m$ is covered by affine spaces and is smooth over $\mathbb C$. Now by [F7] the closed immersion $C\cap U\hookrightarrow U$ of step 1.4 is, at each of its points, locally in the étale topology the inverse image of the coordinate inclusion $\mathbb A^n\subset\mathbb A^m$: there are a Zariski open $V\subseteq U$ and an étale morphism $\varphi:V\to\mathbb A^m_{\mathbb C}$ with $\varphi^{-1}(\mathbb A^n)=C\cap V$ as closed subschemes. Since $\varphi$ is flat and blowups commute with flat base change along the inverse image ideal, $\operatorname{Bl}_{C\cap V}V\cong\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathbb A^n}\mathbb A^m\times_{\mathbb A^m}V$. The projection of this fibre product to $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathbb A^n}\mathbb A^m$ is the base change of the étale morphism $\varphi$, hence étale, and étale morphisms are smooth; a composite of smooth morphisms is smooth, so the model base change, and therefore $\operatorname{Bl}_{C\cap V}V$, is smooth over $\mathbb C$.

Conclusion for one blowup and for sequences. With $\pi:\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y\to Y$ and $x\in C$ as in step 1.4, choose the open $V$ of step 2.3 around $x$; the open subscheme $\pi^{-1}(V)$ of the blowup is smooth over $\mathbb C$. Points of $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y$ mapping outside $C$ lie in the open subscheme $\pi^{-1}(Y\smallsetminus C)$, which is isomorphic to the smooth scheme $Y\smallsetminus C$; as $x$ ranges over $C$, these opens cover $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y$, and smoothness is local on the source, so $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}Y$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$. The blowup is finite type over $\mathbb C$, so the same statement applies to it in place of $Y$: if $C_1\subseteq Y_1$ is a regular closed subscheme of a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme $Y_1$, then $\operatorname{Bl}_{C_1}Y_1$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$. By induction, every scheme obtained from a smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme by a finite sequence of blowups along regular closed subschemes is smooth over $\mathbb C$.

The model construction: desingularizing the closure. Let $P$ be a smooth projective $\mathbb C$-scheme, $Z\subseteq P$ a reduced closed subscheme and $W\subseteq Z$ an open dense subscheme that is smooth over $\mathbb C$. Apply [F3] to $Z\subseteq P$: there is a sequence $P=P_0\leftarrow P_1\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow P_r$ of blowups of regular centers with strict transforms $Z_i\subseteq P_i$, and $Z'=Z_r$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$ with the composite $P_r\to P$ an isomorphism over the smooth locus of $Z$, hence over $W$. Each $P_i$ is a finite disjoint union of integral projective $\mathbb C$-schemes: $P_0=P$ is smooth projective, so it is such a union by step 2.1, and each step is a blowup along the ideal sheaf of a regular closed subscheme, a coherent ideal, so step 2.2 applies inductively. Let $W'$ be the preimage of $W$ in $Z'$; it is open in $Z'$ and isomorphic to $W$. Every irreducible component of $Z'$ meets $W'$: the composite $Z'\to Z$ is proper and birational on every component, so a component of $Z'$ maps onto a component of $Z$; a component of $Z'$ disjoint from $W'$ would have image contained in $Z\smallsetminus W$, a closed set, but every component of $Z$ meets the dense open $W$ by step 2.1, a contradiction. Consequently the ideal $\mathcal I\subseteq\mathcal O_{Z'}$ of the reduced closed subscheme $Z'\smallsetminus W'$ is coherent and is not identically zero on any irreducible component of $Z'$.

The model construction: principalizing the boundary. Keep step 3.2 and decompose $Z'=\bigsqcup_\alpha Z'_\alpha$ into its finitely many components, open and closed in $Z'$ by step 2.1. For each $\alpha$, apply [F4] to the smooth finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme $Z'_\alpha$ and the restricted ideal $\mathcal I_\alpha$ if $\mathcal I_\alpha\ne\mathcal O_{Z'_\alpha}$, and take the identity sequence if $\mathcal I_\alpha=\mathcal O_{Z'_\alpha}$; the centers lie in the successive supports, which map into $\operatorname{supp}\mathcal I_\alpha$, so at every step the blowup is an isomorphism over the complement of the preimage of $\operatorname{supp}\mathcal I_\alpha$, and the composite $\sigma_\alpha:X_\alpha\to Z'_\alpha$ is an isomorphism over $Z'_\alpha\smallsetminus\operatorname{supp}\mathcal I_\alpha$. Set $X=\bigsqcup_\alpha X_\alpha$ and $\sigma=\bigsqcup_\alpha\sigma_\alpha$. Each $X_\alpha$ is a finite sequence of blowups of the integral projective scheme $Z'_\alpha$ along regular centers: by step 2.2 each intermediate scheme is a finite disjoint union of integral projective $\mathbb C$-schemes, and by step 3.1 it is smooth; hence each $X_\alpha$ is integral (or empty), smooth and projective, and $X$ is smooth and projective by step 1.3. On each $Z'_\alpha$ with $\mathcal I_\alpha\ne\mathcal O_{Z'_\alpha}$, the total transform $\sigma_\alpha^*\mathcal I_\alpha$ is the ideal of an effective Cartier divisor with SNC support; on pieces with $\mathcal I_\alpha=\mathcal O_{Z'_\alpha}$ it is the unit ideal, defining the zero divisor with empty support. Let $D\subseteq X$ be the union of these supports with reduced structure: its ideal is, locally, generated by the products of the components' equations, so $D$ is a reduced effective Cartier divisor with simple normal crossings support. Finally $\sigma$ is an isomorphism over $Z'\smallsetminus\operatorname{supp}\mathcal I=W'$, so $X\smallsetminus D\cong W'\cong W$, and the composite morphism $c:X\to P_r\to\cdots\to P$ restricts to the given open immersion $W\hookrightarrow Z\subseteq P$. This proves: (C) for every smooth projective $P$, reduced closed $Z\subseteq P$ and open dense smooth $W\subseteq Z$, there are a smooth projective $X$, a reduced SNC divisor $D\subseteq X$, an isomorphism $X\smallsetminus D\cong W$ and a morphism $c:X\to P$ inducing the inclusion of $W$; moreover $X$ is a finite disjoint union of integral projective pieces.

Existence of an SNC projective compactification. By [F1] there is a quasi-compact immersion $\iota:U\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$; let $Z\subseteq\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ be its scheme-theoretic image, so that $U\cong Z\cap V$ is open and dense in the reduced closed subscheme $Z$, with $U$ contained in the regular locus, by steps 1.1 and 2.1. Apply (C) of step 4.1 with $P=\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ and $W=U$: the output $X$ is a finite disjoint union of integral projective smooth $\mathbb C$-schemes with a reduced SNC boundary divisor $D$ and $X\smallsetminus D\cong U$. The exceptional boundary divisor misses the generic point of every component, so its intersection with each irreducible component is a proper closed subset and hence nowhere dense; therefore $X\smallsetminus D$ is dense in $X$, and $j:U\cong X\smallsetminus D\hookrightarrow X$ is a smooth projective compactification with reduced SNC boundary. If $U=\varnothing$ the same construction with $Z=\varnothing$ returns $X=\varnothing$ and the empty divisor, and all claims are vacuous.

Common domination. Let $U\hookrightarrow X_1,\dots,U\hookrightarrow X_t$ be smooth projective compactifications, and put $P=X_1\times_{\mathbb C}\cdots\times_{\mathbb C}X_t$. Each $X_i$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$ and H-projective, so $P$ is smooth over $\mathbb C$ by stability of smoothness under base change and composition, and projective over $\mathbb C$: the product of closed immersions $X_1\times_{\mathbb C}\cdots\times_{\mathbb C}X_t\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^{N_1}_{\mathbb C}\times_{\mathbb C}\cdots\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^{N_t}_{\mathbb C}$ is a closed immersion by iterated base change, and the iterated Segre embeddings are closed immersions. The diagonal morphism $\delta:U\to P$ is an immersion: it is the composite of the diagonal $U\to U\times_{\mathbb C}\cdots\times_{\mathbb C}U$, a closed immersion because $U$ is separated over $\mathbb C$, with the product of the open immersions $U\hookrightarrow X_i$, which is an open immersion; it is quasi-compact because $U$ is Noetherian and $P$ is quasi-compact. Let $Z$ be its scheme-theoretic image; by step 1.1, $Z$ is reduced with $W:=\delta(U)\cong U$ open, dense and contained in its regular locus. Apply (C) of step 4.1 to $(P,Z,W)$ and compose the resulting morphism $c:X\to P$ with the projections: the composites $X\to X_i$ restrict to the identity of $U$ under the identifications $X\smallsetminus D\cong U$, and $X$ is a smooth projective compactification of $U$ with reduced SNC boundary dominating all $X_i$. For the empty family, step 5.1 already supplies a compactification.

Extension of morphisms. Let $\varphi:U\to V$ be a morphism of smooth quasiprojective complex varieties and let $U\hookrightarrow\tilde U$, $V\hookrightarrow\tilde V$ be smooth projective compactifications. Set $P=\tilde U\times_{\mathbb C}\tilde V$; as in step 6.1 it is smooth and projective. Consider the morphism $\gamma=(\iota,\varphi):U\to P$, where $\iota$ is the open immersion $U\hookrightarrow\tilde U$; it factors as the graph morphism $U\to U\times_{\mathbb C}V$, a closed immersion because $V$ is separated over $\mathbb C$, followed by the open immersion $U\times_{\mathbb C}V\hookrightarrow\tilde U\times_{\mathbb C}\tilde V$, so $\gamma$ is an immersion, and it is quasi-compact because $U$ is Noetherian. Let $Z$ be the scheme-theoretic image of $\gamma$; by step 1.1, $Z$ is reduced and $W:=\gamma(U)\cong U$ is open, dense and smooth inside $Z$. Apply (C) of step 4.1 to $(P,Z,W)$, obtaining a smooth projective compactification $X$ of $U$ with reduced SNC boundary and a morphism $c:X\to P$ inducing $\gamma$ on $U$. Then the composite of $c$ with the second projection $P\to\tilde V$ is a morphism $X\to\tilde V$ restricting to $\varphi$ on $U$, and the composite with the first projection is a morphism $X\to\tilde U$ restricting to the identity on $U$; so $\varphi$ extends after modifying the source compactification outside $U$. Two extensions obtained from the same data coincide on $U$, and the construction of step 6.1 applied to the two source modifications makes the resulting pullback maps agree on $U$.

Choice accounting and boundaries. AC is assumed in the statement and is consumed exactly through the suppliers of [F1]--[F8]: the scheme-theoretic image theorem and the quasi-coherent ideal correspondence, the weak embedded desingularization and principalization algorithms with their canonical regular centers and finite blowup sequences, the Serre-generation theorem behind global generation, the graph-closure corollary and the Segre and ample-pullback items, the étale-local model of regular immersions together with flat base change of blowups, and the coherence identification; all of these either assume AC directly or inherit it from the relative Proj and blowup constructions. The construction uses no further selection: components, divisors and morphisms are constructed canonically or transported along given maps, and the finite disjoint unions, diagonal and graph arguments are choice-free. Boundary cases: if $U=\varnothing$ then $X=\varnothing$ and $D=\varnothing$, the empty divisor being SNC with the empty parameter set, and all three clauses are vacuous; if $U$ is disconnected, $X$ is the finite disjoint union of the compactifications of its components and is projective by step 1.3; if a compactification already has empty boundary, the boundary ideal is the unit ideal and contributes the identity sequence and $D=\varnothing$; the statements are insensitive to replacing $X$ by another compactification, as shown in step 6.1.

boundaries.evidence: If $U=\varnothing$ the construction returns $X=\varnothing$ with the empty SNC divisor and all clauses are vacuous, as recorded in step 5.1.
A zero center ideal has empty blowup (step 1.2); an empty boundary has unit ideal, whose identity principalization defines the zero divisor (steps 4.1 and 8.1).
The one-component case of a connected $U$ and of a single compactification is steps 5.1 and 6.1, which compactify each component and then assemble the finite disjoint union.
Degenerate inputs (reducible or disconnected $U$, a compactification with empty boundary, multiplicities zero) are handled componentwise in steps 3.2, 4.1 and 8.1.
Step 4.1 uses the unit ideal and identity sequence for empty boundary; step 5.1 includes dimension zero and empty input.
AC is consumed exactly through the resolution, principalization and Serre-generation suppliers listed in [A1] and accounted for in step 8.1.

boundaries.reason: The lemma asserts existence and two domination/extension clauses, not a biconditional, so there is no forward implication to check beyond the clauses proved in steps 5.1, 6.1 and 7.1.
No converse is asserted; the uniqueness statement for two extensions is the agreement on $U$ proved at the end of step 7.1.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
Jacobian-criterion, ample-powers, Chern-form and comparison suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex scheme of pure dimension $n\ge0$.

Then the closed points of $X$ carry a structure of **complex manifold**
$X^{\mathrm{an}}$, its **analytification**: if $X\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge1$
this is a compact Hausdorff second-countable smooth complex manifold of complex
dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]); if $n=0$ it is the
finite discrete set $X(\mathbb C)$ with its unique complex structure in the
convention of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]; and if
$X=\varnothing$ then $X^{\mathrm{an}}=\varnothing$. Every standard smooth
algebraic chart of $X$ supplies holomorphic coordinate charts of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$
after shrinking to local analytic graph neighbourhoods around its complex points;
the whole algebraic chart need not be a single holomorphic coordinate chart.
More generally, every morphism between smooth separated finite-type complex schemes of pure dimensions induces a holomorphic map between their analytifications. These analytifications are constructed by the same local charts and need not be compact; separatedness and finite type ensure that they are Hausdorff and second-countable.

Moreover, for every ample invertible sheaf $A$ on $X$ there is a smooth
positive closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta_A$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ whose de Rham
class is the real image of the topological first Chern class
$c_1(A):=c_1(A^{\mathrm{an}})\in H^2(X^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Z)$:
$$J_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}[\eta_A]=\rho_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\bigl(c_1(A)\bigr),$$
where $J$ is the de Rham comparison and $\rho$ the change of coefficients
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$
([[lem-rational-cohomology-scalar-comparison-for-compact-smooth-manifolds]]).
In dimension $n=0$ and for $X=\varnothing$ every $2$-form and every degree-two
cohomology class is zero and $\eta_A=0$, so the identity holds trivially.

Throughout this page, assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]): the
analytic and cohomological suppliers invoked by the results below assume full
AC, and each item records its exact use. The definitional content below uses no
choice.

**(1) Compact Kähler manifolds.** Let $n\ge1$. A **Kähler manifold** is a complex
manifold $X$ of complex dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]) with complex structure
$J$ and a **Hermitian metric** $g$ — a Riemannian metric
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$ — whose **real fundamental form**
$\omega(v,w)=g(Jv,w)$ is

- a smooth real 2-form, the section of $\Lambda^2T^*X$ obtained by alternating
  $g(J\cdot,\cdot)$;
- **positive**: $\omega(v,Jv)=g(Jv,Jv)>0$ for every nonzero tangent vector $v$;
- **closed**: $d\omega=0$.

The manifold is **compact Kähler** when the topological space $X$ is compact.

**Orientation.** For a complex basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of a tangent space $T_xX$,
the ordered real basis $(v_1,Jv_1,\dots,v_n,Jv_n)$ is declared **positive**. This
is well defined: two complex bases differ by a complex-linear automorphism, whose
real determinant is the square of the modulus of its complex determinant and so
is positive, and the local orientations therefore glue along holomorphic charts
to a global orientation of $X$. Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a $g$-orthonormal complex
frame, so $g(v_j,v_k)=\delta_{jk}$ and $g(v_j,Jv_k)=0$, and let $e_j=g(v_j,\cdot)$ and
$f_j=g(Jv_j,\cdot)$ be the metric-dual covectors. Then
$(e_1,f_1,\dots,e_n,f_n)$ is a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe,
$f_j=-Je_j$ for the pullback action $(J\alpha)(v)=\alpha(Jv)$ of $J$ on
covectors, and

$$\omega=\sum_{j=1}^n e_j\wedge f_j .$$

The **oriented volume form** is the top form

$$dV:=\frac{\omega^n}{n!}=e_1\wedge f_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n\wedge f_n ,$$

which evaluates to $1$ on each positively oriented $g$-orthonormal frame.

**Complex dimension zero.** For $n=0$ a complex manifold is a discrete space and
compactness makes it a finite set of points with its unique complex structure;
there are no tangent vectors and no forms of positive degree, $\omega=0$, and the
operators $L,\Lambda,\partial,\bar\partial,d,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ and
all Laplacians introduced below are zero. The Hodge star is the identity on
degree zero, and $dV$ is the counting measure.

**(2) Complex-valued forms and Kähler operators.** Let $X$ be compact Kähler.
Write $\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth $k$-forms, the
complex-linear extension of the real forms of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]; the Hodge star $*$ of
[[def-riemannian-hodge-star]] extends complex-linearly, and for
$\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ the **integral inner product**

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\int_X\alpha\wedge*\bar\beta$$

is complex-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second; the
integral is that of
[[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-top-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]] and
the integrand is $\lvert\alpha\rvert^2\,dV$ when $\beta=\alpha$, so the pairing
is a positive definite Hermitian form. In holomorphic charts

$$\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(X),\qquad d=\partial+\bar\partial ,$$

with $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ of bidegree $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$
([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]); the decomposition is independent
of the holomorphic chart because holomorphic chart changes preserve bidegree.

Put $L=\omega\wedge$, so that $L:\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)\to\Omega^{k+2}(X;\mathbb C)$,
and let $\Lambda,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ be the formal adjoints of
$L,\partial,\bar\partial,d$ with respect to $\langle\,,\rangle$; existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[lem-formal-adjoints-of-differential-operators-exist-and-are-unique]], applied
to the bundle of complex-valued forms with the metric of
[[prop-riemannian-metrics-induce-metrics-on-dual-tensor-and-exterior-bundles]]
and the density $dV$. The **Laplacians** are

$$\Delta_d=dd^*+d^*d,\qquad \Delta_\partial=\partial\partial^*+\partial^*\partial,\qquad \Delta_{\bar\partial}=\bar\partial\bar\partial^*+\bar\partial^*\bar\partial ,$$

and $\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

**(3) Rational pure Hodge structures.** Let $k\in\mathbb Z$. A **rational pure
Hodge structure of weight $k$** is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space
$V$ together with a direct-sum decomposition by $\mathbb C$-subspaces

$$V_{\mathbb C}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}V^{p,q},\qquad \overline{V^{p,q}}=V^{q,p},$$

where conjugation is the $\mathbb C$-antilinear involution
$v\otimes\lambda\mapsto v\otimes\bar\lambda$. The sum is finite because
$V_{\mathbb C}$ is finite dimensional, and it is direct by definition. The **Weil
operator** $C$ is the $\mathbb C$-linear endomorphism of $V_{\mathbb C}$ acting
as $i^{p-q}$ on $V^{p,q}$; the conjugation symmetry makes $C$ commute with
conjugation, so $C$ is the complexification of a real-linear endomorphism
of $V_{\mathbb R}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$. It need not preserve $V$.

A **polarization** of such a Hodge structure is a nondegenerate $\mathbb Q$-bilinear
form $Q:V\times V\to\mathbb Q$, extended $\mathbb C$-bilinearly to $V_{\mathbb C}$,
such that

- $Q(y,x)=(-1)^kQ(x,y)$ for all $x,y$;
- $Q(V^{p,q},V^{a,b})=0$ unless $(a,b)=(q,p)$;
- $h(x,y)=Q(Cx,\bar y)$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V_{\mathbb C}$.

A **rational sub-Hodge structure** is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace
$U\subseteq V$ with $U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$.
The **Tate shift** $V(-r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, keeps the underlying $\mathbb Q$-vector
space, the Weil operator and $Q$ as they are and moves the bidegrees to
$(p+r,q+r)$, so that the weight becomes $k+2r$; equivalently, $(V(-r))^{p,q}=V^{p-r,q-r}$.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). For $n=0$, $\mathbb C^0$ is the
singleton of empty tuples with its unique topology. On an overlap of two
affine charts, the transition isomorphism and its inverse are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and let
$x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring
$\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring
whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$
([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a
classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every
point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski
neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic
stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition
$X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected
locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ — the **strata** — where locally
closed means $S_\alpha=U\cap Z$ for a Zariski-open $U\subseteq X$ and a
Zariski-closed $Z\subseteq X$, such that each
$S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure, is a smooth algebraic
subvariety of $X$; and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure
$\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is
the **frontier condition**: the frontier
$\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata
([[def-connected-space]], [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**The induced structure is the polynomial-quotient function sheaf, not a
restriction of $\mathcal O_X$.** A locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is, locally
inside an affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the set of points with $h\neq0$
and $f_1=\dots=f_r=0$ for polynomials $h,f_1,\dots,f_r$ on $Z$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]); the map
$z\mapsto(z,1/h(z))$ identifies it with the affine model
$\{(z,t):th(z)=1,\ f_1(z)=\dots=f_r(z)=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^{n+1}$, and its
**reduced induced structure sheaf** is the one transported along this
identification: locally functions of the form $a/b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the
set. The ambient restriction $\mathcal O_X|_S$ is not used, since already at the
origin of the affine line the ambient stalk is the local ring of the line while
the stalk of the reduced point is $\mathbb C$. An open subset of an affine model
is a union of finitely many principal open subsets: finite generation of the
ideal of its closed complement supplies finitely many defining polynomials,
whose nonvanishing loci cover the open subset. Each principal open subset is
again an affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety
for the induced structure sheaf. No existence theorem for stratifications, no
common-refinement theorem is asserted. The given chart data and elementary
locally closed condition above require no choice principle.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless $n$-manifold with a specified $R$-orientation $\mu$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring. Its **fundamental class** is
$$[M]=[M]_M\in H_n(M,M\setminus M;R)=H_n(M;R),$$
using [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]] with the compact support $K=M$. The final equality holds at the chain-complex level: $C_*(\varnothing;R)=0$, so quotienting by it leaves $C_*(M;R)$. The cited lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this class with point restriction $\mu_x$ at every $x\in M$. Thus the notation denotes a class determined by the

The **Kronecker pairing** on quotient classes is the rule
$$\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c),\qquad H^n(X;G)\times H_n(X;\mathbb Z)\to G.$$
Its descent through both quotients, biadditivity and naturality are justified by the following lemma [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]], before any use of the quotient pairing. It is not an assertion that evaluation gives an isomorphism to the full dual of homology.

The Kronecker rule $\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c)$ is independent of both cocycle and cycle representatives and is additive in both variables. For a continuous $f:X\to Y$, $\alpha\in H^n(Y;G)$ and $z\in H_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, it satisfies
$$\langle f^*\alpha,z\rangle=\langle\alpha,f_*z\rangle.$$
For a coefficient homomorphism $u:G\to G'$, it satisfies $\langle u_*\alpha,z\rangle=u\langle\alpha,z\rangle$. The same representative-independence argument gives the $R$-bilinear pairing for $R$-linear cochains on chains over a commutative ring $R$.

Assume AC. For every field $k$, every space $X$, and $n\ge0$, evaluation gives a natural $k$-linear isomorphism
$$H^n(X;k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_n(X;k),k).$$
There is no finite-dimensional hypothesis. The right side is the full algebraic dual.

A continuous map $f:X\to Y$ induces $f^*:H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$ for every integer $n$ and abelian group $G$, by $f^*[\varphi]=[\varphi f_\#]$. These maps satisfy $(1_X)^*=1$ and $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$. A coefficient homomorphism $u:G\to G'$ induces $u_*:H^n(X;G)\to H^n(X;G')$, covariantly functorial in coefficients and commuting with $f^*$.

For each abelian group $G$, the assignments
$$X\mapsto C_\bullet(X;G),\qquad f\mapsto f_\#$$
and
$$X\mapsto H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G),\qquad f\mapsto H_n(f_\#)$$
define covariant functors from topological spaces to chain complexes and to
abelian groups, respectively. Equivalently,
$$\operatorname{id}_{X,\#}=\operatorname{id}_{C_\bullet(X;G)},\qquad (g\circ f)_\#=g_\#\circ f_\#,$$
and for every $n\geq 0$,
$$H_n((g\circ f)_\#)=H_n(g_\#)\circ H_n(f_\#),\qquad H_n(\operatorname{id}_{X,\#})=\operatorname{id}_{H_n(X;G)}.$$

Let $X$ be a space and $R$ a commutative unital ring. For $p,n\ge0$, $\varphi\in C^p(X;R)$, and a singular $n$-simplex $\sigma$, define
$$\varphi\cap\sigma=\begin{cases}\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p])\,\sigma[p,\ldots,n],&n\ge p,\\0,&n<p.\end{cases}$$
Extend $R$-bilinearly in $\varphi$ and the finite chains of [[def-singular-simplex-and-singular-chain-group-with-coefficients]]. An $R$-linear cochain is a function on simplex generators; each value multiplies one specified back-face generator. Thus the formula is well-defined on finite formal chains and is $R$-balanced in its two inputs. It

For $\varphi\in C^p(X;R)$, $c\in C_n(X;R)$, $p,n\ge0$, over a commutative unital ring,
$$\partial(\varphi\cap c)=(-1)^p\bigl(\varphi\cap\partial c-\delta\varphi\cap c\bigr).$$
Consequently cap induces an $R$-bilinear map
$$H^p(X;R)\otimes_R H_n(X;R)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X;R).$$
Negative chain groups are zero, and no AC is assumed.

For continuous $f:X\to Y$, $\alpha\in H^p(Y;R)$ and $x\in H_n(X;R)$,
$$f_*(f^*\alpha\cap x)=\alpha\cap f_*x.$$
For $\alpha\in H^p(X;R)$, $\beta\in H^q(X;R)$ and $x\in H_n(X;R)$,
$$(\alpha\smile\beta)\cap x=\beta\cap(\alpha\cap x).$$
Here $R$ is commutative unital and cap evaluates the front face, retaining the back face. Both identities hold already on cochains and chains. No AC is needed.

The **reduced singular chain complex** $\widetilde C_\bullet(X;G)$ is obtained
from the singular chain complex by replacing degree $0$ with the kernel of the
augmentation:
$$\widetilde C_n(X;G):= \begin{cases} C_n(X;G),& n\geq 1,\\ \ker\varepsilon_X,& n=0,\\ 0,& n<0. \end{cases}$$
Its differential is the singular boundary in degrees $\geq 1$ and the zero map
$\widetilde C_0(X;G)\to 0$ in degree $0$.

For every topological space $X$ and every abelian group $G$,
$$\varepsilon_X\partial_1=0:C_1(X;G)\to G.$$
Consequently $\operatorname{im}\partial_1\subseteq\ker\varepsilon_X$, so the
reduced singular chain complex of
[[def-zero-simplex-augmentation-and-reduced-singular-homology]] is well
defined.

Let $X$ be a space, $R$ a commutative unital ring, $a\in H^p(X;R)$ and $b\in H^q(X;R)$, with $p,q\ge0$. Then
$$a\smile b=(-1)^{pq}b\smile a.$$
The defining cochain operation need not be graded commutative. No AC is required.

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space, and let $G$ be an abelian group, or an $R$-module if an $R$-module structure is desired. Its **compactly supported singular cohomology** is
$$H_c^p(X;G)=\varinjlim_{K\subseteq X\text{ compact}}H^p(X,X\setminus K;G).$$
The relative groups use [[def-relative-singular-cochain-complex]]. If $K\subseteq L$, the identity map of pairs $(X,X\setminus L)\to(X,X\setminus K)$ induces the transition from the $K$ group to the $L$ group. Concretely, a cochain vanishing on all simplices outside $K$ also vanishes on all simplices outside $L$, so this transition

If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X A$, inclusion induces an isomorphism
$$H^n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z;G)$$
for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

Assume AC. Every smooth quasiprojective complex variety $U$ admits a smooth projective compactification $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ with reduced boundary a simple normal crossings divisor $D$. Given finitely many such compactifications, there is another dominating all of them and restricting to the identity on $U$. A morphism of smooth quasiprojective varieties extends to a morphism of such compactifications after modifying the source compactification outside its open variety.
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes and let
$\Delta_{X/S}:X\to X\times_S X$ be its diagonal morphism
([[def-diagonal-morphism-scheme]]).

- $f$ is **separated** if $\Delta_{X/S}$ is a closed immersion
  ([[def-closed-immersion-schemes]]).
- $f$ is **quasi-separated** if $\Delta_{X/S}$ is a quasi-compact morphism
  ([[def-quasi-compact-and-quasi-separated-morphism]]).

A scheme $Y$ is called separated, respectively quasi-separated, when the
structure morphism $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ is separated, respectively
quasi-separated. The affine-intersection condition recorded under
[[def-quasi-compact-and-quasi-separated-morphism]] is the earlier definition;
its equivalence to quasi-compactness of $\Delta_{X/S}$ is proved in
[[lem-diagonal-quasi-compact-iff-quasi-separated]] on this page. Both properties are
properties of the morphism $f$ and of its diagonal, and neither is a condition
on the point-set topology of $X$ alone.

A morphism $i:Z\to X$ is a **closed immersion** if its underlying map is a
homeomorphism onto a closed subset and the morphism
$\mathcal O_X\to i_*\mathcal O_Z$ is surjective.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). A regular local ring $R$ of dimension $d$ is a domain and Cohen–Macaulay. For every regular system $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$, the tuple is $R$-regular and $R/(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$ is regular local of dimension $d-c$ for all $0\le c\le d$.

derivations.claim: Structure of the spaces. For the first sentence, discard the open-and-closed components of $X$ and $X'$ that do not meet $U$. Smooth projective components are integral by the regular-local-domain argument [F9], so the remaining open $U$ is dense in each. On each retained component of $X'$, its dense part in $U$ maps to one component of $X$; continuity makes the entire component map into that closed target component. Thus $p$ restricts to the retained unions. Singular chains split over these finitely many open-and-closed components, so discarding the others does not change either restriction image in $H^n(U)$. We may therefore assume the embeddings dense. By [F1], $X$ and $X'$ are compact oriented boundaryless $2d$-manifolds, $U$ is an oriented boundaryless $2d$-manifold, and $j,j'$ are orientation-preserving open embeddings; $p$ is continuous with $p\circ j'=j$. The cohomology groups and maps below are those of these analytic spaces. When $d=0$ the spaces are finite discrete, the dense open embeddings are bijective, and the assertions hold by inspection.

The morphism is the identity over $U$. Put $V=p^{-1}(j(U))$, an algebraic open subset of $X'$ containing the dense open $j'(U)$. The maps $V\to X'$ given by inclusion and $j'\circ j^{-1}\circ p$ agree on $j'(U)$. Their equalizer is a closed subscheme by separatedness, and its defining sections vanish on the dense open $j'(U)$; reducedness and [F9] make those sections zero. Thus the two maps agree on all of $V$, and every point of $V$ belongs to $j'(U)$. Hence $p^{-1}(j(U))=j'(U)$ and $p$ restricts there to $j\circ(j')^{-1}$. In particular, for every compact $K\subseteq U$, $p^{-1}(j(K))=j'(K)$ on the analytic spaces.

The augmentation evaluates the Kronecker pairing through cap. For every space $M$, $\alpha\in H^n(M;\mathbb Q)$ and $z\in H_n(M;\mathbb Q)$ one has $\Phi(\alpha,z)=\varepsilon_*([\alpha\cap z])$. Choose a cocycle $\varphi$ and a cycle $z=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\sigma$ representing the two classes; the defining cap formula in degree $n$ gives $\varphi\cap z=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)[\sigma(n)]$, a finite sum of last-vertex generators, and $\varepsilon_*$ of its class is $\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)=\Phi(\alpha,z)$. Both sides are well defined on classes: cap descends by [F4] and $\varepsilon$ descends by [F5].

The pairings. For $M=X$ or $X'$ define $\Lambda_M(\alpha, eta):=\Phi(\alpha,D_M eta)$ for $\alpha\in H^n(M;\mathbb Q)$ and $ eta\in H^{2d-n}(M;\mathbb Q)$, and define $\Lambda_U(\alpha,c):=\Phi(\alpha,D_Uc)$ for $\alpha\in H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ and $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$. Each $\Lambda$ is $\mathbb Q$-bilinear and perfect: $D_M$ and $D_U$ are isomorphisms by [F2], so for $\alpha
e0$ there is $z$ with $\Phi(\alpha,z)
e0$ and $z=D eta$ for a unique $ eta$, whence $\Lambda(\alpha, eta)
e0$; conversely, if $ eta
e0$ then $D eta
e0$ and evaluation at the nonzero class $D eta$ is a nonzero functional on the full dual of homology, realized by some $\alpha$ because $\Phi$ identifies cohomology with that full dual by [F3].

Cap, cup and the fundamental class. For a closed oriented $2d$-manifold $M$, $\alpha\in H^n(M;\mathbb Q)$ and $\beta\in H^{2d-n}(M;\mathbb Q)$, one has $\Phi(\beta,D_M\alpha)=\langle\alpha\smile\beta,[M]\rangle$, where the right side abbreviates $\Phi(\alpha\smile\beta,[M])$ for the top-degree Kronecker pairing. Indeed $D_M\alpha=\alpha\cap[M]$ by [F2], and the second cap identity of [F4] gives $(\alpha\smile\beta)\cap[M]=\beta\cap(\alpha\cap[M])=\beta\cap D_M\alpha$; applying $\varepsilon_*$ and step 1.3 in degrees $2d-n$ and $2d$ gives the stated equality.

Compatibility of the pairings with the open inclusion. For $\theta\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$ or $\theta\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$ and $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$, one has $\Lambda_U(j^*\theta,c)=\Lambda_X(\theta,e_Xc)$ and $\Lambda_U((j')^*\theta,c)=\Lambda_{X'}(\theta,e_{X'}c)$. Indeed $\Lambda_U(j^*\theta,c)=\Phi(j^*\theta,D_Uc)=\Phi(\theta,j_*D_Uc)=\Phi(\theta,D_X(e_Xc))=\Lambda_X(\theta,e_Xc)$ by the naturality in [F3] and the duality naturality in [F2], and the primed identity is identical.

The identity over compact supports. For every $n$ and every $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$ one has $p^*(e_Xc)=e_{X'}c$ in $H_c^{2d-n}(X';\mathbb Q)$, where $p^*$ acts on the relative groups, possible by step 1.2. Choose by [F7] a compact $K\subseteq U$ and $c_K\in H^{2d-n}(U,U\setminus K;\mathbb Q)$ representing $c$; the extension maps send $c$ to the colimit classes represented by $(j^*)^{-1}c_K$ and $((j')^*)^{-1}c_K$. By step 1.2, $p^{-1}(K)=K$, so $p$ induces a map of pairs $(X',X'\setminus K)\to(X,X\setminus K)$ and $p^*$ is defined on these relative groups. Functoriality of pullback gives $(j')^*\circ p^*=(p\circ j')^*=j^*$, so $(j')^*(p^*((j^*)^{-1}c_K))=j^*(j^*)^{-1}c_K=c_K=(j')^*((j')^*)^{-1}c_K$, and injectivity of the excision isomorphism $(j')^*$ gives $p^*((j^*)^{-1}c_K)=((j')^*)^{-1}c_K$; the two colimit classes therefore coincide.

The transfer and its adjointness. For each $n$ let $T_n:=D_X^{-1}\circ p_*\circ D_{X'}:H^n(X';\mathbb Q)\to H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$, a composite of the duality isomorphisms and the pushforward of [F2] and [F3]. Then, for all $a\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$ and $b\in H^{2d-n}(X;\mathbb Q)$, one has $\Lambda_X(T_na,b)=\Lambda_{X'}(a,p^*b)$. Write $\sigma=n(2d-n)$. Using step 2.1 and the definition of $T_n$, $\Lambda_X(T_na,b)=\Phi(T_na,D_Xb)=\langle b\smile T_na,[X]\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\langle T_na\smile b,[X]\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\Phi(b,D_XT_na)=(-1)^\sigma\Phi(b,p_*D_{X'}a)$, where the third equality is [F6] and the last is the defining property $D_X\circ T_n=p_*\circ D_{X'}$; naturality from [F3] turns the last term into $(-1)^\sigma\Phi(p^*b,D_{X'}a)$. On the other side, $\Lambda_{X'}(a,p^*b)=\Phi(a,D_{X'}p^*b)=\langle p^*b\smile a,[X']\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\langle a\smile p^*b,[X']\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\Phi(p^*b,D_{X'}a)$ by step 2.1 and [F6]. The two displayed values agree.

The identity on $U$. For every $a\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$ one has $j^*(T_na)=(j')^*(a)$ in $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$. By perfectness of $\Lambda_U$ in its first variable (step 1.4), it suffices to test against every $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$: $\Lambda_U(j^*(T_na),c)=\Lambda_X(T_na,e_Xc)=\Lambda_{X'}(a,p^*(e_Xc))=\Lambda_{X'}(a,e_{X'}c)=\Lambda_U((j')^*a,c)$, where the first and last equalities are step 2.2, the second is step 3.1 and the third is step 2.3.

Equality of the images. Let $b\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$. Then $(j')^*(p^*b)=(p\circ j')^*b=j^*b$, by functoriality of pullback [F1, F3], so the image of $H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$ in $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ is contained in the image of $H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$. Conversely, if $a\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$, step 4.1 exhibits $(j')^*a=j^*(T_na)$ with $T_na\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$, so the reverse inclusion holds and the two images agree for every $n$ with $0\le n\le 2d$. For $n<0$ or $n>2d$ both cohomology groups vanish by duality [F2] and the vanishing conventions of [F3], so both images are $\{0\}$; if $U=\varnothing$ then $X=X'=\varnothing$ because $U$ has dense image, and all groups vanish. This proves the first sentence of the statement.

Independence of arbitrary smooth projective compactifications. Let $X$ be an arbitrary smooth projective compactification of $U$, with no SNC hypothesis on its boundary, and let $Z$ be one with reduced SNC boundary, which exists by the first clause of [F8]. Apply the extension clause of [F8] to the identity morphism $U\to U$, viewed with source compactification $Z$ and target compactification $X$: by the closing remark of [F8] the clause is available for arbitrary smooth projective compactifications of the open variety, and it yields a smooth projective compactification $Y$ of $U$ with reduced SNC boundary together with morphisms $Y\to Z$ and $Y\to X$ restricting to the identity on $U$. Since $Y$ is projective and $X$ and $Z$ are separated, the morphisms $Y\to X$ and $Y\to Z$ are proper by [[lem-proper-source-to-separated-target-proper]], and the constructions preserve the component dimensions. Apply step 5.1 on each equal-dimensional component (and take the finite direct sums if dimensions differ); this gives, for every $n$, $\operatorname{im}(H^n(X;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q))=\operatorname{im}(H^n(Y;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q))=\operatorname{im}(H^n(Z;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q))$. Hence the image subgroup attached to a smooth projective compactification of $U$ is independent of the compactification and may always be computed from one with SNC boundary: any identity expressing that subgroup for an SNC compactification, in particular the compactification-image formula of logarithmic weights, holds for every smooth projective compactification. This proves the second sentence of the statement.

Choice accounting and boundary cases. AC is assumed in the statement and is consumed exactly through the suppliers of [F1]--[F9]: the analytification with its Chern-form, Jacobian-criterion, ample-power and comparison inputs, Poincare duality with its orientation classes and exhaustions, the full-dual universal coefficient statement, the compact-support colimit and excision, the resolution, principalization and Serre-generation inputs of [F8], and the regular-local-domain supplier of [F9]; all cap, cup, pairing and sequence computations are choice-free. Boundary cases: for $d=0$ all spaces are finite discrete, the groups vanish above degree $0$, $H^0$ has dimension the number of points, $p$ is bijective over $U$ and both images agree; for $U=\varnothing$ all groups vanish; for $n$ outside $0,\ldots,2d$ both groups vanish; for $p=\operatorname{id}_X$ the transfer $T_n$ is the identity; disconnected $X,X',U$ are covered because [F2] and [F3] decompose along components and all formulas are componentwise; the compact support $K$ of step 2.3 may be enlarged and the class $c=0$ or empty $K$ give zero in the same way. Properness of $p$ is stated but not used beyond continuity and $p\circ j'=j$, both of which hold for any morphism of compactifications; no Hodge theory, strictness or mixed structure is used, and no identification of infinite-dimensional vector spaces with double duals is made.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 discards components disjoint from U without changing restriction images; when U is empty the retained spaces and all images are zero (step 5.1).
The zero class and empty support: $c=0$ or $K=\varnothing$ give the zero compactly supported class, and both sides of the transfer identity vanish, as noted in step 7.1.
Degree zero and dimension zero: $d=0$ makes the spaces finite discrete (step 1.1), and $n=0$ is an endpoint handled in step 5.1.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
Jacobian-criterion, ample-powers, Chern-form and comparison suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex scheme of pure dimension $n\ge0$.

Then the closed points of $X$ carry a structure of **complex manifold**
$X^{\mathrm{an}}$, its **analytification**: if $X\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge1$
this is a compact Hausdorff second-countable smooth complex manifold of complex
dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]); if $n=0$ it is the
finite discrete set $X(\mathbb C)$ with its unique complex structure in the
convention of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]; and if
$X=\varnothing$ then $X^{\mathrm{an}}=\varnothing$. Every standard smooth
algebraic chart of $X$ supplies holomorphic coordinate charts of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$
after shrinking to local analytic graph neighbourhoods around its complex points;
the whole algebraic chart need not be a single holomorphic coordinate chart.
More generally, every morphism between smooth separated finite-type complex schemes of pure dimensions induces a holomorphic map between their analytifications. These analytifications are constructed by the same local charts and need not be compact; separatedness and finite type ensure that they are Hausdorff and second-countable.

Moreover, for every ample invertible sheaf $A$ on $X$ there is a smooth
positive closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta_A$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ whose de Rham
class is the real image of the topological first Chern class
$c_1(A):=c_1(A^{\mathrm{an}})\in H^2(X^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Z)$:
$$J_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}[\eta_A]=\rho_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\bigl(c_1(A)\bigr),$$
where $J$ is the de Rham comparison and $\rho$ the change of coefficients
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$
([[lem-rational-cohomology-scalar-comparison-for-compact-smooth-manifolds]]).
In dimension $n=0$ and for $X=\varnothing$ every $2$-form and every degree-two
cohomology class is zero and $\eta_A=0$, so the identity holds trivially.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). For $n=0$, $\mathbb C^0$ is the
singleton of empty tuples with its unique topology. On an overlap of two
affine charts, the transition isomorphism and its inverse are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and let
$x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring
$\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring
whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$
([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a
classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every
point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski
neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic
stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition
$X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected
locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ — the **strata** — where locally
closed means $S_\alpha=U\cap Z$ for a Zariski-open $U\subseteq X$ and a
Zariski-closed $Z\subseteq X$, such that each
$S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure, is a smooth algebraic
subvariety of $X$; and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure
$\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is
the **frontier condition**: the frontier
$\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata
([[def-connected-space]], [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**The induced structure is the polynomial-quotient function sheaf, not a
restriction of $\mathcal O_X$.** A locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is, locally
inside an affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the set of points with $h\neq0$
and $f_1=\dots=f_r=0$ for polynomials $h,f_1,\dots,f_r$ on $Z$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]); the map
$z\mapsto(z,1/h(z))$ identifies it with the affine model
$\{(z,t):th(z)=1,\ f_1(z)=\dots=f_r(z)=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^{n+1}$, and its
**reduced induced structure sheaf** is the one transported along this
identification: locally functions of the form $a/b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the
set. The ambient restriction $\mathcal O_X|_S$ is not used, since already at the
origin of the affine line the ambient stalk is the local ring of the line while
the stalk of the reduced point is $\mathbb C$. An open subset of an affine model
is a union of finitely many principal open subsets: finite generation of the
ideal of its closed complement supplies finitely many defining polynomials,
whose nonvanishing loci cover the open subset. Each principal open subset is
again an affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety
for the induced structure sheaf. No existence theorem for stratifications, no
common-refinement theorem is asserted. The given chart data and elementary
locally closed condition above require no choice principle.

Throughout this page, assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]): the
analytic and cohomological suppliers invoked by the results below assume full
AC, and each item records its exact use. The definitional content below uses no
choice.

**(1) Compact Kähler manifolds.** Let $n\ge1$. A **Kähler manifold** is a complex
manifold $X$ of complex dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]) with complex structure
$J$ and a **Hermitian metric** $g$ — a Riemannian metric
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$ — whose **real fundamental form**
$\omega(v,w)=g(Jv,w)$ is

- a smooth real 2-form, the section of $\Lambda^2T^*X$ obtained by alternating
  $g(J\cdot,\cdot)$;
- **positive**: $\omega(v,Jv)=g(Jv,Jv)>0$ for every nonzero tangent vector $v$;
- **closed**: $d\omega=0$.

The manifold is **compact Kähler** when the topological space $X$ is compact.

**Orientation.** For a complex basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of a tangent space $T_xX$,
the ordered real basis $(v_1,Jv_1,\dots,v_n,Jv_n)$ is declared **positive**. This
is well defined: two complex bases differ by a complex-linear automorphism, whose
real determinant is the square of the modulus of its complex determinant and so
is positive, and the local orientations therefore glue along holomorphic charts
to a global orientation of $X$. Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a $g$-orthonormal complex
frame, so $g(v_j,v_k)=\delta_{jk}$ and $g(v_j,Jv_k)=0$, and let $e_j=g(v_j,\cdot)$ and
$f_j=g(Jv_j,\cdot)$ be the metric-dual covectors. Then
$(e_1,f_1,\dots,e_n,f_n)$ is a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe,
$f_j=-Je_j$ for the pullback action $(J\alpha)(v)=\alpha(Jv)$ of $J$ on
covectors, and

$$\omega=\sum_{j=1}^n e_j\wedge f_j .$$

The **oriented volume form** is the top form

$$dV:=\frac{\omega^n}{n!}=e_1\wedge f_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n\wedge f_n ,$$

which evaluates to $1$ on each positively oriented $g$-orthonormal frame.

**Complex dimension zero.** For $n=0$ a complex manifold is a discrete space and
compactness makes it a finite set of points with its unique complex structure;
there are no tangent vectors and no forms of positive degree, $\omega=0$, and the
operators $L,\Lambda,\partial,\bar\partial,d,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ and
all Laplacians introduced below are zero. The Hodge star is the identity on
degree zero, and $dV$ is the counting measure.

**(2) Complex-valued forms and Kähler operators.** Let $X$ be compact Kähler.
Write $\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth $k$-forms, the
complex-linear extension of the real forms of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]; the Hodge star $*$ of
[[def-riemannian-hodge-star]] extends complex-linearly, and for
$\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ the **integral inner product**

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\int_X\alpha\wedge*\bar\beta$$

is complex-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second; the
integral is that of
[[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-top-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]] and
the integrand is $\lvert\alpha\rvert^2\,dV$ when $\beta=\alpha$, so the pairing
is a positive definite Hermitian form. In holomorphic charts

$$\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(X),\qquad d=\partial+\bar\partial ,$$

with $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ of bidegree $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$
([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]); the decomposition is independent
of the holomorphic chart because holomorphic chart changes preserve bidegree.

Put $L=\omega\wedge$, so that $L:\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)\to\Omega^{k+2}(X;\mathbb C)$,
and let $\Lambda,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ be the formal adjoints of
$L,\partial,\bar\partial,d$ with respect to $\langle\,,\rangle$; existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[lem-formal-adjoints-of-differential-operators-exist-and-are-unique]], applied
to the bundle of complex-valued forms with the metric of
[[prop-riemannian-metrics-induce-metrics-on-dual-tensor-and-exterior-bundles]]
and the density $dV$. The **Laplacians** are

$$\Delta_d=dd^*+d^*d,\qquad \Delta_\partial=\partial\partial^*+\partial^*\partial,\qquad \Delta_{\bar\partial}=\bar\partial\bar\partial^*+\bar\partial^*\bar\partial ,$$

and $\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

**(3) Rational pure Hodge structures.** Let $k\in\mathbb Z$. A **rational pure
Hodge structure of weight $k$** is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space
$V$ together with a direct-sum decomposition by $\mathbb C$-subspaces

$$V_{\mathbb C}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}V^{p,q},\qquad \overline{V^{p,q}}=V^{q,p},$$

where conjugation is the $\mathbb C$-antilinear involution
$v\otimes\lambda\mapsto v\otimes\bar\lambda$. The sum is finite because
$V_{\mathbb C}$ is finite dimensional, and it is direct by definition. The **Weil
operator** $C$ is the $\mathbb C$-linear endomorphism of $V_{\mathbb C}$ acting
as $i^{p-q}$ on $V^{p,q}$; the conjugation symmetry makes $C$ commute with
conjugation, so $C$ is the complexification of a real-linear endomorphism
of $V_{\mathbb R}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$. It need not preserve $V$.

A **polarization** of such a Hodge structure is a nondegenerate $\mathbb Q$-bilinear
form $Q:V\times V\to\mathbb Q$, extended $\mathbb C$-bilinearly to $V_{\mathbb C}$,
such that

- $Q(y,x)=(-1)^kQ(x,y)$ for all $x,y$;
- $Q(V^{p,q},V^{a,b})=0$ unless $(a,b)=(q,p)$;
- $h(x,y)=Q(Cx,\bar y)$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V_{\mathbb C}$.

A **rational sub-Hodge structure** is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace
$U\subseteq V$ with $U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$.
The **Tate shift** $V(-r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, keeps the underlying $\mathbb Q$-vector
space, the Weil operator and $Q$ as they are and moves the bidegrees to
$(p+r,q+r)$, so that the weight becomes $k+2r$; equivalently, $(V(-r))^{p,q}=V^{p-r,q-r}$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open. Write $\Omega^k(U;\mathbb C)$ for smooth
complex-valued $k$-forms. For increasing multi-indices
$I=(i_1<\cdots<i_p)$ and $J=(j_1<\cdots<j_q)$, write
$dz^I=dz_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dz_{i_p}$ and
$d\bar z^J=d\bar z_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge d\bar z_{j_q}$. The invertible
change of cotangent basis
$dz_j=dx_j+i\,dy_j$, $d\bar z_j=dx_j-i\,dy_j$ gives the direct sum
decomposition

$$\Omega^k(U;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(U),\qquad \Omega^{p,q}(U)=\left\{\sum_{I,J}a_{I,J}(z)\,dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J:a_{I,J}\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C)\right\},$$

where $0\le p,q\le n$ and every sum is finite. On a $(p,q)$ form
$\eta=\sum_{I,J}a_{I,J}dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J$, define

$$\partial\eta=\sum_{I,J,j}(\partial_{z_j}a_{I,J})\,dz_j\wedge dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J,\qquad \bar\partial\eta=\sum_{I,J,j}(\partial_{\bar z_j}a_{I,J})\,d\bar z_j\wedge dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J.$$

Repeated differentials vanish by alternation; components outside the range
$0\le p,q\le n$ are zero. These operators are the components of $d$ of
bidegrees $(p+1,q)$ and $(p,q+1)$.

Fix $m\ge1$, read $\mathbb C^m$ through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]], and let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be
open and $a\in U$.

A map $L:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C$ is **$\mathbb C$-linear** when
$L(u+v)=L(u)+L(v)$ and $L(\lambda u)=\lambda L(u)$ for all $u,v\in\mathbb C^m$
and **all $\lambda\in\mathbb C$**, the vector-space operations being those of
[[def-vector-space]] over the field $\mathbb C$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Requiring the second clause only for real
$\lambda$ gives the strictly weaker notion of an $\mathbb R$-linear map
([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) read through the dictionary.

A function $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** when there is a
$\mathbb C$-linear $L:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C$ with

$$f(a+h)=f(a)+L(h)+r(h),\qquad \frac{|r(h)|}{\lVert h\rVert}\longrightarrow0 \ \text{ as } h\to0,$$

the quotient being considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$ and the norm being that
of the dictionary ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). The map $f$ is **holomorphic
on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$.

**Such an $L$ is unique**, so the notation $Df(a):=L$ is well posed. If $L_1$ and
$L_2$ both satisfy the condition, then $T=L_1-L_2$ is $\mathbb C$-linear and
$|T(h)|/\lVert h\rVert\to0$; fixing $h\ne0$ and taking $h$ replaced by $th$ for
real $t\in(0,1)$ small enough that $a+th\in U$, $\mathbb C$-linearity gives
$|T(h)|/\lVert h\rVert=|T(th)|/\lVert th\rVert$, whose limit as $t\to0$ is $0$;
so $T(h)=0$ for every $h$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume AC. For a compact Kähler manifold $X$ in the sense of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], every de
Rham class has a unique smooth harmonic representative and
$$H^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(X),\qquad \overline{H^{p,q}(X)}=H^{q,p}(X).$$
Here $H^{p,q}(X)$ is precisely the set of classes with a $d$-closed smooth
representative of type $(p,q)$, so the decomposition is independent of the
Kähler metric. Writing $\Omega_X^p$ for the sheaf of holomorphic $p$-forms (the
kernel of $\bar\partial$ on the sheaf $\mathcal A^{p,0}$ of smooth $(p,0)$-forms),
$H^{p,q}(X)$ is isomorphic to $H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$, the sheaf cohomology of
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]. The Hodge filtration
$F^a=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}H^{p,k-p}$ of $H^k(X;\mathbb C)$ equals the filtration
induced by the holomorphic-degree filtration of the de Rham complex, whose
spectral sequence has $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$ and degenerates at $E_1$.
Pullback by holomorphic maps of compact Kähler manifolds and cup product
preserve Hodge type, so $H^k(X;\mathbb Q)$ is a functorial rational pure Hodge
structure.
