[[def-equivariant-constructible-derived-category-for-complex-algebraic-varieties]]
gives a locally small triangulated category $D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ with conservative

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field of
characteristic zero, let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic
variety ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]),
regarded with its analytic topology as in
[[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]], and let
$G=\prod_i\operatorname{GL}_{n_i}(\mathbb C)$ be a finite product of complex
general linear groups ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]])
acting algebraically on $X$
([[def-algebraic-group-action-and-scheme-theoretic-stabilizer]]). Equip the
finite product $G$ with its usual topology and the product $G^p\times X$ with
the product topology.

**The action nerve.** For $p\ge0$ put $Z_p=G^p\times X$, where $G^0$ is a
one-point space, so that $Z_0=X$, and let
$d_i:Z_p\to Z_{p-1}$ for $p\ge1$ $(0\le i\le p)$ and $s_i:Z_p\to Z_{p+1}$ for $p\ge0$
$(0\le i\le p)$ be the face and degeneracy maps of the nerve of the
translation groupoid $G\times X\rightrightarrows X$: writing
$(g_1,\ldots,g_p,x)\in Z_p$,
$$d_0(g_1,\ldots,g_p,x)=(g_2,\ldots,g_p,x),\qquad d_p(g_1,\ldots,g_p,x)=(g_1,\ldots,g_{p-1},g_px),$$
$$d_i(g_1,\ldots,g_p,x)=(g_1,\ldots,g_{i-1},g_ig_{i+1},g_{i+2},\ldots,g_p,x)\quad(0<i<p),$$
$$s_i(g_1,\ldots,g_p,x)=(g_1,\ldots,g_i,e,g_{i+1},\ldots,g_p,x).$$
These are continuous and satisfy the simplicial identities, so $Z_\bullet$ is a
simplicial space in the sense of
[[def-simplicial-object-and-simplicial-commutative-ring]]; equivalently, a
simplicial operator $\alpha:[p]\to[m]$ acts by a continuous map
$Z_\alpha:Z_m\to Z_p$. In general this action nerve has no augmentation to
$X$: already the two faces $G\times X\rightrightarrows X$ are projection and
action and need not agree. For a free action with principal quotient
$P\to P/G$, its action nerve is instead augmented over $P/G$, as in
[[lem-locally-split-cech-nerves-give-derived-cartesian-sheaf-descent]].

**Simplicial sheaves.** A simplicial sheaf of $k$-vector spaces on
$Z_\bullet$ is a family $F=(F_p)_{p\ge0}$ in which $F_p$ is a sheaf of
$k$-vector spaces on $Z_p$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-module-on-ringed-space]]) together with structure morphisms
$Z_\alpha^{-1}F_p\to F_m$ for every monotone $\alpha:[p]\to[m]$, subject to
the identity and composition identities; a morphism $F\to G$ is a levelwise
family of $k$-linear sheaf maps commuting with the structure morphisms.
Kernels and cokernels are formed levelwise (cokernels after sheafification of
the presheaf cokernel) and exactness is checked levelwise, so the category
$\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_\bullet)$ of simplicial sheaves is abelian; under AC it
carries explicit coinduced injective resolutions and a bounded derived
category, with the conventions recorded in
[[lem-locally-split-cech-nerves-give-derived-cartesian-sheaf-descent]], whose
bounded-below injective model uses
[[lem-field-module-sheaves-have-injective-derived-models]]. Write
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_\bullet))$ for that bounded derived category
([[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]), with its ordinary shift
$[1]$ and cone triangles.

**Cartesian cohomology.** A complex $A$ of simplicial sheaves has **Cartesian
cohomology** if for every monotone $\alpha:[p]\to[m]$ the structure morphism
$Z_\alpha^{-1}H^j(A_p)\to H^j(A_m)$ is an isomorphism for every $j$; this is
the condition that all structure morphisms of the simplicial sheaf $H^j(A)$
are isomorphisms, in the notation of
[[lem-locally-split-cech-nerves-give-derived-cartesian-sheaf-descent]].

**Definition.** The **equivariant constructible derived category**
$D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_\bullet))$ consisting of the complexes $A$
satisfying:

1. $A$ is bounded: the single complex $A$ has only finitely many nonzero
   cohomology simplicial sheaves $H^j(A)$, i.e. there are integers $a\le b$
   with $H^j(A)=0$ for $j<a$ and $j>b$. This is uniform cohomological
   boundedness in the simplicial sheaf category; it is not a degreewise bound
   on the components $A_p$;
2. $A$ has Cartesian cohomology; and
3. the restriction $A_0$ of $A$ to the degree-zero space $Z_0=X$ has
   cohomology sheaves that are algebraically constructible with
   finite-dimensional stalks
   ([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]).

**Ext and restriction.** Morphisms in $D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ are morphisms in the
ambient category $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_\bullet))$; they are not morphisms
in the derived category of naive $G$-equivariant sheaves. Set
$\operatorname{Ext}_G^m(A,B)=\operatorname{Hom}(A,B[m])$ with the ordinary
cochain shift. Evaluation at $p=0$ is exact because kernels, cokernels and
cohomology of complexes of simplicial sheaves are formed levelwise, so it
induces the **forgetful functor** (restriction to $X$)
$D^b_{G,c}(X;k)\to D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$, $A\mapsto A_0$; its target is
the bounded constructible category $D_c^b(X;k)$ of
[[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]].

**Well-formedness.** This definition fixes only the ambient category, the
object class and the conventions; the statements that make it usable — that
$D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ is a locally small triangulated category, that restriction to
$X$ is conservative, that coinduced simplicial injectives compute its derived
morphism groups, and that the finite general linear Stiefel resolutions realize
it inside the bounded resolution triples on $X_N$ — are the content of
[[lem-cartesian-simplicial-sheaves-model-equivariant-constructible-derived-hom]],
which is recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps` because that lemma
depends on this definition. AC is inherited from the two construction
suppliers named above and is used there for injective replacements; no further
choice principle is introduced here, and the shift convention is the ordinary
one of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let
$G=\prod_i\operatorname{GL}_{n_i}(\mathbb C)$ be a finite product of complex
general linear groups acting algebraically on a separated finite-type complex
algebraic variety $X$, and let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero. For
bounded algebraically constructible $A,B$ in the equivariant category
$D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ of
[[def-equivariant-constructible-derived-category-for-complex-algebraic-varieties]]:

1. every $\operatorname{Ext}_G^m(A,B)=\operatorname{Hom}(A,B[m])$ is
   finite-dimensional over $k$ and vanishes for all sufficiently negative $m$;
2. for every field extension $k\to K$ of characteristic-zero fields, the
   canonical map
   $\operatorname{Ext}_G^m(A,B)\otimes_kK\to\operatorname{Ext}_G^m(A_K,B_K)$
   is an isomorphism, natural in $A$ and $B$ and compatible with shifts and
   with Yoneda composition;
3. coefficient extension commutes with the coherent six operations, normalized
   Verdier duality, perverse truncation and intermediate extension on these
   bounded constructible objects.

The total Ext space $\bigoplus_m\operatorname{Ext}_G^m(A,B)$ need not be
finite-dimensional, and simplicity is not asserted to be preserved under
coefficient extension.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field of
characteristic zero, let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic
variety ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]),
regarded with its analytic topology as in
[[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]], and let
$G=\prod_i\operatorname{GL}_{n_i}(\mathbb C)$ be a finite product of complex
general linear groups ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]])
acting algebraically on $X$
([[def-algebraic-group-action-and-scheme-theoretic-stabilizer]]). Equip the
finite product $G$ with its usual topology and the product $G^p\times X$ with
the product topology.

**The action nerve.** For $p\ge0$ put $Z_p=G^p\times X$, where $G^0$ is a
one-point space, so that $Z_0=X$, and let
$d_i:Z_p\to Z_{p-1}$ for $p\ge1$ $(0\le i\le p)$ and $s_i:Z_p\to Z_{p+1}$ for $p\ge0$
$(0\le i\le p)$ be the face and degeneracy maps of the nerve of the
translation groupoid $G\times X\rightrightarrows X$: writing
$(g_1,\ldots,g_p,x)\in Z_p$,
$$d_0(g_1,\ldots,g_p,x)=(g_2,\ldots,g_p,x),\qquad d_p(g_1,\ldots,g_p,x)=(g_1,\ldots,g_{p-1},g_px),$$
$$d_i(g_1,\ldots,g_p,x)=(g_1,\ldots,g_{i-1},g_ig_{i+1},g_{i+2},\ldots,g_p,x)\quad(0<i<p),$$
$$s_i(g_1,\ldots,g_p,x)=(g_1,\ldots,g_i,e,g_{i+1},\ldots,g_p,x).$$
These are continuous and satisfy the simplicial identities, so $Z_\bullet$ is a
simplicial space in the sense of
[[def-simplicial-object-and-simplicial-commutative-ring]]; equivalently, a
simplicial operator $\alpha:[p]\to[m]$ acts by a continuous map
$Z_\alpha:Z_m\to Z_p$. In general this action nerve has no augmentation to
$X$: already the two faces $G\times X\rightrightarrows X$ are projection and
action and need not agree. For a free action with principal quotient
$P\to P/G$, its action nerve is instead augmented over $P/G$, as in
[[lem-locally-split-cech-nerves-give-derived-cartesian-sheaf-descent]].

**Simplicial sheaves.** A simplicial sheaf of $k$-vector spaces on
$Z_\bullet$ is a family $F=(F_p)_{p\ge0}$ in which $F_p$ is a sheaf of
$k$-vector spaces on $Z_p$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-module-on-ringed-space]]) together with structure morphisms
$Z_\alpha^{-1}F_p\to F_m$ for every monotone $\alpha:[p]\to[m]$, subject to
the identity and composition identities; a morphism $F\to G$ is a levelwise
family of $k$-linear sheaf maps commuting with the structure morphisms.
Kernels and cokernels are formed levelwise (cokernels after sheafification of
the presheaf cokernel) and exactness is checked levelwise, so the category
$\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_\bullet)$ of simplicial sheaves is abelian; under AC it
carries explicit coinduced injective resolutions and a bounded derived
category, with the conventions recorded in
[[lem-locally-split-cech-nerves-give-derived-cartesian-sheaf-descent]], whose
bounded-below injective model uses
[[lem-field-module-sheaves-have-injective-derived-models]]. Write
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_\bullet))$ for that bounded derived category
([[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]), with its ordinary shift
$[1]$ and cone triangles.

**Cartesian cohomology.** A complex $A$ of simplicial sheaves has **Cartesian
cohomology** if for every monotone $\alpha:[p]\to[m]$ the structure morphism
$Z_\alpha^{-1}H^j(A_p)\to H^j(A_m)$ is an isomorphism for every $j$; this is
the condition that all structure morphisms of the simplicial sheaf $H^j(A)$
are isomorphisms, in the notation of
[[lem-locally-split-cech-nerves-give-derived-cartesian-sheaf-descent]].

**Definition.** The **equivariant constructible derived category**
$D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_\bullet))$ consisting of the complexes $A$
satisfying:

1. $A$ is bounded: the single complex $A$ has only finitely many nonzero
   cohomology simplicial sheaves $H^j(A)$, i.e. there are integers $a\le b$
   with $H^j(A)=0$ for $j<a$ and $j>b$. This is uniform cohomological
   boundedness in the simplicial sheaf category; it is not a degreewise bound
   on the components $A_p$;
2. $A$ has Cartesian cohomology; and
3. the restriction $A_0$ of $A$ to the degree-zero space $Z_0=X$ has
   cohomology sheaves that are algebraically constructible with
   finite-dimensional stalks
   ([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]).

**Ext and restriction.** Morphisms in $D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ are morphisms in the
ambient category $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_\bullet))$; they are not morphisms
in the derived category of naive $G$-equivariant sheaves. Set
$\operatorname{Ext}_G^m(A,B)=\operatorname{Hom}(A,B[m])$ with the ordinary
cochain shift. Evaluation at $p=0$ is exact because kernels, cokernels and
cohomology of complexes of simplicial sheaves are formed levelwise, so it
induces the **forgetful functor** (restriction to $X$)
$D^b_{G,c}(X;k)\to D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$, $A\mapsto A_0$; its target is
the bounded constructible category $D_c^b(X;k)$ of
[[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]].

**Well-formedness.** This definition fixes only the ambient category, the
object class and the conventions; the statements that make it usable — that
$D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ is a locally small triangulated category, that restriction to
$X$ is conservative, that coinduced simplicial injectives compute its derived
morphism groups, and that the finite general linear Stiefel resolutions realize
it inside the bounded resolution triples on $X_N$ — are the content of
[[lem-cartesian-simplicial-sheaves-model-equivariant-constructible-derived-hom]],
which is recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps` because that lemma
depends on this definition. AC is inherited from the two construction
suppliers named above and is used there for injective replacements; no further
choice principle is introduced here, and the shift convention is the ordinary
one of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]].

By [F4] it computes singular cohomology, and [F5] identifies this with constant-sheaf cohomology: $H^0=H^2=k$ and the other groups vanish. A complex of vector spaces with these cohomology groups is quasi-isomorphic to $k\oplus k[-2]$: choose cocycles representing the two generators to obtain a cochain map from $k\oplus k[-2]$ to the complex inducing these cohomology isomorphisms. Thus $R\Gamma(\mathbb P^1,k)\simeq k\oplus k[-2]$.

The forward corner. For complexes of $k$-vector spaces one has $\operatorname{Hom}(k,C[n])=H^n(C)$, so $\operatorname{Ext}^r(L_1,L_2)=\operatorname{Hom}(k,R\Gamma(\mathbb P^1,k)[1+r])=H^{1+r}(\mathbb P^1,k)$, which by step 1.2 is $k$ for $r=-1$ and for $r=1$ and is zero otherwise; in particular both nonzero groups are one-dimensional.

The reverse corner. Similarly $\operatorname{Ext}^r(L_2,L_1)=\operatorname{Hom}(R\Gamma(\mathbb P^1,k)[1],k[r])=\operatorname{Hom}(R\Gamma(\mathbb P^1,k),k[r-1])=\operatorname{Hom}(k\oplus k[-2],k[r-1])=\operatorname{Hom}(k,k[r-1])\oplus\operatorname{Hom}(k,k[r+1])$, which is $k$ exactly when $r=1$ or $r=-1$ and is zero otherwise; so both corners have the same two nonzero degrees.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

By the convention of the Given, $U$ is the Cech nerve of the proper surjection $U_0\to X$, so [F1] proves both the sheaf and the global augmentation statements for $U$. Levelwise proper surjectivity of $U\to V$. For every $j$ the map $U_j\to V_j$ is proper surjective. For $j\leq n$ it is the identity. For $j>n$ it reads $\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{sk}_{n+1}\Delta[j],U)\to\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{sk}_n\Delta[j],U)$: the domain is obtained from the codomain by adjoining the finitely many nondegenerate $(n+1)$-faces of $\Delta[j]$, whose boundaries already lie in the $n$-skeleton, so this map is a Cartesian pullback of the finite product of the matching map $U_{n+1}\to(\operatorname{cosk}_nU)_{n+1}=V_{n+1}$; a finite product over $X$ of proper surjections, and any base change of it, is proper surjective. No local sections are required, and all limits are the finite matching limits of the Given. [given, construct, algebra]

The bisimplicial Cech model and the double total. Form the bisimplicial object $W_{r,j}=U_j\times_{V_j}\cdots\times_{V_j}U_j$ with $r+1$ factors, horizontally the Cech nerve of $U_j\to V_j$, and pull coefficients from $X$ throughout. By [F1] and step 1.2, for each fixed $j$ the horizontally augmented derived row computes the coefficient complex on $V_j$, before and after pushing forward to $X$: with $B_j:=(V_j\to X)^*F$ and $a_{r,j}:W_{r,j}\to X$ one has $Rb_{j*}B_j\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_rRa_{r,j*}a_{r,j}^*F$, where $b_j:V_j\to X$, the identifications being compatible with composition and finite sums by [F3] and [F4]. By [F2] this double total is naturally chain-homotopy equivalent to the total on the diagonal $D_j:=W_{j,j}$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2]

The retract over $X$. The bounded hypercover $U$ is a retract over $X$ of $D$. The map $i:U\to D$ repeats the same $U_j$-point in all $j+1$ horizontal factors, the horizontal degeneracy; through degree $n$ the map $U_j\to V_j$ is the identity, so $D_j=U_j$ there, and in degree $n+1$ let $r_{n+1}:D_{n+1}\to U_{n+1}$ be the projection to the first horizontal factor. Its faces and degeneracies agree with the degree-$\leq n$ identity identifications, because every horizontal factor of $W$ has the same image in $V$ and the lower-degree maps are identities; this defines a map of $(n+1)$-truncated simplicial objects over $X$, and the universal property $U=\operatorname{cosk}_{n+1}U$ extends it uniquely to $r:D\to U$. The composite $ri$ is the identity through degree $n+1$: in lower degrees because $i$ is the diagonal and $r$ the factor projection on $D_j=U_j$, and in degree $n+1$ because repeating a point and projecting a factor returns it; hence $ri=\mathrm{id}$ in every degree by the same universal property. Coefficient pullback reverses these maps, and since $r\circ i=\mathrm{id}$ the augmented total of $U$ is a retract of the augmented total of $D$; by step 2.1 the cone of the augmentation of $D$ is acyclic, and a retract of an acyclic cone is acyclic, so the augmentation of $U$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the supplied injective-resolution six-functor construction. Let $f:Y\to X$ be a proper surjective morphism of finite-type complex algebraic varieties, and let $F\in D^b_c(X;k)$ for a field $k$. Write $Y_p=Y\times_X\cdots\times_XY$ with $p+1$ factors, $f_p:Y_p\to X$, and $F_p=f_p^*F$. In the analytic topology of [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]] the natural augmented derived Cech map is a quasi-isomorphism:
$$F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Rf_{p*}F_p.$$
Here totalization is the normalized or unnormalized alternating-face total supplied by the simplicial-derived construction. There is one fixed lower cochain bound; consequently its diagonals are finite in every degree. The claim commutes with arbitrary algebraic base change and coefficient morphisms. In particular $R\Gamma(X,F)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_pR\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$. Individual fibers of $f$ need not be cohomologically acyclic, connected, or smooth.

Fix an algebraically closed field $k$. The affine models used here are polynomial zero sets $Z\subseteq k^n$, including empty and reducible sets. Their closed subsets are common zero loci of polynomial families, relative to $Z$. Intersections combine equations, and finite unions use products of equations, so these are the closed sets of a topology.

For an open $U\subseteq Z$, let $\mathcal O_Z(U)$ consist of functions $U\to k$ locally equal to $a/b$ for polynomials $a,b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the chosen neighbourhood. Pointwise operations and restriction make these sets a sheaf of $k$-algebras: quotient expressions persist on restriction, and functions that agree locally glue uniquely with the same local quotient property. At a point z its stalk is the ring of germs of such functions. Evaluation at z maps it onto k, with kernel the germs vanishing at z. A germ nonzero at z is invertible: shrink to where its numerator and denominator are both nonzero and interchange them. Thus the kernel is the unique maximal ideal. These affine models are locally ringed spaces in the sense of [[def-locally-ringed-space]], with residue fields canonically k.

A **classical algebraic prevariety** over k is a quasi-compact locally ringed space with a structure sheaf of k-algebras, covered by open subspaces isomorphic over k to these affine models. Here quasi-compact means every open cover has a finite subcover. Equivalently it admits a finite affine-model cover. To justify the converse, each affine model is quasi-compact: polynomial principal opens $D_Z(h)=\{z:h(z)\ne0\}$ form a basis. Given an open cover, take all h whose principal opens lie in a member. Their principal opens cover Z. The ideal generated by these h in $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ is finitely generated by [[thm-hilbert-basis-theorem]], iterated from the field k. Express finitely many generators using finitely many of the original h. Those finitely many h have the same common zero locus as the whole ideal, hence their principal opens still cover Z and yield a finite subcover. The empty model has the empty subcover. A finite union of quasi-compact subspaces is quasi-compact.

A map is **regular** when it is a morphism of locally ringed spaces as in [[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]] whose sheaf maps respect k. For these function sheaves its sheaf map is necessarily pullback of functions: the local stalk map induces a k-map between residue fields k, hence the identity, so the value of a pulled-back section at x is its value at the image of x. Conversely, continuous pullback of local regular functions gives a local stalk map because a function vanishing at the image vanishes after pullback.

Regularity can therefore be checked on affine charts: near every source point choose a target affine chart containing its image and an open neighbourhood in a source affine chart mapped into it; the target coordinate functions must pull back to locally polynomial quotients. This condition also implies continuity. Indeed zero sets of locally polynomial quotients are locally polynomial zero sets, hence closed; pulling back polynomial equations consequently gives closed sets. Substitution then pulls every local quotient on the target back to a local quotient on the source, using this continuity to restrict to its domain and its nonvanishing denominator. Thus the chart condition and the locally ringed-space definition agree.

A prevariety is **separated** when the equalizer of every pair of regular maps into it, from any classical prevariety, is closed. A **classical algebraic variety** is a separated prevariety. Here varieties may be reducible or empty; an **irreducible classical variety** is nonempty and irreducible in the sense of [[def-irreducible-topological-space-and-subset]]. These definitions and the local verifications above use no Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). For $n=0$, $\mathbb C^0$ is the
singleton of empty tuples with its unique topology. On an overlap of two
affine charts, the transition isomorphism and its inverse are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

**A point outside $X$, named rather than assumed.** Put

$$\infty \;:=\; \{\, y \in X : y \notin y \,\},$$

a set by Separation. Then $\infty \notin X$: were $\infty \in X$, the defining
condition applied to $\infty$ itself would give
$\infty \in \infty \iff \infty \notin \infty$. So no hypothesis about $X$ is
needed to obtain a point outside it, and the construction below is available for
every space.

**The space.** Put $X^{*} := X \cup \{\infty\}$ and

$$\mathcal{T}^{*} \;:=\; \mathcal{T} \;\cup\; \{\, X^{*} \setminus C \;:\; C \subseteq X,\ C \text{ closed in } X \text{ and a compact subset of } X \,\} .$$

The pair $(X^{*}, \mathcal{T}^{*})$ is the **one-point compactification**, or
**Alexandroff compactification**, of $X$. Members of $\mathcal{T}$ are said to be
of the **first kind** and the sets $X^{*} \setminus C$ of the **second kind**; a
set of the second kind is exactly an open set of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ containing
$\infty$, since a member of $\mathcal{T}$ is a subset of $X$, and the set $C$ is
recovered from it as $C = X^{*} \setminus (X^{*} \setminus C)$.

**$\mathcal{T}^{*}$ is a topology on $X^{*}$, and this is discharged here.**
Throughout, "closed" and "compact" without qualification mean closed in $X$ and a
compact subset of $X$ ([[def-compact-space]]); two facts about such sets are used
and both are [[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]: a subset of a
compact $C$ that is closed in $X$ is closed in the subspace $C$
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) and hence compact, and a union of two compact
subsets is compact.

*(T1).* $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$, and $X^{*} = X^{*} \setminus \varnothing$
is of the second kind, $\varnothing$ being closed in $X$ and compact.

*(T2).* Let $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}^{*}$, let $\mathcal{S}_1$ be the
members of $\mathcal{S}$ lying in $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{S}_2$ the rest, so
that every member of $\mathcal{S}_2$ is of the second kind. If
$\mathcal{S}_2 = \varnothing$ then $\bigcup \mathcal{S} = \bigcup \mathcal{S}_1$
lies in $\mathcal{T}$ by (T2) in $X$. Otherwise put
$U := \bigcup \mathcal{S}_1 \in \mathcal{T}$ and
$\mathcal{D} := \{\, X^{*} \setminus O : O \in \mathcal{S}_2 \,\}$, a nonempty
family of closed compact subsets of $X$, and $C_0 := \bigcap \mathcal{D}$. Then
$C_0$ is closed by (C2) of [[def-topological-space]], and it is a closed subset of
any one member of $\mathcal{D}$, hence compact. Now

$$\bigcup \mathcal{S} \;=\; U \cup (X^{*} \setminus C_0) \;=\; X^{*} \setminus (C_0 \setminus U),$$

and $C_0 \setminus U = C_0 \cap (X \setminus U)$ is closed in $X$ and a subset of
the compact $C_0$, hence compact; so $\bigcup \mathcal{S}$ is of the second kind.

*(T3).* For $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ the intersection lies in $\mathcal{T}$ by (T3)
in $X$. For two sets of the second kind,
$(X^{*} \setminus C) \cap (X^{*} \setminus D) = X^{*} \setminus (C \cup D)$, and
$C \cup D$ is closed in $X$ and compact as a union of two compact subsets. For one
of each, $\infty \notin U$ gives
$U \cap (X^{*} \setminus C) = U \cap (X \setminus C)$, an intersection of two
members of $\mathcal{T}$.

**Why the compact sets are also required to be closed.** The complement of a
compact set that is not closed in $X$ would not make $\infty$'s neighbourhoods
behave: the union computation in (T2) uses that an intersection of the discarded
sets is again closed, and the intersection of arbitrary compact subsets of a
non-Hausdorff space need not be compact. When $X$ is Hausdorff every compact
subset is closed ([[thm-compact-subset-of-a-hausdorff-space-is-closed]]) and the
two descriptions agree, which is why many texts state the definition without the
word "closed" and silently assume the Hausdorff case.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$(X^{*}, \mathcal{T}^{*})$ be its one-point compactification, with added point
$\infty$ ([[def-one-point-compactification]]). Then:

1. **$X^{*}$ is compact** ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. **$X$ is an open subspace of $X^{*}$**: $X \in \mathcal{T}^{*}$, and the
   subspace topology that $X$ inherits from $X^{*}$
   ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) is $\mathcal{T}$ itself.
3. **$X$ is dense in $X^{*}$** ([[def-dense-top]]) **if and only if $X$ is not
   compact.**
4. **$X^{*}$ is Hausdorff** ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) **if and only if $X$ is
   locally compact** ([[def-locally-compact-space]]) **and Hausdorff.**

In particular, a locally compact Hausdorff space is an open subspace of a compact
Hausdorff space, which is the reason the construction is made. **No choice
principle is used**: the only cover thinned below is thinned by the indexed form
of [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], which returns its own indices.

Let
$$S^2:=\{(x,y,t)\in\mathbb R^3:x^2+y^2+t^2=1\}.$$
Define
$$\Sigma(z)=\left(\frac{2\operatorname{Re}z}{1+|z|^2},\ \frac{2\operatorname{Im}z}{1+|z|^2},\ \frac{|z|^2-1}{1+|z|^2}\right)\qquad(z\in\mathbb C)$$
and $\Sigma(\infty)=(0,0,1)$. Then $\Sigma:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to S^2$ is a
homeomorphism, with inverse
$$\Pi(x,y,t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x+iy}{1-t},&(x,y,t)\neq(0,0,1),\\ \infty,&(x,y,t)=(0,0,1).\end{cases}$$

If $f:X\to Y$ is a homotopy equivalence, then for every $n\geq 0$ and every
abelian group $G$ the induced map
$$H_n(f_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G)$$
is an isomorphism.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

Assume AC. For every field $k$, every space $X$, and $n\ge0$, evaluation gives a natural $k$-linear isomorphism
$$H^n(X;k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_n(X;k),k).$$
There is no finite-dimensional hypothesis. The right side is the full algebraic dual.

A morphism $f:X\to Y$ of classical varieties is projective here if there is an integer $N\ge0$ and a factorization $X\hookrightarrow Y\times\mathbf P_k^N\to Y$ in which the first map is a closed immersion and the second is projection. The product and its standard charts are supplied by [[lem-relative-projective-homogeneous-equations]]. A closed immersion in this classical setting is an isomorphism onto a reduced closed subvariety. Morphisms have the general locally ringed-space meaning of [[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]], checked on affine charts.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Assume AC. Let $f:X\to Y$ be one morphism of reduced quasi-projective complex
algebraic varieties, and prescribe finitely many closed or locally closed
algebraic subsets in source and target. There exist finite smooth complex
algebraic Whitney (a),(b) stratifications with frontier on $X$ and $Y$
respecting all prescribed subsets, such that each source stratum maps
surjectively and smoothly onto one target stratum. A further finite algebraic
stratification may be prescribed and refined. The analytic strata are smooth
complex manifolds and the restrictions are smooth submersions. If $f$ is proper
in the analytic topology, in particular if it is a projective algebraic
morphism, the whole restriction $f^{-1}(T)\to T$ over any target stratum is
proper; no restriction of $f$ to a nonclosed individual source stratum is
asserted proper.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at
every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There
are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective
resolutions supplied by
[[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on
every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this
local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero
otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its
nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.

derivations.claim: The space and its two charts. Glue the affine $z$-line and affine $w$-line along $zw=1$. Their regular transition gives a prevariety with a finite affine cover ([F2], [F3]). Its diagonal is closed: on the two same-chart products equality is $z=z'$ or $w=w'$, and on either cross-chart product it is $zw'=1$ or $wz'=1$. Equalizers of regular maps are inverse images of this diagonal, so $S$ is separated. The formulas of [F5] define a homeomorphism from this glued space to $S^2$: in the $w$-chart they become $(2\operatorname{Re}w,-2\operatorname{Im}w,1-|w|^2)/(1+|w|^2)$, including the north pole at $w=0$; the inverse coordinate there is $w=(x-iy)/(1+t)$, continuous near the north pole. In the other chart the formulas and inverse are those of [F5]. Composing with [F5]'s inverse identifies the analytic topology with the one-point compactification of [F4]. In particular $S$ is compact. [F2, F3, F4, F5, construct, algebra]

The map is proper surjective. The unique morphism $f:S\to\mathrm{pt}$ is surjective because $S$ is nonempty. It is projective in the sense of [F9]: the identity is a closed immersion $S\hookrightarrow\mathrm{pt}\times\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ onto a reduced closed subvariety, and the projection to the point is the structure map. By the properness clause of [F10], a projective algebraic morphism is proper in the analytic topology; hence $f$ is a proper surjective morphism of finite-type complex algebraic varieties, and [F1] applies to it. [F9, F10, F1, given]

The single fiber is not acyclic. Stereographic projection is a homeomorphism $\widehat{\mathbb C}\to S^2$ ([F5]); a homeomorphism is a homotopy equivalence, so it induces isomorphisms on singular homology ([F6]) and $H_2(S;k)\cong H_2(S^2;k)\cong k$ by [F7]. The field-dual corollary [F8] then gives $H^2(S;k)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_2(S;k),k)\cong k\neq0$, since $k$ is a field. The sphere is metric with a contractible-open neighbourhood basis, and these properties transfer through the homeomorphism, so [F11] identifies this singular cohomology group with the actual derived constant-sheaf group $H^2(S,k_S)$. Thus the fiber $S$ of $f$ is not cohomologically acyclic. [F5, F6, F7, F8, F11, algebra]

The rows are still contracted. The fiber of $f$ over the unique point is $S$ and the fiber powers are $S^{p+1}$. Choose one point $y\in S$, for instance the point with $z=0$, and for $r\geq0$ let $\mathrm{ins}_r:S^r\to S^{r+1}$ insert $y$ as first coordinate, with $S^0=\mathrm{pt}$. For the compositions below the deletion maps are $d_i:S^{r+2}\to S^{r+1}$, and they satisfy $d_0\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{id}$ and $d_i\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{ins}_r\,d_{i-1}$ for $i>0$, so with $h_{p+1}:=\mathrm{ins}_{p+1}^*$ and $\delta_p$ the alternating sum of deletion pullbacks one gets $h_{p+1}\delta_p+\delta_{p-1}h_p=\mathrm{id}$ in every internal degree $q$, and $h_0\delta_{-1}=\mathrm{id}$; hence each augmented row is contractible. In the row $q=2$ the term at $p=0$ is $H^2(S;k)\cong k\neq0$, carried injectively into $H^2(S^2;k)$; the nonzero group is retained and does not obstruct exactness. [F1, step 1.3, algebra]

Conclusion. Applying [F1] to $f$ and the constant sheaf $k$, and using that the fiber powers of $f$ are $S^{p+1}$ and that $R\Gamma(\mathrm{pt},k)=k$ is concentrated in degree $0$, the augmented Cech map $k\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}R\Gamma(S^{p+1},k)$ is a quasi-isomorphism; therefore the unaugmented product total has cohomology $k$ in degree $0$ and zero in every other degree. The example shows that proper Cech descent does not require acyclic fibers: the nonvanishing $H^2$ of the fiber is retained throughout the contracted rows. The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the descent lemma and the field-dual corollary, and the construction of $S$, the homeomorphism with $S^2$, the choice of one point and the insertion argument use no further choice. [F1, F8, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.1] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited from the supplied six-functor resolutions. Let $X_\bullet\to X$ be an augmented simplicial finite-type complex algebraic variety ([[def-simplicial-object-and-simplicial-commutative-ring]], [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Assume $X_0\to X$ is proper surjective and, for each $p>0$, $X_p\to(\operatorname{cosk}_{p-1}\operatorname{sk}_{p-1}X_\bullet)_p$ is proper surjective over $X$, where $\operatorname{sk}_{p-1}$ restricts to levels through $p-1$, $\operatorname{cosk}_{p-1}$ is its right Kan extension formed by finite matching limits, and the target is the matching object. Such an object is a proper hypercover; no smoothness or fiber acyclicity is assumed. For $F\in D^b_c(X;k)$ over a field, and $a_p:X_p\to X$, the augmentation gives
$$F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Ra_{p*}a_p^*F,\qquad R\Gamma(X,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}R\Gamma(X_p,a_p^*F).$$
There is a natural strongly convergent spectral sequence $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(X_p,a_p^*F)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X,F)$. If $F$ has cochain lower bound $a$, every diagonal $p+q=m$ is finite; degree $m$ and its differential are determined by levels through $p=m-a+1$. All proper-hypercover refinements induce the same comparison via the base object; any two such hypercovers have a proper common refinement. For $F=k_X$, $a=0$, this is the first-quadrant spectral sequence required for smooth-projective hyperresolutions.

Let $\Delta$ be the **simplex category**: its objects are the finite nonempty
ordered sets $[n]=\{0<1<\dots<n\}$ for $n\ge0$, and its morphisms are the
order-preserving maps. A **simplicial object** in a category $\mathcal C$ is a
functor $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal C$
([[def-category]], [[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]]). A **simplicial
set** is a simplicial object in sets; a **simplicial commutative ring** is a
simplicial object in commutative rings ([[def-commutative-ring]]), so that
each $A_n$ is a commutative ring and the structure maps are ring
homomorphisms ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]); a **simplicial module** over a
simplicial ring $A_\bullet$ is a simplicial object $M_\bullet$ in abelian
groups together with a compatible $A_\bullet$-action, and the resulting
category of simplicial $A_\bullet$-modules is abelian.

Writing $d_i\colon M_n\to M_{n-1}$ for the image of the injection
$[n-1]\to[n]$ omitting $i$ (a **face map**) and $s_i\colon M_n\to M_{n+1}$
for the image of the surjection $[n+1]\to[n]$ repeating $i$ (a **degeneracy
map**), these maps satisfy the usual simplicial identities
$$d_i d_j=d_{j-1}d_i\ (i<j),\qquad s_i s_j=s_{j+1}s_i\ (i\le j),\qquad d_i s_j=\begin{cases} s_{j-1}d_i, & i<j,\\ \mathrm{id}, & i=j\ \text{or}\ i=j+1,\\ s_j d_{i-1}, & i>j+1.\end{cases}$$
Conversely, such a sequence of face and degeneracy maps determines the
functor.

The **Moore complex** of a simplicial abelian group or module $M_\bullet$ is
the chain complex concentrated in nonnegative degrees with $M_n$ in degree
$n$ and differential
$$\partial_n=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i d_i\colon M_n\to M_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1),$$
with $\partial_0=0$; the $d_i$ are the face maps
([[def-chain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]);
the simplicial identities give $\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$. Its homology is
written
$$\pi_n(M_\bullet)=H_n(M_\bullet)\qquad(n\ge0)$$
([[def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex]]). By the Dold-Kan normalization
theorem this agrees with the classical homotopy-group definition
$H_n(NM_\bullet)$ via the normalized subcomplex, so the convention is
canonical; no model-category machinery is introduced here.

For a simplicial commutative ring $A_\bullet$, each $\pi_n(A_\bullet)$ is defined as above, and $\pi_0(A_\bullet)=A_0/(d_0-d_1)(A_1)$ is a commutative ring. The image is an ideal: for $a\in A_0$, multiplying a representative $b\in A_1$ by $s_0a$ gives $a(d_0b-d_1b)$. Every $\pi_n(A_\bullet)$ is a $\pi_0(A_\bullet)$-module. Indeed multiplication by the totally degenerate simplex of a vertex $a\in A_0$ is a chain map on the Moore complex: its faces are the corresponding totally degenerate simplex of $a$ in the preceding degree. If two vertices are the endpoints of $b\in A_1$, multiplication by the simplicial path defined by $b$ gives a homotopy between these chain maps (the alternating prism sum inserts the degeneracies of $b$). Consequently $(d_0-d_1)(b)$ acts as zero on homology, so the action factors through the displayed quotient. Additivity, associativity and the unit descend from levelwise ring multiplication.

A **morphism of simplicial commutative rings** is a natural transformation
$A_\bullet\to B_\bullet$ ([[def-natural-transformation]]). Such a morphism is
a **weak equivalence** when it induces isomorphisms
$\pi_n(A_\bullet)\to\pi_n(B_\bullet)$ for all $n\ge0$. The **category of
derived rings** is the localization of the category of simplicial commutative
rings at the weak equivalences; constructions on derived rings are used below
only through statements that are independent of the chosen replacement up to
canonical isomorphism.

derivations.claim: Degree bookkeeping. In the total complex of the hypercover, the term in bidegree $(p,q)$ has $p\geq0$ and $q\geq a$ and contributes to total degree $p+q$. For a fixed total degree $m$ this gives $0\leq p\leq m-a$. The differentials entering and leaving total degree $m$ involve terms of total degree $m-1$, $m$ and $m+1$, so the largest simplicial level appearing in the data of $H^m$ and of its differential is $p=(m+1)-a=m-a+1$. [F1, given]

The truncation computes the same cohomology. By [F1], the comparison of $X_\bullet$ with its $N$-coskeleton truncation $\operatorname{cosk}_N\operatorname{sk}_NX_\bullet$ is the identity through simplicial degree $N$, and the total complex in a fixed total degree uses only finitely many levels. Choosing $N\geq m-a+1$ makes the two total complexes agree in degrees $m-1$, $m$ and $m+1$; hence they have the same $H^m$ and the same augmentation maps there. Since $m$ was arbitrary, every truncation with $N$ at least the stated bound computes the same cohomology $H^m(X,F)$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

Constant coefficients and sharpness for hard truncation. For $F=k_X$ the lower bound is $a=0$, so the actual total-degree computation uses the outgoing map from level $n$ to level $n+1$. To see that omitting that map can change the answer in every degree, take the proper surjection from two reduced points $S=\{0,1\}$ to a point and its Cech nerve. The map is proper since preimages of compact sets are finite, and its fiber powers are finite discrete spaces. A sheaf on a finite discrete space is a family of vector spaces, so global sections are a finite product and exact. Hence the derived section model has internal degree zero only. The normalized degree-$p$ cochains are $k^2$, indexed by the two alternating nondegenerate strings of length $p+1$. Interior deletions give degenerate strings and vanish in the normalized differential; the two endpoint deletions give $\delta_p(v_0,v_1)=(v_1+(-1)^{p+1}v_0,v_0+(-1)^{p+1}v_1)$, which has rank one over every field. The full augmented complex is contracted by inserting one point, as in [F1], so its positive cohomology is zero and $H^0=k$. If one retains only cochain levels $0,\ldots,n$ and discards $\delta_n$, its top cohomology is $k$ for $n>0$ and $k^2$ for $n=0$, giving the wrong answer. Thus level $n+1$ is necessary in general for this hard truncation of the cochain data. A coskeleton truncation is different: it reconstructs higher levels from matching limits, so no claim that $\operatorname{cosk}_n\operatorname{sk}_nX_\bullet$ itself fails descent is made. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be an integral finite-type $k$-scheme,
let $L$ be invertible, and let $s_0,\ldots,s_n$ be meromorphic sections of
$L$, not all zero. Their ratios define $\varphi:X\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^n_k$.
Put $F=\sum_i\mathcal O_Xs_i\subseteq K_X(L)$ and define the finite-type
quasi-coherent fractional ideal $I=F\otimes L^{-1}\subseteq K_X$.
Its fractional blowup is
$$B=\operatorname{Proj}_X\Bigl(\bigoplus_{d\ge0}I^d\Bigr),\qquad I^0=\mathcal O_X.$$
Then $B$ is integral, its projection $\pi:B\to X$ resolves $\varphi$, and
$(\pi,\psi):B\hookrightarrow X\times_k\mathbb P^n_k$ is the schematic
closure of its graph. The generating line bundle is
$M=\pi^*L\otimes(I\mathcal O_B)$.
If $f:Y\to X$ is a $k$-morphism from an integral scheme, $D\subseteq X$
is the domain of a representative of $\varphi$, $f^{-1}(D)\ne\varnothing$,
and $\theta:Y\to\mathbb P^n_k$ extends that representative composed with
$f$, then $f$ factors uniquely through $B$. The nonempty inverse-image
condition ensures that this induced rational map is defined.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be integral, let $\mathcal I\subseteq
\mathcal O_X$ be a quasi-coherent ideal of finite type, and let
$J\subseteq\mathcal K_X$ be an invertible fractional ideal. Its product
$F=J\mathcal I$ is a subsheaf of $\mathcal K_X$; it need not be contained in
$\mathcal O_X$. Define its **fractional Rees algebra** and blowup by
$$\mathcal R(F)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}F^n,\qquad F^0=\mathcal O_X, \qquad \operatorname{Bl}_{F}X=\operatorname{Proj}_X\mathcal R(F).$$
Here $F^n\cong J^{\otimes n}\otimes\mathcal I^n$, with multiplication induced
inside $\mathcal K_X$, so the algebra is quasi-coherent and generated in degree
one. When $F\subseteq\mathcal O_X$, this is the ordinary ideal blowup of
[[def-blowup-scheme-along-ideal]].

On a nonempty affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ trivializing $J$, choose
$g\in\operatorname{Frac}(A)^\times$ with $J|_U=gA$. Multiplication by $g^n$
is an $A$-module isomorphism $I^n\to(gI)^n$ for every $n$, with inverse division
by $g^n$. These maps respect multiplication and give a graded algebra
isomorphism $R(I)\to R(gI)$. The inverse of its contravariantly induced Proj
map defines
$$\rho_{\mathcal I,J}|_U:\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}U \longrightarrow\operatorname{Bl}_{J\mathcal I}U.$$
No assertion that $g\in A$ is needed.

Replacing $g$ by $ug$, $u\in A^\times$, changes the degree-$n$ map by $u^n$.
This automorphism induces the identity on Proj: on any homogeneous
localization, numerator and denominator of a degree-zero fraction acquire the
same power of $u$, which cancels. Thus the local maps agree on overlaps and
glue to a canonical isomorphism of $X$-schemes
$$\rho_{\mathcal I,J}:\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X \xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Bl}_{J\mathcal I}X.$$
Division by $g^n$ gives its inverse, including when the original ideal is zero
and both blowups are empty. This construction uses relative Proj and is
compatible with restriction to opens.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited through the quasi-coherent interfaces
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a locally Noetherian scheme
([[def-locally-noetherian-and-noetherian-scheme]]). Then:

1. A quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module is coherent
   ([[def-coherent-module-scheme]]) if and only if it is of finite type
   ([[def-finite-type-finite-presentation-module-sheaf]]).
2. For every morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of coherent
   $\mathcal O_X$-modules the kernel, image and cokernel of $\varphi$ are
   coherent, and finite direct sums of coherent modules are coherent.
3. Extensions: if $0\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal E\to\mathcal G\to0$ is a short
   exact sequence of quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_X$-modules
   ([[def-exact-sequence-sheaves]]) with $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal G$
   coherent, then $\mathcal E$ is coherent. Thus $\operatorname{Coh}(X)$ is
   closed under extensions inside $\operatorname{QCoh}(X)$.

The equivalence in (1) is the theorem's essential content: the relation
kernel condition in the definition of coherence is automatic for finite type
quasi-coherent modules over a locally Noetherian base, but not over an
arbitrary base.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a Noetherian
commutative ring ([[def-noetherian-ring-and-module]]) and let $X$ be a scheme
projective over $A$ in the finite-dimensional H-projective convention
([[def-projective-morphism-pre-proj]]): the structure morphism
$X\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ ([[def-affine-scheme-spectrum]]) factors over
$\operatorname{Spec}A$ as a closed immersion
$X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^n_A$
([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]]) followed by the projection,
for some $n\ge0$. Let $L$ be an ample invertible $\mathcal O_X$-module
([[def-ample-invertible-sheaf]], [[def-invertible-sheaf]]) and let $F$ be a
coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module ([[def-coherent-module-scheme]]). Then there is
an integer $m_0$ such that
$$F\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}L^{\otimes m}$$
is globally generated ([[def-globally-generated-sheaf]]) for every $m\ge m_0$;
the bound may depend on $F$. The empty scheme $X$, the zero module $F=0$ and
the cases $n=0$ and $\operatorname{Spec}A=\varnothing$ are included, and no
effectivity of $m_0$ is claimed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited from the projective-space suppliers.
Let $k$ be a field and let $n\ge0$, and write
$\mathbf P^n_k=\mathbb P^n_{\operatorname{Spec}k}$ for the relative projective
space with its standard charts and twisting sheaf $\mathcal O(1)$
([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]],
[[def-very-ample-invertible-sheaf-relative]]). Then
$\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^n_k}(1)$ is closed H-very ample relative to
$\operatorname{Spec}k$: the identity morphism of $\mathbf P^n_k$ is a closed
immersion over $\operatorname{Spec}k$ and pulls $\mathcal O(1)$ back to a sheaf
isomorphic to $\mathcal O(1)$. Consequently

1. $\mathcal O(1)$ is ample on $\mathbf P^n_k$
   ([[def-ample-invertible-sheaf]]);
2. for every integer $d\ge1$ the tensor power
   $\mathcal O(d)=\mathcal O(1)^{\otimes d}$ is ample on $\mathbf P^n_k$;
3. for every finite morphism $g:Y\to\mathbf P^n_k$ the pullback
   $g^*\mathcal O(1)$ is an ample invertible $\mathcal O_Y$-module.

Let $S$ be a scheme and let $n\ge0$. Denote by
$$\pi:\mathbb P^n_S\longrightarrow S$$
the relative projective space with its standard charts $U_0,\dots,U_n$ and
transition isomorphisms
$\theta_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to U_j\cap U_i$ carrying the coordinates by
$x^{(i)}_\ell\mapsto x^{(j)}_\ell/x^{(j)}_i$ and
$x^{(i)}_j\mapsto1/x^{(j)}_i$
([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]]). Write
$x^{(i)}_j$ for the coordinate $t_j/t_i$ on $U_i$.

*The twisting sheaf on relative projective space.* On each chart $U_i$ let
$\mathcal O_{U_i}e_i$ be a free rank-one $\mathcal O_{U_i}$-module with basis
$e_i$. On the overlap $U_i\cap U_j$, identify
$$(\mathcal O_{U_i}e_i)|_{U_i\cap U_j}\longrightarrow (\mathcal O_{U_j}e_j)|_{U_i\cap U_j},\qquad e_i\longmapsto x^{(j)}_i\,e_j ,$$ that is, $e_j=x^{(i)}_j e_i$ on $U_i\cap U_j$; this is the standard normalization under which the coordinate section $x_j$ restricts to $x^{(i)}_je_i$ on $U_i$ and to $e_j$ on $U_j$. This is an isomorphism of invertible sheaves: $x^{(j)}_i$ is a unit on $U_i\cap U_j$ by construction. The transition data are compatible on triple overlaps, $$x^{(j)}_i\cdot x^{(k)}_j=x^{(k)}_i \quad\text{on }U_i\cap U_j\cap U_k,$$ because $x^{(k)}_i=(t_i/t_k)$ and $x^{(j)}_i x^{(k)}_j=(t_i/t_j)(t_j/t_k)$; equivalently, the identifications obtained from $e_i\mapsto x^{(j)}_i e_j$, $e_j\mapsto x^{(k)}_j e_k$ and $e_i\mapsto x^{(k)}_i e_k$ agree on the triple overlap. Hence the trivial invertible sheaves on the $U_i$ glue to an invertible sheaf on $\mathbb P^n_S$, denoted $$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n_S}(1)\qquad\text{or}\qquad\mathcal O(1)$$
when the ambient space is clear, with $e_i$ a frame on $U_i$. For integers
$d$ put $\mathcal O(d)=\mathcal O(1)^{\otimes d}$ for $d\ge0$ and
$\mathcal O(d)=(\mathcal O(-d))^{\vee}$ for $d<0$.

**Definition.** Let $f:X\to S$ be a quasi-compact morphism
([[def-quasi-compact-and-quasi-separated-morphism]]) and let $L$ be an
invertible $\mathcal O_X$-module ([[def-invertible-sheaf]]). Then $L$ is
**H-very ample relative to $S$** if there exist an integer $n\ge0$ and a
quasi-compact $S$-immersion
$$i:X\longrightarrow\mathbb P^n_S$$
of schemes ([[def-locally-closed-immersion]]) such that
$$L\;\cong\;i^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n_S}(1).$$
The value $n=0$ is allowed, with $\mathbb P^0_S\cong S$. If in addition $i$
can be chosen to be a closed immersion, then $L$ is **closed H-very ample
relative to $S$**.

Fix $n\ge0$. For $i\in\{0,\dots,n\}$ let
$$B_i=\mathbb Z[t_0,\dots,t_n]/(t_i-1)\cong\mathbb Z\bigl[x^{(i)}_\ell:\ell\ne i\bigr],$$
where $x^{(i)}_\ell$ denotes the class of $t_\ell/t_i$, so that
$U_i:=\operatorname{Spec}B_i$ is an affine scheme with coordinates
$x^{(i)}_\ell$ for $\ell\ne i$. For $i\ne j$ let $D^{(i)}_j\subseteq U_i$ be the
distinguished open where $x^{(i)}_j$ is invertible. Over it the formula
$$x^{(i)}_\ell=\frac{t_\ell}{t_i}=\frac{t_\ell/t_j}{t_i/t_j}=\frac{x^{(j)}_\ell}{x^{(j)}_i}$$
for $\ell\ne i,j$, together with $x^{(i)}_j=1/x^{(j)}_i$, defines a
$\mathbb Z$-algebra isomorphism
$$\bigl(B_i\bigr)_{x^{(i)}_j}\longrightarrow\bigl(B_j\bigr)_{x^{(j)}_i},\qquad x^{(i)}_\ell\mapsto x^{(j)}_\ell/x^{(j)}_i\ \ (\ell\ne i,j),\quad x^{(i)}_j\mapsto 1/x^{(j)}_i,$$
and these morphisms identify the open subschemes $D^{(i)}_j\subseteq U_i$ and
$D^{(j)}_i\subseteq U_j$ by [[lem-spectrum-localization-open-immersion]]. This is
the reciprocal of the analogous formula with $i,j$ interchanged, and on a triple
overlap $U_i\cap U_j\cap U_k$ both composites send $x^{(i)}_\ell$ to
$x^{(k)}_\ell/x^{(k)}_i$, so the identity and cocycle conditions of
[[thm-gluing-affine-schemes]] hold and the affine schemes $U_i$ glue to a scheme,
denoted $\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb Z}$, whose open subschemes $U_i$ form an affine
cover and are its **standard charts**.

For an arbitrary base scheme $S$ define
$$\mathbb P^n_S=S\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb Z},$$
with structure morphism the projection to $S$ ([[thm-fibre-products-of-schemes-exist]],
[[def-scheme-over-base]]), and call the open subschemes
$U^S_i=S\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z}U_i$ the **standard charts over
$S$**; each is affine over $S$, and they form an open cover of $\mathbb P^n_S$.
When $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ is affine, each $U^S_i$ is the affine scheme
$\operatorname{Spec}A[x^{(i)}_\ell:\ell\ne i]$. Because
base change preserves open immersions and fibre products, the transition
isomorphisms on $U^S_i\cap U^S_j$ are the base changes of the displayed ones, so
the charts and their overlaps commute with base change.

For $n=0$ there is one chart $U_0=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z[t_0]/(t_0-1)\cong
\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$, no gluing takes place, and
$\mathbb P^0_{\mathbb Z}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$, so
$\mathbb P^0_S\cong S$. For $S=\varnothing$ the product is empty, so
$\mathbb P^n_{\varnothing}=\varnothing$. For $n\ge1$ the constructions for the
pairs $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$ are reciprocal as displayed, and the case $i=j$ is the
identity on $U_i$.

Let $X$ be a scheme and let $L$ be an invertible $\mathcal O_X$-module
([[def-invertible-sheaf]]). Recall that $X$ is quasi-compact when its
underlying topological space is quasi-compact
([[def-quasi-compact-and-quasi-separated-scheme]]).

*Nonvanishing loci.* For a global section $s\in\Gamma(X,L^n)$ of a positive
power with $n\ge1$, the **nonvanishing locus of $s$** is
$$X_s=\{\,x\in X\;:\;\text{the image of }s\text{ in the fibre }L^n\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\kappa(x)\text{ is nonzero}\,\}.$$
This set is open: trivialise $L^n$ near a point, writing $s=f e$
with $e$ a frame. In the local ring at $x$, the fibre value is nonzero
exactly when $f_x$ is a unit. A germ inverse of $f_x$ is represented by a
section $g$ on a neighbourhood of $x$; since $(fg)_x=1$, the equality
$fg=1$ holds after shrinking that neighbourhood. Thus $f_y$ is a unit
throughout that neighbourhood, proving openness. The set $X_s$ does not depend on
the chosen trivialisation: the vanishing of the fibre component is an
intrinsic condition on the section.

**Definition.** An invertible $\mathcal O_X$-module $L$ is **ample** when the
following two conditions hold.

1. $X$ is quasi-compact.
2. For every point $x\in X$ there exist an integer $n\ge1$ and a global section
   $s\in\Gamma(X,L^n)$ with
   $$x\in X_s\qquad\text{and}\qquad X_s\ \text{is an affine scheme.}$$

The **empty scheme is allowed**: if $X=\varnothing$ then $X$ is quasi-compact
and condition (2) is vacuous, so every invertible sheaf on $X$ — there is
exactly one, the zero module sheaf, which is invertible because the empty
scheme has no points — is ample on $X$.

Open immersions, closed immersions and immersions (equivalently locally closed immersions) remain of the same kind after arbitrary base change. If a closed subscheme $Z\hookrightarrow S$ has ideal sheaf $\mathcal I$, its pullback under $g:Y\to S$ has ideal
$$\operatorname{Im}(g^*\mathcal I\longrightarrow\mathcal O_Y).$$
On affine charts $A\to C$ this is the extended ideal $IC$. No injectivity of $g^*\mathcal I\to\mathcal O_Y$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $i:Z\to Y$ be a closed immersion, where
closed immersion has the published convention that the map on structure sheaves
is surjective. For every affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $Y$, there is
a unique ideal $I\subseteq A$ such that, over $U$,
$$i^{-1}(U)\cong\operatorname{Spec}(A/I).$$
Conversely, every quotient map $A\to A/I$ induces a closed immersion
$\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\to\operatorname{Spec}A$. Every base change of a
closed immersion is a closed immersion. In particular, the empty subscheme of
$\operatorname{Spec}A$ corresponds to $I=A$.

A morphism $i:Z\to X$ is a **closed immersion** if its underlying map is a
homeomorphism onto a closed subset and the morphism
$\mathcal O_X\to i_*\mathcal O_Z$ is surjective.
For $m,n\ge0$ and $a,b\ge1$, the map from $\mathbf P^m_k\times\mathbf P^n_k$ taking $([x],[y])$ to all monomials $x^\alpha y^\beta$ of bidegree $(a,b)$ is a closed embedding.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the relative Proj construction
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be an integral scheme
([[def-integral-scheme]]) and let $\mathcal I$ be a nonzero quasi-coherent
ideal sheaf of finite type on $X$ ([[def-quasi-coherent-ideal-sheaf]]). Then
the blowup $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X$ of
[[def-blowup-scheme-along-ideal]] is integral: the affine blowup algebras
$A[I/a]$ are domains because $A$ is a domain and $a$ is nonzero, and they glue
along localisations. More generally, if $X$ is reduced then
$\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X$ is reduced, because the affine blowup
algebras of a reduced ring are reduced.

An **integral scheme** is a nonempty scheme that is reduced and whose
underlying topological space is irreducible. Equivalently, it is nonempty and
every nonempty affine open is the spectrum of a domain. The latter criterion is
independent of the chosen affine open cover.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: $X$ carries the closed immersion $i:X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}$ given by its projectivity, and $L_0=i^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}}(1)$ is invertible. The standard charts $U_0,\dots,U_N$ are affine and cover $\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}$, so the finitely many intersections $X\cap U_j=X_{s_j}$, where $s_j=i^*(x_j)\in\Gamma(X,L_0)$, are affine: each is a closed subscheme of the affine chart $U_j$, hence $\operatorname{Spec}(A_j)$ for a quotient $A_j$ of the polynomial ring over $\mathbb C$ [lem-closed-immersion-affine-quotient-and-base-change]. Every $A_j$ is Noetherian [lem-field-is-noetherian, cor-finite-variable-polynomial-ring-noetherian, thm-noetherian-ring-quotients-and-localisations], so this finite affine cover exhibits the scheme $X$ as locally Noetherian and quasi-compact [def-locally-noetherian-and-noetherian-scheme, def-quasi-compact-and-quasi-separated-scheme]. The coordinate section $x_j$ has nonvanishing locus $U_j$ and pullback along a closed immersion of an invertible sheaf has as nonvanishing locus the preimage of the original one [def-very-ample-invertible-sheaf-relative, def-closed-immersion-schemes], so the charts $X_{s_j}=X\cap U_j$ are affine and cover $X$; the ampleness criterion of [def-ample-invertible-sheaf] therefore makes $L_0$ ample on $X$.

By [F2] the quasi-coherent finite-type ideal sheaf $\mathcal I$ is coherent on the locally Noetherian $X$, and since $X$ is projective over the Noetherian ring $\mathbb C$ and $L_0$ is ample there is $d_0$ such that $\mathcal I\otimes L_0^{\otimes d}$ is globally generated for every $d\ge d_0$. Fix $d\ge\max(1,d_0)$, put $L=L_0^{\otimes d}$ and $\mathcal F=\mathcal I\otimes L\subseteq L$, and choose finitely many global sections $s_0,\dots,s_n\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$ generating $\mathcal F$. To justify finiteness, global generation supplies finitely many such sections generating each finite-type stalk; their coherent cokernel vanishes on a neighbourhood of that point (on an affine chart, each of its finitely many generators is killed after localizing away from that point). Quasi-compactness of $X$ supplies finitely many of these neighbourhoods, and the union of their finite section tuples generates $\mathcal F$ everywhere. Since $\mathcal I\ne0$ and $L$ is invertible, $\mathcal F\ne0$, so not all $s_i$ are zero and $\mathcal F=\sum_i\mathcal O_Xs_i$ as subsheaves of $L$.

Apply [F1] to the integral finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme $X$, the invertible sheaf $L$ and the meromorphic sections $s_0,\dots,s_n$: the fractional blowup $B=\operatorname{Proj}_X\bigoplus_{k\ge0}(\mathcal F\otimes L^{-1})^k$ is integral and $(\pi,\psi):B\to X\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ is the schematic closure of the graph of the induced rational map, hence a closed immersion.

The canonical isomorphisms $\mathcal F\otimes L^{-1}=(\mathcal I\otimes L)\otimes L^{-1}\cong\mathcal I\otimes(L\otimes L^{-1})\cong\mathcal I$ of $\mathcal O_X$-modules [def-invertible-sheaf] identify the graded $\mathcal O_X$-algebras $\bigoplus_{k\ge0}(\mathcal F\otimes L^{-1})^k$ and $\bigoplus_{k\ge0}\mathcal I^k$, hence induce an $X$-isomorphism $B\cong\operatorname{Proj}_X\bigoplus_{k\ge0}\mathcal I^k=\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X$ [def-blowup-scheme-along-ideal, def-blowup-fractional-ideal]. Composing with the closed immersion of step 3.1, the blowup $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X$ is a closed subscheme of $X\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ over $X$.

Base change of the closed immersion $X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}$ along $\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$ is a closed immersion $X\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}$ [F4], and the Segre embedding of [F5] is a closed immersion $\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}\times_{\mathbb C}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb C}\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$ with $M=(N+1)(n+1)-1$. A composite of closed immersions is again a closed immersion [F4], so $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X$ is a closed subscheme of $\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$; all exhibited maps are morphisms over $\mathbb C$, so the structure morphism $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$ factors as this closed immersion followed by the projection, and $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X$ is projective over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of [def-projective-morphism-pre-proj].

For the composition clause argue by induction on the number of factors: let $X_0$ be integral projective over $\mathbb C$ and $X_{k+1}=\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I_k}X_k$ for nonzero finite-type quasi-coherent ideal sheaves $\mathcal I_k\subseteq\mathcal O_{X_k}$. If $X_k$ is integral projective then steps 1.1-5.1 applied to $(X_k,\mathcal I_k)$ show that $X_{k+1}$ is projective over $\mathbb C$, and [F6] shows that it stays integral, so the induction runs through every finite composition.

Boundaries and Choice accounting. An integral scheme is nonempty and $\mathcal I\ne0$ by hypothesis, so the empty and zero cases are excluded; the chosen twist satisfies $d\ge1$; the endpoint $n=0$ of a single generator is allowed, the Segre factor then being $\mathbb P^0_{\mathbb C}$ with $M=N$; and $N=0$ is covered by the same argument with the single chart $U_0$. The Axiom of Choice [F7] is inherited exactly from [F1] and [F2]; no further selection is made.

boundaries.reason: X is integral and nonempty, and the zero ideal is excluded. The unit ideal with empty centre is allowed.
The zero ideal is excluded by the hypothesis $\mathcal I\ne0$.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1 covers a generating tuple with a single section and step 7.1 records the endpoint $n=0$.
Statement: The unit ideal gives the identity blowup, included by the proof and induction.

risk_review.notes: Read all seven proof steps, facts, and 24 declared supplier interfaces. A finite affine cover makes X Noetherian and the pulled-back coordinate line bundle ample. Coherence plus eventual global generation and quasi-compactness give finitely many nonzero generators; their coefficient ideal is exactly I, not the twist treated as an ordinary ideal. The graph-closure supplier is applied only to integral finite-type X and not-all-zero meromorphic sections. Untwisting identifies the Rees algebra, and the (1,1) Segre dimension is (N+1)(n+1)-1. Integral blowups permit finite iteration; unit ideal, N=0, n=0 and zero-step composition work, while I=0 and empty X are excluded. AC inherited from the supplied Proj and coherent-twist results is stated. Stacks 31.33.9 and 31.33.13 cross-check integrality and projectivity.
