citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be an integral projective complex scheme of
finite type, with structure morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$
([[def-projective-morphism-pre-proj]]), and let $\mathcal I\subseteq\mathcal O_X$
be a nonzero finite-type quasi-coherent ideal sheaf
([[def-quasi-coherent-ideal-sheaf]]). Then the blowup
$\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X$ of [[def-blowup-scheme-along-ideal]] is
projective over $\mathbb C$: for some $M\ge0$ its structure morphism factors as
a closed immersion
$\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^M_{\mathbb C}$
followed by the projection. Consequently every composition of blowups of an
integral projective complex scheme along nonzero finite-type ideal sheaves
remains integral and projective over $\mathbb C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $S$ be a Noetherian
scheme ([[def-locally-noetherian-and-noetherian-scheme]]) and let
$f:X\to S$ be a separated morphism of finite type
([[def-separated-morphism-schemes]],
[[def-locally-finite-type-and-finite-type-morphism]]). Then there exist an
integer $N\ge0$, a scheme $X'$ and morphisms
$$\pi:X'\longrightarrow X,\qquad \iota:X'\longrightarrow\mathbb P^N_S,$$
with $\iota$ an immersion over $S$ ([[def-locally-closed-immersion]]) and
$\pi$ proper and surjective ([[def-proper-morphism]]), and there is a dense
open subscheme $U\subseteq X$ such that $\pi^{-1}(U)\to U$ is an isomorphism.

The construction passes through the schematic closure of $U$ in $X$: in the
proof $X$ is first replaced by the schematic closure $X^*$ of a dense open
$U\subseteq X$, a closed subscheme of $X$ through which $U\hookrightarrow X$
factors, over which $U$ is schematically dense and which is a surjective
closed immersion over $X$ restricting to an isomorphism over $U$; a solution
for $X^*$ composes with $X^*\to X$ to a solution for $X$.

If $f$ is proper, then $\iota$ is a closed immersion, so $X'$ is projective
over $S$ ([[def-projective-morphism-pre-proj]]). The case $X=\varnothing$ is
included with $X'=U=\varnothing$.

Fix a base scheme $S$ and work in the category of $S$-schemes
([[def-scheme]]), in which finite limits and coproducts exist
([[def-fibre-product-schemes-universal-property]],
[[cor-product-schemes-over-base-exists]]). An **augmented simplicial
$S$-scheme** is a simplicial object in this category
([[def-simplicial-object-and-simplicial-commutative-ring]]) augmented over $S$:
$S$-schemes $X_p$ for $p\ge0$ with face maps $d_i:X_p\to X_{p-1}$ and
degeneracy maps $s_i:X_p\to X_{p+1}$ satisfying the simplicial identities,
together with structure morphisms $X_p\to S$ compatible with all of them; write
$a:X_0\to S$ for the augmentation. A **$k$-truncated** such object consists of
the data in degrees $p\le k$.

For $p\ge1$ the **matching object** $M_p(X_\bullet)$ is the finite limit
over the boundary of $[p]$: there is one copy of $X_q$ for every
order-preserving injection $\theta:[q]\hookrightarrow[p]$ with $q<p$.
For $\theta=\theta'\alpha$, compatibility is imposed by the structure map
$X(\alpha):X_r\to X_q$, where $\alpha:[q]\hookrightarrow[r]$ and
$\theta':[r]\hookrightarrow[p]$. Equivalently,
$M_p(X_\bullet)=(\operatorname{cosk}_{p-1}\operatorname{sk}_{p-1}X_\bullet)_p$,
the value at $[p]$ of the right adjoint of the $(p-1)$-skeleton truncation;
set $M_0(X_\bullet)=S$. The **canonical boundary map** $X_p\to M_p(X_\bullet)$
is the morphism whose components are the structure maps of $X_\bullet$, and it
exists by the universal property of the limit.

A **splitting** consists of subobjects $N_q\hookrightarrow X_q$, called
the **nondegenerate parts**, such that the degeneracy maps induce isomorphisms
$$m_p:\coprod_{\delta:[p]\twoheadrightarrow[q],\ 0\le q\le p}N_q\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }X_p$$
for every $p\ge0$. The surjections are order-preserving, and the identity
surjection contributes $N_p$, not the whole $X_p$. Each component map is
$N_q\hookrightarrow X_q\xrightarrow{s_\delta}X_p$; in particular $N_0=X_0$.
The object is **split** (Deligne: *s-scinde*) if it admits such a splitting;
for a $k$-truncated object the same condition is required only for $p\le k$.
For schemes these subobjects are open-and-closed coproduct summands. Thus the
$N$-construction records nondegenerate parts, rather than adding copies of
already degenerate simplices a second time.

An augmented simplicial $S$-scheme $X_\bullet\to S$ is a **proper hypercover**
of $S$ if the augmentation $X_0\to S$ and every canonical boundary map
$X_p\to M_p(X_\bullet)$, $p\ge1$, is proper and surjective
([[def-proper-morphism]]). Neither smoothness, separatedness, finiteness nor
properness of the individual terms is part of the definition; those enter as
hypotheses where they are used.

Let $\Delta$ be the **simplex category**: its objects are the finite nonempty
ordered sets $[n]=\{0<1<\dots<n\}$ for $n\ge0$, and its morphisms are the
order-preserving maps. A **simplicial object** in a category $\mathcal C$ is a
functor $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal C$
([[def-category]], [[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]]). A **simplicial
set** is a simplicial object in sets; a **simplicial commutative ring** is a
simplicial object in commutative rings ([[def-commutative-ring]]), so that
each $A_n$ is a commutative ring and the structure maps are ring
homomorphisms ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]); a **simplicial module** over a
simplicial ring $A_\bullet$ is a simplicial object $M_\bullet$ in abelian
groups together with a compatible $A_\bullet$-action, and the resulting
category of simplicial $A_\bullet$-modules is abelian.

Writing $d_i\colon M_n\to M_{n-1}$ for the image of the injection
$[n-1]\to[n]$ omitting $i$ (a **face map**) and $s_i\colon M_n\to M_{n+1}$
for the image of the surjection $[n+1]\to[n]$ repeating $i$ (a **degeneracy
map**), these maps satisfy the usual simplicial identities
$$d_i d_j=d_{j-1}d_i\ (i<j),\qquad s_i s_j=s_{j+1}s_i\ (i\le j),\qquad d_i s_j=\begin{cases} s_{j-1}d_i, & i<j,\\ \mathrm{id}, & i=j\ \text{or}\ i=j+1,\\ s_j d_{i-1}, & i>j+1.\end{cases}$$
Conversely, such a sequence of face and degeneracy maps determines the
functor.

The **Moore complex** of a simplicial abelian group or module $M_\bullet$ is
the chain complex concentrated in nonnegative degrees with $M_n$ in degree
$n$ and differential
$$\partial_n=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i d_i\colon M_n\to M_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1),$$
with $\partial_0=0$; the $d_i$ are the face maps
([[def-chain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]);
the simplicial identities give $\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$. Its homology is
written
$$\pi_n(M_\bullet)=H_n(M_\bullet)\qquad(n\ge0)$$
([[def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex]]). By the Dold-Kan normalization
theorem this agrees with the classical homotopy-group definition
$H_n(NM_\bullet)$ via the normalized subcomplex, so the convention is
canonical; no model-category machinery is introduced here.

For a simplicial commutative ring $A_\bullet$, each $\pi_n(A_\bullet)$ is defined as above, and $\pi_0(A_\bullet)=A_0/(d_0-d_1)(A_1)$ is a commutative ring. The image is an ideal: for $a\in A_0$, multiplying a representative $b\in A_1$ by $s_0a$ gives $a(d_0b-d_1b)$. Every $\pi_n(A_\bullet)$ is a $\pi_0(A_\bullet)$-module. Indeed multiplication by the totally degenerate simplex of a vertex $a\in A_0$ is a chain map on the Moore complex: its faces are the corresponding totally degenerate simplex of $a$ in the preceding degree. If two vertices are the endpoints of $b\in A_1$, multiplication by the simplicial path defined by $b$ gives a homotopy between these chain maps (the alternating prism sum inserts the degeneracies of $b$). Consequently $(d_0-d_1)(b)$ acts as zero on homology, so the action factors through the displayed quotient. Additivity, associativity and the unit descend from levelwise ring multiplication.

A **morphism of simplicial commutative rings** is a natural transformation
$A_\bullet\to B_\bullet$ ([[def-natural-transformation]]). Such a morphism is
a **weak equivalence** when it induces isomorphisms
$\pi_n(A_\bullet)\to\pi_n(B_\bullet)$ for all $n\ge0$. The **category of
derived rings** is the localization of the category of simplicial commutative
rings at the weak equivalences; constructions on derived rings are used below
only through statements that are independent of the chosen replacement up to
canonical isomorphism.

For every scheme $S$, the category of $S$-schemes has binary products $X\times_S Y$, terminal object $S\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}S$, and initial object $\varnothing\to S$. A product with the empty scheme is empty. Disjoint unions, including the empty disjoint union, are coproducts of $S$-schemes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). For every proper morphism $f:X\to S$ and
every morphism $S'\to S$, the base-changed morphism
$$f_{S'}:X\times_S S'\longrightarrow S'$$
is proper.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). For proper morphisms of schemes
$X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}S$, the composition
$g\circ f:X\to S$ is proper.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to S$ be proper and let $g:Y\to S$ be
separated. Then every $S$-morphism $h:X\to Y$ is proper. No Noetherian,
reducedness or nonemptiness hypothesis is used, and the empty source is
included.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every closed immersion of schemes is finite, hence
proper; the empty closed immersion is included, no Noetherian, reducedness or
nonemptiness hypothesis is used, and the Axiom of Choice enters through the
affine quotient structure of closed immersions and the properness of finite
morphisms.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every projective morphism in the finite-dimensional
H-projective convention of this page is proper: if $f:X\to S$ factors over $S$
as
$$X\xrightarrow{i}\mathbb P^n_S\longrightarrow S$$
with $n\ge0$, $i$ a closed immersion and the second arrow the projection, then
$f$ is proper. The empty source, the empty base and the case $n=0$ are
included, and no Noetherian, field, reducedness or nonemptiness hypothesis is
imposed.

Assuming the Axiom of Choice, a surjective scheme morphism $f:X\to S$ remains surjective after every base change $S'\to S$. In particular, for a field extension $K/k$, a nonempty $k$-scheme $X$ has nonempty $X_K$.

For an arbitrary base scheme $S$, a morphism $f:X\to S$ is **projective on
this page** if for some integer $n\ge0$ it factors over $S$ as
$$X\xrightarrow{i}\mathbb P^n_S\longrightarrow S,$$
where $i$ is a closed immersion and the second arrow is the projection. The
relative projective space and its projection are those of
[[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]], and closed immersion has
the meaning in [[def-closed-immersion-schemes]]. This is the finite-dimensional
H-projective convention of Stacks Definition 29.44.1(2). That source's clause
(1) separately uses a projective bundle $\mathbb P(\mathcal E)$; this page
does not conflate the two conventions. The value $n=0$ is allowed, with
$\mathbb P^0_S\cong S$.
For $m,n\ge0$ and $a,b\ge1$, the map from $\mathbf P^m_k\times\mathbf P^n_k$ taking $([x],[y])$ to all monomials $x^\alpha y^\beta$ of bidegree $(a,b)$ is a closed embedding.

Let $f:X\to S$ and $g:Y\to S$ be morphisms of schemes. A **fibre product** is a scheme $P$, with projections $p:P\to X$ and $q:P\to Y$, such that $fp=gq$ and, for every scheme $T$ and morphisms $a:T\to X$, $b:T\to Y$ with $fa=gb$, there is exactly one $h:T\to P$ satisfying $ph=a$ and $qh=b$. Thus, naturally in every test scheme $T$,
$$\operatorname{Hom}(T,P)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(T,X)\times_{\operatorname{Hom}(T,S)}\operatorname{Hom}(T,Y).$$
Write $P=X\times_S Y$. The commutative square with edges $p,q,f,g$ is **Cartesian** when it has this universal property. Morphisms here are morphisms of locally ringed spaces, as in [[def-morphism-of-schemes]]. No existence assertion is part of the definition.

Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes and let
$\Delta_{X/S}:X\to X\times_S X$ be its diagonal morphism
([[def-diagonal-morphism-scheme]]).

- $f$ is **separated** if $\Delta_{X/S}$ is a closed immersion
  ([[def-closed-immersion-schemes]]).
- $f$ is **quasi-separated** if $\Delta_{X/S}$ is a quasi-compact morphism
  ([[def-quasi-compact-and-quasi-separated-morphism]]).

A scheme $Y$ is called separated, respectively quasi-separated, when the
structure morphism $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ is separated, respectively
quasi-separated. The affine-intersection condition recorded under
[[def-quasi-compact-and-quasi-separated-morphism]] is the earlier definition;
its equivalence to quasi-compactness of $\Delta_{X/S}$ is proved in
[[lem-diagonal-quasi-compact-iff-quasi-separated]] on this page. Both properties are
properties of the morphism $f$ and of its diagonal, and neither is a condition
on the point-set topology of $X$ alone.

A morphism $i:Z\to X$ is a **closed immersion** if its underlying map is a
homeomorphism onto a closed subset and the morphism
$\mathcal O_X\to i_*\mathcal O_Z$ is surjective.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Smooth projective covers. Let $Z$ be a reduced projective complex scheme with its closed immersion $Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}$. The ambient scheme $\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}$ is smooth of finite type over the characteristic-zero field $\mathbb C$, so [F1] applies to the reduced closed subscheme $Z$: the embedded desingularization is a tower $\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb C}=X_0\leftarrow X_1\leftarrow\dots\leftarrow X_r$ of blowups along regular centers with strict transform $\widetilde Z=Z_r$ smooth, mapping to $Z$ properly and birationally on every irreducible component and isomorphically over the smooth locus. Each $X_i$ is integral projective over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-blowups-of-projective-schemes-are-projective]], so the closed subscheme $\widetilde Z\subseteq X_r$ is smooth projective, and $\widetilde Z\to Z$ is surjective because its image is closed and contains a dense open of every irreducible component of the reduced $Z$.

Degree zero. Apply [F2] with $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$ Noetherian and $T=Y$ proper, hence separated and of finite type: there are a projective $X'$ over $\mathbb C$ and a proper surjective $\pi:X'\to Y$. Replacing $X'$ by its reduction ([[def-reduction-of-scheme]]) is a closed immersion $X'_{\mathrm{red}}\hookrightarrow X'$ that is proper and surjective onto $X'$, and the reduced projective $Z=X'_{\mathrm{red}}$ still maps properly and surjectively to $Y$; step 1.1 applied to $Z$ produces a smooth projective $Y_0$ with a proper surjective $Y_0\to Y$. This is the degree-zero term of the construction, and the one-term object $\{Y_0\to Y\}$ is a split $0$-truncated proper hypercover in the sense of [F3], its only boundary map being the augmentation.

Matching objects are projective. Suppose a split $(p-1)$-truncated proper hypercover $Y_0,\dots,Y_{p-1}$ of $Y$ with all terms smooth projective has been constructed, for some $p\ge1$. Let $B_p$ be the finite set of order-preserving injections $\theta:[q]\hookrightarrow[p]$ with $q<p$, and write $q(\theta)=q$. The matching object $M_p$ is cut out in $\prod_{\theta\in B_p,Y}Y_{q(\theta)}$ by the boundary compatibility equations. Each equation is an equality into a separated lower term, so [F5] makes it closed. This fibre product is closed in $\prod_{\theta\in B_p,\mathbb C}Y_{q(\theta)}$ by the closed diagonal of $Y$. The factors are projective over $\mathbb C$; their finite product and its closed subscheme $M_p$ are projective by [F5]. Hence $M_p$ is projective over $\mathbb C$.

Extension step. Choose a smooth projective proper surjection $N_p\to M_p$ by applying step 1.1 to the reduction of the projective $M_p$; the reduction inclusion is proper surjective by [F4]. Set $Y_p=\coprod_{\delta:[p]\twoheadrightarrow[q],\,q\le p}N_q$, using the previously chosen $N_q$ for $q<p$. Here is the explicit extension of the structure maps. Write $i_q:N_q\to Y_q$ for the summand inclusions. For any $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$ with $m,n\le p$, on the summand $N_q$ of $Y_n$ indexed by $\delta:[n]\twoheadrightarrow[q]$, factor $\delta\alpha=\iota\epsilon$ with $\epsilon:[m]\twoheadrightarrow[t]$ and $\iota:[t]\hookrightarrow[q]$. Its map into $Y_m$ is $Y(\epsilon)Y(\iota)i_q$. The injection part is an old structure map if $q<p$, a component of the chosen boundary tuple if $q=p$ and $t<p$, and the identity if $t=q=p$. The surjection part, when $m=p$ and $t<p$, sends each old summand $N_u$ indexed by $\eta:[t]\twoheadrightarrow[u]$ into the new summand indexed by $\eta\epsilon$; otherwise it is old or the identity. Boundary compatibility supplies the relations between injections; concatenation supplies the relations between surjections; refactoring their composites gives the mixed relations. Thus these prescriptions obey contravariant composition and define the $p$-truncated simplicial object. Its splitting is precisely the displayed coproduct. Each summand is smooth projective, and each map to the separated projective $M_p$ is proper by [F4]. The finite union map is proper (finite type and separatedness hold on its open-and-closed summands, and every base change has closed image as a finite union of closed images); it is surjective on the $N_p$ summand. This extends the proper hypercover through degree $p$.

Existence and finite stages. AC permits successive choices in step 4.1 for all $p$, giving one compatible augmented simplicial object; each term is smooth projective and each matching map proper surjective. In a first-quadrant cochain simple complex $K^{p,q}$ attached to this object, total degrees $n-1,n,n+1$ involve only $p\le n+1$. Thus its degree-$n$ cohomology uses only this finite skeleton. No splitness of the higher terms of $\operatorname{cosk}_N\operatorname{sk}_NY_\bullet$ is asserted or needed.

Relative refinement construction. More generally let $T_\bullet\to Y$ be a proper hypercover with projective complex terms, without a smoothness or splitting assumption. Construct a split smooth projective $V_\bullet\to Y$ with a map to $T_\bullet$. At degree zero take a smooth projective proper cover of $T_0$. Once the lower degrees and their maps are constructed, form $P_p=T_p\times_{M_p(T)}M_p(V)$. This is projective by [F5], and $P_p\to M_p(V)$ is a proper surjection by base change of the matching map of $T$. Choose a smooth projective proper cover $N_p\to P_p$, and apply step 4.1 to its composite into $M_p(V)$. On $N_p$ define the map into $T_p$ by the other projection; on each degenerate summand $N_q$ define it by its existing map to $T_q$ followed by the corresponding degeneracy of $T$. The fibre-product condition and the composition check of step 4.1 give a simplicial map. Its new matching map is proper surjective on $N_p$, so the induction constructs the required $V$. This uses no inference that termwise surjections induce surjections on matching limits.

Common refinements and morphisms. For two given hypercovers $A_\bullet,B_\bullet$ of $Y$, put $T_p=A_p\times_YB_p$. Matching limits commute with these products, so the matching map of $T$ is the product over $Y$ of the matching maps of $A,B$; it is proper surjective by [F4]. Its terms are projective by [F5]. Step 6.1 gives a split smooth projective hypercover mapping to $T$ and hence to both given systems. For a morphism $g:Y\to Z$, and fixed hypercovers $A_\bullet\to Y$ and $B_\bullet\to Z$, instead put $T_p=A_p\times_ZB_p$, using $A_p\to Y\xrightarrow{g}Z$. This is the product over $Y$ of $A$ with the base-changed hypercover $Y\times_ZB$, so its matching maps are again proper surjective; its terms are closed in $A_p\times_{\mathbb C}B_p$ by separatedness of $Z$, hence projective. Apply step 6.1 over $Y$. The resulting maps to $A$ and $B$ give the required refinement of the source and lift of $g$.

Boundaries and Choice accounting. For empty $Y$ take every term empty; degree zero is step 2.1. If $Y$ is a point, the constant one-point hypercover is allowed (its $N_p$ are empty for $p>0$). Zero-dimensional and mixed-dimensional smooth terms are finite disjoint unions covered by [F5]. AC is inherited from Chow's lemma and desingularization and permits the countable sequence of cover choices, including the relative constructions; any fixed finite truncation uses only finitely many such choices.

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff topological space and let $R$ be a
commutative ring. For $k\ge0$ let $S_k(X)$ be the set of continuous maps
$\Delta^k\to X$ from the standard simplex
([[def-singular-simplex-and-singular-chain-group-with-coefficients]]); the
convention of [[lem-a-locally-compact-hausdorff-space-has-a-base-of-open-sets-with-compact-closure]]
supplies neighbourhood bases by open sets with compact closure. A formal sum
$c=\sum_{\sigma\in S_k(X)}a_\sigma\,\sigma$ with $a_\sigma\in R$ is **locally
finite** if every point $x\in X$ has an open neighbourhood meeting only
finitely many of the images $\sigma(\Delta^k)$ of the simplices with
$a_\sigma\ne0$ ([[def-compact-space]] for compactness). The **locally finite
$k$-chains** are the $R$-module
$$C_k^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)=\bigl\{c:\ \text{the sum is locally finite}\bigr\},\qquad C_k^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)=0\ \ (k<0),$$
with addition and scalar multiplication defined coefficientwise. The **boundary**
$$\partial\Bigl(\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma\Bigr)=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\,\partial\sigma$$
is again locally finite, because every face of $\sigma$ has image contained in
the image of $\sigma$, and $\partial^2=0$ because $\partial^2\sigma=0$; thus
$(C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R),\partial)$ is a chain complex and its homology is the
**Borel-Moore homology** $H_k^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)$
([[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]] for the ordinary chain
complex, which is the special case of sums with finite support).

A **proper** continuous map $f:X\to Y$ (inverse images of compact sets are
compact) induces $f_*:C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)\to C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(Y;R)$ by
$\sigma\mapsto f\circ\sigma$: for $y\in Y$ choose a compact neighbourhood $K$
of $y$; the compact set $f^{-1}(K)$ is covered by finitely many of the
neighbourhoods furnished by local finiteness of $c$, by
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], so only finitely many
simplices meet $f^{-1}(K)$, and a neighbourhood of $y$ contained in $K$ then
meets only finitely many images $f(\sigma(\Delta^k))$. This is a chain map
because $f\circ\partial\sigma=\partial(f\circ\sigma)$, so it induces
$f_*:H_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)\to H_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(Y;R)$. Coefficients and degree
are otherwise unused below. No choice principle is used in the definition; a
homeomorphism and, more generally, a proper continuous map act functorially.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$.
Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]].

$f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the
preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$.

$f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$.

**The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only
if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open
$U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is
continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of
$f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$,
which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and
a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and
then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$,
so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the
same statement written twice.

**Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$
is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is
defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being
asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the
corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later
item, which are different notions.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a Hausdorff topological space
([[def-hausdorff-space]], [[def-topological-space]]), with compact subsets as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **A point and a disjoint compact set are separated.** If $K \subseteq X$ is
   compact and $x \in X \setminus K$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$x \in U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
2. **Two disjoint compact sets are separated.** If $K, L \subseteq X$ are compact
   and $K \cap L = \varnothing$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$L \subseteq U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
3. **Compact implies closed.** Every compact subset of $X$ is closed in $X$.
4. **In a compact Hausdorff space the two classes coincide.** If in addition
   $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact, then a subset of $X$ is compact if and only if
   it is closed.

**The proof is written choice-free, and that is not a stylistic preference.** The
textbook argument says "for each $y \in K$ choose disjoint open $U_y, V_y$",
which is a selection over an arbitrary index set and therefore an appeal to the
full Axiom of Choice. What is done below instead is to take the family of **all**
open $V$ that admit some open $U \ni x$ disjoint from them — a family cut out by
a formula, with nothing selected — extract a finite subcover from it, and only
then make finitely many selections, which [[lem-finite-choice]] supplies as a
theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), with
subspaces as in [[def-subspace-topology-top]] and compactness as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **Closed in compact is compact.** If $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed in $X$, then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$.
2. **Finite unions.** If $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $K_0, \dots, K_n$ are compact
   subsets of $X$, then $K_0 \cup \dots \cup K_n$ is a compact subset of $X$. The
   union of the empty list is $\varnothing$, which is a compact subset of every
   space.

Claim 1 needs $X$ to be compact and claim 2 does not; no hypothesis of any kind
is placed on $X$ in claim 2. **No choice principle is used**: claim 1 selects
nothing, taking a least index where a selection would be natural, and claim 2
makes finitely many selections through [[lem-finite-choice]], a theorem of ZF.

derivations.claim: Every ordinary singular chain is locally finite: a sum with finite support has only finitely many distinct images, so any neighbourhood of any point meets at most those finitely many images. The inclusion $C_k(X;R)\hookrightarrow C_k^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)$ is therefore defined, commutes with the coefficientwise boundary, and is injective.

Conversely let $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ be locally finite on the compact $X$. Local finiteness provides an open cover of $X$ by neighbourhoods $U$ each of which meets only finitely many images of simplices with nonzero coefficient; by compactness [F2] finitely many such neighbourhoods $U_1,\dots,U_m$ cover $X$. If $\sigma$ has $a_\sigma\ne0$, then its image is nonempty, so it meets some $U_j$, and for each $j$ only finitely many such $\sigma$ meet $U_j$; hence only finitely many coefficients are nonzero and $c$ lies in the image of the inclusion.

By steps 1.1 and 1.2 the inclusion is a bijection on every chain group, hence an isomorphism of chain complexes; it induces isomorphisms on homology. For a continuous map $f:X\to Y$ of compact Hausdorff spaces, for every compact $K\subseteq Y$, Hausdorffness makes $K$ closed, continuity makes $f^{-1}(K)$ closed in the compact $X$, and this preimage is therefore compact by [F2]. Thus $f$ is proper, and the pushforward $f_*$ of [F1] restricts on finite chains to the ordinary singular chain map, so the isomorphisms are natural. No choice principle was used.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 and step 1.2 both hold for the empty compact space: there are no simplices and no points to test.
step 1.1 covers the zero chain and step 2.1 the zero coefficient case.
step 1.1 handles a single simplex and step 2.1 the single-neighbourhood cover.
The comparison is coefficientwise, so degenerate simplices are included without change in step 1.1.
The statement is for every degree and step 2.1 applies to each chain group separately.
step 2.1 uses only compactness of an open cover and makes no selection; the proof is choice-free.

boundaries.reason: The lemma asserts no equivalence in the forward direction beyond the isomorphism.
The lemma asserts no equivalence in the reverse direction beyond the isomorphism.

Finite support implies local finiteness; conversely the cover by all locally finite neighbourhoods has a finite subcover, and every nonzero simplex has nonempty image meeting it. This includes empty X, every k>=0, zero coefficient ring and degenerate simplices. Boundary equality is literal, hence the inclusion is a chain isomorphism and its inverse induces the displayed BM-to-singular map. Continuous maps between compact Hausdorff spaces are proper because compact target subsets are closed and their inverse images are closed in compact source. citations.quote:
Assume AC. Every proper complex algebraic variety $Y$ admits a split simplicial
proper hypercover $a:Y_\bullet\to Y$ with every $Y_p$ smooth projective. Here
proper hypercover means that $Y_0\to Y$ and each map
$Y_p\to(\operatorname{cosk}_{p-1}Y_\bullet)_p$ is proper and surjective. Two
such systems admit a third smooth projective proper hypercover mapping to both
over $Y$. Every morphism between proper varieties can be lifted to a morphism
between such hypercovers after refining the source. Degree-$n$ cohomology uses
only the finite skeleton through degree $n+1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited from the supplied six-functor resolutions. Let $X_\bullet\to X$ be an augmented simplicial finite-type complex algebraic variety ([[def-simplicial-object-and-simplicial-commutative-ring]], [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Assume $X_0\to X$ is proper surjective and, for each $p>0$, $X_p\to(\operatorname{cosk}_{p-1}\operatorname{sk}_{p-1}X_\bullet)_p$ is proper surjective over $X$, where $\operatorname{sk}_{p-1}$ restricts to levels through $p-1$, $\operatorname{cosk}_{p-1}$ is its right Kan extension formed by finite matching limits, and the target is the matching object. Such an object is a proper hypercover; no smoothness or fiber acyclicity is assumed. For $F\in D^b_c(X;k)$ over a field, and $a_p:X_p\to X$, the augmentation gives
$$F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Ra_{p*}a_p^*F,\qquad R\Gamma(X,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}R\Gamma(X_p,a_p^*F).$$
There is a natural strongly convergent spectral sequence $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(X_p,a_p^*F)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X,F)$. If $F$ has cochain lower bound $a$, every diagonal $p+q=m$ is finite; degree $m$ and its differential are determined by levels through $p=m-a+1$. All proper-hypercover refinements induce the same comparison via the base object; any two such hypercovers have a proper common refinement. For $F=k_X$, $a=0$, this is the first-quadrant spectral sequence required for smooth-projective hyperresolutions.

(i) Let $K$ be a rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex
([[def-cohomological-mixed-hodge-complex]]). Then for every $n$ the vector
space $H^n(K_{\mathbb Q})$ carries a mixed Hodge structure whose weight
filtration is the shifted image filtration
$W_mH^n(K)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(W_{m-n}K)\to H^n(K))$ and whose Hodge
filtration is the image filtration
$F^pH^n(K_{\mathbb C})=\operatorname{im}(H^n(F^pK_{\mathbb C})\to H^n(K_{\mathbb C}))$.
In the weight spectral sequence $E_1^{p,q}=H^{p+q}(\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-p}K)$
one has $E_1^{p,q}$ pure of weight $q$, the sequence degenerates at $E_2$, and
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH^n(K)\cong E_2^{n-m,m}$ compatibly with the Hodge
filtrations. A morphism of cohomological mixed Hodge complexes induces, on
every $H^n$, a morphism of the resulting mixed Hodge structures.

(ii) Let $K^\bullet$ be a cosimplicial system of weight-zero rational Hodge
complexes concentrated in nonnegative cohomological degrees: cochain complexes
$K^{p,q}$ with coface maps and an internal differential satisfying the
cosimplicial identities, with $K^{p,q}=0$ unless $p,q\ge0$, whose differentials
are strict for the Hodge filtration, and with $H^q(K^p)$, together with the
induced $F$ and the rational comparison, a pure Hodge structure of weight $q$
for all $p,q$ (the axioms (GH1)-(GH2) of a cohomological Hodge complex of
weight zero). The Hodge filtration is finite on each cochain group; the coface
and codegeneracy maps are chain maps preserving it and commuting with the
levelwise rational comparisons. Form its simple
complex $sK$ with the standard total differential and the increasing filtration
$L$ by cosimplicial degree, $L_{-p}sK^n=\bigoplus_{i\ge p}K^{i,n-i}$. Then $sK$
is a rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex for the filtration $L$ and the
Hodge filtrations of the $K^p$, the cosimplicial spectral sequence
$E_1^{p,q}=H^q(K^p)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(sK)$ degenerates at $E_2$, and
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_qH^n(sK)\cong E_2^{n-q,q}$; consequently all weights of
$H^n(sK)$ are at most $n$.

A **rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex** consists of

(a) a bounded-below cochain complex $K_{\mathbb Q}$ of $\mathbb Q$-vector
spaces with an increasing filtration $W$ by subcomplexes, finite on each
cochain group;

(b) a cochain complex $K_{\mathbb C}$ of $\mathbb C$-vector spaces with an
increasing filtration $W$ by subcomplexes and a decreasing filtration $F$ by
subcomplexes, again finite on each cochain group;

(c) a morphism of complexes
$\alpha\colon K_{\mathbb Q}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\to K_{\mathbb C}$
compatible with the weight filtrations, such that for every $w$ the induced map
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_w\alpha$ is a quasi-isomorphism,

subject to the following axiom: for every integer $w$ the weight-graded
complex $\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK$ has finite-dimensional cohomology, its
differential (induced by $d_K$) is strict for the induced filtration $F$, and
for every $r$ the induced filtration $F$ on
$H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb C})$, together with the induced rational
comparison
$H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb Q})\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\to
H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb C})$, is a pure Hodge structure of weight
$r+w$ ([[def-rational-mixed-hodge-structure]]).

Here a cochain complex is a complex in the sense of
[[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], a filtration by subcomplexes is
a filtered complex in the sense of [[def-filtered-chain-complex]], a morphism
compatible with the weight filtrations is a filtered chain map in the sense of
[[def-filtered-chain-map]], quasi-isomorphism means
[[def-quasi-isomorphism]], and finiteness on a cochain group $K^n$ means
$W_aK^n=0$ for all sufficiently negative $a$ and $W_aK^n=K^n$ for all
sufficiently positive $a$, with bounds depending on $n$; dually $F^pK^n=K^n$
for $p\ll0$ and $F^pK^n=0$ for $p\gg0$.

**The weight filtration on cohomology** is the shifted image filtration
$$W_mH^n(K):=\operatorname{im}\bigl(H^n(W_{m-n}K)\to H^n(K)\bigr).$$
The shift is essential: it is what makes the axiom's weight $r+w$ on the graded
complexes compatible with the weight of $H^n$, and pole-count weight on a
logarithmic complex is not the weight on its cohomology. The differential
strictness in the axiom is Deligne's condition (GH1); the equivalent
formulation that the $F$-spectral sequence of the graded complex degenerates at
its first page is recorded in the sources but is neither asserted nor used
here, so no degeneration theorem enters this definition.

**Morphisms and the sheaf case.** A morphism of cohomological mixed Hodge
complexes is a pair of chain maps $K_{\mathbb Q}\to L_{\mathbb Q}$ and
$K_{\mathbb C}\to L_{\mathbb C}$ compatible with both filtrations and with the
comparisons; compatible filtered homotopies are permitted. The same
definitions apply to bounded-below complexes of sheaves on a topological space
when the complexes are replaced by their derived global sections and the
resolutions used preserve the graded pieces; the existence of such resolutions
for the concrete complexes used later is proved where those complexes are
constructed, not here.

Assume AC. For a compact Kähler manifold $X$ in the sense of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], every de
Rham class has a unique smooth harmonic representative and
$$H^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(X),\qquad \overline{H^{p,q}(X)}=H^{q,p}(X).$$
Here $H^{p,q}(X)$ is precisely the set of classes with a $d$-closed smooth
representative of type $(p,q)$, so the decomposition is independent of the
Kähler metric. Writing $\Omega_X^p$ for the sheaf of holomorphic $p$-forms (the
kernel of $\bar\partial$ on the sheaf $\mathcal A^{p,0}$ of smooth $(p,0)$-forms),
$H^{p,q}(X)$ is isomorphic to $H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$, the sheaf cohomology of
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]. The Hodge filtration
$F^a=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}H^{p,k-p}$ of $H^k(X;\mathbb C)$ equals the filtration
induced by the holomorphic-degree filtration of the de Rham complex, whose
spectral sequence has $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$ and degenerates at $E_1$.
Pullback by holomorphic maps of compact Kähler manifolds and cup product
preserve Hodge type, so $H^k(X;\mathbb Q)$ is a functorial rational pure Hodge
structure.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
Jacobian-criterion, ample-powers, Chern-form and comparison suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex scheme of pure dimension $n\ge0$.

Then the closed points of $X$ carry a structure of **complex manifold**
$X^{\mathrm{an}}$, its **analytification**: if $X\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge1$
this is a compact Hausdorff second-countable smooth complex manifold of complex
dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]); if $n=0$ it is the
finite discrete set $X(\mathbb C)$ with its unique complex structure in the
convention of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]; and if
$X=\varnothing$ then $X^{\mathrm{an}}=\varnothing$. Every standard smooth
algebraic chart of $X$ supplies holomorphic coordinate charts of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$
after shrinking to local analytic graph neighbourhoods around its complex points;
the whole algebraic chart need not be a single holomorphic coordinate chart.
More generally, every morphism between smooth separated finite-type complex schemes of pure dimensions induces a holomorphic map between their analytifications. These analytifications are constructed by the same local charts and need not be compact; separatedness and finite type ensure that they are Hausdorff and second-countable.

Moreover, for every ample invertible sheaf $A$ on $X$ there is a smooth
positive closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta_A$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ whose de Rham
class is the real image of the topological first Chern class
$c_1(A):=c_1(A^{\mathrm{an}})\in H^2(X^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Z)$:
$$J_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}[\eta_A]=\rho_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\bigl(c_1(A)\bigr),$$
where $J$ is the de Rham comparison and $\rho$ the change of coefficients
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$
([[lem-rational-cohomology-scalar-comparison-for-compact-smooth-manifolds]]).
In dimension $n=0$ and for $X=\varnothing$ every $2$-form and every degree-two
cohomology class is zero and $\eta_A=0$, so the identity holds trivially.

Every morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures is strict for
$W$ and for $F$:
$$f(W_nH)=f(H)\cap W_nK,\qquad f(F^pH_{\mathbb C})=f(H_{\mathbb C})\cap F^pK_{\mathbb C}$$
for all $n,p$. Its kernel, image and cokernel, with the induced or quotient
filtrations, are mixed Hodge structures; the functor $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n$ is
exact; and a morphism from a structure of weights at least $n$ (that is
$W_{n-1}H=0$) to a structure of weights at most $n$ (that is $W_nK=K$) has
pure image of weight $n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at
every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There
are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective
resolutions supplied by
[[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on
every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this
local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero
otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its
nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a quasi-projective complex algebraic variety, $k$ a
field, and $F$ a bounded complex of analytic $k$-sheaves whose cohomology is
locally constant of finite rank on a finite complex algebraic stratification.
Fix finitely many algebraic supports and locally closed inclusions to be
respected. There is a finite compatible smooth complex algebraic Whitney
refinement, a projective compactification with its algebraic boundary
respected, and a finite pair of simplicial complexes $(K,D)$ such that
$X^{\mathrm{an}}\cong|K|\setminus|D|$, every open simplex lies in one complex
stratum, and the marked supports are unions of simplices. One can take
$\dim K\le2\dim_{\mathbb C}X$; in particular constant-sheaf cohomology vanishes
above that real dimension. The same construction applies individually to the
compact controlled links supplied by the conical-neighborhood theorem.

On these models, actual ordinary and compact-support cohomology, ordinary
derived Hom, internal derived Hom and local cohomology with a prescribed
algebraic support have bounded finite-dimensional cochain models. Internal Hom
is constructible on a finite complex Whitney refinement. The local link and
support models vary locally constantly along the corresponding complex strata;
thus their cohomology has finite rank there. Every such model commutes with
extension of the coefficient field. Inclusions and supports are chosen in
finite collections for a given construction; no compatible triangulation of
arbitrary algebraic maps or cyclic diagrams is asserted. Perverse dimensions
remain the dimensions of the complex strata, independent of the auxiliary real
simplices.

Let $K$ be a finite simplicial complex and let $\sigma$ be a nonempty simplex.
Let $\operatorname{lk}_K\sigma$ be the subcomplex of simplices $\tau$ disjoint
from $\sigma$ with $\sigma\cup\tau\in K$, and let $\operatorname{st}_K(\sigma)$
be the open star of $\sigma$
([[def-simplicial-subcomplex-star-closure-and-link]]). Then
$$\operatorname{st}_K(\sigma)\cong\operatorname{relint}|\sigma|\times c_{<1}(|\operatorname{lk}_K\sigma|),$$
where $c_{<1}(L)=(L\times[0,1))/(L\times\{0\})$ with the quotient topology, and
the cone on the empty space means a single apex. The homeomorphism takes each
simplex interior containing $\sigma$ to the product with the corresponding
link-simplex interior and positive radial coordinate; the simplex $\sigma$
itself maps to the apex. The link is compact and has finitely many simplices.
If $D\subseteq K$ is a subcomplex and $\sigma\notin D$, this star lies in
$|K|\setminus|D|$.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). For $n=0$, $\mathbb C^0$ is the
singleton of empty tuples with its unique topology. On an overlap of two
affine charts, the transition isomorphism and its inverse are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and let
$x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring
$\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring
whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$
([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a
classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every
point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski
neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic
stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition
$X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected
locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ — the **strata** — where locally
closed means $S_\alpha=U\cap Z$ for a Zariski-open $U\subseteq X$ and a
Zariski-closed $Z\subseteq X$, such that each
$S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure, is a smooth algebraic
subvariety of $X$; and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure
$\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is
the **frontier condition**: the frontier
$\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata
([[def-connected-space]], [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**The induced structure is the polynomial-quotient function sheaf, not a
restriction of $\mathcal O_X$.** A locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is, locally
inside an affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the set of points with $h\neq0$
and $f_1=\dots=f_r=0$ for polynomials $h,f_1,\dots,f_r$ on $Z$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]); the map
$z\mapsto(z,1/h(z))$ identifies it with the affine model
$\{(z,t):th(z)=1,\ f_1(z)=\dots=f_r(z)=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^{n+1}$, and its
**reduced induced structure sheaf** is the one transported along this
identification: locally functions of the form $a/b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the
set. The ambient restriction $\mathcal O_X|_S$ is not used, since already at the
origin of the affine line the ambient stalk is the local ring of the line while
the stalk of the reduced point is $\mathbb C$. An open subset of an affine model
is a union of finitely many principal open subsets: finite generation of the
ideal of its closed complement supplies finitely many defining polynomials,
whose nonvanishing loci cover the open subset. Each principal open subset is
again an affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety
for the induced structure sheaf. No existence theorem for stratifications, no
common-refinement theorem is asserted. The given chart data and elementary
locally closed condition above require no choice principle.

Let $X$ be a compact ([[def-compact-space]]) Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) topological space. Then:

1. $X$ is **regular** ([[def-regular-and-t3-spaces]]);
2. $X$ is **normal** ([[def-normal-and-t4-spaces]]);
3. $X$ is $T_1$ ([[def-t0-and-t1-spaces]]), and hence $X$ is $T_3$ and $T_4$.

Following [[def-regular-and-t3-spaces]] and [[def-normal-and-t4-spaces]],
*regular* and *normal* name the separation conditions alone and the numerals
$T_3$ and $T_4$ name their conjunctions with $T_1$; claim 3 is what supplies the
$T_1$ half, and it is stated separately for that reason.

**Nothing stronger is claimed.** In particular it is not asserted here that a
compact Hausdorff space is completely regular
([[def-regular-and-t3-spaces]] distinguishes the two conditions), and no
continuous real-valued function is produced anywhere below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Dependent Choice. Every open cover
of a compact Hausdorff space admits a finite partition of unity subordinate to
that cover.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume AC. Let $U$ be smooth quasiprojective over $\mathbb C$, and choose an SNC smooth projective compactification $j:U\hookrightarrow X$, boundary $D$. The logarithmic de Rham complex with Hodge filtration by degree and pole-count weight filtration constructs a functorial rational mixed Hodge structure on $H^n(U,\mathbb Q)$, independent of the compactification. Its weights are at least $n$, and
$$W_nH^n(U,\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(X,\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H^n(U,\mathbb Q)).$$

**Assume the Axiom of Choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), which is what
[[thm-zorn]] is proved from. Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$
([[def-vector-space]]) and let $L \subseteq S \subseteq V$ with $L$ linearly
independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and $\operatorname{span}(S) = V$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). Then there is a basis $B$ of $V$
([[def-linear-basis]]) with

$$L \;\subseteq\; B \;\subseteq\; S .$$

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff topological space and let $R$ be a
commutative ring. For $k\ge0$ let $S_k(X)$ be the set of continuous maps
$\Delta^k\to X$ from the standard simplex
([[def-singular-simplex-and-singular-chain-group-with-coefficients]]); the
convention of [[lem-a-locally-compact-hausdorff-space-has-a-base-of-open-sets-with-compact-closure]]
supplies neighbourhood bases by open sets with compact closure. A formal sum
$c=\sum_{\sigma\in S_k(X)}a_\sigma\,\sigma$ with $a_\sigma\in R$ is **locally
finite** if every point $x\in X$ has an open neighbourhood meeting only
finitely many of the images $\sigma(\Delta^k)$ of the simplices with
$a_\sigma\ne0$ ([[def-compact-space]] for compactness). The **locally finite
$k$-chains** are the $R$-module
$$C_k^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)=\bigl\{c:\ \text{the sum is locally finite}\bigr\},\qquad C_k^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)=0\ \ (k<0),$$
with addition and scalar multiplication defined coefficientwise. The **boundary**
$$\partial\Bigl(\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma\Bigr)=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\,\partial\sigma$$
is again locally finite, because every face of $\sigma$ has image contained in
the image of $\sigma$, and $\partial^2=0$ because $\partial^2\sigma=0$; thus
$(C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R),\partial)$ is a chain complex and its homology is the
**Borel-Moore homology** $H_k^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)$
([[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]] for the ordinary chain
complex, which is the special case of sums with finite support).

A **proper** continuous map $f:X\to Y$ (inverse images of compact sets are
compact) induces $f_*:C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)\to C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(Y;R)$ by
$\sigma\mapsto f\circ\sigma$: for $y\in Y$ choose a compact neighbourhood $K$
of $y$; the compact set $f^{-1}(K)$ is covered by finitely many of the
neighbourhoods furnished by local finiteness of $c$, by
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], so only finitely many
simplices meet $f^{-1}(K)$, and a neighbourhood of $y$ contained in $K$ then
meets only finitely many images $f(\sigma(\Delta^k))$. This is a chain map
because $f\circ\partial\sigma=\partial(f\circ\sigma)$, so it induces
$f_*:H_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)\to H_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(Y;R)$. Coefficients and degree
are otherwise unused below. No choice principle is used in the definition; a
homeomorphism and, more generally, a proper continuous map act functorially.

Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff topological space and let $R$ be a commutative
ring. The inclusion of the ordinary singular chain complex into the complex of
locally finite chains of [[def-borel-moore-homology]] is an isomorphism of chain
complexes, and it induces isomorphisms
$$H_k^{\mathrm{BM}}(X;R)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H_k^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;R)$$
in every degree, natural for continuous maps of compact Hausdorff spaces
([[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]). In particular the class
map of a proper complex algebraic variety may be computed using ordinary
singular homology.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Assume AC. For every field $k$, every space $X$, and $n\ge0$, evaluation gives a natural $k$-linear isomorphism
$$H^n(X;k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_n(X;k),k).$$
There is no finite-dimensional hypothesis. The right side is the full algebraic dual.

For continuous $f:X\to Y$, $\alpha\in H^p(Y;R)$ and $x\in H_n(X;R)$,
$$f_*(f^*\alpha\cap x)=\alpha\cap f_*x.$$
For $\alpha\in H^p(X;R)$, $\beta\in H^q(X;R)$ and $x\in H_n(X;R)$,
$$(\alpha\smile\beta)\cap x=\beta\cap(\alpha\cap x).$$
Here $R$ is commutative unital and cap evaluates the front face, retaining the back face. Both identities hold already on cochains and chains. No AC is needed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups
on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]). For $x\in X$ let $\mathcal F_x$ be
the stalk at $x$ ([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]], [[def-germ-of-section]]) and let
$i_{x,*}A$ be the skyscraper sheaf at $x$ with value an abelian group $A$
([[def-skyscraper-sheaf-abelian-group]]): $(i_{x,*}A)(V)=A$ when $x\in V$ and
$(i_{x,*}A)(V)=0$ otherwise.

Put
$$C^0(\mathcal F):=\prod_{x\in X}i_{x,*}\mathcal F_x,$$
the product in $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ of the skyscraper sheaves of the stalks of
$\mathcal F$; since products of sheaves are computed open by open, for an open
$V\subseteq X$ one has
$$C^0(\mathcal F)(V)=\prod_{x\in V}\mathcal F_x .$$
The germ maps $\mathcal F(V)\to\prod_{x\in V}\mathcal F_x$,
$s\mapsto(s_x)_{x\in V}$ ([[def-germ-of-section]]) are compatible with
restrictions and assemble into a morphism of sheaves
$\varepsilon_{\mathcal F}:\mathcal F\to C^0(\mathcal F)$, the **germ map** of
$\mathcal F$. Let
$$Q^0(\mathcal F):=\operatorname{coker}(\varepsilon_{\mathcal F})$$
be the cokernel sheaf of $\varepsilon_{\mathcal F}$
([[def-kernel-cokernel-image-sheaves]]). Recursively, having defined a sheaf
$Q^n(\mathcal F)$ of abelian groups on $X$, put
$$C^{n+1}(\mathcal F):=C^0\bigl(Q^n(\mathcal F)\bigr),\qquad Q^{n+1}(\mathcal F):=\operatorname{coker}\bigl(Q^n(\mathcal F) \xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon_{Q^n}\ }C^{n+1}(\mathcal F)\bigr),$$
with $\varepsilon_{Q^n}$ the germ map of $Q^n(\mathcal F)$. The **Godement
resolution** of $\mathcal F$ is the coaugmented complex
$$0\to\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon_{\mathcal F}\ } C^0(\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\ d^0\ }C^1(\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\ d^1\ }\cdots,$$
where $d^n:C^n(\mathcal F)\to C^{n+1}(\mathcal F)$ is the composite of the
quotient morphism $C^n(\mathcal F)\to Q^n(\mathcal F)$ with the germ map
$\varepsilon_{Q^n}:Q^n(\mathcal F)\to C^0(Q^n(\mathcal F))=C^{n+1}(\mathcal F)$.
Its terms are sheaves of abelian groups on $X$ and its differentials are
differentials of the cochain complex $\Gamma(X,C^\bullet(\mathcal F))$ after
applying global sections.

The construction is functorial: a morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of
abelian sheaves induces morphisms of stalks $\varphi_x$, hence morphisms
$C^0(\varphi)$, $Q^0(\varphi)$, and by recursion morphisms $C^n(\varphi)$ and
$Q^n(\varphi)$ commuting with the germ maps and the differentials, so that
$C^\bullet$ is a functor from $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ to the category of coaugmented cochain complexes in $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ ([[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]). The germ
map $\varepsilon_{\mathcal E}:\mathcal E\to C^0(\mathcal E)$ is injective for
every abelian sheaf $\mathcal E$, by [[lem-section-zero-if-all-germs-zero]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $X$ be a topological space and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$ with Godement resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\ }C^0(\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\ d^0\ } C^1(\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\ d^1\ }\cdots$$
([[def-godement-resolution]]). Then

1. every term $C^n(\mathcal F)$ is flasque
   ([[def-flasque-sheaf]]);
2. the coaugmented complex is exact, so that $0\to\mathcal F\to C^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
   is a resolution of $\mathcal F$ by flasque sheaves;
3. for every $q\ge0$ there is an isomorphism
   $$H^q(X,\mathcal F)\cong H^q\bigl(\Gamma(X,C^\bullet(\mathcal F))\bigr),$$
   natural in $\mathcal F$, where $H^q(X,-)$ is sheaf cohomology from the
   supplied functorial injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$
   ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]).

In particular the Godement complex is a $\Gamma$-acyclic resolution of
$\mathcal F$ ([[def-acyclic-sheaf-global-sections]]) that computes sheaf
cohomology.

derivations.claim: (Actual cosimplicial Hodge complexes.) Choose the smooth projective proper hypercover $a:Y_\bullet\to Y$ of [F1]. For sheaves of rational or complex vector spaces, construct the Godement resolution of [F10]. Its first functor $C^0$ is exact because stalks are exact and products of surjective linear maps are surjective under AC. In a short exact sequence of sheaves, the corresponding germ embeddings into $C^0$ form a diagram with exact rows and columns; the kernel-cokernel exact sequence makes the three cokernels short exact. Iteration proves that every successive cokernel functor, every $C^t$ and every $\Gamma C^t$ is exact, the last again being a product of stalks. In particular resolutions and global sections preserve filtration levels, their finite intersections and associated gradings. Their first-quadrant totals compute derived global sections: termwise flasque acyclicity from [F10] applies to each sheaf of the bounded de Rham complex, and each total diagonal is finite. Apply this construction on every $Y_p$ and put $K_{\mathbb Q}^{p,q}=\Gamma(Y_p,C^q(\mathbb Q_{Y_p}))$ and $K_{\mathbb C}^{p,q}=\bigoplus_{k+t=q}\Gamma(Y_p,C^t(\Omega^k_{Y_p}))$, for $p,q\ge0$, with $F^b$ given by $k\ge b$. These are the resolved global de Rham complexes, not the complex of global holomorphic forms. Godement pullback along each face is induced by pulling a germ collection at a point to the stalk over its image; the successive cokernels preserve these maps, so their composites obey the simplicial identities and preserve $F$. The constant inclusion $\mathbb Q\otimes\mathbb C\to\Omega^0$ gives the functorial rational comparison; on cohomology it is the scalar-extension comparison of [F4]. Exactness and acyclicity of the resolution show $H^q(K_{\mathbb C}^p)=H^q(Y_p;\mathbb C)$, with the holomorphic-degree image filtration, and $H^q(K_{\mathbb Q}^p)=H^q(Y_p;\mathbb Q)$. The compact Hodge theorem [F4] gives pure weight $q$ and Hodge-de Rham $E_1$ degeneration on each smooth projective component. The latter makes the actual internal differential $F$-strict: if $dx\in F^b$, degeneration lifts the leading lower-filtration class of $x$ to a cycle up to a higher-filtration term and a boundary; subtracting the cycle and boundary raises the preimage filtration without changing $dx$, and finite induction supplies a preimage in $F^b$. This proves differential strictness directly. Thus every level is an actual weight-zero rational Hodge complex. Each internal total diagonal is finite, and $F^{q+1}K^{p,q}=0$, so [F3] applies to its first-quadrant simple complex, giving the mixed Hodge structure and $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(Y_p;\mathbb Q)$, $E_2$ degeneration and $\operatorname{Gr}^W_qH^n(sK)=E_2^{n-q,q}$. The terms have $p=n-q\ge0$, so weights are at most $n$, and the finitely many $E_1^{p,q}$ entries on every total diagonal are finite-dimensional by [F4]. Descent [F2] identifies the rational simple cohomology naturally with $H^n(Y;\mathbb Q)$, carrying this structure.

Singular comparison. The point map $Y_0^{\mathrm{an}}\to Y^{\mathrm{an}}$ is a continuous surjection: a nonempty finite-type fibre over a complex point has a complex closed point, as in the residue-field argument of [F4]'s analytification supplier. Thus $Y^{\mathrm{an}}$ is compact. A finite affine cover makes it second-countable, and separatedness makes its diagonal closed in the products of these affine point loci; hence it is Hausdorff. The topology of a nonreduced scheme is that of its reduction. On each affine chart [F6] supplies a finite deleted-boundary triangulation. At a point of a retained simplex, its open star is $\operatorname{relint}|\sigma|\times c_{<1}(L)$. Small convex neighbourhoods of the point in the first factor and small radial cones in the second give a contractible open neighbourhood basis: compactness of the link gives a uniform radial bound at the apex. To obtain a metric, take a finite partition of unity $\phi_j$ subordinate to the affine charts, with supports contained in the charts, using [F6]. If $z_j$ are the finite affine coordinate vectors, define $\Phi(y)=(\phi_j(y),\phi_j(y)z_j(y))_j$, extending each product by zero outside its chart. These extensions are continuous because the supports are closed and contained in their charts. If $\Phi(y)=\Phi(y')$, choose $j$ with $\phi_j(y)>0$; equality of the scalar coordinates puts both points in that chart with equal positive $\phi_j$, and equality of the product coordinates gives $z_j(y)=z_j(y')$, hence $y=y'$. A continuous injection from this compact space to Hausdorff Euclidean space is a homeomorphism onto its image: images of closed subsets are compact and therefore closed. Pulling back the Euclidean metric gives the analytic topology. The sheaf-singular comparison of [F6] now identifies the descended cohomology with $H^n_{\mathrm{sing}}(Y^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Q)$, naturally in $Y$. The partition and comparison consume their stated AC hypotheses; no claim of a DC-only construction is made.

Independence and functoriality. If $a':Y'_\bullet\to Y$ is a second split proper hypercover with smooth projective terms, [F1] supplies a third such hypercover dominating both; the two refinements give filtered comparison maps between the corresponding cosimplicial systems and hence morphisms of the mixed Hodge complexes of step 1.1, and by [F2] both simple complexes compute the constant-sheaf cohomology of $Y$, so the induced maps on $H^n(Y,\mathbb Q)$ are the identity; strictness [F5] upgrades this to an isomorphism of mixed Hodge structures, so the structure is independent of the diagram. A morphism $g:Y\to Y'$ of proper varieties lifts, after refining the source hypercover, to a morphism of the chosen hypercovers [F1], pullback of holomorphic forms along it is a morphism of the cosimplicial mixed Hodge complexes compatible with the comparisons, and independence of the hypercovers makes the induced map $g^*:H^n(Y',\mathbb Q)\to H^n(Y,\mathbb Q)$ well defined and compatible with identities and composition.

(The smooth-open clause and comparison compatibility.) Let $g:Y\to U$, and use the logarithmic mixed Hodge complex realizing [F7] on an SNC compactification $X\supset U$. On its complex side, pullback along $g_0=ga_0:Y_0\to U$ takes logarithmic forms to regular forms: a boundary equation pulls back to a nowhere-zero holomorphic function, whose $d\log$ is regular. Resolve this map by the pullback construction of step 1.1 and place it in cosimplicial degree zero of $sK_{\mathbb C}$. Its first alternating face differential vanishes because $g_0d_0=g_0d_1$ on $Y_1$, so this is a chain map preserving $F$ by form degree. Its cohomology map is $g^*\otimes\mathbb C$: on $U$, $\Omega_X^\bullet(\log D)$ restricts to $\Omega_U^\bullet$, and the constant-sheaf de Rham comparison in the logarithmic construction restricts to the usual natural comparison; descent and the augmentation then identify this degree-zero map with pullback to $Y$. To obtain a rational chain map, split each source and target cochain group into boundaries, representatives for cohomology, and a complement to cycles, under AC. The differential identifies the last summand with the next boundary summand. Send cohomology representatives by the actual rational $g^*$ and send the other two summands to zero. This is a chain map $K_{\mathbb Q}(U)\to(sK)_{\mathbb Q}$ inducing $g^*$. Its scalar extension and the complex map commute with the rational comparisons up to homotopy: their difference induces zero on cohomology, and the same decompositions contract each boundary-complement pair, giving a homotopy for any such zero-cohomology map. All these maps and homotopies preserve weight, since the source pole filtration is zero for $a<0$ and the target $L_a$ is the whole simple complex for $a\ge0$; no filtration constraint is placed on the chosen complements. Thus the two chain maps, with this weight-filtered comparison homotopy, are a morphism of the mixed Hodge complexes. By [F3] the actual rational $g^*$ is a mixed Hodge morphism.

The class map. Let $h:Y\to X$ be proper with $X$ smooth projective of pure dimension $d$. By step 2.1 and [F8], Borel-Moore homology of $Y$ equals ordinary homology. The Kronecker isomorphism $H^i(Y)=H_i(Y)^*$ and finite-dimensionality of $H^i(Y)$ imply that $H_i(Y)$ is finite-dimensional: any finite independent tuple extends to a basis by [F8] under AC and gives that many independent coordinate functionals, so its length is bounded by $\dim H^i(Y)$. Consequently evaluation identifies $H_i(Y)=H^i(Y)^*$ canonically. Give it the dual filtrations of [[def-rational-mixed-hodge-structure]]. Their weight-$a$ graded piece is $(\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-a}H^i(Y))^*$, with pure types $(p,q)$ changed to $(-p,-q)$; this proves the mixed Hodge axiom and the lower weight bound $-i$. Transposes of filtration-preserving maps preserve the annihilator filtrations. Naturality of the Kronecker pairing identifies $h_*$ with the transpose of $h^*$, a mixed Hodge morphism by step 3.1. For $X$, cup product preserves Hodge type by [F4], and the top cohomology on each connected component is of type $(d,d)$: forms with total degree $2d$ have only that possible type. Evaluation on the oriented fundamental classes therefore gives a Hodge morphism $H^{2d}(X)\to\mathbb Q(-d)$ (sum the component traces). Poincare duality and the cap/cup identity [F8] make the resulting cup/trace pairing $H^i(X)\otimes H^{2d-i}(X)\to\mathbb Q(-d)$ perfect. After twisting the second factor by $(d)$ it identifies $H^{2d-i}(X)(d)$ with $H^i(X)^*=H_i(X)$ as pure Hodge structures of weight $-i$: the complementary types become $(-p,-q)$ on the dual factor. The composite with $h_*$ is the asserted class map. By [F5] its image is pure of weight $-i$; untwisting gives weight $2d-i$. For mixed-dimensional $X$, apply this on its finitely many open-and-closed connected components and the corresponding inverse images in $Y$, obtaining the stated direct sum.

Boundaries and Choice accounting. For $Y=\varnothing$ every group is zero with the trivial structure and all clauses are vacuous; the degree $n=0$ case has all weights equal to $0$, consistent with the bound; the smooth hypercover terms of differing dimensions are handled componentwise in [F4], without assuming that the singular components of $Y$ are disjoint; and the case $Y=X$ of pure dimension $d$ reduces the class map to Poincare duality itself. The Axiom of Choice [F9] is inherited from [F1], [F2] and [F7], including the sheaf-singular comparison; the exact Godement resolutions of step 1.1 and the comparison homotopy in step 3.2 use AC for products and linear complements; it also licenses the partition in step 2.1 and the duality argument in step 4.1.
